name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Are Fairfield teenagers getting the mental health care they need?
description: Having mental health resources does not automatically mean every teenager knows about them, feels comfortable using them, or can access the right care.
text:
Growing up in Fairfield, I saw how much mental health can affect a person, a family, and an entire community. I had multiple friends who struggled with their mental health, and some died by suicide. I have also struggled with my own mental health.
These experiences have shown me how important it is for people to feel comfortable asking for help and know where to find it. Fairfield has brought people together to discuss mental health, especially after difficult experiences and losses. These conversations are important, but we also need to make sure teenagers know how to find support. Having resources available is one thing. Knowing how to access them and feeling comfortable using them are different things.
Fairfield should make it easier for teenagers to understand their mental health options and access support without feeling embarrassed or unsure where to begin.
When I have needed mental-health support, I have struggled to find a therapist in Fairfield who was the right fit, including someone who offered talk therapy or cognitive behavioral therapy. I have ended up looking in nearby towns, including Westport, Norwalk, and New Milford. My experience does not mean Fairfield lacks mental-health providers, but it has made me question how easy it is to find the right support when someone needs it. 
 For teenagers, this process can feel even more overwhelming. They might not know which services are available, how to contact a provider, whether their family can afford treatment, or what information will remain private. Some may fear judgment from friends, while others may not realize they need help. Parents may also struggle to know where to start. When someone is already having a difficult time, figuring out how to get support should not become another challenge. 
Research supports these concerns. A 2021 review by Jerica Radez and colleagues found that stigma, embarrassment, confidentiality concerns, costs, transportation, and limited knowledge can affect whether young people seek mental-health care. A 2022 study by Alice Villatoro and colleagues also found differences between how adolescents approach mental-health help for themselves and how they recommend it to peers. Encouraging a friend to seek help may feel easier than asking for it personally.
Schools can be part of the solution. Research by Mylien Duong and colleagues found that school-based mental-health services were used by about 7% of youth in the general population and about 22% of youth with elevated symptoms or diagnoses. Schools cannot solve every mental-health problem, but they can help students understand what support exists and how to take the next step. Students should not have to search through multiple websites or depend on word of mouth to learn where to turn.
Fairfield Public Schools already share social-emotional learning resources, and the town has a Collaborative for Youth Mental Health. These are important starting points. Instead of automatically creating more programs, Fairfield should examine whether teenagers and families can easily find and use the resources already available.
 Fairfield Public Schools, town officials, families, and local mental-health organizations should work together on three steps. First, they should create one clear, regularly updated guide to local resources, including how to make appointments, available cost and insurance information, and where to ask about confidentiality. Second, schools should regularly discuss mental health in age-appropriate ways and explain how students can seek support. Third, students should have a way to share their concerns anonymously so community leaders can better understand what prevents them from getting help. 
 These efforts should be evaluated over the next school year. Schools could ask students whether they know where to find support before and after these changes. This would help show whether the information is reaching young people instead of assuming that making resources available means students are using them. Listening directly to students would also help Fairfield understand which changes would be most useful. 
 Some may argue that Fairfield already has mental-health resources and community programs. That is a fair point. However, having resources does not automatically mean every teenager knows about them, feels comfortable using them, or can access the right care. Improving access does not mean ignoring what Fairfield already does. It means building on existing efforts and identifying what still gets in the way of young people. 
 Mental health should not become a community conversation only after a tragedy. Teenagers deserve to know where to turn before they reach a crisis point. Fairfield can build on the conversations already happening and make support easier to find and use. Sometimes, helping someone starts with making sure they know help is available and that they do not have to figure everything out alone. 
Maddie Reed of Fairfield is a fourth-year Human Services major at Elon University interested in youth well-being, mental health, and improving access to support for adolescents.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Is the ‘Connecticut Option’ a good one?
description: Gov. Ned Lamont wants a state-designed health insurance model that will lover costs. Will it work?
text:
Rising health insurance premiums remain a growing concern for Connecticut households. For 2027, average increases of 11.3% and 15.1% have been approved for individual and small-group health insurance plans, respectively. 
Connecticut needs policies that make health insurance and healthcare services more affordable, especially for people living with chronic diseases.
The problem of high healthcare costs in Connecticut is not new. Historically, healthcare costs have gone up faster than household income in Connecticut. A 20-year comparison of average healthcare cost increases and median household income growth shows a 2.8-percentage-point difference: 4.8% compared with 2%. This means healthcare costs increased more than twice as much as household income. 
Health insurance premiums are rising for several reasons. Medical services and prescription drugs are becoming more expensive, and people are using more healthcare services. Insurance companies are also paying more for medical claims than they expected. Changes in federal financial help for people buying health insurance can also affect premiums.
Many Connecticut residents are already struggling with healthcare costs. A 2025 survey of over 1,400 adults found that about 64% had trouble affording healthcare during the previous year. Also, 61% reported delaying or going without healthcare because of cost. So, what does this mean for people living with chronic conditions?
Chronic conditions often require ongoing care. People living with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, or chronic kidney disease may need regular visits with healthcare providers, lab tests and medicines to manage their conditions and prevent serious health problems. Missing or delaying these services can make their conditions worse and may even put their lives at risk. For these individuals, high insurance premiums add to the financial burden of paying for medicines, frequent visits with healthcare providers, and medical equipment they may need. Moreover, paying for healthcare while also meeting basic needs, such as food, housing, and family expenses, can make life more difficult.
Although the Connecticut Insurance Department has made efforts to reduce the yearly premium increases requested by insurance companies, there’s still more to do. The state must put in place policies to ensure that people with chronic conditions can get the medicines, medical equipment, and follow-up care they need without having to pay more than they can afford.
Gov. Ned Lamont has proposed the “Connecticut option” as a possible solution to high healthcare costs in the state. This would be a state-designed model managed by private insurance companies. It would include a network of healthcare providers offering quality care at lower costs, which people would be encouraged to use. The Office of Policy and Management has been directed to study whether the plan could work under Public Act 26-68, and the governor plans to propose legislation in 2027.
Organizations such as the Connecticut Hospital Association have raised concerns about the Connecticut option. They worry that the plan could limit patients’ choices of healthcare providers and lead to higher healthcare costs. These concerns are especially important for people living with chronic diseases, who may have regular healthcare providers familiar with their conditions and treatment needs.
As the state studies whether the Connecticut Option could work, officials should consider these concerns and work toward a plan that lowers healthcare costs without limiting patients’ access to healthcare providers. Legislators should also consider these concerns when reviewing the proposed plan.
Dorothy Wilson is a graduate student at the Elisabeth DeLuca School of Nursing, University of Connecticut.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT has built something healthcare can’t afford to waste
description: Connecticut has an opportunity to turn connected health information into more coordinated care and healthier communities.
text:
Connecticut has spent the past several years building the connections needed to make health information sharing a reality across the state. Now comes the more important work: putting that information to use in ways that change lives.
As healthcare providers face growing demands to address disparities and do more with limited resources, timely access to reliable health information has never mattered more.

Michelle Puhlick

As I step into the role of interim executive director of the Health Information Alliance, Inc. (HIA), I see an opportunity to build on the foundation we’ve established through Connie, Connecticut’s statewide Health Information Exchange, and turn connected data into more informed decisions and better health outcomes. We’ve built the infrastructure. Now, we’re focused on what it can make possible.
I’ve been part of Connie’s journey since before it launched in 2021, helping establish the operational foundation and connections for statewide information sharing. This transition is built on years of collaboration and a shared vision for what Connie can become. We’re now entering the phase where that groundwork starts to pay off, as we put the data to work for patients and providers in even more meaningful ways, and I’m committed to carrying that mission forward with energy and focus.
Connie now connects more than 4,000 provider locations across Connecticut, helping healthcare providers, payers and public health entities securely share information that supports coordinated, high-quality care. We’ve expanded participation among skilled nursing facilities and pharmacies, connected our first behavioral health electronic medical record systems and brought our first emergency medical services provider onto the network.
These milestones give care teams more opportunities to see the bigger picture and make informed decisions. They also reflect our participants’ trust in Connie and Connecticut’s collective commitment to improving care.
 Additionally, we’re:
 • Demonstrating Connecticut’s leadership in addressing health information exchange challenges nationwide, with Connie among just nine organizations selected nationally for a pilot grant to advance electronic consent management for patients receiving behavioral health care.
 • Helping providers improve race, ethnicity and language data, enabling more complete, accurate information to inform efforts to make healthcare more equitable.
 • Developing tools that give home and community-based services providers access to timely health information to support more coordinated, whole-person care.
These accomplishments give us a strong foundation, but I believe our greatest opportunity lies ahead. Our next phase is about putting the information and infrastructure we’ve built to work in more meaningful ways.
That means using data to help identify patients who may benefit from earlier intervention, strengthening public health response and supporting more equitable outcomes across Connecticut. It also means continuing to improve data quality and expand the network while ensuring the organizations that depend on Connie can realize its full value.
Rural health will be an important focus. Through Connecticut’s Rural Health Transformation Program, we’re working on initiatives to help providers identify rural patients at risk of avoidable hospitalizations and unnecessary emergency department visits. Better information and earlier insights give care teams more opportunities to intervene before a health concern becomes a crisis.
We’re pursuing this work in partnership with the providers, state agencies and community organizations that understand Connecticut’s needs firsthand. Technology alone cannot solve the challenges facing healthcare. Progress depends on listening to providers and patients and acting on what they tell us as we build practical solutions together. That includes guidance from our Clinical Advisory Council, Patient and Family Advisory Council and the feedback we gather at community events across the state.
My commitment is to carry forward Connie’s mission while continually asking how we can do more with the foundation we’ve established. Our leadership team and staff remain focused on supporting our participants and state partners, and the services and relationships people rely on will continue. 
What will evolve is how we use our capabilities to create even greater value for the people and communities we serve.
I’m proud of what we’ve built so far, but I’m even more energized by what comes next. Connecticut has an opportunity to turn connected health information into more coordinated care and healthier communities. With our partners, we intend to help make that opportunity a reality.
Michelle Puhlick is interim executive director and COO of the Health Information Alliance, Inc., the operating entity charged with running Connecticut’s Health Information Exchange, Connie.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Are you shopping as you read this? Black Friday moves to different days, ways to buy
description: Black Friday might not be the “shopping extravaganza” it once was, but that doesn't mean people won't be spending for the holidays like always -- and then some, with total sales expected to top $1 trillion this year nationwide.
text:
Shoppers will be spending for the holidays, but the traditional Black Friday scrums won't be as much a part of the season, which has stretched out over a longer period and moved to online and other platforms. (Photo by Getty Images)Black Friday might not be the “shopping extravaganza” it once was, but that doesn’t mean people won’t be spending for the holidays like always — and then some, with total sales expected to top $1 trillion this year.
The National Retail Federation predicted in October that retail sales during the November and December holiday season will grow 4.2% more than the 2025 rates. Total spending is set to hit $1.013 trillion compared to last year’s $972 billion.
But with additional holidays like Small Business Saturday and Cyber Monday, and weeklong deals at online shopping platforms like Amazon, the sales have moved past the exclusivity of a single day as the years go on, economic experts say.
University of Maryland marketing professor Jie Zhang said retailers have begun introducing sales earlier each year. Tariffs, rising gas prices and inflation continue to drive up the cost of living, making consumers less willing to buy and retailers less willing to discount.
Zhang, who specialized in retail management, said this year’s average discounts are projected to be similar to last year’s, which were already scaled back after hits to the nation’s economy.
“[Retailers] just simply could not afford to offer really deep discounts anymore because many of them absorbed a substantial part of tariffs … unfortunately, this year they’re not seeing much relief,” she said. “Because of that … some retailers might feel the pressure to actually raise prices and then offer discounts. The prices consumers end up paying, even with the discounts, are certainly higher than they have ever been.”
While the NRF is predicting sales will increase this holiday season, consumers shouldn’t take the growth rate at face value, said Henry Boyd, a clinical marketing professor at the University of Maryland who has a focus in consumer spending. The higher totals don’t factor in higher prices and costs of goods due to inflation and tariffs.
“You’re going to probably buy less stuff, but the stuff you buy is more expensive,” Boyd said in an interview last week.
The Maryland Retailers Alliance noted in a November press release that the outcome for Maryland retailers might be more of a mixed bag. According to the organization’s annual member survey, about 64% of participating businesses experienced lower sales in September and October compared to the previous year. The other 36% said they expect their sales to decline this holiday season.
Alliance President Cailey Locklair said these numbers could largely be influenced by the small businesses that make up a sizable portion of Maryland retailers. Small businesses tend to be more cautious about their forecasts, as online shopping and larger retailers become and tend to be more popular during sales events.
Consumers are also becoming more comfortable using artificial intelligence as a way to surf the internet for the best deals, which has the power to change consumer habits and increase the holiday spending activity, Boyd noted.
“We take it for granted: information at your fingertips,” he said. “It used to be the hardest part was figuring out where is the deal. You can do that now instantly.”
The national foundation’s additional late-October report notes that online shopping continues to rank as the top method, but the percentage of individuals planning to shop online has begun to decrease, with only 52% of consumers –  compared to last year’s 56% –  saying they plan to do so.
“It’s online fatigue. So much of our lives now are lived online,” Locklair said. “For a lot of people, it’s not just shopping; it’s an experience. It’s a whole-day adventure.”
Consumer behavior isn’t the only thing that drives the holiday season. Retailers are beginning to prioritize different marketing strategies during the busiest months for their income, Zhang said.
In addition to the holiday no longer being limited to a singular day of shopping, she said large retailers are starting to stagger sales to draw consumers in. This is where a retailer hikes up their prices, offers a sale for a short time period and gets rid of it before reintroducing a similar sale, giving the illusion of better discounts.
“For retailers, the end-of-the-year holiday shopping season is the single most important shopping season for their business,” Zhang said. “Because of that, competition amongst retailers has become more and more fierce over the years.”
But Boyd said that even with an influx of ways to shop online or grab the best discounts using AI platforms, shoppers still tend to appreciate the social experience holidays like Black Friday provide.
Even if people aren’t in a line wrapped around the store early Friday morning, people won’t be ditching the brick and mortar stores, he added.
“It’s like a form of entertainment,” Boyd said. “For a lot of folks, the magic lies … with your family, you’re with your friends… you look at a couple things, you grab something to eat, and those are the memories.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: John A. Peoples Jr., beloved former Jackson State president, dies at 100
description: President Emeritus John A. Peoples, addresses members of the Jackson State Class of 1970, Saturday, May 15, 2021, during a special graduation ceremony at the historically black university in Jackson, Miss. The class was honored 51 years after the school canceled its 1970 graduation ceremony after white law enforcement officers marched onto campus near the en[...]
text:
John A. Peoples Jr., a beloved leader who shepherded Jackson State’s evolution from a teachers college to a university, died Thursday. He was 100.  
Lisa M. Ross confirmed Peoples’ death on behalf of his family. Ross, a Jackson-area attorney and JSU alumna, praised Peoples’ leadership. 
“Dr. Peoples was an extraordinary leader,” Ross said. “He prepared us to believe in ourselves and never abandon our dreams.”
Former Jackson State University President John A. Peoples, second from right and his wife, Mary Peoples, second from left, join attendees at a convocation honoring Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., in singing “We Shall Overcome,” Thursday, Feb. 25, 2010 in Jackson, Miss. Andrew Young, a civil rights activist who worked alongside Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., delivered the address noting America’s civil rights fight must move to an economic front and he encouraged black college students should pursue degrees in economics rather than law. (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
Peoples was the first Jackson State alumnus to also serve as its president, leading the university from 1967 to 1984. When he stepped down, he continued teaching for a year at JSU before retiring in 1985.  
Peoples also led Jackson State during one of the darkest periods in its history. In May 1970, law enforcement officers opened fire on campus, killing Phillip Lafayette Gibbs, a Jackson State student, and 17-year-old James Earl Green, a high school student, and injuring others. 
Sen. Sollie Norwoord, a Democrat from Jackson, was a student during the Jackson State tragedy. He said the aftermath of the campus shootings was Peoples’ finest hour as president.
Norwood recalled Peoples walking around campus and sitting with students and faculty in what is now known as the Gibbs-Green Memorial Plaza to restore calm and reassure the university community. His leadership during those turbulent years set a standard for future presidents, Norwood said.
John A. Peoples Jr., a beloved former president of Jackson State University, died on Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. He was 100. Peoples led JSU through civil rights struggles and its transition from a teachers college to a university. Credit: Jackson State University
“We’ve had many presidents since Peoples’ tenure that have had some of his qualities but there was only one John A. Peoples Jr.,” said Norwood, who graduated from JSU in 1974. “He was a genuinely good person.”
Peoples supported efforts to desegregate Mississippi’s public higher education system through the landmark Ayers lawsuit, which challenged racial inequities in the state’s public universities. 
“We weathered difficult times, times of tragedy and of opposition to our progress, but we came through,” Peoples said in a video posted by the JSU National Alumni Association commemorating his 100th birthday in August.
“Looking back from this long vantage point, I have been happy to see the continued growth of our dear institution, and to boast about achievements and contributions that you Jackson State alumni have made,” he said.
Jackson State alumni (from left) Lee Bernard, Quilly Turner and Gailya Porter attended the 56th Gibbs-Green Commemoration at the university campus on Thursday, May 14, 2026. They were classmates of Phillip Lafayette Gibbs. Police shot and killed Gibbs and Jim Hill High School student James Earl Green during protests at JSU on May 15, 1970. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
During Peoples’ 17-year tenure, student enrollment grew from 2,200 to 7,800, and Jackson State expanded its academic offerings beyond its traditional focus on teacher education. 
Peoples pressed the state’s college board to grant university status to Jackson State College. It did so in 1974. Jackson State awarded its first doctoral degrees eight years later, becoming the first historically Black college or university in Mississippi to do so. 
Peoples established new academic schools, launched an Army ROTC program and, in 1975, introduced a meteorology program, making JSU the first HBCU to offer a bachelor’s degree in the field.
Born Aug. 26, 1926, in Starkville, Peoples graduated from Oktibbeha County Training School in 1944. He enlisted in the U.S. Marine Corps the following year and served until 1947. 
A photograph of President Emeritus John A Peoples, Jr., appears in the Jackson State University’s 144th Founders’ Day Convocation program in Jackson, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 28, 2021. Peoples was awarded an honorary doctorate of humane letters during the ceremony. (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
He earned a bachelor’s degree in mathematics from Jackson College in 1950 before earning a master’s degree in mathematics and a doctorate in higher education from the University of Chicago. 
Peoples is widely regarded as one of Jackson State’s best presidents. When the state college board began searching last year for the next JSU president, alumni and others tied to the university said they wanted a leader like Peoples. They shared stories of their experience under Peoples’ leadership and how he emphasized the need to respect the campus community.
Sen. Hillman Frazier, a Democrat from Jackson and JSU alum, said he often turned to Peoples for advice on higher education issues after joining the Mississippi House of Representatives in 1980. 
At the time, Frazier said, the state’s college board prohibited the university president from lobbying lawmakers. The two often discussed funding disparities at Mississippi’s historically Black universities and Jackson State’s needs for better faculty pay, campus improvements and student housing. 
“JSU is surviving because of him.”

name: VTDigger
title: A pilgrimage at 60 on bad knees taught me to let go
description:
Fear of losing the people you love can be handed down like an heirloom. My Camino de Santiago pilgrimage helped me accept that I am not in control. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A pilgrimage at 60 on bad knees taught me to let go.
text:
This commentary is by Geeta Anand, the former editor-in-chief of VTDigger. She lives in Plainfield.
Many Asian spiritual traditions believe you are reborn at the age of 60. To facilitate my own rebirth, this year I set out on the Camino de Santiago, an ancient pilgrimage through Europe that ends in the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in northwestern Spain. The remains of one of Jesus’ apostles, St. James, are believed to be buried there.
My first 60 years were focused on caring for my children and parents as I built a meaningful journalism career. For the next chapter, I wanted to journey inward to learn to accept the things I’ve feared most in life, and so in September I set out to walk the last 75 miles of the Camino with three girlfriends, two of whom I have known since first grade in India. 
We all carried spiritual grief, but I was also encumbered by the physical burden of severe osteoarthritis in my knees. I trained for months, increasing my daily walks from 20 minutes in the hills around my house in Plainfield to the four hours it takes to walk to my favorite cafe and back home again, but I knew the pilgrimage would test me. 
In September, we set out from Baiona, a medieval Spanish town of red-tiled rooftops and bright white beaches overlooking quiet coves of the azure Atlantic Ocean. The first day was easy, but reality hit hard the next morning. I ended up calling a taxi to get to our hotel. The following day, I needed to rest on benches every 30 minutes to relieve my knee pain, and once more finished the day in a taxi. 
Taking taxis on a daily basis was not my idea of how best to navigate this pilgrimage. I took the next day off to do what I should have done before beginning the journey: study the route and develop a feasible plan for each day. 
My knees barely hurt for the first two hours of walking — these were my golden hours, I was learning, so my strategy became to leave early at 7 a.m. and move my legs as fast as I could so I covered as many miles as possible before the knee pain set in. 
From then on, I lay down and stretched on almost every wall along the route. I worried that someone might perceive me as irreverent lying on a church wall with legs aloft, but I was desperate enough to take the risk. To my relief, no angry priest or parishioner ever shooed me away.
I thought of my parents and how judgmental I had been of them when they found a way to sit down at every bench they passed. I had been so sure I wouldn’t be like them, and yet here I was.
My Camino journey was about letting go of my fear of loss. Thoughts of my parents flooded my mind as I walked, as they have since they died — my dad in 2017 and my mom in 2023. I thought of how terrified they had been of losing the ones they loved. 
I remembered my American grandmother, who sent five sons off to fight in World War II. How scared she was about losing them, and how grateful when all five returned safely. Beside the telephone in her house in Catonsville, Maryland, she kept five framed telegrams, one from each saying he was coming home.
My parents carried this intergenerational trauma into our lives. They were so worried about losing me that they called me many times a day to make sure I was OK. If I didn’t pick up after a flight was due to land, they concluded it had gone down. 
I vowed I wouldn’t call my kids as relentlessly as my mother called me. But I often find myself calling them more than they seem to want to answer. It is harder than I had understood to forge a different way of being than your parents. That’s why I was on the Camino, I realized. It took intention; it took a journey like this to cut a different trail. 

READ MORE

At 60, I have seen enough of life to understand there’s no avoiding losing the people you love. Tina, another friend on the Camino, said she was on the journey to try to find a way to accept her husband’s death three years earlier. He had lived a healthy life focused on exercise, meditation and a vegetarian diet. And still cancer had taken him at the age of 64. 
You can try with every ounce of your being to protect yourself and your family from illness and death, and it can still come calling. I tried to protect my children from the addiction that plagued my family for generations, and yet my daughter Tatyana suffered from the same life-threatening substance use disorder. She has been sober now for 16 months, but her success has little to do with me or anything I have ever said or might advise. 
My pilgrimage was not dedicated to her recovery but instead about letting her go and accepting that I was not in control of her journey in this world.
I managed a challenging physical journey in spite of my disabling arthritis. I did so not by being careless with myself, as I have done in years past, but by honoring my injuries and attending to them. In doing so, I emerged from my Camino feeling stronger, and yes, perhaps even reborn to a wiser and more accepting version of myself.

name: Delaware
title: The Thanksgiving Thank-You That Can’t Wait for Pie
description: By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE There comes a moment at Thanksgiving dinner when someone asks where the gravy is, someone else remembers the rolls are still in the oven, and the person who cooked most of the meal finally gets to sit down. At our table, somewhere in the middle of all that, we bow our heads ... Read More
text:
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
There comes a moment at Thanksgiving dinner when someone asks where the gravy is, someone else remembers the rolls are still in the oven, and the person who cooked most of the meal finally gets to sit down. At our table, somewhere in the middle of all that, we bow our heads and say grace.
I thank God for the food and for the people gathered around the table. And then my mind wanders a little. I start thinking about people who won’t be sitting with us, people who did something during the year that I’m still grateful for. I wonder how many of them know it.
Most of us can think of someone. Maybe it’s the neighbor who brought your trash cans up the driveway while you were recovering from surgery. Or the friend who called a few weeks after the funeral, when the house had gone quiet and there were fewer reasons for the phone to ring. Maybe it’s a grandchild who called just to tell you something funny that happened at school, on a day when you could use a good laugh.
We usually manage a quick thank-you when these things happen. What the other person may never hear is that we were still thinking about that phone call a week later. Or that seeing those trash cans beside the garage made us feel a little less alone.
Around Bear, where I live, some folks will spend Thanksgiving morning cooking for a houseful. Others will work a shift, bring a plate to a neighbor or have a quiet meal at home. There will be tables where everyone talks at once and tables where somebody’s absence is felt every time the conversation goes quiet. Sometimes relief and sorrow sit so close together you can feel both while passing the mashed potatoes.
If this has been a hard year, your thank-you can be as small and plain as it needs to be. “I remember you called that Sunday. I was having a rough day, and I’m glad you called.” If you’ve ever wondered whether to reach out to someone going through a difficult time, imagine how it would feel to hear those words from them months later.
As a writer, I spend a fair amount of time looking for the right words. That may be why I’m tempted to wait until I can write a proper note, preferably on a card I’ve remembered to buy. Meanwhile, my phone is usually within reach, and I could have typed “I’m glad you called” in less time than it took me to decide I needed a card.
So, here’s my Thanksgiving invitation. Think of one person you’ve been meaning to thank. Tell them what they did and why you remember it. If they’re across the table, you can lean over and say it. If they’re across the country, a text will get there while the coffee is still hot. And if the person you’re thinking of is gone, tell someone at the table a story about them. You may find out they remember the same thing, or that they have a story you’ve never heard.
You can also thank the person who finally got to sit down. If you know how early they got up to get the turkey in the oven, say so. Then offer to do the dishes. Some thank-you’s are even better with a dish towel in hand.
This Thanksgiving, when I bow my head, I’ll thank God for the people who showed up when I needed them. After grace, I’m going to tell one of them exactly what I remember.
If somebody asks whether I’m ready for pie, tell them I’ll be there in a minute.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas teen competes for national civics championship after leading drive for hygiene products
description: LAWRENCE — Salina South High School freshman Colin Burke represented the state of Kansas at the National Civics Bee Championship, placing fourth in the competition with plans to further the community wellness project that began his journey to the national stage. Colin competed at the local, regional and state level on civics, American government and […]
text:
Finalists, including Colin Burke, center, compete Oct. 14, 2026, during the National Civics Bee Championship at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Erin Scott/U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation)LAWRENCE — Salina South High School freshman Colin Burke represented the state of Kansas at the National Civics Bee Championship, placing fourth in the competition with plans to further the community wellness project that began his journey to the national stage.
Colin competed at the local, regional and state level on civics, American government and the constitution, making his way to the national competition in October that was livestreamed on C-SPAN. Even with technical difficulties in the final round that made contestants go from using buzzers to whiteboards, he stayed calm under pressure, and finished just five points behind the contestant in third place.
“ This experience has just taught me so much,” he said. “ It’s helped me connect with a lot more people around our community through doing my project and how to speak in public. I kept telling my mom  even if I didn’t place at this, I’ll just be really prepared for AP American Government.”
Colin wrote an essay and speech about teen wellness, a demographic he said is overlooked. He wrote about a plan to bring hygiene supplies at schools to make them available for students who can’t drive.
“ It’s more accessible than a traditional adult-led effort,” Colin said. “I want students providing input so we can create a wider base of opinion.”
After winning regionals last spring, Colin decided he would implement the idea from his essay at his middle school, organizing a hygiene drive by working with local charities and collecting 500 items.
His principal at Salina South Middle School describes Colin as the type of student that every principal hopes to have in their building.
“Colin’s project has provided our students with an opportunity to see what can happen when someone takes an interest, works hard, and commits themselves to making a difference,” principal Dustin Dooley said. “He is a young man of tremendous character, leadership, humility, and determination. He consistently set a positive example for those around him.”
Colin said he’s working on getting a student committee together at his high school to expand the project from his middle school. Dooley said he hopes to see current students build upon what Colin started.
Colin credits much of his success to his parents, with his mom, Elizabeth Burke, editing his essays and helping him study, he said. Elizabeth said he has grown academically and personally in the past year.
“ He loves learning, and he’s curious about the world, and that’s what you want in a learner,” she said. “That’s what you want in somebody who lives in a democracy. He’s constantly challenging things too, which I think is a great quality to have.”
To prepare for the competition, Colin said he would try to study at least an hour per day after school and his extracurriculars. He also utilized his good luck charm, the Hamilton musical soundtrack, which he says he listened to all the way through more than 1,000 times.
“ I tried to make sure that I prioritized school,  but I really wanted to make sure that I studied at least an hour a day,” he said. “ I didn’t have any reason to be like, ‘I wish I would’ve crammed just a little bit more in at nationals.’ ”
He said that going into politics isn’t off the table, but his main focus for now is school — specifically educating his fellow students about staying politically and civically informed.
“ I would tell students it may seem boring, but in four years you’ll be voting, and I think it’s important for us all to understand how our government works,” Colin said. “ It’s really important for safeguarding our democracy.”
Before his interest in government, Colin had plans to go into genetics to find a cure for Type 1 diabetes to help find a diagnosis for his younger brother. He said he will have a tough decision deciding if he wants to go into politics or genetics.
“It kind of relates back to I want to help people,” Colin said. “I want to be a politician  and make changes in the world. There’s a lot of problems that we have in our world, and I want to help solve them.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Young People Get Cash To Keep Them Off The Streets
description: The hope is that the new program, funded by private foundations, will be so effective that government will decide to support it.
text:
Holli-Jae Macanas’ downtown Honolulu apartment is about a three-minute walk to her daughter’s childcare program. It’s a 20-minute walk from her part time job in a nonprofit’s planning department. It’s five minutes from the Liliʻuokalani Trust offices where twice a week she, her partner and daughter study Native Hawaiian culture and values with the goal of giving back to their community and building pilina — a connection — as a young family.
“Our whole life is around our home,” Macanas said on a recent Thursday in the one-bedroom apartment she shares with Micah Naniole-Furutani and their 19-month old daughter, Hunny. 
The apartment was crowded with baby supplies — from boxes of diapers to a stroller to a lacy white child’s tent where Hunny keeps her stuffed flower pillows. In the kitchen was a small square table where last month Macanas, 24, sat down with a case manager to plot out her finances and a plan for moving forward.
Their share of Hunny’s state-subsidized childcare had gone up $218 a month, and they had fallen behind in payments. Their rent was due to rise in four months. With a combined take-home income of about $2,500 a month — Naniole-Furutani is an assistant swim coach at a Honolulu high school and attends community college — things were getting too tight, too fast.
“I was spending countless nights up awake, and Micah said, ‘Why can’t you go to sleep?’” said Macanas, who experienced homelessness as a teenager on the Big Island. “I said, ‘I’m stressing out.’ And he was stressing out, too.”
Barely a month later, the couple are on firmer financial footing as they look to the future. The difference: a program new to Hawaiʻi intended to keep young people off Oʻahu’s streets through one-time cash grants paired with an array of classes, counseling and workshops on topics such as credit repair and financial planning.
Micah Naniole-Furutani and his partner, Holli-Jae Macanas, play with their daughter, Hunny, in their downtown Honolulu apartment. Macanas is one of the first participants in a program overseen by the nonprofit Hawaiʻi Health and Harm Reduction Center that gives one-time cash grants to young people aged 18 to 24 to help keep them from falling into homelessness. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
In Macanas’ case, a $3,300 grant put breathing room between her family and a financial crisis that could have cost them their housing. 
The theory of the Targeted Housing Assistance Program is that for many people, a few thousand dollars is the difference between stability and homelessness. The point is to catch them before they fall.
To be eligible, participants must be between the ages of 18 and 24, experiencing a crisis that could lead them to homelessness, and not already on the streets or in homeless shelters.
The Hawaiʻi Health & Harm Reduction Center in Honolulu oversees the program, which was started by a New York nonprofit, Point Source Youth, that partners with local organizations.
It’s “an upstream intervention,” said center Executive Director Heather Lusk, aimed at “finding folks that are having housing insecurity, but are still housed, and keeping them housed.” 
A Flexible Approach
Launched in the Midwest five years ago with philanthropic funding, the program is now up and running in 10 states including California, Texas and Georgia. So far, only Maryland, California and Oregon have committed public funds to it, said Point Source Youth executive director and co-founder Larry Cohen.
Hawaiʻi is starting small. As of Tuesday, 11 people had been enrolled since early October in the Oʻahu program, which focuses largely on Native Hawaiian and LGBTQ young people because both groups are overrepresented among homeless youth. Lusk said grants are generally delivered within 48 hours after someone is approved.
The grant is given out via a debit card that participants can redeem and use as they see fit.
A critical component is working with participants to find out what they need money for beyond keeping their housing or finding a new place to live, Cohen said. For example, he said, if someone needs a laptop to complete their schooling, addressing that need would help ensure their future stability in ways that a housing grant alone might not. 
“The question isn’t ‘What’s the least amount of money possible to solve the problem?’” he said. “It’s, ‘What is the amount of money that’s going to be most effective as a one-time payment to set this young person on a positive life journey?’”
A participant in the Targeted Housing Assistance Grant program received a grant for a security deposit and first month’s rent for a new apartment and to pay off her credit card debt. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Also key to the process is discussing with young people how to use the grant to arrive at a spending plan, rather than placing tight restrictions on what it can be used for from the outset. 
“It works better because it really puts the young person at the center of the decision making and of the problem solving and of the energy to execute the solution,” Cohen said, “because we’re supporting them, and they really feel that.”
Macanas was able to fashion a plan in which her $3,300 grant would cover two months of rent, a month of childcare and the start of a savings fund.
For one single mother on the Windward side, a $5,900 grant covered a security deposit and first month’s rent on a two-bedroom apartment, and it allowed her to pay off her credit card so debt doesn’t drag her back down.
“Receiving it was unreal,” said the 24-year-old woman, who asked not to be identified, saying she is living in an unsafe situation while waiting for a new apartment. Going through her finances with the Hawaiʻi Health and Harm Reduction Center staff was eye opening, she said, helping her realize she could save money through changes such as buying fewer groceries and dropping subscriptions to publications she didn’t read.
“They don’t just want a handout. They want a partnership and they want to show that they can make it on their own.”Heather Lusk, Executive Director, Hawaiʻi Health & Harm Reduction Center
“The budgeting process that they do with you really opens up like what your needs are and what you’re actually putting your money toward,” she said. 
Other participants include another 24-year-old fleeing an abusive partner who just needed enough to cover a security deposit to get into public housing. A 21-year-old had aged out of a housing support program but lacked money for a deposit and month’s rent to stay in her apartment. The program covered that, plus money for a bicycle for her husband to get to and from work. 
In another case, a 23-year-old Kapiʻolani Community College student expecting her second child got a grant to pay off a credit card and move into a two-bedroom apartment near Pearl Harbor with a view of the Skyline tracks.


A Note On Anonymous Sources
Civil Beat generally uses on-the-record sources. However, we occasionally use unnamed sources when a source is sharing important information we wouldn’t have otherwise been able to obtain and when they could face negative consequences for speaking publicly. The reporter and at least one editor must know the identity of the source and the use of anonymity must be approved by a senior editor. You can read more about our anonymous sources policy here.


“I still don’t even think I’m in here, I really don’t believe it,” said the woman as she sat on a bench in her new home, which was still largely empty of furniture that the grant had paid for but had yet to arrive. 
She, too, did not want to be named for safety reasons. She doesn’t want certain people in her life to know that she received a grant and has found a new place to live.
She said she had been living in a moldy, rodent-infested one-bedroom unit in Honolulu with her partner and daughter and a relative, while her poor credit rating doomed her applications for at least 20 apartments. 
Besides getting her into a new living situation, she said, a course through the program had helped her improve her credit score.
First 50, Then 200
The program has a goal of reaching 50 young people on Oʻahu in its first year. It is privately funded, Cohen said, by the Harry and Jeanette Weinberg and Doris Duke foundations in Hawaiʻi and the Zilber Family Foundation of Wisconsin.
The hope is to demonstrate that it’s effective and gain enough government funding to reach 200 young people a year statewide, Cohen said. That’s about the number of 18-to-24-year-olds tallied as homeless across Hawaiʻi during the January 2026 Point in Time count — a number the program hopes to keep from rising.
Keeping someone from becoming homeless saves money that would otherwise be spent on shelter and support services, which can reach $32,000 a year in Hawaiʻi, plus policing, criminal justice and emergency room costs. It can also keep people in jobs or school – or both.
“It’s a reasonable amount of money, and it saves money that you’re going to spend in six months, when or if a young person enters the homeless system,” Cohen said.
While the national average grant size is $3,700, Hawaiʻi’s high cost of living has increased the average grant here to about $4,300, said Michelle Wilkins, housing and outreach manager at Hawaiʻi Health and Harm Reduction Center.
A Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health study this year of the seven states already participating examined outcomes for 345 youth. It found that six months after receiving the grant, 93% of them reported they had not turned to shelters or other homeless services. All told, the study found 623 people were helped by the program.
That’s promising, say experts who have researched similar cash support programs and homelessness, but more research is needed to be certain other factors aren’t also keeping the recipients off the streets.
“I think it’s a great program design … but it’s hard to prove something prevented something from happening if you don’t have the control group to compare it to,” said Ben Henwood, a professor of social policy and health at the University of Southern California and director of its Homelessness Policy Research Institute.
Cohen is aware of that critique. He said a new Johns Hopkins study will take in the experiences of more than 800 participants, including in Hawaiʻi, and will include a control group of people not receiving grants.
Direct cash programs have attracted criticism that recipients will spend the money unwisely. But studies have largely refuted those fears and shown that, instead, they spend it on daily necessities, said Jiaying Zhao, a psychology professor at the University of British Columbia.
The Point Source Youth program’s approach of working with participants to determine their best spending choices, and leaving them to carry out the plan, is important, Zhao said. She said it distinguishes it from others where someone like a case manager or trustee manages the funds.
Referring to how the program tries to empower participants, she said, “We want independence. We want freedom. So that feature actually could be good.”
Other aspects of the program portend success, too, said Zhao, who has directed research projects focused on cash grants for people who are homeless.
“Unconditional cash works better than conditional, and the size matters, too: The larger the payment … the larger impact it has,” she said. “And the other thing is timing: The cash has to be delivered at the time of need rather than, let’s say, tax time as a once-a-year payment.”
Lusk, of Hawaiʻi Health & Harm Reduction Center, said the first grant recipients have been determined to prove the investment is a good one.
Michelle Wilkins, program manager for outreach and housing with Hawaiʻi Health & Harm Reduction Center, greets Hunny, daughter of Holli-Jae Macanas. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
“They don’t just want a handout. They want a partnership, and they want to show that they can make it on their own,” she said.
Another common refrain among the young people who have received grants so far, she said, is essentially: “Why me?”
“We’ve actually had to say, ‘Hey, you qualify for this. I know that you’re feeling like you’re taking something because you already have a home, but you’re not taking this away from anybody else. And you deserve to implement your housing stability plan,’” Lusk said.
In her downtown apartment, with Hunny and Naniole-Furutani beside her on a small, extra bed in the living room, Macanas said they hope to move to the Big Island next year to be closer to her family. She will be able to work her job remotely while her partner plans to attend the firefighter academy.
“The best thing that our family can do is to keep on hustling, going to work, attending school and making sure we make time to give back to our community,” she said. “We need to keep on putting in our savings, building our credit and paying our bills.”
“In my heart I feel we aren’t on full solid financial ground,” she said, “but we are getting there.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Honolulu Studios For $800 A Month? One Developer Is Pulling It Off
description: Two new affordable housing projects in town are breaking ground as Hawaiʻi residents face escalating living costs amid a stagnant economy and slow wage growth.
text:
Honolulu real estate developers are building something rare in Honolulu’s urban core: new one-bedroom apartments for rent around $866 per month.
Tradewind Group and Stanford Carr Development earlier this month began construction on the 23-story, 247-unit Olohana on Piʻikoi complex. The $150 million project at Piʻikoi and Young is expected to open in the summer of 2028.
Meanwhile, not far from Olohana on Piʻikoi, at 1142 Kīnaʻu St., Kailua-based Ahe Group is planning a $130 million, 206-unit tower, with two units reserved for families experiencing or at risk of homelessness. It’s expected to open in December 2028.
The private projects on private land defy a recent trend in which federally supported affordable housing projects are typically being developed as public-private partnerships, on public land or both.
Olohana on Piʻikoi will reserve units exclusively for individuals earning between $32,000 and $65,000 a year and families of four earning $46,200 to $92,400, according to the most recent guidelines set by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.
The 1142 Kīnaʻu building will reserve all but six units for residents at those income levels: four, two-bedroom units will be set aside for individuals earning up to $86,240 and four-person households earning up to $123,200. Two additional apartments will be manager units.
Trandewind Group and Stanford Carr Development broke ground in November on their $150 million Olohana on Piʻikoi project, which will offer 247 affordable units in Honolulu’s urban core. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
The result at Olohana on Piʻikoi will be 13 studio apartments starting at $808, including utilities. Combined, the two projects will provide 188 one-bedroom apartments with rent and utilities capped at between $866 and $1,732 a month, depending on the renters’ household income, according to the guidelines.
Tradewind’s president and chief executive, Robert Nobriga, said the goal is to create truly affordable housing, which is in woefully short supply for working people.
 “If we wanted more return on the land,” Nobriga said, “we would have a different business plan.”
The projects break ground as Hawaiʻi residents face escalating living costs amid a stagnant economy and slow wage growth. A report released earlier this month by the Aloha United Way found that 52% of households in Hawaiʻi are struggling to get by financially, up from 40% in 2024, and housing costs are a big reason for that.
It’s long been expensive to rent a home in Hawaiʻi, and it’s only gotten worse since the Covid-19 pandemic. Rents in Honolulu have increased more than 28% since 2019, according to the University of Hawaiʻi Economic Research Organization. Rents have stabilized in the last few years, UHERO reported in its latest housing report, but the median monthly price published on Craigslist in 2025 still topped $2,000 on Oʻahu.
The result has been an exodus of people from the state, with a significant percentage of those who stay burdened by high rents. UHERO found nearly one in three renters on Oʻahu were spending more than half their income merely to cover their rent.
Federal Tax Credits Are Key
The developers are using state and government housing programs to build and pay for the projects while keeping rents low. A state law allows affordable housing developers to exceed normal density limits, which in the case of Olohana at Piʻikoi is allowing a 200-foot condo tower and seven-story parking garage in an area of mostly one-story and low-rise apartments and commercial buildings.
The 1142 Kīnaʻu project is also saving money by including only 24 parking stalls for the 20-story tower, which Ahe Group is positioning as a transit-oriented project because of the development’s close proximity to bus and bike-share stops, McKinley High School, a Safeway grocery store and Straub Benioff Medical Center.
“Everybody wants affordable housing. But there’s no such thing as an affordable carpenter or affordable concrete or affordable rebar.”Kaloa Robinson, Stanford Carr Development
Tradewind and Stanford Carr are covering about 50% of Olohana at Piʻikoi’s costs with state and federal low-income housing tax credits and another 25% with a low-interest loan from the state’s Rental Housing Revolving Fund, said Chris Fong, Tradewind’s vice president of development. The rest will come from private bonds.
The 1142 Kīnaʻu project is also using state and federal low-income housing tax credits and a loan from the state Rental Housing Revolving Fund. Ahe Group didn’t respond to requests for comment about the plans, but it provides details on its website and in documents filed with the Hawaiʻi Housing Development and Finance Corp., a state housing agency.
The federal tax credits are “the difference between making a project like this work and not work,” said Kaloa Robinson, vice president of development for Stanford Carr.
“Everybody wants affordable housing,” he added, “but there’s no such thing as an affordable carpenter or affordable concrete or affordable rebar.”
The empty lot of the project Olohana where  Stanford Carr Developers is partnering with a local financial services conglomerate to build something rare in Honolulu’s urban core: new apartments for rent as low as $808 per month.  (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
The result is a condo unit that costs $550,000 to $650,000 to build, and the only way to pay for that if developers foot the bill alone is to charge rents of around $4,000 a month, Robinson said.
Tax credits are generally sold by developers for cash used as equity in the projects, reducing the amount developers have to borrow and pay back through rents. That allows projects such as Olohana at Piʻikoi and 1142 Kīnaʻu to pencil out financially even with lower rent revenue.
Olohana on Piʻikoi and 1142 Kīnaʻu are hardly the only developments to rely on the federal tax credits. The Hawaiʻi Housing Finance and Development Corp., which administers the program, has awarded approximately $140 million in annual federal low-income housing tax credits to 42 projects in the last five years.
And they’re not the largest. For instance, the Hawaiʻi Public Housing Authority in October broke ground on the first phase of its redevelopment of the Mayor Wright Housing Project, which it is building with the private developer Highridge Costa. A 308-unit tower will replace 64 public housing units spread out over eight low-rise buildings with a 308-unit tower, part of a long-term plan to replace 364 units with 2,450 new homes in 10 towers on state land.
Still, Olohana at Piʻikoi and 1142 Kīnaʻu stand out. The finance and development corporation in recent years has prioritized steering housing tax credits to government projects or public-private partnerships, typically located on public land, said Dean Minakami, the corporation’s executive director.
In that context, he said, Olohana at Piʻikoi and 1142 Kīnaʻu are unusual as private projects being built on private land using federal tax credits that limit rents to truly affordable levels.
Units To Stay Affordable For 66 Years
The federal low-income housing tax credit program requires units to be rented at affordable levels for only 15 years, meaning developers could benefit from government subsidies to build housing, then raise rents to market rates.
The practice is much different, Minakami said. Developers usually commit to far more than that when submitting proposals to receive tax credits under a competitive process in which the housing corporation ranks projects according to benefits they provide the community. 
In the past, that’s often meant developers committing to 30-year affordability periods.
These days, the duration is typically closer to 60 years, Minakami says, or “the economic life of the building.”
“When we evaluate projects, the longer they commit, the higher they score,” he said.
The lot formerly occupied by Meadow Gold is seen with demolition work in progress in November.  (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
The shortest duration for the current round of tax credit financing is 55 years, he said. Olahana at Piʻikoi and 1146 Kīnaʻu have committed to 66 years. 
Tradewind hopes to build more such affordable housing projects in Honolulu, Nobriga and Fong said. One candidate is the site of a former Meadow Gold milk processing facility on Sheridan and Elm streets near the Ala Moana Walmart, land that Tradewind bought for $17.7 million in 2025.
The challenge, Fong said, is that the parcels don’t currently qualify for the federal low-income housing tax credits, which the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development calls “the most important resource for creating affordable housing in the United States today.”
Regardless of whether that parcel works, Nobriga said Tradewind is committed to doing more truly affordable projects like Olohana on Piʻikoi.
“We’re not trying to make loads of money on every transaction,” he said. But, he added, “I’m reluctant to toot our own horn because we have such a long way to go.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Maui Strives For A More Ethical Government
description: The county is updating its rules for lobbyists and strengthening protections against nepotism in government.
text:
One of the first things Lauren Akitake noticed after she was tapped to become Maui County’s first full-time ethics director — and the state’s first full-time county-level ethics employee outside of Honolulu — was that there were multiple puka, or holes, in Maui’s ethics policy.
“We needed to fill those,” she said. 
Aspects of Maui’s Code of Ethics were much weaker than in other parts of the state, Akitake said, and it failed to adequately address important ethical questions on issues like lobbying and nepotism. 
Since Akitake was brought on board in the summer of 2025, she has helped push through a bill that gives the Board of Ethics greater authority to investigate ethical complaints filed against current and former county officials, and she has appeared before members of the Maui County Council to discuss additional changes to the county’s rules for lobbyists and a proposal for a countywide anti-nepotism policy. 
Since she was hired to be Maui County’s first full-time ethics director, Lauren Akitake has worked to strengthen the county’s code of ethics.  Erin Nolan/Civil Beat/2026
Akitake was hired to be the Board of Ethics director and legal counsel following a string of high-profile local public corruption scandals and amidst declining public trust in government across the country. 
She has spent the past year working with the Board of Ethics to help county officials better understand what constitutes an ethical violation and advocating for policy changes intended to promote integrity in local government. Over time, Akitake said that she hopes their efforts will translate into an improved relationship between residents and the county government. 
“It has been tough,” Akitake said, sitting behind her desk at the David K. Trask Jr. office building in Wailuku. “There are those people who are not going to like change or ethics rules, but we see that it’s working on a daily basis, and the reception by those who are using our services makes it worth it.”
Some of the current initiatives have been discussed by the Board of Ethics for years, said Michael Lilly, a former Hawaiʻi attorney general and the current board chair. But until recently, the all-volunteer board lacked the resources to effectively advocate for policy changes while also staying on top of responsibilities such as training county employees, reviewing financial disclosures and investigating ethics complaints against public officials and workers.
“It’s completely night and day,” Lilly said, referring to the board’s productivity since it was able to hire Akitake and a handful of other full-time employees. “We’re not dealing with minutiae. That makes us so much more effective. It’s been transformational.”

Maui County Ethics Director Lauren Akitake said that she hopes her efforts will translate into an improved relationship between residents and the county government.  Marina Riker/Civil Beat/2022

Akitake, who has lived most of her life on Maui and spent many years as a per diem District Court judge and lawyer on Maui and Oʻahu, said she and the board strive for fairness and transparency. 
Still, some residents have criticized her work with the board. In particular, she faced backlash last year after the board adopted several rule changes, including one that critics said looked like an attempt to silence anyone who filed a complaint against a county employee or elected official. The board ultimately said it would not enforce the new confidentiality rule, pending further discussion.
Most of the proposed changes were based on the rules for the state and Honolulu ethics commissions, and they were intended to promote efficiency and impartiality. 
‘Now People Know That We’re Effective’
The board’s increased capacity came about after Maui voters approved a 2024 charter amendment authorizing the county to hire a full-time Board of Ethics staff. 
Akitake has issued more than 200 informal advisory opinions to county employees and officers seeking ethics advice or policy clarification since she started the job in 2025.
“Two years ago, we didn’t have informal opinions. All the opinions were by the board, and they were formal,” Lilly said. “Because we only meet once a month, we can’t do very many formal opinions very often.”
Having staff issue informal opinions gives the board more time to investigate complaints and focus on formal requests for advisory opinions.

Maui County Board of Ethics Chair Michael Lilly in 2016 (Cory Lum/Civil Beat/2016) Cory Lum/Civil Beat/2016

Recently, the board issued a formal advisory opinion addressing the considerations that county employees and elected officials should take when writing letters of recommendation, and they have begun reviewing a permitted interaction group’s report examining when it is and is not appropriate for local government officials to accept gifts. 
Akitake and Lilly said officials seem to be much more educated about the county’s ethics policies compared to previous years, and more people have been seeking ethics advice before problems arise.
“Now people know that we’re effective,” he said. “They know that they can come to us, and they can not only get opinion, but they can get action.”
In the first year that the board had a full-time staff, it received 48 complaints, reviewed hundreds of financial disclosure statements and administered lobbyist registrations and terminations.
Legislative Priorities
Lilly said the board reached a major milestone this month: The council approved legislation allowing the board to pursue ethics violations by any current or former public employee or officer up to six years after the alleged misconduct occurred. In cases in which misconduct was fraudulently concealed, the legislation grants the board jurisdiction for up to six years after the violation was or reasonably should have been discovered.
“Until now, if a person left public employment, we lost jurisdiction over them. We had three recent examples where there was an ethics complaint that we would have pursued, but it got dismissed because the person was no longer employed by the county,” Lilly said, adding that he was not able to disclose specific details about those examples. 
The statute of limitations to investigate ethics violations had previously been one year after the potential violation occurred, Akitake said.
The bill had been in the works for years, Lilly and Akitake said, and the final version was the result of extensive board deliberation, research and discussion with council members.
The council is currently reviewing the board’s proposed changes to rules for lobbyists, which have been developed over the past year with guidance from the executive director of the Hawaiʻi State Ethics Commission. 
Akitake said Maui is the only county in Hawaiʻi that does not have comprehensive rules for lobbyists, and its existing lobbyist registration system is outdated and difficult to use. The existing framework lacks clear registration standards, and it does not require periodic expenditure reporting. 
“It will be such an achievement to fill that hole, that puka,” she said, adding that the council has already approved the first reading of the lobbyist legislation, and the second and final reading is expected next month. 
Council Member Kauanoe Batangan, who chairs the council’s Government, Ethics and Transparency Committee, has taken an interest in some of the Board of Ethic’s initiatives. (Erin Nolan/Civil Beat/2026) Erin Nolan/Civil Beat/2026
Council members have also begun to discuss the board’s proposal for a countywide anti-nepotism policy, guidance which already exists in Honolulu and Hawaiʻi counties, according to Akitake. 
Akitake and other ethics employees drafted the proposed nepotism bill after meeting with the state ethics commission’s enforcement director, Kee Campbell.
“He researched nepotism across the country to look at best practices and to inform the state’s rule,” Akitake said. “That was really helpful for us.”
She added that the new rules are not intended to be a prohibition on hiring friends and family to work for the government, but rather an assurance that hiring, supervision and employment decisions are based on an individual’s qualifications and abilities.
Expanded ethics training is critical to making current and proposed policies effective and is one of the achievements of the last year that Lilly and Akitake both pointed to.
“It’s as important for the public employees to know the ethics laws,” Lilly said, “as it is for the public to know that we are on top of them, and that we’re carrying out our mandate.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC list that recognizes 10 ‘angels’ also aims to help donors give smartly
description: The secretary of state’s office released its annual list ahead of the holiday giving season of 10 “angel” charities.
text:
Prepared boxes cover the floor of a food pantry in Auburn, Maine. The Sandalwood Community Food Pantry of Hilton Head Island is among 10 South Carolina charities recognized this year by the secretary of state's office. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/ Maine Morning Star)COLUMBIA — A river conservancy, horse rescue farm and veterans’ support network are among the 10 South Carolina charities recognized as “angels” in this year’s list from the secretary of state’s office. 
The program, started in 1998, annually promotes charities that spend at least 80% of their funding on their charitable cause, effectively use volunteers and don’t rely significantly on government grants. Other eligibility criteria include operating for at least three years and adhering to state laws governing charities. 
The goal, Secretary of State Mark Hammond said, is to help donors know where their money is going. 
“It’s our job to inform our charitable donors so that they will make wise charitable decisions when they decide to donate to these organizations,” Hammond, who was just reelected to a seventh term, told the SC Daily Gazette. “We like to pick 10 charities from the state and recognize them for the good work that they do, and this is also part of our public service announcement during the holiday season because we know that that’s a time of giving.” 
The secretary of state’s office has several programs to help people choose charities. The office runs an app called Give Smart SC. Its website also includes a search feature to look up charities and how much they’re giving to their cause. 
This year, Hammond said, three of the angel charities were nominated by community members: Sandalwood Community Food Pantry of Hilton Head Island, Equine Rescue of Aiken and Camp Canaan, which operates on a 100-acre island of the Catawba River in York County. The other seven were picked by people in his office. 
The following lists the 2026 angel charities, with the percentage of their spending that goes to their charitable cause: 

Backpack Buddies Seabrook Island, 90.5%
Camp Canaan of Rock Hill, 90.9%
Chattooga Conservancy, Inc. of Oconee County, 80.9%
Equine Rescue of Aiken, 87.7%
Freshwater Coast Community Foundation of Abbeville, 99.6%
Helping Florence Flourish, 89.8%
Midlands Special Needs Foundation of Lexington, 96.7%
Patriot Housing Project (Tri-County Veterans Support Network) of Summerville, 95.2%
Samaritan Health Clinic of Pickens County of Easley, 89.3%
Sandalwood Community Food Pantry of Hilton Head Island, 88.2%

South Carolinians receiving phone calls from people soliciting donations, Hammond said, should ask callers whether they’re professional fundraisers, what percentage of their donation goes to the charitable cause and if they’re complying with the state’s Solicitation of Charitable Funds Act. 
Professional fundraisers must register with the state, so the chunk they keep for payment is public. That amount can be significant. It can reach 85 cents of every dollar they raise, Hammond said. By law, the callers must disclose that they’re professional fundraisers when asked. 
Nonprofits can keep overhead and fundraising costs low by using volunteers, Hammond said.
To comply with the Solicitation of Charitable Funds Act, nonprofits must register with the state and keep their information updated. That includes submitting forms used to determine what percentage they spend on their reported purpose. 
The guidelines and mandates aren’t about punishing nonprofits, Hammond said, but rather informing donors.  
“We want to make sure that our donors get the best bang for their buck, give from the heart, and please give smart,” Hammond said.
