title: Read President Abraham Lincoln’s proclamation upon declaring a national day of Thanksgiving
description: Editor’s note: At the urging of magazine editor Sarah Josepha Hale, President Abraham Lincoln declared an annual national holiday of Thanksgiving in 1863. Most remarkably, Lincoln made his proclamation at the height of the bloodiest war in American history. Bit of trivia: The text was written by Secretary of State William Seward. Here’s the proclamation:  […[...]
text:
Abraham Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C.Editor’s note: At the urging of magazine editor Sarah Josepha Hale, President Abraham Lincoln declared an annual national holiday of Thanksgiving in 1863. Most remarkably, Lincoln made his proclamation at the height of the bloodiest war in American history. Bit of trivia: The text was written by Secretary of State William Seward. Here’s the proclamation: 
The year that is drawing towards its close, has been filled with the blessings of fruitful fields and healthful skies. To these bounties, which are so constantly enjoyed that we are prone to forget the source from which they come, others have been added, which are of so extraordinary a nature, that they cannot fail to penetrate and soften even the heart which is habitually insensible to the ever watchful providence of Almighty God. 
In the midst of a civil war of unequalled magnitude and severity, which has sometimes seemed to foreign States to invite and to provoke their aggression, peace has been preserved with all nations, order has been maintained, the laws have been respected and obeyed, and harmony has prevailed everywhere except in the theatre of military conflict; while that theatre has been greatly contracted by the advancing armies and navies of the Union. 
Needful diversions of wealth and of strength from the fields of peaceful industry to the national defence, have not arrested the plough, the shuttle or the ship; the axe has enlarged the borders of our settlements, and the mines, as well of iron and coal as of the precious metals, have yielded even more abundantly than heretofore. Population has steadily increased, notwithstanding the waste that has been made in the camp, the siege and the battle-field; and the country, rejoicing in the consciousness of augmented strength and vigor, is permitted to expect continuance of years with large increase of freedom. 
No human counsel hath devised nor hath any mortal hand worked out these great things. They are the gracious gifts of the Most High God, who, while dealing with us in anger for our sins, hath nevertheless remembered mercy. 
It has seemed to me fit and proper that they should be solemnly, reverently and gratefully acknowledged as with one heart and one voice by the whole American People. 
I do therefore invite my fellow citizens in every part of the United States, and also those who are at sea and those who are sojourning in foreign lands, to set apart and observe the last Thursday of November next, as a day of Thanksgiving and Praise to our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the Heavens. 
And I recommend to them that while offering up the ascriptions justly due to Him for such singular deliverances and blessings, they do also, with humble penitence for our national perverseness and disobedience, commend to His tender care all those who have become widows, orphans, mourners or sufferers in the lamentable civil strife in which we are unavoidably engaged, and fervently implore the interposition of the Almighty Hand to heal the wounds of the nation and to restore it as soon as may be consistent with the Divine purposes to the full enjoyment of peace, harmony, tranquillity and Union.
In testimony whereof, I have hereunto set my hand and caused the Seal of the United States to be affixed.
Done at the City of Washington, this Third day of October, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three, and of the Independence of the United States the Eighty-eighth.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Colom once displayed leadership, as well as grit and tenacity, on the Millsaps College basketball team
description: Scott Colom, right, played basketball for Millsaps College during the 2003-04 season.
text:
Twenty-five years ago John Stroud, the Ole Miss basketball great and former NBA player, recruited Scott Colom to Millsaps College and coached him during Stroud’s last two seasons at the Jackson school.
Rick Cleveland
Colom went on to earn a law degree and become a district attorney in four counties. He won a U.S. Senate election in Mississippi this month, unseating Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.
I asked Stroud, who now works in private business in New Albany, what he thought back then Colom would wind up doing later in life.
“Well, my first guess wouldn’t have been United States senator,” Stroud answered. “But I knew he would be successful. I knew he was really, really intelligent, and I knew he was a leader. I knew he was a people person. Scott will talk to anybody about anything. I knew for sure he would make something of himself.”
Stroud will tell you up front young Scott Colom was not a great basketball player, even at the NCAA Division III level. He was a back-up point guard, better at guarding on defense and setting up the offense than at scoring points himself. 
Scott Colom, right, plays in a Millsaps College basketball game during the 2003-04 season. Credit: Courtesy of Millsaps College
“What I most remember about Scott is that when I would come into the locker room before a game to talk to the team, Scott was already talking to them, already coaching them about what we needed to do to win,” Stroud said. “When I say he was a leader, he really was. He was an enthusiastic leader. I believe he’ll be a great senator.”
Colom came to Millsaps from Columbus, where his parents were lawyers and one of his best friends was Thomas Adams, a doctor’s son who was two years older and already at Millsaps. Thomas Adams was a four-year starter and star, now a member of the Millsaps Athletics Hall of Fame.
Thomas Adams Credit: Madison Public Schools
Says Adams, now the principal at Madison Middle School, “Our families were close. We spent a lot of time together growing up. We played together, went to church together. Either I would spend the night at their house or Scott and Andrew (Scott Colom’s twin brother) would spend the night at our house.”
While Andrew chose to attend Ivy League Columbia, Scott picked Millsaps, at least in part to play basketball with Adams.
“I remember Scott and his family would drive down to our games to watch Thomas play,” Stroud said. “They had played together in high school. Scott could have gone to college anywhere because of his academics, and in his family, academics came first, but Millsaps gave him a chance to do both.”
Asked to describe Colom as a player, Adams responded, “He was always so competitive. He’d scrap and claw to make the team better. He was all about the team.”
When Stroud left Millsaps for private business, Tim Wise, who had played at Millsaps and was the school’s all-time assists leader, was elevated from assistant to head coach. Wise remembers Colom, as a smart, strong, physical guard, “who played a lot that first year I was the head coach.”
“Scott was a team player, the kind that who get a group of guys going in the right direction,” Wise said. “He was a great encourager, the kind of guy who makes the guys around him better.”
Colom decided not to play his senior year of eligibility, opting to concentrate fully on academics to prepare for law school. He eventually landed at the University of Wisconsin, where he flourished. But, says Wise, “I always thought he would come back to Mississippi and made a difference, which he has.”
John Stroud
Stroud and Colom remain good friends and talk often. Even so, Stroud says, he marveled at Colom’s successful campaign. 
“I mean the president of the United States comes down to campaign for his opponent, and Scott goes to the event and walks down the line of people waiting to get in, shaking hands and greeting folks,” Stroud says. “Who else does that? But if you know Scott Colom, you’re not surprised.”
Adams, his childhood friend and former teammate, certainly was not surprised.
“Scott has taken the same mindset he had on the basketball floor into the political arena. He’s always been a competitor,” Adams said. “When he got in the race, I thought he was a long shot, but I went to some of his campaign events and saw how he connected with people, how hard he worked. He just wasn’t going to be denied.”
Wise joked that Colom’s election gives Stroud a unique status.
“I told John not many people can say what he can,” Wise said. “He coached a senator in Scott. There are only a hundred of those. A few years before, he coached Tate Reeves, the governor. There are only 50 of those. He coached two of 150. I wonder how many coaches there are in America who can say that. Not many, I suspect.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri prepares for SNAP purchase restrictions as court battles continue
description: Missouri plans to give nearly 5,000 retailers a list of candy, sugary drinks and desserts that shoppers will no longer be able to purchase with federal food benefits starting Feb. 15. But grocers worry the list could quickly become outdated as products change. To create the list, the Missouri Department of Social Services has received […]
text:
The restrictions planned for Feb. 15 will impact the almost 5,000 retailers who are authorized to accept SNAP benefits in Missouri (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).Missouri plans to give nearly 5,000 retailers a list of candy, sugary drinks and desserts that shoppers will no longer be able to purchase with federal food benefits starting Feb. 15. But grocers worry the list could quickly become outdated as products change.
To create the list, the Missouri Department of Social Services has received permission to forgo competitive bidding and make a one-time purchase of a Missouri-specific product database from global market research firm NielsenIQ.
The restrictions, approved by the federal government at the state’s request last year, will prohibit purchases of candy, prepackaged, shelf-stable desserts, sugary beverages and energy drinks through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. They will also apply to a program called SUN Bucks that gives families of eligible children a one-time benefit of $120 to buy groceries during the summer.
The list is intended to help almost 5,000 SNAP retailers statewide implement the changes consistently, according to the department’s single feasible source purchase notice.
“Without this centralized procurement, approximately 4,944 SNAP-authorized Missouri retailers would each need to independently acquire the data, risking inconsistent implementation and federal noncompliance penalties,” according to the department posting. 
But the Missouri Grocers Association, which advocates for the state’s grocery industry, says that unless the department provides regular updates to the list, retailers will struggle to implement SNAP restrictions uniformly as product formulations change and manufacturers release new products. 
Dan Shaul, the association’s executive director, told The Independent he also worries retailers will be punished for inconsistencies that will be difficult to avoid.
“Yes, we’ll go ahead and program that list in,” Shaul said. “But then how do we make changes as our products change? I don’t think people understand the depth of product changes or (Universal Product Code) changes from retailer to retailer. Those things change constantly.” 
Missouri’s plans are unfolding against the backdrop of federal court battles over the legality of SNAP restrictions in 23 states where the U.S. Department of Agriculture has approved waivers. 
A class action lawsuit filed Nov. 18 and led by the National Center for Law and Economic Justice seeks to strike down proposed and current SNAP restrictions in 18 states, including Missouri, arguing federal officials lacked authority to use waivers to undertake such large-scale change to SNAP. 
The lawsuit builds on the center’s ongoing legal challenge of SNAP restrictions in the five other states where USDA approved waivers. A judge blocked  those waivers, in Colorado, Iowa, Tennessee and West Virginia in June, though the USDA has appealed the decision. 
Missouri’s updated waiver, approved by USDA in June, defines candy as products that combine sugar or artificial sweeteners with “chocolate, fruit, nuts, caramels, gummies and hard candies…in the form of bars, drops or pieces.” The definition excludes items that contain flour or require refrigeration.
The waiver prohibits the use of SNAP benefits to purchase energy drinks, as well as “soda, juice, punch and tea,” which are defined as containing more than 10 grams of sugar per serving or 50% or less of vegetable or fruit juice. But SNAP participants can use benefits to buy beverages containing milk and sports drinks marketed to increase hydration.
The waiver’s ban on SNAP purchases of pre-packaged, ready-to-eat desserts does not include items baked fresh in grocery stores that aren’t considered shelf-stable.
To qualify for SNAP, Missourians can earn a gross income of no more than 130% of the federal poverty level, or $41,796 per year for a family of four before taxes and other deductions.
As researchers study the impacts of SNAP restrictions, the effectiveness of the waivers at improving nutrition remains unclear.
Kate Bauer, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Michigan School of Public Health, told The Independent that while studies conducted before the first waivers took effect showed little impact on participants’ diets — suggesting people used resources besides their benefits to buy restricted products — more recent research suggests SNAP restrictions can decrease purchases of sugary drinks.
Bauer said she worries SNAP restrictions will heighten existing stigma against people who use food benefits.
“A big concern for me is that with these restrictions and really a lot of confusion over what foods and beverages are eligible, that stigma would increase,” Bauer said.
 A “good day one list”

Shaul said several other states are using product lists from NielsenIQ and that “it’ll be a very good day one list.”
But, he said, “my responsibility now is to try to find (retailers) tools beyond the day one list that will allow them to comply” with the coming SNAP changes.
In an email to The Independent, Baylee Watts, the department’s media director, said the department could not disclose the cost of the contract because procurement is still underway.
But Watts said “requiring each store to independently license and maintain this product data would cost Missouri retailers an estimated aggregate of more than $7.4 million — and that figure excludes additional fees for larger retailers.”
The department’s single feasible source posting also indicates that because of the “urgent federal implementation timeline,” a competitive request for proposals would have been “impractical and detrimental to compliance efforts.”
The department applied for federal permission to restrict SNAP purchases at the behest of Gov. Mike Kehoe in a September 2025 executive order. The department postponed the original start date of Oct. 1, 2026, to better support Missouri retailers, Kehoe said in a June press release. Retailers had warned they needed clearer guidance to enforce the new restrictions.
Watts said the list the department plans to provide “is designed to eliminate guesswork.”
“Rather than requiring individual store owners to manually audit tens of thousands of inventory items, this standardized electronic dataset allows retailers and their point-of-sale (POS) software providers to perform direct, batch updates across their systems,” Watts said.
Shaul said the association is searching for a solution that would provide a dynamic list, so that product changes won’t require manual updates to retailers’ systems.
The definitions in Missouri’s SNAP waiver, Shaul said, are “up for interpretation.
“I would hope that the department would interpret it the exact same way as every retailer in the state that has SNAP,” Shaul said. “That is not going to happen.
 Fundamental changes

Neither of the two Missourians named in the class action lawsuit filed Nov.18 have funds other than their SNAP benefits to purchase food, according to court documents.
Nicole Noblet, of Kansas City, has celiac disease, gastroparesis and, her doctor suspects, hypoglycemia. Her conditions make it difficult for her body to absorb sugar from solid foods, so she uses soda or energy drinks to raise her blood sugar. 
Gerard Rogers, of Springfield, has diabetes and sometimes uses candy bars to manage low blood sugar, according to the lawsuit.
Katharine Deabler-Meadows, a senior attorney working on the lawsuit, told The Independent many SNAP participants don’t have other resources they can reallocate to buy items restricted by state waivers.
“Probably the simplest and most classic example that we’ve run across as we’re talking to people about these waivers is a person who is diabetic who relies on soda or candy to manage blood sugar crashes when they’re working or running errands or caring for their children,” Deabler-Meadows said. “…They’re going to have to choose: Do I manage my chronic health condition, or do I not buy something else that my household needs?”
Deabler-Meadows said throughout the history of SNAP, USDA’s definition of SNAP-eligible food has matched the definition in the federal Food and Nutrition Act and has been consistent across states. 
Changing this definition of food through federal regulations — and making different changes in different states — is “a fundamental change to the way this program works” and a “backdoor method to restrict access to SNAP,” Deabler-Meadows said.
“This is not the sort of change that can or should be done by an administrative agency through the waiver process,” she said. “This should be done via open debate in Congress.”
 Getting on the same page

Bauer said research shows programs that incentivize purchases of healthy food can improve the quality of people’s diets.
She gave the example of Double Up Food Bucks, which allows SNAP participants to get twice as much fresh produce when they use their benefits to buy fruits and vegetables.
“People want to eat healthy, and they want to feed their kids fruits and vegetables,” Bauer said. “They know what’s healthy. That’s not the limiting factor. The limiting factor is the amount of money they have.”
Bauer also pointed to difficulties retailers could face implementing SNAP restrictions. One recent study shows that since states began implementing the waivers this year, slightly fewer convenience stores are accepting SNAP benefits.
Shaul said he wants to make sure grocers making a good-faith effort to comply with the coming SNAP restrictions don’t get penalized for noncompliance.
“We’re going to continue to work with the department to try to get to a point where everybody is in the same — I won’t even say the same page, but the same book,” Shaul said. “I’d love to be in the same chapter.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Commentary: The real story behind that Thanksgiving turkey that prompted the Kentucky Capitol haz-mat response
description: Frankfort’s small army of state workers, fresh from four days off for Thanksgiving on Dec. 1, 1997, slipped from their cars in normal morning sun and almost as one looked to the sky with twisted, stricken faces. The Capitol Annex parking lot seemed misted with some indelible flesh-rot that despised humankind. It wasn’t just a […]
text:
This is not the maintenance worker who responded to an unusual post-Thanksgiving emergency outside the Kentucky Capitol Annex. That incident went unphotographed, as far as we know, though not forgotten. (Getty Images)Frankfort’s small army of state workers, fresh from four days off for Thanksgiving on Dec. 1, 1997, slipped from their cars in normal morning sun and almost as one looked to the sky with twisted, stricken faces.
The Capitol Annex parking lot seemed misted with some indelible flesh-rot that despised humankind. It wasn’t just a smell but a Presence. It sucked life from you; your soul departed and you knew it would not return. Your eyes glazed toward opaque. You could not breathe but for shallow, burning gasps that presaged death rattle.
Of all possible causes, you wouldn’t at this moment imagine a turkey.
Yet. Over there, 30 feet yonder, a maintenance lad in a white haz-mat suit with a stout black bag and a muscular garbage picker crept toward a thing on the Annex lawn. It looked like a yellowed stew of plastic and flesh. It seemed to glow and quiver. Some brave parking-lot sufferer managed to croak out toward the creeping lad, “Dear God, son … What … Why?”
“Some a-hole threw a turkey on the lawn,” the lad said, in a voice that echoed death. It was a sentence as final and direct as, “They launched the nuclear missiles.”
When he’d kissed his wife goodbye that morning, the young man had no clue what this day would bring. He was about to be a hero. He retrieved the turkey. He lost his sense of smell. “Like starin’ at the Sun and goin’ blind,” he told the Workers Comp Board weeks later, I heard. It was a metaphor nailed down tight.
So this is a story I’ve been badgered to tell since then. It started when Rep. Jim Callahan of Southgate gave me a Thanksgiving turkey.
Jim was House Democratic Caucus chairman. In the happy event he liked you, you could have no finer friend in the stinging spin-drift of the Kentucky legislature. If he didn’t, he was one of the few people who could and would get you fired. A man to be trusted and feared. A perfect politician.
I had just lately and reluctantly been put in charge of the Legislative Research Commission’s Public Information Office, a communications shop whose future was in doubt because of some early Republican restiveness. They didn’t find the office deferential enough. It likely wasn’t.
I made it my strategic purpose in life to become indispensable to Jim, so he (and the House Dems, then lazy with a comfortable majority) would protect me against the new restive Republican hordes. I succeeded with Jim, the caucus obeyed his instructions re: me, and in late 1997 Jim started rewarding me for my many good works with appreciated tokens like holiday meats.
The day before this particular Thanksgiving — five days before the maintenance lad’s heroics — Jim’s lanky assistant presented me with my first turkey, laid the sweaty sucker on my desk, bagged in plastic, pristine, frozen and promptly forgotten.
Forgotten, that is to say, in my windowless, steam-heated office, 80 degrees at least, with four black holidays awaiting it and a billion turkey-flesh bacteria awakening to yawn, scratch themselves, and eat.
Flash forward: 9:27 p.m., Payton Residence, Louisville. Sat. Nov. 29.
Quick scene:
“Aw, MAN! NO!”
“What?”
“I forgot the damn TURKEY!”
“What turkey?”
“The one Jim C. gave me three days ago that’s sitting on my desk like a bomb about to explode, if it hasn’t already! I have to get it.’
(Indistinct squabbling).
Even quicker scene:
“You’re not driving a hundred miles round-trip to Frankfort in the dead of night to retrieve a turkey that’s wrapped in plastic and perfectly fine. No.”
Note to young husbands: There are many days coming in your marriage when you simply look at your wife’s slant eyes and surrender. I surrendered. Fifty miles east, the turkey-flesh bacteria ate and ate.
The rest of the weekend was like waiting for biopsy results. Monday morning I drove to work early, dreading what I’d find, hoping against hope the turkey hadn’t exploded but otherwise wanting to get things cleaned up and tended to as best I could before anyone else arrived. Pretty sure I was first in the parking lot slammed by the Presence, the living thing I’d birthed.
The Kentucky Capitol and Annex are in the author’s hometown of Frankfort along the Kentucky River. (University of Kentucky Libraries, Special Collections Research Center, Post Card Collection)
But hope withstood its first assault. As a Frankfort native, I was accustomed to its distilleries, specifically the smell of its distilleries burning mash. The signature smell of the Kentucky River valley. In many ways, Frankfort is a smell. It’s not necessarily a good smell; many find it rank. But all share in it. Every redneck boy, every doctor’s son, every lawyer’s daughter and governor’s privileged kid walks out on fall mornings into its egalitarian embrace. It is hillbilly Marxism: Share the stink.
So for no more than half a second I thought/hoped this stink might be mash. For the second half-second I thought, “Whew, did they throw some rotting sheep cadavers into the mash vats this morning?” Then of course I knew: Turkey. Hissing from my office. Into the Annex HVAC system. Leaking out the old building’s windows. Filling the river valley. Soon to make me the laughing stock of Frankfort. Republicans would say this proved my liberalism.
I try to be relatively accurate in memoirish accounts like this (facts are critically important until they interfere with a good laugh). So I’ll admit the next half hour is a blur that resists disinterment.
The grotesque bird was still on my desk, its plastic bag ripped open by the force of its eruption. I recall an echoey dripping sound onto the floor, a yellowish oozing slime, thick like molasses, that seemed alive itself (remember, it teemed with a billion chomping necrobiomes). It looked like some bad special-effects alien from the first season of Star Trek in 1966.
I cannot remember how I managed to scoop up the carcass itself, make some quick impossible decision about disposing of it, and rush it down the still-deserted Annex hall to the bronze entry doors, where I flung it mightily onto the front lawn and the Presence began spreading in earnest, as did its legend.
At some point the heroic haz-mat kid was called, he gave the remains their final scoop, yet the smell snaked through the Capitol campus (HVAC circulation and filters are eternal, and the river valley itself a thermal trap). Many workers went home for an extra day or two of Thanksgiving celebration. Every sentence at home began “You won’t believe…”
Me, I suffered the derision I deserved, and have at least once a year for 27 years been hectored into telling “Scott’s Turkey Story” to wildly laughing, knee-slapping audiences. I’ve hated it every time, knowing they’re not exactly laughing with me, and sworn for many years I’d “write it up” and just hand the sucker out at every such request.
So now I’ve done that. Here you are. Don’t ask again.
But.
Coda: There is more to the story, and it’s good, but it doesn’t belong to me. It belongs to a fellow Capitol staffer who worked a mysterious deskless job for people who seemed powerful. His name recalls that of a major world capital. He would “borrow” your desk without asking if he needed one. Jim Callahan gave him a turkey every year too.
This is a grand fellow, as all in politics must be, but a bit absent-minded, as most in politics are. To his credit though, and unlike me, he miraculously got his gifted bird to his car that afternoon. Threw it in the trunk. Promptly forgot it.
A week or so later, troubled by some mystery problem with the car — couldn’t quite put his finger on it, snap, snap! — he dropped it off at the repair shop.
From memory:
FRANKFORT STATE JOURNAL
Police Reports 12/8/97
Police responded at 8:19 a.m. to call from Willie and Joe’s Auto Service on East Main of a suspected dead body, decomposed in trunk of customer’s vehicle. Officers opened trunk, discovered turkey.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Cost of Thanksgiving dinner went up 6% from last year
description: A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people costs on average $58.63 in 2026, which is a 6% increase from the cost in 2025, according to the annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation.  The biggest cost increase from 2025 to 2026: turkey. The Thanksgiving centerpiece was 10% more expensive, according to the grocery shopping survey, […]
text:
The cost of a Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people increased 6% in 2026 according to an annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people costs on average $58.63 in 2026, which is a 6% increase from the cost in 2025, according to the annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation. 
The biggest cost increase from 2025 to 2026: turkey. The Thanksgiving centerpiece was 10% more expensive, according to the grocery shopping survey, with an average price of $23.68 per 16-pound bird in 2026. 
Farm Bureau reported the cost of the meal is nearly $3.50 higher than 2025’s meal — but in inflation-adjusted figures, that’s a difference of about 38 cents, or a 2% increase. Last year’s Thanksgiving meal was also the lowest cost, according to the survey, since 2022. The 2026 average cost is similar to the cost of the meal in 2024. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to Gov. Kim Reynolds’ turkey pardoning proclamation, Iowa is seventh in the nation for turkey production, raising about 12 million turkeys annually. 
The Farm Bureau report said strong demand for turkey and tight inventories have led to increased prices for turkey in 2026. U.S. Department of Agriculture outlooks from October predicted turkey prices will continue to increase in 2027 and showed an increase in turkey production in 2026 compared to the year prior. 
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig read a proclamation from Gov. Kim Reynolds pardoning Early and Bird. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The highly pathogenic avian influenza continues to impact the turkey industry. While Iowa has had fewer than 10 cases in 2026, a Sac County commercial turkey flock of about 44,400 birds had a case of bird flu at the end of October. The virus impacts poultry production and supply, but turkey and chicken products remain safe to consume. 
Reporting from Stateline noted that labor shortages caused by changes to immigration policy also contribute to higher turkey prices. 
Turkey wasn’t the only item on the menu that increased in price this year. Boneless ham, milk, dinner rolls, sweet potatoes, russet potatoes, frozen peas, frozen green beans, cranberries and cubed stuffing also went up this year from last year.
Farm Bureau said there are myriad factors driving price increases that “aren’t a complete surprise.” Higher input costs including diesel fuel, fertilizers and labor make food production more expensive. 
A regional analysis of Thanksgiving meal prices show feasters on the East Coast will pay the highest price for their meal, with an average cost of $61.57 for the 10-person meal. Midwesterners will shell out $56.89 for the meal, which was more expensive than shoppers in the South, but slightly cheaper than Western states. 
The cost of vegetable trays and frozen pie crusts declined in 2026 compared to 2025, according to Farm Bureau. Heavy whipping cream also decreased from the year prior. 
Farmers receive a relatively small share of the food dollar, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The latest data showed farmers make, on average, just under 13 cents per dollar spent by U.S. consumers on domestically produced food.
Farm Bureau said this means when consumers pay higher prices at the grocery store, it might translate into higher revenues on farms but they can be “quickly offset” by mounting production costs. 
A National Farmers Union analysis of the farmer share of the dollar shows farmers receive less than 10 cents per consumer dollar spent on Thanksgiving foods like turkey, sweet corn, stuffing and dinner rolls. 
National Farmers Union President Rob Larew said in a statement that the consumer price only tells “part of the story.”
“But higher grocery prices don’t mean farmers are earning more,” Larew said. “When a handful of powerful companies dominate agricultural and food markets, farmers and families are left with fewer choices and less power. We need a fairer food system that works better for everyone.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Health insurers are dropping Idaho Medicare Advantage plans that cover tens of thousands
description: Nearly a third of Idaho seniors who have private Medicare coverage are set to lose those health insurance plans next year. More than 60,000 Idahoans are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans that are set to be canceled statewide or in their county, according to federal data analyzed by Idaho health insurance brokers.  With a week […]
text:
With a week and a half left in Medicare open enrollment, insurance brokers are encouraging Idaho seniors to read mailed notices from their insurer to understand if their plan is being canceled, and reach out for help. (Photo by Getty Images)Nearly a third of Idaho seniors who have private Medicare coverage are set to lose those health insurance plans next year.
More than 60,000 Idahoans are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans that are set to be canceled statewide or in their county, according to federal data analyzed by Idaho health insurance brokers. 
Your Health Idaho is in open enrollment. Insurance premiums hikes might be tamped down.

With a week and a half left in Medicare open enrollment, insurance brokers are encouraging Idaho seniors to read mailed notices from their insurer to understand if their plan is being canceled, and reach out for help.
“It’s actually causing a lot of panic with seniors,” Coeur d’Alene based broker Malia Rogers said.
This year, she said seniors are navigating plan cancellations, trying to make sure their medical providers are still accepting their Medicare Advantage plan, and checking that their prescriptions are still covered.
“Don’t try to do it on your own, because there’s so many things … to watch out for,” Rogers said. “My recommendation is to find a broker. Brokers have a trained set of eyes, and we never charge for our services, so our services are free.”
Nearly half of the people who are on Medicare in Idaho are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, which tend to cover extra benefits than traditional Medicare. 
Some seniors are being hit harder by the cancellations because their Medicare Advantage plans were tailored to their needs. Marcia Benton, a broker in Meridian, said some people in North Idaho won’t be able to find comparable plans. Rural areas, she said, will also be hit hard. 
 If your Medicare Advantage plan is being terminated, what can you do?

Open enrollment for Medicare ends Dec. 7. 
In a statement last month, Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron encouraged Medicare members to tap free help from a licensed agent or a Medicare counselor with Senior Health Insurance Benefits Advisors, a state service available by phone at 1-800-247-4422 or online at https://doi.idaho.gov/shiba/about-shiba/ask-shiba/.
“While some carriers are exiting the market, Idaho still offers a competitive selection of plans and strong consumer protections,” Cameron said.
But if your Medicare Advantage plan is being terminated, you may be able to switch to another plan or traditional Medicare after through a special enrollment period.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Insurers haven’t seen federal pay rates keep up with inflation, broker says

State insurance officials say the scalebacks in Idaho and across the nation are caused by a mix of regulations, federal pay structures and rising costs. This is the second year of major Medicare Advantage cancellations in Idaho, but brokers say that less Idahoans are enrolled in plans being terminated this year than last year. 
Insurance carriers haven’t seen federal pay rates keep up with sharp medical inflation, Benton said. She called the Medicare Advantage market unstable and said plan closures can result in higher costs for consumers.
“But we do need to stop having these closures. Because moving mass amounts of people from plan to plan is not good for any carrier,” Benton said.
UnitedHealthcare is closing two Idaho plans, along with withdrawing from several counties across the state. About 16,500 Idaho seniors are enrolled in the plans affected. In a statement, a spokesperson for the insurer said its moves in Idaho are meant to “help ensure long-term sustainability of our plans.”
“UnitedHealthcare is making targeted changes to our Medicare Advantage offerings for 2027 to help ensure long-term sustainability of our plans,” the spokesperson said. “We are here to support members through any necessary transition and remain committed to helping everyone understand their options.”
Other health insurers that are canceling plans in Idaho could not be immediately reached for comment.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Auburn University Board of Trustees approves partial enrollment policy suspension
description: Auburn University will partially suspend its enrollment policy to allow a broader study of the school’s admission process.   Under Auburn’s enrollment policy, undergraduate enrollment must be “maintained at approximately 25,000 students,” and each incoming freshman class cannot exceed about 5,000 students. Alabama residents have to make up about 60% of each [...]
text:
A sign identifying Auburn University on the university's campus on August 14, 2023 in Auburn, Alabama. The Auburn University Board of Trustees voted on Nov. 20 to temporarily suspend enrollment policies that cap undergraduate enrollment and the total number of freshmen on campus. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)Auburn University will partially suspend its enrollment policy to allow a broader study of the school’s admission process.  
Under Auburn’s enrollment policy, undergraduate enrollment must be “maintained at approximately 25,000 students,” and each incoming freshman class cannot exceed about 5,000 students. Alabama residents have to make up about 60% of each freshman class; “qualified” undergraduate transfer students should be recruited; and prospective students should be encouraged to apply to Auburn University Montgomery if there is no space available on the main campus. 
The Auburn University Board of Trustees on Nov. 20 approved a resolution temporarily removing the caps on undergraduate enrollment and the total number of freshmen at the university. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
B.T. Roberts, an Auburn trustee and chair of the academic affairs committee, said the board “takes great pride” in the experience Auburn offers students and wants to protect it.
“As we respond to growing demand, we want our policies to help preserve what makes Auburn student experience so special,” he said.
The enrollment policy suspension will remain in place until an enrollment task force tasked with reviewing Auburn’s enrollment policies and guidelines – created by the Nov. 20 resolution – presents its findings to the trustees in February. 
The resolution said the task force will review the school’s enrollment policies and guidelines, “taking into consideration perspective provided by university students, administrators, faculty and alumni, and recommend such changes as may be appropriate to advance the university’s institutional priorities and preserve its exceptional student experience.”
Roberts said the task will recommend changes “that would advance the university’s institutional priorities.”
Auburn’s total enrollment rose from 35,172 in 2025 to 35,733 in the Fall 2026 semester, a 1.6% increase. Undergraduate enrollment went from 28,953 in the Fall 2025 semester to 29,693 in the Fall 2026 semester, an increase of 740 students (2.6%). 
Graduate and professional student enrollment at the university declined, going from 6,219 in 2025 to 6,040 in Fall 2026, a 2.9% decline.
It’s unclear if other universities in the state will act similarly. The University of Alabama reported 42,431 total students in the Fall 2026 semester, an increase of 71 students enrolled in Fall 2025. A message seeking comment was left with university officials Tuesday.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: S&P upgrades West Virginia bond rating
description: Standard and Poor’s has upgraded West Virginia’s bond rating for the first time in 15 years.  Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced the upgrade from AA- to AA, crediting the state’s tax cuts, fiscal discipline and $2 billion Rainy Day Fund for the move.  “We’re cutting taxes, living within our means, and laying the foundation for long-term […]
text:
The West Virginia State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)Standard and Poor’s has upgraded West Virginia’s bond rating for the first time in 15 years. 
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced the upgrade from AA- to AA, crediting the state’s tax cuts, fiscal discipline and $2 billion Rainy Day Fund for the move. 
“We’re cutting taxes, living within our means, and laying the foundation for long-term economic growth, and Wall Street is taking notice,” said Morrissey. “By maintaining fiscal discipline, protecting our reserves, and making smart investments that will grow our economy, we’re putting West Virginia on stronger financial footing. A higher credit rating means the potential for lower borrowing costs and more taxpayer dollars staying in West Virginia communities.”
Bond ratings affect the state by making it cheaper for the government to borrow money for infrastructure projects like roads. 
It’s like a credit rating a person might have when they go look for a car. Typically, people don’t have $30,000 on hand to buy the newest Toyota Camry, so they have to take out a loan and make payments. 
The state has to do the same for its roads and bridges. And like a car loan, the state has to also pay on interest for those projects. 
A higher bond rating means lower interest rates. 
But part of achieving that bond rating involves having reserves on hand in the form of the Rainy Day Fund, which hasn’t been tapped since 2017. That fund is a proverbial piggy bank that’s only to be cracked in case of emergencies. 
But what constitutes an emergency appears to be up to interpretation by state leaders.  
In 2025, Democratic lawmakers had proposed dipping into it to address flood preparation and recovery, but it was shot down. Floods killed 12 people in the state that year. 
This year, Democratic and Republican lawmakers proposed taking $250 million from the Rainy Day fund to address the water sanitation crisis in the southern part of the state. That proposal ultimately went nowhere.

title: El Niño is already scrambling your ski season
description: This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here. Being open for Thanksgiving has long been a goal for major ski resorts, including Sugarbush in Vermont. It had planned to have its lifts running and its slopes swarming by now. But with highs approaching 60 degrees Fahrenheit for much of […]
text:
A skier takes a run at Wolf Creek in Colorado last Sunday. (Photo by Kevin Bruce/Courtesy of Wolf Creek Ski Area)This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here.
Being open for Thanksgiving has long been a goal for major ski resorts, including Sugarbush in Vermont. It had planned to have its lifts running and its slopes swarming by now. But with highs approaching 60 degrees Fahrenheit for much of the past week, that hasn’t happened.
”It’s been a really warm November,” said John Bleh, director of communications at Sugarbush. “New snowmaking technology has helped a ton, but it’s not the ultimate cure-all.”
The popular destination is one of a slew throughout the East, from Sugarloaf in Maine to Snowshoe Mountain in West Virginia, that have had to delay opening due to unseasonably balmy conditions.
On the other side of the country, skiers in California are gloating. Resorts in the Lake Tahoe area received more than 4 feet of snow after a recent series of storms. The bounty was so generous that the Sierra Avalanche Center was warning of a “considerable” risk of slides and Kirkwood Mountain Resort opened nearly two weeks ahead of schedule. “It’s always exciting to get the season underway, but being able to open this early is a huge win,” Ricky Newberry, the resort’s general manager, said in a statement.
It’s a bit more complicated in the Rockies. Some resorts in Utah and Colorado got off to a slow start before recent storms brought snow, but Wolf Creek in the southern end of the state has opened all of its terrain.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
These wildly different starts to the ski season are a clear sign that the “super” or “Godzilla” El Niño, the strongest on record, is already shaping what could be a weird winter on the slopes.
El Niño occurs every three to five years when a band of unusually warm water forms off the coast of South America, altering weather patterns worldwide. The effects will vary widely: California is expected to be wetter than normal, the Northwest drier, and the Northeast wetter and warmer.
With El Niño’s impacts sticking around through March, the contrasts playing out at resorts right now may become more pronounced as winter settles in, said meteorologist Chris Tomer, who specializes in mountain and snow forecasting. “All roads run through the Sierra,” noted Tomer, referring to the Sierra Nevada mountain range. He expects the region’s resorts to receive 100 to 200 inches more snow than usual over the season. The Northeast will see its share of storms, but with temperatures expected to run warmer than normal, the question is whether that precipitation will fall as snow or rain.
“It’s a little off-putting at times,” said Bryan Rivard, who handles media relations at the trade group Ski Vermont. Still, he’s trying to remain optimistic. “If the weather comes, it could bring some pretty big stuff.”
In some ways, this year may be a repeat of 2015 and 2016, another “super” El Nino season that blessed the West and stressed the East. But as climate change accelerates warming patterns in general, the guarantee of skiable snow is increasingly difficult to come by even in normal years. That’s one reason that resorts have been investing millions of dollars in advanced snowmaking equipment.
“It’s enabling us to make snow in much tighter windows,” said Rivard. Modern snow guns and systems allow crews to work even when the temperatures dip for only a matter of hours. Bleh agrees that this has changed the dynamic considerably, but cautions against overreliance on the technology. “Every year we are making snowmaking upgrades,” he said. “But we need the temperatures to be able to do anything, and a long enough window to make it worth it.”
Those temperatures are set to arrive at Sugarbush this week, and the resort hopes to open by Thanksgiving or the day after. By then, some places in California will have seen nearly two weeks of skiing, an early glimpse of a winter that promises plenty of snow — just not where or when skiers might want it.
Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Commentary: Thanksgiving is perfect the way it is, thanks very much
description: You’ve probably heard the terrible news: Thanksgiving is an endangered holiday. Turkey Day is getting squeezed out by longer seasons for its big, noisy calendar neighbors Halloween and Christmas. That’s been the talk for decades. The late CBS curmudgeon Andy Rooney opined in 2002, “It ought to be against the law to start Christmas before […]
text:
Most Americans still celebrating Thanksgiving as a time for food and family. (Stock photo via Getty Images)You’ve probably heard the terrible news: Thanksgiving is an endangered holiday.
Turkey Day is getting squeezed out by longer seasons for its big, noisy calendar neighbors Halloween and Christmas.
That’s been the talk for decades.
The late CBS curmudgeon Andy Rooney opined in 2002, “It ought to be against the law to start Christmas before December.”
In the early 2000s and 2010s, people fretted that stores opened for holiday shopping on Thanksgiving Day — forcing employees to work on the holiday so retailers could squeeze a few extra bucks out of the biggest consumer season of the year.
The pandemic ended that. The stores moved their Black Friday deals online.
The big stores with actual buildings — Walmart, Costco, Home Depot, Target, Lowe’s, Best Buy and Kohl’s — are all closed this Thanksgiving.
Still, air raid sirens wail in anticipation of the great Thanksgiving apocalypse.
National Review pleaded, “Don’t let Thanksgiving be squeezed out of the calendar,” in November 2023. A year later, CBS News reported that “holiday creep starts even earlier this year.”
Last October, a lecturer in the business and economics department of Colorado College told The Denver Gazette: “Thanksgiving is a single-day event based around a meal with family and friends. It’s very home-centered and hasn’t been successfully experience-ized or productized.”
To quote the 20th-century philosopher Col. Sherman T. Potter: “Horse hockey.”
Thanksgiving is absolutely an experience. It need not be “ized” in any way, unless you’re talking about iodized salt to lightly sprinkle on your turkey.
Some 93% of Americans celebrated Thanksgiving in 2023, according to research by Collage Group, a market research firm. The participation was tied with Christmas for the most popular holiday of the year.
The seasons for Halloween and Christmas are undeniably lengthy. Hershey’s reported sales of Halloween candy in July and August increased 11% in 2025.
Nielsen, the TV ratings company, found holiday shopping advertising rose 11% this September compared with the previous year and was six times the airtime the same month in 2021.
Thanksgiving, like everything else in the country, has gotten caught in the culture wars crossfire, but not with any serious damage. A 2021 Economist/YouGov poll asked respondents about the holiday’s historical origins in European colonialism.
Some 49% said Pilgrims stole the land from Indigenous people, yet 53% planned to celebrate the holiday as normal. Just 5% wanted to abandon the holiday.
More than a quarter of those polled wanted more emphasis on American history during Thanksgiving.
Happy to oblige, but don’t expect a mythical tale of pious Pilgrims inviting their Indigenous neighbors over for a turkey dinner in 1621.
The real meeting had more in common with a diplomatic summit than modern Thanksgiving. Deer meat was the dish du jour, not turkey.
The Pilgrims and the Wampanoag leaders came together because they both needed each other.
About half the Mayflower passengers died during the first winter in modern-day Plymouth, Mass. The Wampanoag suffered catastrophic losses from an epidemic.
Both groups were vulnerable separately, but allied they would be stronger. The Wampanoag taught the Pilgrims farming.
The English brought firearms, which strengthened their alliance with the Wampanoag against competing tribes, particularly the Narragansett.
The alliance lasted about 50 years and ended in war and death the way so many stories of relations between colonists and Indigenous people do.
President George Washington first issued a Thanksgiving proclamation in 1789, but it was not related to the meeting between the Pilgrims and Wampanoag — and the first president did not make the event a formal national holiday.
The idea for Thanksgiving as a national holiday came from Sarah Josepha Hale.
Hale was the 19th-century version of a social media influencer. The New Hampshire widow supported her five children by becoming one of the most successful writers of the early 19th century, publishing poems and a novel before becoming a magazine editor.
Hale also wrote the popular children’s poem “Mary Had a Little Lamb.”
She used her platform as editor of Ladies’ Magazine and later Godey’s Lady’s Book to rally for a day of thanksgiving to strengthen national unity — it was not tied to the 1621 gathering.
She published editorials and wrote government officials and presidents for 36 years, until her message reached President Abraham Lincoln in September 1863.
Lincoln favored anything that would inspire unity amid the bloody Civil War. In 1863, he proclaimed a national Thanksgiving observance on the last Thursday in November.
Congress established the fourth Thursday in November as the permanent date for Thanksgiving in 1941, and President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the legislation into law.
Despite a complex and misunderstood history, Thanksgiving is as strong as ever and, contrary to the advertising and marketing wonks who would turn everything into a sale, Thanksgiving is perfectly sized at just one day.
Bakers and cooks might strongly disagree with the notion that Thanksgiving is just one day, but how it is widely celebrated is exactly right.
Thanksgiving is a pause between the garish bacchanalia of Halloween and the harried Christmas season.
American culture moves pedal-to-the-metal fast, from the endless scroll on our phones to the constant pressure to grow practically everything bigger, faster and stronger.
One day a year — Thanksgiving Day — we press pause. We gather with family and friends to enjoy a great meal, sit, talk and watch a football game or three.
We welcome newcomers to the family from newborns to significant others and spouses. And remember those no longer with us.
One day centered around food and fellowship is just enough time for us to recognize just how blessed we truly are.
The only Thanksgiving squeeze you need to worry about is the pressure on the top button of your trousers after that last slab of pumpkin pie.



				This column first appeared on Daniel P. Finney’s blog, The Paragraph Stacker on Substack.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Could a data center’s waste heat warm a North Carolina town?
description: In the Carolinas, Ohio, Texas, and many other states, Democrats routed incumbent Republicans in this month’s elections at least in part because voters fear an onslaught of AI data centers — the massive computer warehouses that threaten to suck up water supplies, increase climate and air pollution, and drive up energy costs. Voters didn’t just […]
text:
Data centers are energy-intensive, running servers around the clock to power streams of computer computations. (Image: Adobe Stock)In the Carolinas, Ohio, Texas, and many other states, Democrats routed incumbent Republicans in this month’s elections at least in part because voters fear an onslaught of AI data centers — the massive computer warehouses that threaten to suck up water supplies, increase climate and air pollution, and drive up energy costs.
Voters didn’t just take their anger out on politicians. In red and blue areas alike, they also approved dozens of ballot measures pausing or restricting data centers, adding to the over 450 moratoriums already in place across the country.
The backlash has left state and local leaders grappling with how to put guardrails on the facilities and ensure they benefit nearby communities.
A forthcoming deal between a data center and Enfield, North Carolina — an overwhelmingly poor, majority Black town of 2,000 — could offer a groundbreaking example of what such development might look like.
New group seeks to help US small towns lead the clean energy transition

For years, Enfield leaders and their allies have been working toward a clean energy vision that includes a solar farm to supply residents with power, a new substation to help distribute those renewable electrons, and a thermal energy network — a shallow form of geothermal that could replace inefficient water heating, space heating, and cooling. But they’ve faced a dearth of funding and fierce policy headwinds under President Donald Trump.
Then, this summer, Halifax County, where Enfield sits, announced it was selling property to Wyoming-based Quiet Data Centers, a land development firm, for a 100,000 square-foot facility. The industrial site is 2 miles outside the town but needs to tap into its wastewater systems.
For Enfield Mayor Mondale Robinson, that presented a bargaining opportunity. Now, he and top officials from Quiet are negotiating a community benefits agreement, a legally binding document that ties developers to certain benchmarks. Among other commitments, Robinson wants the company to fund the entire $16.2 million clean energy plan.
Duke University student Arka Solanki explains how a nearby data center could connect to a planned thermal energy network at a community event in Enfield, North Carolina, in September. (Photo by Elizabeth Ouzts/Canary Media)
What’s more, he wants the data center to join the thermal energy network, which could provide a surge of excess heat to meet the whole town’s needs. If the plans come to fruition, it would be the first time in the U.S. that a data center has connected to such a system.
Brendan Morris, Quiet’s chief development officer, confirmed to Canary Media that the discussions were ongoing and that all of Enfield’s aims were on the table. “I think things are possible,” he said. “We’re new to this community and new to the county. We look around and see how a new business and a new data center coming into the area can make a positive impact.”
Robinson, a self-proclaimed progressive, acknowledges that the midterms were a rebuke of the tech sector’s buildout. “Everybody should be against dirty data centers,” he said. But he believes the not-in-my-backyard approach has too often stuck communities like Enfield with polluting projects rejected by wealthier areas. That’s why he wants a data center that’s built sustainably and with community input. “There’s nothing progressive about saying we are against something, without saying what we are for,” he added.
A cheap, quiet option for cooling data centers
A year ago, Lancaster, Pennsylvania, became the first local government in the country to sign a community benefits agreement with a data center project, according to researchers at the World Resources Institute. The agreements have long been used for other types of developments, from manufacturing plants to solar farms, said Danielle Riedl, research associate at the nonprofit.
“But now, of course, the conversation — seemingly everywhere — is focused on data center development,” she said. Still, the agreements are no silver bullets. “You really want to see CBAs as one tool, together with zoning policies, development agreements, and other accountability mechanisms.”
In Halifax County, Quiet has pledged to mitigate some common data center complaints. At a public meeting this summer, the company said the 88-megawatt facility will plug into the Dominion Energy grid on its own dime and pay for all the electricity it needs, according to the local news outlet RRSpin. It will run backup generators for no more than 30 minutes a month, on average, unless there is an outage.
But the company also has to alleviate the immense heat generated by racks of computers inside the facility. And while Quiet has pledged to use closed-loop cooling — a less-water-intensive process than sending waste heat to cooling towers, where water then evaporates — the technology is expensive and noisy.
That’s where the thermal energy network comes in. The system is essentially a network of ground-source heat pumps. They’re analogous to air-source heat pumps, but move heat between the buildings and the earth rather than the outside air, thanks to a water-based solution that flows through a system of buried pipes.
Some data centers in Europe are already plugged into such systems as a way to release excess heat. The same technology could be used in Enfield, providing cooling without the noise and at less cost, said Eric Bosworth, a pioneer on utility-run thermal energy networks who runs his own consultancy called Thermal Energy Insights.
“It gives a layer of resiliency, and it’s going to save them money on cooling, too,” Bosworth said, referring to Quiet. “Every [unit] of heat that they send to the network is going to be cheaper than putting it up through their chillers.”

The nonprofit Enfield Energy Futures won a seed grant earlier this year to design the thermal energy network. But receiving funding from Quiet for the geothermal project — and the entire clean energy plan — would be game-changing.
A transparent, robust community benefits agreement with Quiet, said William Munn, Enfield Energy Futures executive director, would be “an incredible opportunity to take some of this unfettered wealth and set Enfield on course to take care of itself, make decisions for itself, and to be able to grow and sustain itself for the long term.”
The data center’s participation in the thermal energy network would be a boon in wintertime, when residents face extreme utility bills of $500 a month or more. During the region’s sweltering summers, Quiet’s excess heat could prove more challenging to handle.
“There’s no free lunch in physics,” Bosworth said. Solutions could include disconnecting the data center from the network or installing a technology called absorption chillers. “You’re essentially using a chemical reagent to produce cooling from waste heat. So, you could put in one of those systems and continue to harvest heat through the summer months, and benefit the network with cooling.”
Workers drill cores in Enfield, North Carolina, so that researchers can assess heat and soil properties for a thermal energy network. (Photo by Brian McAdoo)
As part of the seed grant, Brian McAdoo, associate professor at Duke University’s Nicholas School of the Environment, and his students have already been testing heat levels and soil properties to fine-tune specs for the network. Now, his team is also reworking the system plan for the potential addition of the data center.
“One possible way of getting rid of heat from a data center would be through groundwater,” McAdoo said. “Since we have so much water in the coastal plain sediments, if you put heat in one place, it can take that heat and move it.”
McAdoo will weigh all the options with Morris and the rest of the Quiet team. “We’re going to look at the plumbing. We’re going to look at the mechanical. We’re going to look at the heat that’s being produced,” Morris said. ?“Every climate is different. North Carolina is different than North Dakota, which is different than Helsinki. That’ll give us the parameters to go back to Enfield.”
The research and design work is time-consuming, part of why a final community benefits agreement, if it materializes, is likely still weeks, or even months, away.
“Rushing to get something on the books that is incomplete does a disservice to what the data center may be able to offer our community, but it also does a disservice to our residents,” Mayor Robinson said. “I don’t think any of us are living up to our full potential by signing agreements before things are completely understood.”
This story was originally published by Canary Media. It is republished here with permission.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia could pay up to $948M to fix busted PATH system; $332M already invested
description: Fixing West Virginia's busted online database for social services programs could cost up to $948 million. The costly fix comes after the state already spent $332.9 million in federal and state dollars on the PATH system, a massive online apparatus.
text:
The offices of the West Virginia departments of Health, Health Facilities and Human Services are located on Capitol Street in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)Fixing West Virginia’s busted online database for social services programs could cost up to $948 million. The costly fix comes after the state already spent $332.9 million in federal and state dollars on the PATH system, a massive online apparatus. 
The state is entering its 10th year of a contract with Optum, a Minnesota-based company, and the system still doesn’t work properly.
As Morrisey officials seek a new vendor to take over PATH, new documents show companies competing for that new contract estimate it could cost anywhere from $534 million to $948 million to build a new system that is crucial to programs that West Virginians use every day. 
Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell, speaks on the House of Delegates floor on Jan. 23, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“I’m very, very concerned about the numbers that have come forward,” said House Health Chair Evan Worrell, R-Cabell. “That’s over a 10-year contract, it’s still big numbers.”
PATH stands for People’s Access to Help, an online system that operates Medicaid, the foster care system, low-income assistance programs and more. It’s also where residents apply online for safety net programs. 
Over the last decade, there has been an exhaustive list of issues with the PATH system, including a disrupted workflow during the COVID-19 pandemic. 
Initiated in 2017 under Gov. Jim Justice, PATH launched four years later than expected in 2024. Now, with three years left on the contract, it still has issues processing data and delivering payments on time to vendors, including companies working with foster children.
Sen. Eric Tarr, R-Putnam, speaks on the Senate floor on Feb. 12, 2026. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“We paid an awful lot of money for a car we’ve never really got to drive,” said Sen. Eric Tarr, R-Putnam.”I’m not aware of any other states that I’ve seen in the media anywhere that are having these kinds of issues.”
Hundreds of millions of dollars in lives are at stake, Tarr said. 
Worrell stressed that fixing the system is critical.
“We owe it to the children of West Virginia to get this right because it is not working for anybody. Whether you’re an agency, legislator, government, anybody in government or any citizen, it is not working,” he said. “It is affecting everybody across the state, and it is affecting them in a negative way.”
The state is on the hook to give Optum another $36 million under the current contract with the company to continue PATH’s operation through 2027.
“DoHS is in the final year of the original contract the state signed with Optum in 2017,” said Angelica Hightower, communications specialist for the state Department of Human Services. “Most of the cost is paid with federal dollars. Of the $36.7 million operating cost, about $26.6 million is federal and about $10.1 million is state.”
“The contract also allows up to $4.25 million for changes and improvements. However, that money can only be spent if the department identifies and approves a specific change or improvement,” she said. 
According to public records, three companies have bid on taking over the PATH system: Deloitte, Infosys Public Services Inc and Optum. 
“PATH is how West Virginia families apply for SNAP, Medicaid and other benefits, and it has to keep running while the state chooses who will operate it next. The bids submitted for the next contract are under review, and state purchasing rules prevent us from discussing them until an award is made,” Highertower said. 
Worrell raised concerns that just two vendors alongside the current operator, Optum, bid on the project.
“I’m scared that it’s become so bad that that is why vendors have not bid on this (Request for Proposal), because they are worried that it can’t be fixed,” Worrell said.
“I don’t know how to go forward as a legislator, other than saying we are not going to commit monies for the next 10 years of that contract,” he continued. “I would like to kind of hold the line and say I’m willing to support funding for the next three years for a vendor to get it right and prove to us to get it right, then they will receive subsequent funding after that.” 
He also noted always-changing technology may be a reason to limit the timeframe of the contract. 
Tarr worried about the vendor transition impact since the program is used every day, and how that could play into the state’s decision with what vendor they’ll choose. It’s out of the hands of lawmakers. 
“I’m wondering what’s involved in the transition. Is PATH required to assist in that transition to a new contract, or is PATH done and they got to start building new? Because and if so, how are they preparing to flip that switch?” Tarr said. “There needs to be some sort of warm handoff, and I wonder how they’re planning to do that.”
An agency audit initiated by Gov. Patrick Morrisey earlier this year showed that the department could see $18.5 million in potential savings by addressing technology constraints and mainframe dependency related to PATH.

title: Commentary: West Virginia’s unfinished work: Finishing the economic dreams of Dr. Leon Sullivan, Walter Reuther
description: Dr. Leon Sullivan and Walter Reuther are two West Virginians worth knowing about. In the 1960’s and ’70s they blazed a path towards racial and labor justice — and now, we are losing the way.
text:
Civil rights Leaders hold hands as they lead a crowd of hundreds of thousands at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom in Washington D.C., on Aug. 28, 1963. Those in attendance include (front row, left to right): James Meredith and Martin Luther King, Jr.,  Roy Wilkins  light-colored suit), A. Phillip Randolph and Walther Reuther. (Photo by Express/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)Dr. Leon Sullivan and Walter Reuther are two West Virginians worth knowing about. In the 1960’s and ’70s they blazed a path towards racial and labor justice — and now, we are losing the way.
Here are the facts: Dr. Leon Sullivan was Black and Walter Reuther was white. Reuther grew up in Wheeling; Sullivan in Charleston. They were named West Virginian of the Year back-to-back. Sullivan in 1965; Reuther in 1966.
Sullivan became the first Black man appointed to the board of a top-tier U.S. corporation: General Motors in 1971. Sullivan decided that by joining he could, in the “short run and long run make things better for my people,” the New York Times reported in 1971.
He went on to be the architect of the Sullivan Principles and recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
The Sullivan Principles were business guidelines for companies to support human rights in apartheid South Africa. Some of the original principles included nondiscrimination, equal pay, integration and community development.
And Walter Reuther’s activism has overlapping racial and economic goals. And the two both catalyzed change through cars.
Reuther served as president of the United Auto Workers from 1946 until 1970 and marched alongside Dr. King in Selma, Alabama. He and his brother survived assasination attempts and risked their lives to fight for unions.
So what’s the status of unions now? Rocky. Between 1985 and 2025, West Virginia experienced the largest percentage-point drop in private-sector union membership of any U.S. state, writes the Center for Economic and Policy Research. It fell 16.7 percentage points from 22.2% to 5.5% in 2025. It’s staggering.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, across America, union membership fell from 20.1% in 1983 to 10% in 2025. Since then, there has been greater income inequality, lower bargaining power for workers and lost rights.
For the last 30 years, intense corporate opposition and threats, jobs shipped overseas and a dwindling manufacturing sector have contributed to the decline.
So what would Reuther and Sullivan have to say about it? First they’d have a little talk with Gov. Patrick Morrisey. They’d scrutinize his lofty job promises connected to data centers and AI computing, new natural gas power plants and defense technology.
They’d want to know: How many union jobs? What are the healthcare benefits? What percentage of jobs are guaranteed for West Virginians? Retirement security?
Equal access for women and people of color?
It absolutely matters. Because in these times, such concepts are far from guaranteed. The Trump administration is clawing back worker protections.
For example, the Trump administration ended affirmative action requirements for federal contractors that involved years of fighting for change. It revoked Executive Order 11246. This policy dated back to 1965 and was a requirement to promote equal opportunity for workers of color and women.
Trump also directed the Department of Labor to stop enforcing those workplace protection requirements and reporting. And companies are now no longer required to report racial and gender demographics, such as who is most represented in management positions.
Third, the Trump administration is taking active steps to undermine the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. This weakens tools to address workplace discrimination.
And, though attacked, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 still remains, as well as the equal pay act. Thank goodness. But let’s keep our eye on the ball to ensure it stays that way. Nothing is sacred anymore.
Because here’s the deal: West Virginia’s poverty proves that financial success is not always measured by the almighty dollar. It is measured by safe conditions, worker protections and if people of all types have access to opportunities in the workplace.
Sullivan and Reuther knew racial justice and economics are inextricably intertwined
and that both matter for America’s future.
The pair lead us far in union organizing and racial harmony, but who will take the baton?
The economic center cannot hold. And when conditions get bad — rock bottom — people finally rise up. We’ve had enough. The ghosts of Sullivan and Reuther are waiting.
