name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Longer lines, anxious people: SNAP changes are straining Kentucky food pantries
description: During the COVID-19 pandemic, Daryl Caldwell recalls receiving around $300 a month in food assistance.  Now, he’s down to $24.  When he got $300 — thanks to pandemic-era reimbursement increases — he didn’t need help from his local food bank in Louisville, he said.  Now, he’s getting a box every month from Exodus Family Ministries, […]
text:
Bags of potatoes in the Dare to Care food bank in Louisville, May 14, 2025. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd) During the COVID-19 pandemic, Daryl Caldwell recalls receiving around $300 a month in food assistance. 
Now, he’s down to $24. 
When he got $300 — thanks to pandemic-era reimbursement increases — he didn’t need help from his local food bank in Louisville, he said. 
Now, he’s getting a box every month from Exodus Family Ministries, he said, which includes items like juice, cereal, vegetables and powdered milk. 
“Same things I like, some I don’t,” he said. “So what I don’t use, I give to the needy, so somebody could use it.”  
Food banks are already struggling to keep up with the demand brought on by changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, more commonly referred to as SNAP, in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
Dare to Care president and CEO Vincent James said that while the government rose to meet the surge of hunger during COVID, it has not done so now as grocery prices, gas and energy costs rose this year. 
Vincent James, president and CEO of a Louisville-based food bank, says more people in the region are unsure where their next meal will come from. Flanked by anti-hunger advocates and religious leaders, he spoke in a Dare to Care warehouse, May 14, 2025. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)
“For the first time in Dare to Care’s history, we’ve exceeded 200,000 individuals in our service area that are experiencing food insecurity,” James said. “I think the drivers are what is affecting everyone: It’s the gas prices, it’s grocery prices, it’s the economy as a whole.” 
And food banks just can’t keep up with the increase in hungry people as around 80,000 Kentuckians have lost access to food benefits: He’s had to turn people away. As of September, James said Dare to Care has seen a 115% increase in demand for food this year.
“For those who are on the margins,” James said, “they are now over.”  
Longer lines 
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a sweeping budget bill passed by Congress in 2025, made several changes to the SNAP program. 
Last November, for example, veterans, the homeless, recent foster care youth and adults ages 54-64 were no longer exempt from work requirements to receive food benefits for themselves and their families through SNAP. 
KFF Health News reported in October that around 5 million, or 13%, fewer people, were enrolled in SNAP in June 2026 than July 2025.
Danielle Bozarth, the interim president and CEO of God’s Pantry, said in the 50 counties her organization serves, demand for food is also on the rise. 
“What our … partner agencies are reporting is longer lines, running out of food. People are lining up earlier, before it opens, and just anxious,” she said. “Just making sure that they’re able to leave with food that day while they’re in line.” 
Danielle Bozarth. (Photo provided)
Supply is a challenge right now. James and Bozarth both pointed to a shortage in food commodities coming in from the United States Department of Agriculture. 
“That typically will ebb and flow with the administration, and we recognize that; it’s ebbed and flowed for years,” said James, who said Dare to Care is down 3 million pounds of food from federal commodities. 
This is the first time, though, that he’s seen federal food commodities decrease while demand for food is increasing. 
Bozarth said God’s Pantry served around 280,000 people last year. As of Nov. 18, it was up to 314,000 people in 2026. James said Dare to Care saw a 115% increase in food demand from January to September. 
Looking to the holidays, winter 
Winter can exacerbate hunger, experts said: Kids who got lunches at school are leaving the classrooms for break; heat bills are higher. 
“I think families will struggle trying to put food on the table,” Bozarth said. “I think it will be a tough, tough December for families. And then with heat bills and buying Christmas presents, and … providing additional food for the kids when they’re home. I think January will probably be really hard for the families.” 
James doesn’t expect the increase in hunger to slow down. 
“We’re consistently seeing more and more people entering into the roles of food insecurity,” he said. 
This is also a time of giving, for many: Thanks to bulk buying, many food banks have better purchasing power than the average person. Therefore, monetary donations are often appreciated, though food donations and volunteering are also welcome, James said.  
“Food banks have such a large buying power that we’re able to buy more food at less cost than someone who would be purchasing a can of soup for $1,” James said. “We can provide two meals where for $1 purchasing some soup is only going to get you one can of soup.” 
Could the ‘blue wave’ help? 
The power in Washington D.C. shifted during the 2026 midterm elections. Democrats now have control of Congress, and they have already signaled they want to restore funding to social service programs cut in recent years. 
“We just simply need every elected official to be able to, at every level of government, understand that charitable food assistance again cannot make up for the reduction in the federal nutrition programs that we’ve seen already, and we need that continued support,” James said. 
Melissa McDonald, the executive director of Feeding Kentucky, said during a Nov. 18 meeting of the Race and Access to Opportunity Committee that “SNAP provides nine meals for every one meal that a food bank is able to provide.” 
“My hope is that we can work towards a Kentucky where no family has to worry about where their next meal is coming from, where farmers have opportunities to succeed, and where food we produce helps our people thrive,” McDonald said. “I believe these goals go hand in hand.”  
Persistent myths 
Many people receiving food assistance are working already, experts say, contrary to the idea that people getting government assistance aren’t in the workforce. 
James called it a “classic myth.” 
“For the first time, we’re seeing two-income families that are still not able to make ends meet,” he said. “The math simply isn’t mathing; it’s not working. And so these families are turning to charitable food assistance for relief because they’re having to make tough decisions. Because the gas inflation prices, they can’t afford to fill up a truck that they need for their job and work, and it’s costing them $100 a week when they were used to paying $70 a week. That $30 is a huge difference for someone who’s on the margin already.”  
Volunteers begin to unpack turkeys to give to meal recipients as part of God’s Pantry Food Bank Sharing Thanksgiving program in the parking lot of Big Sandy Community and Technical College on Nov. 24, 2025, in Prestonsburg, Kentucky. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)
This year, Dare to Care has seen a 30% increase in two-income families turning to food banks for the first time, James said. 
“Some of these are hardworking families, or these are seniors choosing between food and medicine,” Bozarth said. “There could be an unexpected expense or setback. It could happen to any of us.” 
For Caldwell, 63, it was a storm of crises that hit him back to back. 
He broke his ankle in 2013 and got an infection, he said. He filed for disability because he couldn’t work. In 2019, he had a heart attack and had to get a stent. Then he became homeless. 
“I couldn’t afford housing, so I started drinking heavy,” he recalled. 
He eventually got help from a Louisville nonprofit that helped him get settled in a reduced-rent apartment. 
“I get very little…SNAP, but other things help me,” he said. “I’m doing all right. I’m blessed. I’ve got a roof over my head.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: Be thankful for Colorado’s county clerks
description: You probably don’t know their names. You might be shaky on exactly what they do. But, in this season of giving thanks, Coloradans owe a huge amount of gratitude to the state’s county clerks. In the run-up to the election this month, they faced immense pressures as election deniers and democracy haters, starting with President […]
text:
An election worker feeds ballot envelopes through a machine that scans for signatures at the Adams County clerk and recorder's office in Brighton on Nov. 3. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)You probably don’t know their names. You might be shaky on exactly what they do. But, in this season of giving thanks, Coloradans owe a huge amount of gratitude to the state’s county clerks.
In the run-up to the election this month, they faced immense pressures as election deniers and democracy haters, starting with President Donald Trump, piled on threats and trafficked in rhetoric that was meant to undercut and intimidate them. Some Trump allies suggested an election that didn’t go their way could result in civil war.
The clerks weren’t having it. These professionals stood their ground, upheld their oaths and performed most honorably under fire. They demonstrated that authoritarian bullies can be defeated with unwavering pursuit of impartial processes. They showed Coloradans that an unflinching defense of democracy can come in the form of dispassionate competence and conscientious professionalism.
We’re all the beneficiaries of their courage.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sixty-four clerk-and-recorders oversee local election offices throughout the state, one for each county. They’re elected to the position. They are Republicans, Democrats and, increasingly, independents. The secretary of state is often the face of statewide elections, and that position does play a crucial role in issuing rules, coordinating local activity and tallying results. But it’s the clerks who do the real work of election administration. They are the main point of contact for voters. And they are the most exposed to threats and disruptions.
Consider their work environment this year. The Trump administration sued the state to obtain sensitive voter data, presumably to bar some residents from voting. Trump issued an executive order that would have allowed the administration to meddle with mail ballot systems, an alarming prospect in the handful of universal mail-ballot states like Colorado. Colorado was 1 of 15 states flagged by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security for “election integrity” monitoring ahead of the June primary, and the administration deployed a dozen election monitors to the Democratic-leaning region of a toss-up congressional district in Colorado, clearly an act of partisan intimidation.
This was all in addition to the more ominous threats to elections nationwide, such as potential deployment of military members to polling places, invocation of the Insurrection Act, and seizure of ballots and election machines. An attorney close to Trump less than a month before the election mused about Trump seizing ballots and being in a position to win a “civil war.”
And you thought your job was stressful.
The pressures, which began when Trump falsely claimed the 2020 election was stolen from him, have taken a toll. In 2024, high turnover meant that 24 Colorado counties, representing half the state’s population, had new clerks administering elections. Jena Griswold, the secretary of state, attributed the turnover to “election deniers” and “an environment of threats.” Clerks in the state have had to fortify their facilities, take unpredictable routes to and from work, and hire private security.


It could take a generation to cleanse American culture of election disinformation after Trump did so much to normalize it among Republicans.


But as rumors of war and other forms of lawlessness swirled around their offices this year, the clerks were undeterred. They did the job their constituents elected them to do: create secure conditions for free and fair elections and count votes without partisan favor. The result was an election so beyond reproach that not even Republican Lauren Boebert, who after 2020 did more than anyone in Colorado to boost Trump’s election lies, accepted her defeat in the state’s most Republican congressional district. Her loss came as part of a “blue tsunami” that elevated Democrats in districts long thought to be impenetrable Republican strongholds.
Enemies of democracy might have been muffled since Nov. 3, but they haven’t gone away. Two days after the election, influential MAGA podcaster Joe Oltmann and former Colorado governor candidate Heidi Ganahl went full election denial on Oltmann’s show. Extremist Colorado “election integrity” activist Mark Cook seems only to have doubled down on ludicrous claims. The most famous county clerk in Colorado history, Tina Peters, an election-denying MAGA champion who when she oversaw the elections office in Mesa County committed crimes that landed her in prison, has hardly changed her tune.
It could take a generation to cleanse American culture of election disinformation after Trump did so much to normalize it among Republicans, and it retains the power to disrupt the 2028 cycle as would-be Trump successors seek advantages.
But, for the moment, clerks in Colorado and around the country have proved that democracy is stronger than autocracy. For that we can’t thank them enough.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Food aid started in Appalachia; it’s still needed and it’s being cut back
description: As President Kennedy perused the New York Times from his White House bedroom on the Sunday morning of Oct. 20, 1963, he was startled by a Whitesburg, Kentucky datelined story on page one. He immediately picked up the phone and ordered an emergency cabinet meeting to address the issues in the article. The byline was […]
text:
The Letcher County Food Pantry in Whitesburg. (Photo courtesy Letcher County Food Pantry)As President Kennedy perused the New York Times from his White House bedroom on the Sunday morning of Oct. 20, 1963, he was startled by a Whitesburg, Kentucky datelined story on page one. He immediately picked up the phone and ordered an emergency cabinet meeting to address the issues in the article.
The byline was that of Homer Bigart, a two-time Pulitzer Prize winner and star war correspondent. He had just returned from a visit to Letcher County with Tom and Pat Gish, publishers of the Mountain Eagle, and attorney Harry Caudill, author of “Night Comes to the Cumberlands.” The headline said, “Kentucky Miners: A Grim Winter; Poverty, Squalor and Idleness Prevail in Mountain Area.”
The statement that most affected the president quoted Dr. Randall D. Collins, the Letcher County health officer, saying he had seen pot-bellied, anemic children who ate dirt out of chimneys. Caudill said in the same story that the mountaineers had been given just enough food to stay alive and then told to go to hell. Kennedy ordered food aid and other relief to begin immediately for the unemployed miners in Eastern Kentucky.
I recalled Tom Gish telling this history as I read reporter Sam Adams’ reporting in the Mountain Eagle last month about the impact of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on food supplies in Letcher County. Adams reported that the Letcher County Food Pantry handed out food to 139 families in three days. They do it in an aging building still showing damage from the July 2022 flood, with a sagging floor, a failing heating system, and a leaking roof.  Harold D. Bolling, the pantry’s treasurer, put the repair bill at about $40,000. 
“We’re desperate to get some things done,” he told Adams.
Vicki Holbrook, who runs the pantry, said the people coming through the door have been battered by grocery and gas prices. The ones she worries about most are the oldest. “The elderly, they slashed it down,” she said. “Some of them don’t get even $100 in food stamps, and most of them get the least Social Security they can get.”
Bolling said this week that donations totaling $30,000 had come in from readers who saw the Eagle article. In addition, he said, a local vendor had cut the price of a new heat pump by a third, ensuring the building is properly heated and cooled. 
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025, is projected by the Congressional Budget Office to reduce federal SNAP spending by nearly $187 billion through 2034. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities calls it “the largest cut to the program in history.”
One major piece is the work rule. Adults without young children must now show 80 hours a month of work, volunteering or job training to keep their benefits past three months. That rule used to stop at 54. It’s now 64, which in a coal county covers a lot of people in their late 50s and early 60s who haven’t had steady work since the mines closed. Parents used to be exempt if they had a child under 18. Now the child has to be under 14. And the law eliminated exemptions that had applied to veterans, homeless people and young adults who had been in foster care.
The Kentucky Center for Economic Policy counted 42,870 Kentuckians, roughly one in 14 of the people who had been getting help, who lost SNAP in the first seven months after the law took effect, through May 2026. More than a quarter of them, 11,168, were children. “Hunger is increasing, and yet Kentuckians are losing our best resources against it,” the center wrote. At the same time, the federal food that stocks those shelves has been shrinking. Holbrook told Adams the pantry has received almost no apples this year, far fewer potatoes and very little meat.
A news search across the coalfields shows Letcher County is not alone. In Wayne County, West Virginia, a church pantry manager told NBC News this month that there was a decent chance his pantry could run out. In Lincoln County, West Virginia Watch told of a woman whose monthly benefit fell from about $400 to $24 after she was told she had to meet the new work rules. In St. Paul, Virginia, a pantry director told Cardinal News she can no longer put as much in a food box as she used to. Second Harvest in Tennessee says demand is up 10 percent. The Southeast Ohio Foodbank serves half again as many people as it did in 2019.
There is a bit of irony here for those who know the history of federal food aid and concern about food insecurity in Appalachia. On May 29, 1961, Agriculture Secretary Orville Freeman passed out the first food stamps in Welch, the county seat of McDowell County, West Virginia. The first went to Alderson and Chloe Muncy of Paynesville, who were feeding a household of 15.
In February 1968, fresh from hunger hearings in Mississippi the previous year, Robert Kennedy brought his Senate poverty subcommittee to Eastern Kentucky, holding a field hearing in the Fleming-Neon High School gym. Hunger was part of what he came to see. He stopped at a one-room school at Barwick where the teacher managed somehow to cook hot meals for the children. 
From all of that came a promise, made by presidents of both parties and kept for most of my life.  In a country this rich, nobody should go hungry because of where they happen to live or where there are no jobs available. Yet, things are apt to get worse. As of Oct. 1, Kentucky and every other state must pay 75 percent of the administrative cost of running SNAP, up from half. Beginning in October 2027, most states will also have to pay part of the food benefits themselves for the first time, with their share tied to how accurately they administer the program. States with payment error rates below 6 percent pay nothing toward benefits. Those above that threshold can be required to pay 5, 10 or 15 percent. An error does not necessarily mean fraud. It can be an overpayment or an underpayment caused in administering an enormously complicated program.
 Kentucky policy analysts initially estimated that the new law could eventually cost the state as much as roughly $250 million a year in additional SNAP expenses, including administration and benefit costs. A much lower error rate for Kentucky (4.7%, down from the previous 10%) last year has now lowered that figure as the state is now one of only nine states that don’t have to match a portion of SNAP benefits. The cost that is real right now is administrative. The cabinet is seeking $43.5 million in fiscal year 2027 and $58 million in fiscal year 2028 from the legislature to cover the administrative shift.
Things are far better in the mountains today than when Bigart came. I know of nothing now like what he described. But a lot of mountain families still don’t know whether the groceries will last until the end of the month. Across Appalachia, where so much of the nation’s history of ensuring food security began, we are seeing the reversal of the concern that drove that history. It is easier to believe that the Kentucky River will start to flow backwards than it is to believe that the political majority in Washington now would stir from their beds or their church pews on a Sunday to address this emerging emergency.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: Twin conquering heroes return to Richmond to treat patients
description: Drs. Travan and Travis Jasper, twin brothers who are Richmond born and bred, have returned to their hometown in a notable way: After decades working elsewhere, they recently became co-medical directors of the emergency department at HCA Virginia Chippenham Hospital in the state’s capital city. I’m featuring the doctors as part of my sometimes-annual “things [...]
text:
Dr. Travan Jasper (left) and his twin brother, Dr. Travis Jasper, Co-Directors of the Emergency Department pose for a portrait in Chippenham Hospital August 31, 2026 in Richmond, Virginia.(Photo by Max Posner/ For The Washington Post via Getty Images)Drs. Travan and Travis Jasper, twin brothers who are Richmond born and bred, have returned to their hometown in a notable way: After decades working elsewhere, they recently became co-medical directors of the emergency department at HCA Virginia Chippenham Hospital in the state’s capital city.
I’m featuring the doctors as part of my sometimes-annual “things I’m thankful for” column as Thanksgiving descends.  
They decided to enter the medical field after watching their uncle struggle in the intensive care unit when they were just 12 years old. A doctor treated the twins as if they had no clue what was happening to their uncle, and the incident made them “want to do better than that” as physicians, Travan Jasper said. 
When the chance arose to come back home to lead the ER this year, they leapt at it.
“It’s a real honor to have that opportunity to care for people you know and you’re close to,” Travis Jasper told ABC News. They’re now 57, according to news and social media reports.
Call it the latest example of “the return of the conquering heroes.” The Jaspers grew up without running water sometimes and were often hungry, but they became top hurdlers and co-valedictorians at John Marshall High School in Richmond in the late 1980s. 
They attended the same college and the University of Chicago medical school, and the Jaspers spent many years working in various hospitals in Georgia.
The brothers said they initially didn’t want to practice medicine in Richmond because they were nervous about treating people they grew up with, ABC News reported. But they said their fears subsided as they got further along in their careers.
Through a hospital spokesperson, the Jaspers declined talking to me. I assume it’s because they did so many interviews a few months ago, including from national and local outlets. No matter: Theirs is a story that deserves to be shared.
Randall Johnson probably figured his February flight would be uneventful as he headed from Houston to Atlanta, with Virginia as his final destination. But Johnson, a Virginia Union women’s basketball assistant coach who was returning from a recruiting trip, was one of 85 passengers on the Delta flight when a man rose during the plane’s incline and began banging on the cockpit door.
An altercation ensued as the 300-pound-plus man became more aggressive, and Johnson and other passengers intervened to subdue him. A flight attendant eventually zip-tied the man as Johnson and others held him down, and the plane returned to Houston. Police detained the suspect, and medics assisted injured passengers. 
Delta’s president contacted Johnson afterward, and he received several perks. Johnson, an employee at Norfolk International Airport, also got a $5,000 award from his employer.
“I didn’t see myself as a hero,” he said. His fellow passengers and employer disagree.
Keeping a promise to his wife, who was suffering the effects of Alzheimer’s disease, Jim Thornton kept her at home in Hampton, rather than send her to a nursing facility. Donna Thornton, his high school sweetheart and wife of nearly 56 years, got his full attention: He became her full-time caregiver and managed her everyday needs. 
The Thorntons also received help from Riverside Health’s palliative care team on the Peninsula.
Donna, 78, died in February.
Jim, who along with Donna had careers in the shipyard industry, wanted to provide comfort to other people who face similar challenges. He made a “transformational” gift of seven figures to establish the Donna S. Thornton Hospice Home for patients whose needs can’t be met at their own homes.
The Riverside Foundation announced the site will have four private rooms where patients will receive specialized care in a home-like setting. Groundbreaking was Nov. 18 on the campus of Riverside’s Warwick Forest in Newport News.
The home is a tribute to both Thorntons.
Jim Thornton holds a photo of his wife, Donna, who died this year after battling Alzheimer’s disease. He recently donated money to establish a hospice home in her name on the campus of Riverside’s Warwick Forest campus in Newport News. (Photo courtesy of Riverside Health)
I don’t write enough about science – I did poorly in the subject back in my high school years, so I’m a mite gun shy – but I perk up when the topic is NASA Langley Research Center. I had the pleasure of touring the 764-acre facility in Hampton back when I was an editorial writer at the Daily Press.
So I was fascinated by the news that NASA Langley this summer celebrated construction of its first major wind tunnel in more than 40 years.
WHRO covered the story about the $57 million Flight Dynamics Research Facility. As my former colleague Katherine Hafner wrote: “The futuristic-looking building resembles a giant, concrete version of the Liberty Bell display – twin pillars flanking a sloped structure in the center.”
Among the projects scheduled at the tunnel: something called the Transonic Truss-Braced Wing. The aircraft design could help lower fuel and operational costs for future airliners. Facilities like this make science intriguing.
No one can ever doubt that Charlie Hill loves Virginia State University, his alma mater. (It was called Virginia State College when he graduated in 1966.) He’s served on the Board of Visitors. In 2015, he donated $100,000 to establish an endowment honoring his late wife; she earned her bachelor’s and master’s degrees in microbiology from VSU. 
He did that gift one better this year, when he committed $1.5 million to Virginia State. The university said it’s the largest gift ever made to the university by a living alumnus.
“Over the course of my time at Virginia State University, I built the foundation for a successful corporate career,” Hill said. “I want today’s students to have that same opportunity for transformation so their lives can be even richer than mine.” Bravo to him. 
As we celebrate this holiday built around family, food and football, I hope you find something to be thankful for, too.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Schools and tribes are bringing Native foods and culture to the cafeteria
description: The tall, dense stalks of blue Hopi corn were a burst of green among the dry grassland of southeastern Wyoming. As the small patch of crops whipped in the wind, Lisa Ansell Frazier led the way into the rows and gently touched the leaves, tassels and budding silk. If you talk to the corn and […]
text:
Lisa Ansell Frazier talks to the blue Hopi corn, which she manages on the Mitákuye Ówahe Farm in southeastern Wyoming. (Photo by Lauren Wagner/ The 74)

This article originally appeared in The 74, a non-profit, independent news organization focused on education in America.

The tall, dense stalks of blue Hopi corn were a burst of green among the dry grassland of southeastern Wyoming. As the small patch of crops whipped in the wind, Lisa Ansell Frazier led the way into the rows and gently touched the leaves, tassels and budding silk. If you talk to the corn and say hi, she said, it will reach out and touch you.
“These are our babies,” she said. “This is the corn that is going to our schools.”
On a hot August afternoon, the corn still had weeks to mature alongside Huckleberry Gold potatoes and Jerusalem artichokes on the Mitákuye Ówahe Farm near Cheyenne. The produce would eventually travel more than 300 miles west to the Wind River Reservation, where it would be delivered to schools and pantries called food lodges.
The farm is just one facet of the Buffalo Youth Nation Project, a Wyoming nonprofit working to restore food sovereignty — which ensures Indigenous communities have the right to make decisions about what they grow, harvest and eat, according to the Native American Food Sovereignty Alliance. Key components include the protection of ancestral knowledge; revitalization of ancestral foods; and the integration of traditional customs in food production.
Across the nation, organizations, educators, tribal members and schools are working to supply student cafeterias with Indigenous foods that federal policy spent more than a century working to eliminate. They aim to address high rates of diet-related disease in Indigenous communities while expanding food access and Native education through lunch trays.
In 2018, Frazier founded the Buffalo Youth Nation Project — called Wakanyeja Tatanka Oyate in Lakota — to strengthen Indigenous food sovereignty and access to resources for Wyoming youth, families and communities.
This year is Mitákuye Ówahe Farm’s first providing blue Hopi corn, often ground into cornmeal for recipes, and other fresh produce across the region to schools and school-based food lodges — public pantries that serve local children, families and communities.
The nonprofit has its own herd of 16 buffalo at the Standing Rock Reservation, located on the border of North and South Dakota. Buffalo, the term many Native communities use, refers to the American bison. The organization’s work includes restoring buffalo across the Great Plains and distributing the meat to local communities, such as three schools on the Wind River Reservation: Wyoming Indian Elementary, St. Stephens Indian School and Fort Washakie Schools, alongside the University of Wyoming’s Native Student Center in Laramie.

Lisa Ansell Frazier points to rows of crops, including Jerusalem artichokes, on the Mitákuye Ówahe Farm in southeastern Wyoming. (Photo by Lauren Wagner)
“We have sourced thousands of pounds of buffalo meat for the schools,” Frazier said. “It depends on availability. Bison is a highly sought-after source of protein, and our herd health is the utmost priority — we do not want to take too much from our herds. I source mainly from my tribe, the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe, (and) we have sourced from the Shoshone-Bannock tribe in Idaho.”
Frazier said delivery of buffalo meat sparks a lot of conversations between elders and children, and she hears from students about how they’ve never tasted bison before. One girl she recently met experimented with cooking it in milk and fed it to her family, who loved it.
“When we go back to our ancestral foods, it’s a win-win. Indigenous food sovereignty, when you break it down, it’s about healing the earth, and the people, and the animals, and creating a relationship with all of that,” Frazier said. “The education part comes through the schools (and) the community. If we don’t have it there, then the education doesn’t happen, but when we introduce it, that’s when the education starts.”
St. Stephens Indian School uses the buffalo meat in its lunches and food lodge. Wyoming Indian Elementary and Fort Washakie Schools currently distribute it only in their own food lodges.
Cheryl Coleman, a behavior support coordinator at Wyoming Indian Elementary, said the school’s food lodge wouldn’t be possible without the Buffalo Youth Nation Project. The nonprofit purchased refrigerators and freezers for the local schools to store buffalo meat.
“We could serve it in our school lunches if we had the infrastructure to do that,” she said. “But right now, she orders it, we get it and it’s distributed to our families that need it.”
More than two centuries ago, the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho tribes — which now live together on the Wind River Reservation — traveled across a landscape populated by up to 60 million buffalo. By the early 1900s, that number was down to the hundreds because of mass hunting by white settlers and colonization — a conscious strategy by the federal government to starve Native communities.
The impact on Native Americans was devastating: Autonomy and traditional ways of life were destroyed, contributing to trauma that remains today, according to the nonprofit North American Traditional Indigenous Food Systems. Highly nutritious traditional foods were replaced with processed, shelf-stable government rations, with the goal of keeping Native populations alive, rather than healthy. Other wild plants and foods disappeared after the buffalo were killed, because in order to thrive, native seeds needed the natural aeration of soil from the bisons’ powerful hooves.
Indigenous populations were left with high rates of diabetes, obesity and other diseases. In 2024, 18% of Native American children were reported as not being in excellent or very good health, according to the Annie E. Casey Foundation. That was the largest percentage for any demographic, the lowest being 7% for white children.
Frazier is one of several advocates betting that part of the solution lies in what students eat.
While the Buffalo Youth Nation Project sources and delivers Indigenous ingredients, the Wind River Food Sovereignty Project has created Native recipes for school cafeterias. In June, the nonprofit was one of five organizations nationwide to complete a two-year USDA grant to do so.
The funding helped school nutrition staff develop Native recipes that could be standardized and count toward federal meal requirements. Last summer, it helped Wind River Reservation schools establish raised garden beds and greenhouses so students could plant Indigenous produce for lunches.

A geometric dome greenhouse at Wyoming Indian Elementary on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming. (Photo by Lauren Wagner)
“When we first began this work, there was a lot to learn,” said Krystal Northcott, food service director at Fort Washakie Schools. “We had to learn about the Indigenous foods themselves, how they were traditionally used, and how we could take those ingredients and prepare them in a way that would work in the school kitchen.”
The project created dishes like huckleberry bison sliders, pumpkin bison chili, blue cornmeal lemon blueberry muffins and chokecherry gravy. The recipes are in the final stages of USDA approval after two years of consulting with tribal elders, experimenting with ingredients, sampling at schools, adapting the meals for hundreds of servings, going back-and-forth with the federal agency and dealing with piles of documentation paperwork.
Northcott’s favorite part of the process was watching students taste the recipes and give feedback. When sampling the chokecherry gravy — a creamy, deep purple pudding dessert made from cooked chokecherries and honey — a group of kids were asked to put stickers with either a smile or frown on a board to express their thoughts. All four recipes received mostly smiles, Northcott said.
“We could develop what we thought was a great recipe, but ultimately our students were the ones who were going to eat it. We wanted to know what they thought — did they like it?” she said. “We were really lucky at that because I was thinking, ‘Oh my God, all that time and effort putting into a recipe, and then (what if) the kids tell us it sucked?’ ”

A Wyoming Indian Elementary School student taste tests chokecherry gravy. (Wind River Food Sovereignty Project)
Even though the federal grant has expired, the Wind River Food Sovereignty Project still has a long list of plans. It’s publishing a cookbook with the school cafeteria recipes, plus more Indigenous meal ideas. It also plans to launch a K-12 Native education curriculum about nutrition, traditions and culture by next fall. The first release will be for grades K-3, with older students included in later years.
“Bringing Indigenous foods into a school cafeteria is about much more than changing a menu,” Northcott said. “It is about education. It is about giving our students an opportunity to taste something connected to their culture. It is about giving our food service staff the knowledge, equipment, training and confidence to prepare those foods, and it is about creating a connection between what our children learn from the land and what they see on their lunch break.”
The effort to expand food sovereignty in schools isn’t just happening on the Wind River Reservation. Minneapolis Public Schools has incorporated culturally relevant food into its cafeterias since 2012, said Madison Taylor, the district’s farm-to-school coordinator.
Its central kitchen and capacity for cooking meals from scratch allows the district to serve all of its nearly 30,000 students Native foods. Every second Thursday is deemed “Minnesota Thursday,” and Indigenous recipes are often the focus.
In December, the menu will include a bison grain bowl over wild rice pilaf with roasted vegetables and a maple vinaigrette. School cafeterias have also served dishes like bison pozole and turkey wild rice soup.
“Every student is receiving the same meal, and we’re doing promotion and education about that meal in a bigger way — we have posters in all of the schools that shows the meal, where it’s coming from, who’s supplying the products, and then we also create a video that teachers share with their classes about why this meal is good for them and the cultural connections,” Taylor said.
One of her main jobs is to obtain local ingredients, when possible. More than 1,000 pounds of wild rice for next month’s meal was sourced through North American Traditional Indigenous Food Systems. The Minneapolis-based nonprofit was founded by local chef Sean Sherman, who owns the state’s first full-service Indigenous restaurant. The organization was one of the USDA grant recipients along with the Wind River Food Sovereignty Project.
Currently, it is planning a program called Meals for Native Institutions that will sell and deliver ready-to-eat foods to schools, health care centers, tribal programs and senior facilities. Only Indigenous ingredients will be used — no beef, pork, wheat or dairy — and they will be purchased from Native producers when possible.
“It was about 2020 when Sean started the first steps of this program,” said Andrea Weber, director of Meals for Native Institutions. “When he started to talk to me about it a few years ago, it was like, ‘We really want to get Indigenous foods to the youth because we want them to have access to these foods for most of their life, and make that part of their understanding of their culture and and then their diet, too.’”
State and federal regulations have made progress slow, but Weber said she hopes to officially launch by the end of this year, at first selling to tribally managed schools and community facilities.
Other districts are also working to incorporate Native foods into their school cafeterias.
Umoⁿhoⁿ Nation Public Schools, a K-12 district on the Umoⁿhoⁿ (Omaha) Reservation in Macy, Nebraska, operates a farm-to-school program and food sustainability initiative that centers around Indigenous food sovereignty. Teens grow and harvest more than 25,000 plants each summer for their school’s culinary department.
Beginning in third grade at the Service to All Relations School, a public charter bordering the Navajo Nation near Flagstaff, Arizona, students grow traditional crops like corn, beans and squash — a trio referred to as the three sisters.
Food service staff at Rocky Boy School District in north-central Montana are moving away from heavily processed foods and toward Indigenous ingredients that are grown and harvested in the local Chippewa Cree community. Other recent efforts can be found in New York, Washington and Alaska.
In Wyoming, Frazier is in the middle of preparing to ship 200 pounds of blue Hopi cornmeal to each Wind River Reservation school. Northcott and other district staff are finalizing the four recipes they’ve been crafting for two years, and they will soon begin another spring planting season with students, growing produce on school grounds.
“When a student recognizes an Indigenous food in the cafeteria, I hope they don’t just see another school lunch,” Northcott said. “I hope they see a piece of who they are. I hope that as we continue this work, Indigenous foods will become a normal and valued part of our school meals, because our children deserve to see their culture reflected in their schools, and that includes what is on their plates.”

Ka nota a ka luna hoʻoponopono: Unuhi ʻia na Kamalani Johnson. Click here to read this article in English.
Hiki ke pālua ka waiwai o ka ʻoihana mahiʻai o ka mokuʻāina inā ua māmā mai nā lula pekelala pili ponoʻī iā Hawaiʻi e ʻoi aku ai ka papaha no nā mahiʻai e kūʻai aku ai i nā hua ma ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa.



Civil Beat stories ma ka ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi 
'Ka Ulana Pilina' is an ongoing collection of news articles and opinion pieces written in the Hawaiian language to better connect with our Indigenous readers, identify underreported stories and improve our engagement with an underserved community.





Read All

Pēlā mai ka Hawaiʻi Institute for Public Affairs ma ka moʻolelo hope iho nei, kahi i wānana ʻia ai ka lilo o ka $800 miliona kālā i nā mahiʻai ma ka waiwai e loaʻa paha mai ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa i kēlā me kēia makahiki — he huinanui i ʻoi aku i ka waiwai pau loa o ka ʻoihana kāʻokoʻa.
Nānā ʻia ʻo Hawaiʻi he ʻāina ʻē ma ka ʻōnaehana pekelala e hōʻoia ana i ka palekana no nā mea ola e kū nei, he mea e ʻāʻumeʻume nei nā mahiʻai me nā lula pekelala ʻoʻoleʻa, a wahi a ka hui noiʻi, he mea e hiki ke hoʻonōhie ʻia no ke kōkua i ka mahiʻai ʻana. Ua hoʻokumu ʻia ia mau lula no ke kaupale ʻana iā ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa mai nā ʻelala mahiʻai he nui wale o Hawaiʻi, e laʻa ka nalo, he mea nō naʻe ia e pilikia nei nā mahiʻai o ka pae ʻāina ma ka mālama ʻana i ko lākou kaʻawale mai nā mākeke o ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa, wahi a ka moʻolelo.
Pāpā ʻia ma lalo o kekahi mau lula nōhihi ka hoʻouna ʻia o nā hua ʻai a lauʻai he nui i ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa e laʻa ke cacao. ʻAʻole hiki ke hoʻouna ʻia ka hua ʻai maoli inā ʻaʻole hoʻomaloʻo a hoʻomākaukau mua ʻia. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2025) Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2025
E pono e lilo kēia he hopohopo ʻoihana hoʻokele waiwai no ka mokuʻāina, wahi a ka moʻolelo. He kōkua nui ka lapaʻau ʻana i kēia pilikia no ka mokuʻāina, e ʻae ana i nā mahiʻai e komo ma nā mākeke hou me nā hua hou a kahiko pū, wahi a Cameron Deptula, kekahi o nā mea kākau o ka moʻolelo.
Ua hoʻohiki nā alakaʻi mokuʻāina e hoʻonui i ka nui ʻai e hoʻoulu ʻia ma ka pae ʻāina a me ka lawa o ka ʻai no nā makahiki he nui, ua lilo nō naʻe nā ʻāʻumeʻume me ka pipiʻi o ka ʻāina, ka hana ʻana a nā kānaka, ka wai, a me ka nui wahi he ālaina. He 0.4% o ka ʻoihana hoʻokele waiwai o ka mokuʻāina ka ʻoihana mahiʻai, ma kahi o ka $554 miliona i ka makahiki 2025.
Ma ka mokuʻāina ka mole o ka nui o ia waiwai ʻoiai, kākaʻikahi ka haʻalele ʻana o kahi mea iā Hawaiʻi.
“Hoʻouna ʻia aku ka ʻuala kahiko, ka hēʻī, basil, a ʻo ia wale nō paha, wahi a Brian Miyamoto i ʻōlelo ai, ka luna hoʻokele hoʻokō o Hawaiʻi Farm Bureau.
Pōkole ka papa helu o nā hua a lau ʻai e ʻae ʻia. No nā mea hou, e laʻa nā ʻano maiʻa a hua ʻai ʻālani ponoʻī, aia ma ka ʻōnaehana ʻāpono nā hōʻoia ʻana e loʻohia ai nā ʻāina mahiʻai i ka wā e hoʻāʻo ana e hoʻonui i kahi e kūʻai ʻia ai nā hua, wahi a Deptula.
E pono e lilo ka hoʻēmi ʻana i nā luhi o nā lula — ʻo ka nui, ʻo ka hoʻēmi ʻana i ka nui manawa e ʻāpono ʻia ai kahi hua hou, a he ʻelima makahiki i kekahi manawa — he makakoho, wahi a Deptula, he mea e noho nei he aʻoaʻo kūikawā i ke Kiaʻāina Josh Green.
Ma ka nui, e pono ko Hawaiʻi e hoʻonui i ka palekana o nā mea ola e huli ai ka manaʻo o ke aupuni pekelala no ka hoʻomāmā ʻana i nā lula a me ka hoʻopōkole ʻana i ka wā ʻāpono no nā hua a lau ʻai hou, wahi āna.
Aia he ʻelua hale mahiʻai ma ka ʻōnaehana ʻāpono: ʻo Mahi Pono ma Maui no nā lemi, a ʻo Volcano Wasabi ma Hawaiʻi mokupuni.
Aia ka nui o ka nānā ʻia o nā hua a lau ʻai i ka nui o ka makaʻu i ka hopena e loaʻa paha no nā hua a lau ʻai o ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa, ma ka nui loa. For nā lemi, he nui loa nō ia, keu hoʻi ma nā wahi e like me Kaleponi. No laila, inā ua makemake ʻo Mahi Pono e hoʻouna he lemi ʻokoʻa i ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa, e pono ana e komo hou i ka ʻōnaehana ʻāpono.
“ʻO ka pololei, ʻaʻole nānā ʻia ke ʻano o ka pea, ke ʻano o ka manakō,” i ʻōlelo ai ʻo Ken Love, ka luna hoʻokele hoʻokō o Hawaiʻi Tropical Fruit Growers.
A no Volcano Wasabi e hoʻoulu nei i ka wasabi ma Hawaiʻi mokupuni, ua hoʻomaka ka ʻōnaehana ʻāpono he ʻehā a ʻoi makahiki aku nei me kahi loiloi i ka makaʻu i ka hopena no nā ʻelala. No ka loiloi e koi ʻia ai ka noiʻi hohonu i nā hopena e pili pū ana me nā ʻelala ma luna o nā mea ola, he ʻelua paha makahiki ka lōʻihi o ia hana. A he ʻelua hou aku makahiki no ka ʻōnaehana loiloi i kō ʻole a i kēia.
Wānana ʻia ma ka moʻolelo ka pā a lilo o ka ʻoihana ma ka $760 miliona kālā, a he $40 miliona a ʻoi kālā ma ka hōʻoia ma mua o ka hoʻouna ʻana a me ka hahai lula.
“ʻAʻole nō nānā ʻia inā he ʻāina mahiʻai nui a kahiko kou nona nā lako e hana pū ai me nā kānaka loaʻa o ke kālā a no ka ʻimi i ke kākoʻo kānāwai, ʻo ia paʻa nō ia o nā ʻōnaehana liʻiliʻi a nui pū,” wahi a Deptula.
A laila, loaʻa nā lula hou aku e pākuʻi ʻia, ʻo ia hoʻi nā kiʻina koi ʻia, e pā ai paha ka maikaʻi o ka hua a lau ʻai, a pau ai ka pono. No ko Hawaiʻi mau manakō e pono e mālama ʻia i loko o ka wela ma mua o ka hoʻouna ʻia, makehewa ka hoʻouna ʻana a haʻalele i ka mokupuni, i ʻōlelo ai ʻo Love.
ʻOiai penei, he ʻelua wale nō ala no nā mahiʻai: ʻO ke kūʻai wale nō ma Hawaiʻi a ʻo ka ʻimi i nā ala e hoʻolilo ʻia ai ia mau mea he mau lako no ka hakakau i loaʻa ʻole nā ʻelala.
He ala nā kiʻina mālama e laʻa ka pepehi ʻelala a mūhune ma ka wela e hōʻoia ʻia ai ka loaʻa o ka nui kālā e hiki i nā mahiʻai a e hoʻēmi ʻia ai ka ʻōpala ma ke kiʻi i ka hua a lau ʻai i kū ʻole i nā lula o ka nānā ʻana. He ala pū nō naʻe ia e emi ai ka makaʻu i ka hopena no nā mahiʻai e lilo ana paha ka hua a lau ʻai ma muli o ka manawa i lilo i nā lula hoʻokaʻawale pekelala, wahi a Deptula, ʻo ia kekahi o nā kumu i hoʻokaʻawale ai nā ʻelele kau kānāwai i ke kālā ma nā miliona ma luna o nā hale mālama meaʻai ma ka mokuʻāina.
Ua ʻōlelo ʻo Miyamoto o ka Farm Bureau, ua kūkā ʻia kēia pilikia ma Wakinekona me ko Hawaiʻi mau ʻelele ʻahaʻōlelo. Ua hāpai pū ʻo ia i ke kuhina o ke Keʻena Mahiʻai o ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa.
Ua ʻōlelo ʻo Love, e pono ka mokuʻāina e hānai mua i kona poʻe iho nō. Hoʻouna aku ka mokuʻāina he 20 miliona paona ʻālani a he 45 miliona paona maiʻa, wahi āna.
No laila, i loko nō o ka maikaʻi o ka hoʻonui ʻana i nā mea e hoʻouna ʻia aku ma kekahi mau ʻano, e pono pū e lilo he mea maʻamau nā papahana e ʻimi ana i nā pani no nā mea e hoʻouna ʻia mai i Hawaiʻi. Ua kākaʻahi iho nei ko Love hui he 12,000 kumu ʻālani a pūmaiʻa ma lalo o kahi papahana o ia ʻano e “kaulike” ai, wahi āna.

title: Free holiday parking returns to Providence Saturday, with tree lighting and festivities ahead
description: Free parking at designated metered parking spaces in Providence returns for the holiday shopping season starting Saturday, with up to two hours of free parking through Jan. 1, 2027. text:
Holiday revelers gather around an illuminated Christmas tree outside Providence City Hall during the city's annual tree-lighting celebration on Dec. 6, 2024. (Photo courtesy of Providence City Council)Free parking at designated metered parking spaces in Providence returns for the holiday shopping season starting Saturday, with up to two hours of free parking through Jan. 1, 2027.
The holiday break applies to the city’s main shopping and commercial hubs, including portions of downtown, Federal Hill, College Hill, Fox Point, Olneyville Square, Wayland Square and Hope Street. The free parking begins on Small Business Saturday as part of the returning PVD Holiday Festival, which will take place from Dec. 3 through Dec. 7. 
The city’s annual Christmas tree lighting is set for Saturday, Dec. 5, on the front steps of City Hall on Dorrance Street. Performers scheduled to entertain revelers at this year’s lighting include the Lillian Feinstein School Choir, Brown University’s Jabberwocks, TEN31 Productions Dance Company and R&B singer Lisa Bello.
Also scheduled to make a public appearance: Santa Claus himself, who will “arrive in style just in time to count down to the spectacular tree lighting,” according to the city. 
A free “Candy Cane Express Train” will operate on the evenings of Thursday, Dec. 3 and Friday, Dec. 4, and make stops throughout downtown. On Saturday, Dec. 5, a downtown holiday trolley will make stops at shops, restaurants, and festival events between Biltmore Park, Downtown, Federal Hill and Track 15. 
A holiday market will run throughout the weekend, at Grant’s Block, located at the corner of Westminster and Union Streets, featuring entertainment, workshops and a showcase of local artists and small business.
The Providence Rink will open Friday, Nov. 27, for public skating and ice bumper cars through March. The rink will also host free ice skating performances on Dec. 4.
City Hall will host its annual Hanukkah Spectaculah on Monday, Dec. 7, from 4:45 to 6 p.m., with a menorah lighting, traditional foods, art activities and live klezmer music.
A full schedule of holiday events and transportation options is available at the PVD Holiday Fest website.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: The dream of farming is alive and well in New Hampshire — but it’s still a tough row to hoe
description: Sustainable, local, farm-to-table food can sound especially appealing in a world of hyper-processed products and periodic food-safety scares.  That’s just one of several ideals cited by some of the newest small-scale farmers to take the plunge into the world of New Hampshire agriculture. “Food security is the main goal here,” said Walter Alce, who dreams […]
text:
Running a small farm in New Hampshire requires a strong community and support system, said Jesse Wright, field specialist in agricultural business management with UNH Extension. Here, she speaks with new and aspiring farmers during an Extension New Farmer School session in Rochester on Oct. 14. From left: Walter Alce, Maria Elena Potter, Deborah Stacy, Sam Monohon, Wright, and Lisa Aquizap. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Sustainable, local, farm-to-table food can sound especially appealing in a world of hyper-processed products and periodic food-safety scares. 
That’s just one of several ideals cited by some of the newest small-scale farmers to take the plunge into the world of New Hampshire agriculture.
“Food security is the main goal here,” said Walter Alce, who dreams of running a self-sustaining family farm with his wife and four children — and who, last year, took a major step toward that goal when he purchased Elm Farm in Francestown.
It’s not an unusual dream. Others across New Hampshire also aspire to work the state’s land to produce crops and livestock for their families and neighbors. But for those new to the field, there’s lots to learn about the realities and limitations of farming in New Hampshire. And sometimes that journey comes with hard lessons along the way, experts and new farmers said.
Standing in a wood-heated greenhouse, Sam Monohon, co-owner of Nerdy Turnip Farm, addresses a group of new and aspiring farmers on Wednesday, Oct. 14, at Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester. Monohon has co-owned Nerdy Turnip Farm for four growing seasons. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Food and community
Small family farms make up about 86% of all agricultural operations in the U.S., according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. In New Hampshire, that proportion is similar. According to 2022 data from the department, the median size of the state’s farms, by land area, is 37 acres; that year, the average operator took home $6,568 in net profit.
New and aspiring farmers come from diverse backgrounds, drawn to farming for many different reasons, said Jesse Wright, field specialist in agricultural business management with the University of New Hampshire Extension. 
With Caroline Beaton, Wright helps run the extension’s New Farmer School program, where some of those fledgling farmers gather. The class welcomes recent retirees and young adults; transplants and lifelong New Hampshire residents; and people who have dreamed of farming their whole life alongside people suddenly plunged into the field when they, say, inherited a family member’s land or married into a farming family, Wright said. 
Many, like Alce, were drawn to farming as a way to provide healthy food or other natural products for their family and community.
“This is where science and food and community and practicality all kind of meet together,” said Sam Monohon, who for four years has co-owned Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester, where New Farmer School students arrived for a tour of the grounds this fall.
Kale plants soak up October sunlight at Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Finding a field to plant in
One of the first and biggest barriers many aspiring farmers face is land access.
The high cost of property and limited amount of well-suited farmland coming onto the market are major hurdles for many, Wright said. 
“If you don’t have space, or a space that’s well suited to growing, it’s kind of a non-starter,” she said.
Alce and his wife searched for over three years before finding the right property that could support the chickens, pigs, cows and other livestock they wanted to raise. Navigating fluctuating interest rates and a competitive market for land was a frustrating and drawn-out process, he said.
At the same time, it felt like the puzzle piece that would make everything else fall into place.
“Land is something you can’t make more of,” Alce said. “You find the land, then anything else, and everything else, is possible.”
In the end, Alce said, success came down to “being in the right place at the right time and sending out the right email.”
But for others — some of whom cannot afford to purchase land themselves or struggle to find a suitable property — newer, creative approaches to secure land access can help, said Beaton. These include joining forces with other aspiring farmers to make joint land purchases; renting fields instead of buying land; and working with land trusts and other groups to access agricultural conservation land. 
A turnip launched by Sam Monohon, co-owner of Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester, sails over new farmer Allyson Traeger’s head and into the waiting hands of Robbin Ray, media relations director with the University of New Hampshire, on Wednesday, Oct. 14. Monohon welcomed new and aspiring farmers to her property for a tour that day as part of the “New Farmer School” program run by UNH Extension. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Sowing spreadsheets
Like the matter of land, many other parts of the high barrier to entry for beginning farmers are also financial. In a broad sense, one thing most non-farmers may not realize is the sheer amount of business savvy required to run a successful farm, Monohon said.
“Every farmer that I know is secretly a giant spreadsheet nerd,” she joked. “Doing the farming is kind of a small piece of what it ends up being, when you own the farm or when you manage or run the farm.”
Rising costs have also hit farmers, and the price of production for crops and livestock can be staggering for those just getting into farming. For Alce, that realization hit him when he first began looking into raising chickens.
“I think most of us don’t know the true cost of food,” Alce said. 
Government subsidies for large-scale farms can obscure the true cost of food and make it hard for small farms to compete, Alce said.
Turnips are ready for harvest at Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester on Oct. 14. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Wright recalled a conversation with an aspiring farmer and New Farmer School participant who calculated the total cost of producing their goods, from seeds to fertilizer, feed and labor, and concluded that to charge anything over the actual cost of production would price out members of their community.
Farmers must also contend with the normal costs of running a small business: accounting and payment processing, wages for their laborers and insurance, to name a few, Monohon said.
Marketing is a major task for farmers, who must cultivate a reliable customer base in addition to their crops and products. For many, this means reluctantly posting on social media.
“The shiny, beautiful, outside thing is the growing of the things, and the less fun thing is the number crunching and the Facebook posting,” Wright said.
Affording health insurance for themselves as well as their employees is a major burden on many beginning farmers and, in some cases, a barrier to entering the field, Beaton said. 
To make it work, many farmers work a day job. Alce and his wife both work 9 to 5, while Monohon’s husband, Caleb, works full time, allowing the couple and their two toddlers to access health insurance through his work. Many other participants in New Farmer School also said they work day jobs, have a family member who does or are retired.
It’s a difficult reality that can bring up complicated feelings for farmers. 
“There’s a lot of imposter syndrome feelings that I get,” Monohon said. “… It is a difficult thing to do without that kind of tie into society. Farming can kind of make you self reliant, but Caleb and I have not figured out a way to be entirely just on the farm.”
It’s a common struggle, Wright said: Aspiring farmers enter the field with big dreams and wholehearted visions for their future, while societal barriers make those dreams difficult to realize. 
Helping farmers access resources and promoting programs like incubator farms, extension trainings and community support is crucial to helping lessen the burden, as is transparency about the difficulty of the endeavor, she said.
It’s possible to achieve the dream of a small, sustainable farm successfully, she said, but not without multifaceted community support.
“I think we have to be done pretending that you can have a small farm in New Hampshire and support a family, support a lot of folks’ vision for what life can look like without some of these background levers being pulled,” she said. 
Tomatoes that dropped from the summer’s plants and escaped harvest lie on the floor of a greenhouse in Rochester on Oct. 14. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
A committed lifestyle
Beyond the finances, living as a farmer requires near-constant commitment.
One thing that some New Farmer School participants are dismayed to learn is that farmers “can’t necessarily go on vacation,” Beaton said. 
Alce said he decided against raising dairy cows after talking to other farmers, who told him they were a seven-day-a-week commitment. It’s knowledge-sharing and discussions like that, he said, that have helped him gather experience and avoid pitfalls as he gets his footing.
Contending with the unpredictability of growing is one of the biggest struggles of the farming life, said Monohon. Weather, pests and a revolving array of unforeseeable circumstances — like fungus or equipment problems — can turn plans upside down. 
But for Monohon, after four years of running the farm, the plunge has proven worthwhile. After the trial-by-fire days of navigating both farm ownership and parenthood for the first time, Monohon said, she feels a new era beginning. And though her day-to-day is still full of challenges, seeing the farm take on a life of its own has been both fulfilling and exciting.
“There’s something really wonderful about it,” she said. “… I have my little chunk of land that I’m going to do with what I can to make the greatest positive impact on this greater problem, and help protect my family and my friends and my community in future years.”
New and aspiring farmers stand among pieces of twine used to support tomato plants in a greenhouse at Nerdy Turnip Farm, in Rochester, on Oct. 14. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: With weeks until federal law changes, here’s what you need to know about hemp-based THC
description: With just three weeks until a strict new federal definition of hemp takes effect, business owners and consumers are scrambling to understand what the changes will mean for the availability of the intoxicating hemp-derived products like gummies and drinks that have been widely available for years. Minnesota’s top cannabis regulator said his office is preparin[...]
text:
A change in federal law coming next month could change the market for hemp-based THC drinks, seen here at a St. Paul market. (Photo by J. Patrick Coolican/Minnesota Reformer)

With just three weeks until a strict new federal definition of hemp takes effect, business owners and consumers are scrambling to understand what the changes will mean for the availability of the intoxicating hemp-derived products like gummies and drinks that have been widely available for years.
Minnesota’s top cannabis regulator said his office is preparing for either possibility: that the law takes effect, or Congress delays or overturns it.
U.S. Sen. (and Gov.-elect) Amy Klobuchar introduced a bill Tuesday with GOP Sen. Tim Sheehy of Montana that would loosen the definition of hemp and create a regulatory framework for intoxicating hemp products.
If things feel like they are in flux, it’s because they are. Here’s what you need to know about the new hemp law, what could yet happen and what it means for you.
How did we get here?
It all started back in 2018 when the federal Agriculture Improvement Act – better known as the Farm Bill – legalized hemp products containing up to 0.3% by weight of delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary compound in marijuana that produces a high.
That meant all sorts of hemp-derived THC products, such as gummies, beverages and topical ointments, were legal nationwide, as long as they met that 0.3% THC threshold. These products quickly became available in stores nationwide, but Congress did not create any mechanism to regulate them, leaving that to the states.
Some states, like Minnesota and Indiana, created their own regulations for hemp. But many others did not, and these products were essentially unregulated in many places.
In November 2025, Congress attempted to put the toothpaste back in the tube by passing a new definition of hemp that will outlaw most intoxicating hemp products in much of the country. Under the new rules set to take effect Dec. 11, any product containing more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per container will be considered marijuana under federal law. That standard is so strict that many nonintoxicating products, such as a topical balm containing the cannabinoid CBD, along with trace amounts of THC, will also become federally illegal.
What happens next in Washington?
Without further congressional action, the new law goes into effect next month, though a handful of bills have been introduced to either postpone or rewire the new rules. The legislation introduced this week is Klobuchar’s third hemp-focused bill of the session. So far, none have moved forward.
But some industry insiders are cautiously optimistic about the Klobuchar-Sheehy bill, also known as the Hemp Guardrails Act. The bill would raise the potency threshold for hemp products to a maximum of 1% by weight total THC (which includes all forms of tetrahydrocannabinol, not just delta-9); empower the Food and Drug Administration to regulate hemp products and producers; prohibit sales of hemp-derived products to those under the age of 21; create packaging and marketing standards; ban synthetic cannabinoids; and allow states to enact stricter regulations.
“Minnesota is a national leader in hemp, and our state has shown that we can protect kids and support responsible hemp businesses,” Klobuchar said in a statement, adding that the measure “would keep safe hemp products on store shelves, protect consumers from dangerous products, and ensure that farmers and small businesses can continue to operate, grow and create jobs.”
Outgoing Sen. Tina Smith of Minnesota also supports reversing the new law, citing a conversation with a Minnesota brewer. The industry has embraced hemp-based drinks but faces a challenging future in that market segment if the law goes into effect.
“I was just at an event with Utepils where the owner and I agreed that this federal ban is misguided and will hurt our brewers if it isn’t delayed, or better yet, reversed altogether,” Smith said in a statement.
A major potential roadblock remains: A pair of Republican senators — who are still in the majority during the lame-duck session — are vowing to block any bill that “extends, delays or builds a regulatory framework” around hemp products.
It’s possible that no deal is reached before the new Congress is sworn in next year. With large Democratic majorities in both houses and a White House that has signaled support for regulating hemp, the law could get an update in 2027, but passing laws is typically more difficult than blocking them.
In Washington, D.C., Beecher Vaillancourt was in a taxi on Tuesday during a “hill climb” trip to lobby legislators on behalf of the U.S. Hemp Roundtable. Vaillancourt, who owns the Minneapolis-based Foundry Nation and BLNCD Naturals brands of hemp-derived products with his wife, Allison, said his sales to distributors have also dropped off precipitously in recent months. But it’s been counteracted a bit by a spike in online sales, he said.
Vaillancourt’s companies held two “warehouse sales” to move unsold product in recent months. They’re working to build up wholesale and dispensary sales in Minnesota to compensate for the potential loss of out-of-state sales. They’re also in the process of getting an adult-use cannabis license to expand their product lines into the recreational marijuana market, he said.
In the event a deal is reached, Vaillancourt has stocked up on ingredients so they can immediately ramp up production again.
“We’re hedging our bets, optimistically,” he said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Buy Nothing Day free coat exchange in Providence turns 30
description: Head to the sprawling front lawn of the Rhode Island State House on Friday morning and you can get a warm winter coat for the attractive price of nothing. But it does cost a lot of time and effort — plus a 26-foot U-Haul — to gather the hundreds of coats to be given out […]
text:
Bags of donated winter clothing fill a 26-foot rental truck ahead of Rhode Island's 30th annual Buy Nothing Day Coat Exchange, scheduled for Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, at the State House in Providence. A volunteer stands amid the donations in the photo at right. (Photos courtesy of Lauren Testoni)Head to the sprawling front lawn of the Rhode Island State House on Friday morning and you can get a warm winter coat for the attractive price of nothing.
But it does cost a lot of time and effort — plus a 26-foot U-Haul — to gather the hundreds of coats to be given out gratis each year on Smith Hill as part of Rhode Island’s Buy Nothing Day Coat Exchange, which marks its 30th anniversary year. 
Chief organizer Lauren Testoni of East Greenwich said this year’s coat drive runs from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Friday, or until supplies run out, on the State House lawn, across from Providence Place. In the event of rain, Testoni said the event will be held in Gloria Dei Lutheran Church, right down the street.
Annual free coat giveaway set for Black Friday on R.I. State House lawn

The event’s placement across from Providence Place is somewhat ironic given its origins in the late 1990s as a local anticonsumerist effort and part of Buy Nothing Day, an anti-Black-Friday observance founded in 1992. 
The annual giveaway has historically distributed an estimated 1,500 coats a year. Testoni said she doesn’t keep a precise census of how many coats are collected or distributed, but a photo she shared of this year’s haul depicted a mountain of coat-filled bags packing into the interior of a 26-foot rental truck.
“Whatever that comes out to, I would say thousands,” Testoni said.
Demand remains substantial, Testoni noted, and seems to have grown alongside donations and the number of volunteers who help out.
“It’s grown in size, it’s grown in the amount of people that we can help, it’s grown in the number of donations we get and community partners we have,” Testoni said. “But I think the sad part is that the need has never gone away.”
Some former customers, Testoni said, have become part of the exchange’s stable of volunteers.
“We have people come year over year and truly like I only know their first names and I only see them this one day, and they are mostly people who were unhoused at some point,” Testoni said. “It’s nice to see that they stay, come back, help, give back, knowing where they were.” 
Testoni said that, beyond the holiday season when people are “very giving,” she hopes others think of people with unmet needs at other times of the year. 
“Just keep everyone in mind throughout the year would be my one thing that I would ask of everyone,” Testoni said. 
Donations are down slightly compared to previous years, Testoni said, but the items donated this year are generally of better quality. 
“I think the quality has gone up,” Testoni said. “We usually have a lot of filler stuff.”
Testoni and her mom, Pam, started leading the coat drive together about a decade ago, with the two of them working together as lead organizers for about seven years. Pam Testoni stepped down from the leadership role a few years ago, but still volunteers. Now after 10 years, Testoni is hoping to find a new leader for the charitable effort.
“I would just like to step back and be a volunteer rather than kind of running the whole show,” Testoni said in an interview Wednesday.
The most important qualification for her successor?
“Someone with a kind heart. That’s all I care about,” Testoni said.
More information, including where to donate, can be found on the Coat Exchange’s website. Testoni said the drive particularly needs children’s coats and adult sizes 3X and larger.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: How prepared meals are helping fill in food aid gaps in Portland and across Maine
description: Ron Stanley has been unhoused in Portland for six years, but it wasn’t until last October that he found a reliable place to secure a hot lunch. Now, Stanley, along with dozens of others, most of whom are unhoused, gather each day on Cotton Street to get two prepared meals along with dry goods, packaged […]
text:
Volunteers package hot meals at Cotton Street's food distribution site on Nov. 25, 2026. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Ron Stanley has been unhoused in Portland for six years, but it wasn’t until last October that he found a reliable place to secure a hot lunch. Now, Stanley, along with dozens of others, most of whom are unhoused, gather each day on Cotton Street to get two prepared meals along with dry goods, packaged food and drinks.
“I don’t know how people are going to get a hot meal if these guys don’t show up,” Stanley said, gesturing toward the volunteers handing out food.
“It’s always a pretty good meal too,” he said. “They’re always hot, they’re nutritious and they have people here that can support and counsel us, too.”
Ron Stanley at Cotton Street’s food distribution hub on Nov. 25, 2026. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
The meals come from nonprofit Preble Street, which prepares everything served on site at its Food Security Hub in South Portland. The City of Portland collaborates with the nonprofit, providing tables, chairs and a canopy for people to sit under and eat their meals. Volunteers from Milestone Recovery and various faith-based organizations often hand out meals.
“This fills the gap for people who are staying outside for consistent meal services, and it’s the lowest barrier option for consistent food in the city, especially with SNAP changes,” said Andrew Volkers, Preble Street’s director of health services and Street Outreach Collaborative. “In these times, hot food can really feel like a privilege.”
The need for services like the one on Cotton Street comes as food insecurity continues to rise across Maine. According to the latest national food insecurity data from Feeding America’s Map the Meal Gap study, 14.5% of Maine residents experienced food insecurity in 2024, up from 13.8% the previous year.
Since then, President Donald Trump’s administration has cut access to federal food assistance for thousands of Mainers. Combined with rising costs for food, energy and other essentials, an even larger percentage of people currently have limited or uncertain access to food. 
But for people who rely on services like those at Cotton Street, access to food is only part of what makes them important. The opportunity to sit down, share a meal and spend time with others can be just as meaningful, particularly during the holidays, Volkers said. Last year was the first Thanksgiving meal the nonprofit offered in downtown Portland.
“Last year on Thanksgiving when I was here, it just felt happy and lively, and there was a lot of camaraderie,” Volkers said. “Not only food-centric holidays, but family-centric holidays bring up a lot … like trauma, lack of social support, lack of family. So offering hot meals and pie, and just sitting with them for the afternoon I think is really important.”
The Cotton Street location is part of a broader effort by Preble Street to expand access to prepared food across Maine, which accelerated after the nonprofit opened its Food Security Hub in South Portland in 2025. 
There is more demand than ever among food pantries for prepared meals, according to Colin Freeman, the organization’s chief director of community partnerships. Now that the organization has a facility in which it can cook up to 2,000 meals a day, and store thousands of frozen fully prepared meals, they can come closer to meeting it. The kitchen has the capacity for them to eventually scale up to 10,000 meals every day. 
Volunteers and staff prep mushrooms at Preble Street’s Food Security Hub on Nov. 25, 2026. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
Those meals are prepared with produce donated by Maine farms and are distributed within Preble Street’s Portland shelters, on Cotton Street and — most recently — through Good Shepherd Food Bank to pantries across the state.
“Pantries really need to fill this market where there’s people that don’t have the time to be able to produce their own meals, because if you see the kind of food that they’re receiving, it’s dried beans and things that are laborious and take time to really create delicious meals out of,” Freeman said.
“So for somebody that’s trying to work, take care of their kids, keep a house over their head, and cook for their family at the same time, this kind of meal is such a helpful thing.”
Last month, Preble Street announced the partnership with Good Shepherd funded by a $150,000 grant from Hannaford Bros. The program, called Harvest to Home, has already offered more than 10,000 meals in the month since it launched, with the goal being 100,000 meals a year.
“Access to nutritious food means more than having something to eat, it means having food that supports health, well-being and dignity,” Good Shepherd Food Bank President Heather Paquette said in a statement announcing the partnership. “Together, we can reach communities across all 16 counties and strengthen our collective response to hunger.”
