name: Florida Phoenix
title: Commentary: We should all be thankful this powerful Florida senator got the boot
description: Happy Thanksgiving, y’all! This is the most Florida of holidays, and not just because everyone’s so delighted by the extreme Florida-ness of “Grand Theft Auto 6.” Despite what your teachers taught you while you were tracing the turkey-like outline of your hand, Thanksgiving started here, NOT Massa-dang-chusetts. The first Thanksgiving was celebrated in 1565 [...]
text:
High Oaks Ranch in Seminole County became the subject of a lengthy fight involving influential developer Chris Dorworth. Dorworth lost but his latest attempt to wreck the Seminole County rural boundary cost Sen. Jason Brodeur his job. (Photo via Save Rural Seminole)Happy Thanksgiving, y’all! This is the most Florida of holidays, and not just because everyone’s so delighted by the extreme Florida-ness of “Grand Theft Auto 6.”
Despite what your teachers taught you while you were tracing the turkey-like outline of your hand, Thanksgiving started here, NOT Massa-dang-chusetts.
The first Thanksgiving was celebrated in 1565 by the tin-hatted Spanish conquistadors who’d just landed in St. Augustine and the Native Americans who greeted them. If only the Pilgrims who showed up 50 years later had sailed southward to Florida, they could have spent their first winter lounging by the hotel pool.
As a result, I always look for something we Floridians can all be thankful for. Last year, for instance, I was thankful for alligators.
John Lowndes via Florida Senate
Sen. Jason Brodeur via Florida Senate
This year? I’m thankful that Sen. Jason Brodeur got booted from the Legislature, and you should be too.
Brodeur had what might have seemed like a safe seat. He was president pro tempore, the second highest position in the upper chamber. He had endorsements out the wazoo, including from the governor. He enjoyed beaucoup big-bucks contributors too.
But now he is, as Jim Carrey would say, a loo-hoo-hoooooooooser. He lost to an underfunded underdog, a Democratic candidate named John Lowndes, former mayor of Maitland.
It wasn’t even close. He lost by 12 points. Florida hasn’t seen a rout this bad since the Jaguars beat the Dolphins 62-7 in Dan Marino’s final game.
Gov. Ron DeSantis swore this wasn’t Brodeur’s fault. He was merely a victim of the blue tsunami that washed away Republicans across the country.
“That wasn’t a reflection of him,” DeSantis said, according to my Phoenix colleague Mitch Perry. “He got caught up in a wave,”
But Lowndes, in an interview with the Orlando Sentinel, pinpointed another problem, one that I think the entire Legislature should take note of:
Brodeur broke a promise to defend Seminole County’s rural boundary.
“It’s really a matter of trust,” Lowndes said. “I think Jason Brodeur broke faith with the voters when he flipped on the rural boundary.”
And he had some high-powered help with that betrayal, too.
 An embarrassing man
I wouldn’t call Brodeur’s recently extinguished political career “distinguished.”
In 2023, for instance, Brodeur filed a bill to require bloggers critical of state government to register with the state, a strategy I think George Orwell invented. National Review called the bill “an unconstitutional, moronic disgrace” and called Brodeur “an embarrassment to the GOP.”
Yet the man kept getting reelected. He served in the House from 2010 to 2018 and won his Senate seat in 2020. In 2022, the last time he was on the ballot, he won with 54% of the vote.
Not all his elections wins were — oh, what’s a polite word? — “clean.”
When he was elected to the Senate in 2020, Brodeur got a boost from a “ghost candidate” scheme similar to one that happened in South Florida.
In Brodeur’s case, a no-party candidate drained enough votes away from his Democratic opponent to help him triumph. Others involved wound up facing legal consequences, but Brodeur didn’t. However, the scandal did cost him his job as CEO of the Seminole County Chamber of Commerce.
Brodeur denied being involved, but one of the co-conspirators said he was in on it from the get-go.
But that scandal isn’t why a lot of people this year were hoping to mimic Ann-Margaret and warble, “Bye Bye, Brodeur!”
 How many hankies
A story in Politico bemoaned Brodeur’s loss to the environmental community as if he were the second coming of Marjory Stoneman Douglas. He did play a key role in 2021 in creating the Florida Wildlife Corridor.
Yet Florida bear advocates detested the man, and with good reason.
In 2014, Brodeur led a group of legislators calling for the state to hold its first bear hunt since 1994.
Unfortunately, the state wildlife commission listened to Brodeur and his buddies, not to the thousands of residents who opposed a hunt.
The 2015 bear hunt was a colossal disaster. The commission had to shut ir down after just two days. Hunters killed 33 lactating mama bears, leaving more than a few orphaned cubs.
As a result, the state didn’t hold another one until last year.
Why did the wildlife commission revive it? Brodeur again.
Brodeur sponsored a Senate resolution calling for a constitutional amendment enshrining the right to hunting and fishing. The amendment passed and became the FWC’s justification for reviving the bear hunt.
The language in the amendment seemed fairly benign — until you noticed that it insisted that those two recreational pursuits are the “preferred means of responsibly managing and controlling fish and wildlife.”
When bear advocates protested, Brodeur told them, “Hunting and fishing are the preferred methods of population control because, during the last 50 years, game animals are the only ones that seem to be thriving.”
Some smart aleck (OK, it was me), wrote that this was a load of what bears deposit in the woods.
The eagle population soared to the point it could be taken off the endangered list with no help from hunters. Manatees and alligators are two more examples.
When I learned Brodeur had lost, one of the first people i called was Chuck O’Neal of Speak Up Wekiva. He was one of the bear advocates who had tried to persuade Brodeur not to sponsor that resolution. I think O’Neal took the senator’s loss well.
“How many handkerchiefs did it take to dry my tears when I heard he lost?” O’Neal joked. “Zero!”
But even O’Neal said the issue that doomed Brodeur wasn’t bears. It was the Seminole County rural boundary — with help from a guy NAMED Bear.
 Slamming the door
To understand what happened, we have to rewind to the time a different former legislator tried to wreck the boundary.
Chris Dorwood via Florida House
Chris Dorworth wasn’t just any legislator. He had been chosen to become the next speaker of the House, one of the most powerful positions in Florida.
However, the voters had other plans for their ethically challenged representative. In 2012, they threw him out of his carefully drawn district seat.
If Dorworth’s name sounds familiar, it’s probably because of his loooong association with scandal-magnet Matt Gaetz. Just last month, two women sued Gaetz, Dorworth, and a third politician over alleged sex trafficking.
Five years after his electoral defeat, Dorworth was a developer who had his eye on a 669-acre parcel in Seminole County. Located east of the Econlockhatchee River, it was known as the High Oaks Ranch.
In 2017, according to the Orlando Sentinel, Dorworth signed a letter of intent to purchase it for more than $35 million. The deal was contingent on getting approval from Seminole County to rezone the land for (takes a deep breath) 600 single-family homes, 270 townhomes, 500 apartment units, and 1.5 million square feet of commercial and professional space.
The project would be named “River Cross.” What made people cross about River Cross was that it would bust up Seminole County’s rural boundary.
That boundary had been approved by voters in 2004 with more than 56% of the vote. A more modern version was approved in 2024 by 82 — far more than any candidate ever received.
The rural boundary covers almost the entire eastern third of Seminole County, protecting it from the kind of runaway growth that’s hit the rest of Central Florida. Within the boundary, some sections limit development to one home per five acres and others to one home per 10 acres. It’s all an effort to preserve the area’s rural character — something Dorworth seemed determined to wreck.
David Bear via subject
To oppose Dorworth’s project, a lawyer named David Bear helped form a group called Save Rural Seminole. Although Bear was a fellow Republican, he and the other supporters of the rural boundary wanted to slam the door on Dorworth.
The group was remarkably effective. The county commission unanimously rejected River Cross’ rezoning. You could say they Crossed it off the map.
Dorworth sued in both state and federal court — and lost. The federal judge was so disgusted with his specious claims that she ordered him to pay the county’s legal expenses of more than half a million dollars.
But Dorworth wasn’t done. His next attack was through the Legislature.
 Counting on short memories
Sen. Jonathan Martin doesn’t live anywhere near Seminole County. He represents a district 200 miles away in Fort Myers.
That area has no rural boundary. As a result, its rural areas are being rapidly wiped away by sprawl.
James Uthmeier via Office of Attorney General
Jonathan Martin via Florida Senate
Yet Martin asked Attorney General James Uthmeier about the constitutionality of the rural boundaries in both Seminole and Orange counties.
“When I learned about the rural boundary issue that was taking place in Central Florida, I was concerned about its effects down in my district, if that was something that people in Southwest Florida wanted to take a closer look at,” Martin said during a Senate committee meeting.
Last December, Uthemeier’s staff replied to Martin that those rural boundaries were likely unconstitutional because they restricted property owners from doing whatever they wanted with their land. At the least, counties should pay property owners for taking their property, the letter said.
Dorworth gleefully notified Seminole officials about the letter, bragging about getting help from Uthmeier.
Seminole County officials wrote back to Uthmeier, arguing that his analysis was wrong. Nobody’s property was being “taken,” they wrote, just the amount of development was limited. That protected the property rights of people who didn’t want to live in another Fort Lauderdale or Miami.
During a February Senate committee meeting, Martin brought up the AG opinion and announced he’d be offering an amendment to pro-developer Senate Bill 208 that would effectively gut those rural boundaries.
Brodeur had always sworn he was in favor of the rural boundary. But when Martin’s measure got to the Senate floor on the final day of this year’s session, Brodeur announced he now supported that.
He said Uthmeier’s opinion hit him “like a ton of bricks” because of “its clarity and forcefulness” and that’s why he was backing Martin’s amendment.
“If you’re going to take people’s property, if you’re going to restrict the use of your land … you got to give them money,” Brodeur said, according to Florida Politics. “You got to compensate them for it.”
Other senators were unconvinced or outright opposed. They voted against Martin’s last-minute amendment, although it’s likely to come back next year.
Kelly Martinez Semrad via Orange County
Later, when Orange County Commissioner Kelly Semrad saw Brodeur at a political event, she warned him that his flip-flop had angered a lot of voters in both parties.
“He said, ‘The voters have short memories,’” she told me. “He thought he’d be a part of the political landscape for a long time. He thought he’d be governor someday.”
Boy, was HE wrong!
 ‘Not a dang thing’
I tried repeatedly to call Brodeur this week to talk to him about what happened. He never responded.
Florida’s rural areas have been under increasing pressure from developers these days. Dorworth, for instance, popped up last month with a new slab of sprawl he wanted to shove down Seminole County’s throat. The county planning board recommended rejecting it.
A lot of state officials like Uthmeier, Martin, and Brodeur keep siding with the big-money boys like Dorworth and not listening to what the rural residents want.
As a result, the Legislature has worked to tip the scales further toward developers who want to invade rural areas and to block the public from having any say about it.
In an op-ed for the Sentinel, Bear wrote, “We expect our state elected officials to work for the people, not the donor class. We expect them to stand up to those in Tallahassee who are taking away our residents’ right to self-determination, even if they are within their own party.”
Bear’s organization, normally a nonpartisan one, repeatedly reminded the voters about Brodeur’s betrayal. It also pushed Lowndes despite his being a Democrat.
Lowndes is not perfect, Bear told me, “but at least we don’t have our own guy up there leading the charge against us.”
Members of the Legislature up for reelection in 2028 might want to look at what happened to Brodeur and learn from it. But if they continue to act as if (to quote House Speaker Sam Garrison) they didn’t learn a darn thing from this election, it might mean bye-bye for then just like Brodeur.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s food insecurity crisis needs a two-prong response
description: Because of federal cuts, thousands of CT men, women and children will be going hungry unless state legislators step up with emergency and long-term funds.
text:
It has been over a year since federal HR 1 (also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) was signed.  Research and real-life experiences have shown that program cuts within HR 1 have wrought havoc to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and those who depend on it (one in 12 CT residents).   
While this crisis was created at the federal level, the impact on our residents means that we must look to Connecticut leaders to respond to the hunger crisis HR 1 has exacerbated.  Even with the recent changes to the composition of Congress, any federal action to mitigate the damage done to SNAP will take time.   
To prevent further harm to Connecticut and our residents, we believe it is critical for our elected leaders to institute a two-pronged state-funded food assistance program.  Implementation should include both a long-term legislative solution as well as an immediate short-term response through our emergency reserve fund.  The emergency reserve fund was established to address the impact of HR 1 cuts exactly like those to SNAP. 
Connecticut’s former SNAP recipients are struggling to afford food for themselves and their families.  The time to act is now. 
The problem:
Since 2020, Connecticut’s food insecure population has increased by 54%.  Connecticut Foodshare reports that across Connecticut, one in seven people (15.3% or 560,760 people) do not have reliable access to affordable and nutritious food and are considered food insecure.  That includes one in five children, totaling over 137,000 kids statewide. Access to food has clearly been reduced by the cuts to SNAP assistance.   But eating is not optional.
Our organizations work with food providers, clients who are struggling to make ends meet and feed their families and those navigating the new web of expanded work rules and eligibility terminations as a result of HR 1.  SNAP (formerly known as Food Stamps) work requirements no longer exempt those aged 55 to 64, the homeless, veterans or some caregivers.  Additionally, food assistance for asylees, refugees and victims of human trafficking has been eliminated for those not yet legally permanent residents.  All of this is happening while we face astronomical grocery price increases.  
Work requirements have long been a component of SNAP eligibility.  But the jobs available for those with disabilities, limited skills or limited access, generally fail to raise incomes enough to make them self-sufficient.  Those same work limitations may now mean an individual will lose all support from SNAP, severely impacting their ability to afford a basic diet. 
While Connecticut Foodshare and their network of emergency food providers has heroically supplied the equivalent of 44.9 million meals across Connecticut during the 2026 Fiscal Year, access to food through local retailers, including grocery stores, convenience stores and bodegas, has decreased.  SNAP is designed to enable individuals to meet their food needs by purchasing food in their community with their SNAP subsidy. Feeding America reports that for every meal provided through their food bank network, SNAP provides about nine meals for hungry Americans.  
Many previously qualified SNAP recipients are no longer able to buy essentials – like milk, bread or eggs – at the grocery or corner store nearest to them.  Importantly, while food pantries do the best they can to support those in need, their hours and days are necessarily limited.  Working people may not be able to get to a pantry on a given day during specific open hours or have access to transportation to do so.   Grocery stores and neighborhood mom and pop shops are open late, on weekends – times when working people can stop in to get the food they need.
According to a September 2026 report from DataHaven, Connecticut lost approximately $11 million per month in SNAP benefits between June 2025 and June 2026.  Creating a state-funded food assistance program will ease the stress on our overburdened emergency food system and afford recipients the autonomy to shop as needed and align their food choices with their personal dietary and cultural needs.  It will also help food retailers recover from the loss in economic activity the SNAP cuts have forced on them.   
The CT Department of Social Services (DSS), which administers the SNAP program, initially estimated that 36,000 SNAP recipients could be at risk of losing benefits under HR1.  The actual losses are approaching double that estimate.  According to an August 2026 report issued by Connecticut Voices for Children, 62,770 recipients lost access to SNAP in Connecticut between July of 2025 and July of 2026, a decrease of 17.45%. 

SNAP enrollment decreased across Connecticut. Credit: CT Mirror

The two-part solution: 
Connecticut residents cannot wait any longer to receive the food assistance they need.  Connecticut leaders must:

Act immediately to implement an interim solution and use a portion of Connecticut’s remaining Federal Cuts Response Fund (currently holding approximately $250 million) and provide monthly benefits for food purchases to Connecticut residents cut-off from SNAP.


Create a long-term state-funded nutrition assistance program that mirrors SNAP, for those losing benefits.  Such a program will help restore access to food for residents, and access to cash flow for local farmers and retailers.

Every town in Connecticut has SNAP participants who depend on this program.  A state-funded food assistance program is an investment in our future.  We know that SNAP lifts our neighbors out of poverty and improves health outcomes.  We know that it helps our farmers and retailers through the economic activity it generates.  Purchasing power in our communities, at farm stands and farmers markets, must be bolstered.  We need the leadership of our governor and our legislators to meet this challenge.
The combination of rising food prices and energy costs, along with cuts to SNAP and Medicaid, is catastrophic for many of Connecticut’s residents.  They can’t do it alone. Connecticut must meet this challenge.
Submitted by Sara Parker McKernan on behalf of New Haven Legal Assistance,   CT Legal Services, Greater Hartford Legal Aid, Connecticut Voices for Children, United Way of Connecticut, Connecticut Veterans Legal Center, IRIS: Integrated Refugee & Immigrant Services and the Connecticut Food Association.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Beus Harris steps down, Stanek steps up, Madaleno steps forward, in political notes
description: Maryland Republican Party Chairwoman Nicole Beus Harris to step down after the party's drubbing at the polls, Jason Stanek takes a new federal role at PJM, and former state Sen. Rich Madaleno Jr. lands at the University System of Maryland, in political notes.
text:
Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) walks with his wife, Maryland Republican Party Chairwoman Nicole Beus Harris, at the 49th annual J. Millard Tawes Crab and Clam Bake in Crisfield in September. Beus Harris announced she would not run for reelection as chairwoman this fall. (Photo by Steve Crane/Maryland Matters)After a brutal election year for the GOP, the chairwoman of Maryland’s Republican Party announced this week she is stepping down.
“Election results this disappointing require a leader to step up and take responsibility for the losses,” Maryland Republican Party Chairwoman Nicole Beus Harris wrote in an open letter to party members Monday. “For that reason, I have decided not to seek another term.”
Even in already deep-blue Maryland, the Republicans sustained some surprising losses in this election. In Frederick County. state Sen. Bill Folden (R-Frederick) and outspoken Sheriff Chuck Jenkins were unseated by Democrats Lara Westdorp and Karl Bickel, respectively. Democrats also gained two seats in the House of Delegates and flipped county governments in Wicomico and Kent. In total, 27 political offices flipped from red to blue, according to the Maryland Democratic Party.
Beus Harris is the wife of Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st), who won reelection despite a formidable challenge from Democrat Dan Schwartz.
In her letter, posted to X on Monday, Beus Harris pointed to victories during her four-year tenure. The party raised $3.25 million to lift itself out of debt, launched a grassroots candidate recruitment effort and slightly increased Republican registration, Beus Harris said.
“The Maryland Republican Party has the foundation, the tools, and most importantly the people to win in the right election year,” Beus Harris wrote. The party will select a new chair at its winter convention in Annapolis on Dec. 12.
Federal pivot for Stanek
Former Maryland utility regulator Jason Stanek is taking on a new role at electric grid operator PJM Interconnection.
Come Dec. 9, Stanek, a former chairman of the Maryland Public Service Commission, will be the vice president of federal policy at PJM. In his new role, Stanek will “assume responsibility for all of PJM’s engagement and relationships in Washington D.C.,” including with its regulator: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
Jason Stanek, executive director of governmental affairs at PJM, will become the regional electric grid operator’s vice president of federal policy. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Stanek previously served as PJM’s executive director of governmental services, coordinating the grid’s various liaisons to state governments.
Stanek made occasional stops to Annapolis to testify before the state legislature. He also appeared at this year’s Maryland Association of Counties conference in Ocean City.
“I’m honored to be appointed to this role. PJM is important to the continued health and vitality of 67 million consumers, and we need to partner with our regulator and policymakers in Washington to make sure that we tackle the most pressing issues facing the grid today for the benefit of those consumers,” Stanek said in a news release.
PJM, the largest grid operator in the country, has faced pressure from the White House and a host of other elected officials who argue that it must step in to protect customers from the costs of building out the grid to power data centers. The PJM grid includes Northern Virginia, which hosts one of the largest concentrations of data centers worldwide.
Stanek will help the grid “establish a more active DC presence,” said Asim Z. Haque, PJM’s executive vice president of governmental and member services, in the news release.
“Jason’s knowledge, experience and integrity will serve him well as PJM’s chief liaison in Washington D.C.,” Haque said. “He has already established himself as an independent and trusted voice within the energy community, and his background is necessary to ensure that we are being responsive to our regulator and understand the avenues for educating policymakers about the challenges the grid is facing today.”
New gig for Madaleno
A former state senator with a ton of budget experience and legislative street cred is headed to the University System of Maryland next month.
Richard Madaleno Jr., the soon-to-be former chief administrative officer for Montgomery County, joins the system as its next vice chancellor of government relations.
Montgomery County Chief Administrative Officer Richard Madaleno. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Chancellor Jay A. Perman, in a letter Tuesday to staff, lauded Madaleno for his budget expertise and past support of the system.
“Rich believes that no Maryland organization is more critical to the state’s success and growth than the USM,” Perman wrote. “He says the challenges that Maryland faces right now need the USM to solve them. And to do that, he says, we need the state’s support. Rich has exactly the right reputation, the right relationships, and the right résumé to help us win that support.”
Madaleno takes over on Dec. 14 and will succeed Susan Lawrence, who retires next month.
Since 2020, Madaleno has worked in Montgomery County government, first as director of the county’s budget office and more recently as the chief administrative officer overseeing a county budget of $7 billion and roughly 10,000 employees.
Prior to that, Madaleno served four terms in the General Assembly. His tenure included a decade in the Senate where he served as vice chair of the Senate Budget and Taxation Committee.
“Rich’s deep experience and influence in fiscal policy—burnished over decades as an administrative officer, an elected leader, and a legislative analyst—will be vital as we head into another challenging budget year; as we advocate for the investment we need to educate 178,000 students, to produce a competitive Maryland workforce, and to conduct and commercialize the R&D that fuels economic growth statewide,” Perman wrote.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Denby Fawcett: Bishop Museum Races To Save A Shark Named Megamouth
description: Why we should care about a goofy looking fish with Botox-like lips. It’s an astonishing story – a Hawaiʻi story.
text:
I was invited recently by my friend Catherine Cruz to be her “plus one” at a small private party at the Bernice Pauahi Bishop Museum to commemorate the discovery off Oʻahu 50 years ago of the shark Megamouth.
I went mainly to get out of the house after a long day of writing in our cramped kitchen pantry, now my home office. I anticipated nothing more than a change of scenery, free food and conversing with fish scientists.
Instead, I ended up amazed. 
After the wine, spring rolls and kalua pork sliders, the scientists presented the timeless story of how Megamouth was discovered on Nov. 15, 1976.
The historic finding was accidental. A U.S. Navy vessel was doing deep water research 25 miles off Oahuʻs Kahuku Point. It had set two parachute anchors at a 540 feet depth to steady the boat in waters almost three miles deep.
When crew members winched up the anchors, they were stunned to find a nearly 15-foot long, strange-looking shark entangled in one of them. The creature had bitten one of the anchors and suffocated as it tried to free itself. It was dead.

The German chocolate cake prepared to celebrate Megamouth. (Denby Fawcett/Civil Beat/2026)

The German chocolate birthday cake we ate at the party was to commemorate the date of the shark’s discovery – actually the day of its death. But it is better to think of the delicious pastry as marking the day the shark became of service to science. 
Ensign Linda Hubble, aboard the vessel that day, recognized the animal was different, something she had never seen. When the crew returned to shore, she called Leighton Taylor, then director of the Honolulu Aquarium.
When Taylor arrived at the Navy’s dock at Kāneʻohe Bay, he saw only the shark’s tail hanging from the winch. Its 1,500-pound body was so heavy it had fallen back into the ocean and had to be retrieved by divers to make it whole again.
In the scientific paper he later co-authored, Taylor described it in formal scientific language as “a strange shark…extraordinary in its distinctness and its great size.” In layman’s terms it could be characterized as “freaking weird.”
It had a bulbous head, wide flappy lips, a huge mouth that could open three-feet wide and teeny little backward-facing teeth.

Megamouth was brought in to the dock of the U.S. Naval Undersea Laboratory at Kaneohe Bay to be held until Leighton Taylor could arrange for it to be transported to Honolulu for further study. (Courtesy: U.S. Navy)

“It is a goofy-looking shark, more like a cartoon character with its big head, enormous mouth and floppy fins,” said Richard Pyle, the museum’s senior curator of ichthyology.                  
Taylor realized this was not only a new species but a new genus and new family of shark. 
The Megamouth specimen is a holotype, the particular specimen designated as the reference for the scientific name of the species. Scientists can compare a newly found organism to a holotype in determining if it is an already known species or something entirely new. 
Today, 50 years later, Taylor still remembers the discovery with great excitement. “It was very unusual in the 20th century to find not just a new species but an entirely new family of shark. It makes you wonder what else is in the ocean we don’t know about.”
Taylor named the shark Megachasma pelagios, the Greek for “giant yawner of the open sea.” Bruce Dunford, a Honolulu-based reporter for the Associated Press, broke the story of the discovery, giving the shark what became its permanent common name “Megamouth.” 



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

In his research, Taylor determined the shark did not eat hunks of flesh like most other sharks, but was a filter feeder that consumed its food by opening its mouth wide to take in plankton — tiny shrimp and crab-like organisms — while simultaneously flushing water out through its gills.
Megamouth is among just three other filter-feeding shark species known to exist, along with the basking shark and the whale shark. 
Taylor calls it a “gentle giant,” about as far away from Jaws as you could possibly get.
On its discovery day, a flatbed truck delivered the shark to Hawaiian Tuna Packers at Kewalo Basin. There it was flash-frozen until a preservation container could be built to transport it to its permanent home at the Bishop Museum.
It has been in the museum’s fish collection for the last 50 years, resting in a bath of isopropyl alcohol in the original fiberglass box that was supposed to be only temporary.
Dr. Richard Pyle, senior curator of ichthyology and director of natural sciences at Bishop Museum, is reflected as he looks over the first megamouth shark specimen put on scientific record. The specimen — the first of its kind to be discovered, already turned 50 this year but needs a new storage facility and preservation tank. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
The 50-year-old box has chronic leaking problems. Pyle says if the shark is not moved to a new container in the next two years, it could be lost to science forever.       
“It would be totally tragic; an incredibly bad thing to lose it,” said Taylor.
It is the rarest and largest specimen in the museum’s collection. But the museum admits it won’t be easy to raise the $300,000 needed to construct a new room where it will install three new stainless steel tanks, specially ordered from New Zealand; one for Megamouth and the two other tanks for shark specimens from the museum’s fish collection.

Dr. Richard Pyle, senior curator of ichthyology and director of natural sciences at Bishop Museum, looks over the megamouth shark in Honolulu. The specimen turns 50 this year but needs a new storage facility and preservation tank. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026) (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)

The fundraising is challenging because Megamouth is not a warm and fuzzy creature and most people will never get to see it because of preservation concerns, such as light and temperature changes that might deteriorate it.
Fish collection manager Calder Atta says Megamouth’s container is opened only about every two years and then, only to make sure it is intact and to replenish it with alcohol.
“We are very selective about who can view the specimen due to its importance and the fragility of the container. Generally, it’s limited to those involved in megamouth research or who take care of the specimen,” said Atta.
Megamouth’s container sits in a cramped room in an off-limits area the museum likes to call the “fish library.” It includes numerous shelves with tens of thousands of jars containing 130,000 individual specimens of fish.
“It is definitely a challenge to ask the public for money to save something that can never be seen. And Megamouth is not adorable like a puppy or a kitten,” said Janet Bullard, the museum’s vice president for marketing and communications.
Taylor agrees: “Megamouth is a hard sell. There is no way you can call it cute.”
But there’s an extraordinary story behind the shark’s discovery and its subsequent scientific importance. Once that is more widely known, the “sell” will be easier, museum officials say.
“It is Hawaiʻi’s own. It was discovered in Hawaiʻi’s waters. We must try to tie Megamouth to a sense of local pride,” said Liza Lee, the museum’s director of individual giving.
Bishop Museum commissioned Honolulu artist Casey Lee to create this painting to show what Megamouth looks like alive, feeding in the ocean. (Denby Fawcett/Civil Beat/2026)
Artwork has been commissioned to show the shark not as a cadaver but alive, consuming plankton while swimming in the deep ocean. Also, a new video shows the importance of Megamouth to our understanding of the extraordinary biodiversity of the Pacific Ocean. In addition, there is also a plan to create a life-size replica of Megamouth that can be displayed publicly.

The Bishop Museum is reviewing these toy concepts for future sales  its store and donor gifts. (Denby Fawcett/Civil Beat/2026)

And, to accomplish the seemingly impossible task of making cute what can never be cute, the museum is reviewing designs for a new Megamouth plushie toy to sell in its shop and give to donors.
Megamouth will always be priceless to me because of its amazement factor – just to know that a creature so freaking weird had been down in the ocean for tens of millions of years without any of us even knowing it is astonishing.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Independent Jesse Battles remains winner of tight state Senate race after recount
description: Independent conservative candidate Jesse Battles remained the winner of a northeast Alabama Senate race following an automatic recount conducted Wednesday.  Senate District 10 consists of Cherokee and Etowah counties and a part of DeKalb. In Cherokee County, there was one less vote for Battles in the recount than in the original tally, and Jones’ tabulation [...]
text:
Jesse Battles is running as an independent candidate in Senate District 10. Battles remained the winner of Senate District 10 after an automatic recount on Wednesday. (Via jessebattles.com)Independent conservative candidate Jesse Battles remained the winner of a northeast Alabama Senate race following an automatic recount conducted Wednesday. 
Senate District 10 consists of Cherokee and Etowah counties and a part of DeKalb. In Cherokee County, there was one less vote for Battles in the recount than in the original tally, and Jones’ tabulation stayed the same. In DeKalb County, Battles gained one vote, and Jones’ votes remained the same.
The results for Etowah County were not immediately available Wednesday evening. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Battles defeated incumbent Sen. Andrew Jones, R-Centre. In a statement posted to Facebook Wednesday evening, Battles said he looks forward to working with Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville and Senate leadership.
“From the beginning, I have been open and honest about my Republican values, but my promise to District 10 is simple: I am here to serve every one of you. My focus will always be on what is best for our district, and I will work with anyone willing to help move Northeast Alabama forward,” he said.
Jones said in a Facebook post that he called Battles and congratulated him.
“While we came up short following today’s recount, in the end, more votes were found for both candidates. From day one, I have held firmly to the belief that every vote in the Senate District 10 race should be counted,” he said.
Battles’ margin of victory was less than 0.5% in the Nov. 3 election, leading to a recount. The State Elections Canvassing Board on Monday certified the Nov.3 general election, which started the recount process.
Battles originally sought to challenge Jones in the Republican primary for the district, but was removed from the ballot by the Alabama Republican Party in February. According to The Anniston Star, Battles faced allegations that he had done work for former Alabama House Minority Leader Craig Ford, D-Gadsden, who ran against Jones as an independent candidate in 2018.
Battles accused the “Montgomery establishment” of removing him from the primary, and gathered enough signatures to win ballot access as an independent.
Jones, who started the campaign with about $432,000, reported raising $1 million and spending $1.2 million on the race, according to campaign finance reports. Battles raised $142,000 and spent about $135,000.
There will be 24 Republicans, 10 Democrats and one independent in the upper chamber. The Legislature will convene for the 2027 Regular Session on Feb. 2.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Gun-rights groups sue — again — to block law banning ‘machine gun convertible’ pistols
description: Gun-rights advocate Mark Pennak often warns lawmakers their gun legislation will land in court -- and in the case of Senate Bill 344, he was right three times over. That's how many suits have been filed against the law that would ban "machine gun convertible" pistols.
text:
An unloaded Glock 19X handgun sits next to a magazine and 9mm ammunition at a gun range. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)Gun-rights advocate Mark Pennak routinely warns lawmakers in Annapolis that gun legislation they’re proposing will land in court.
In the case of Senate Bill 344, he was right three times over.
That’s how many lawsuits have been filed against the law, which would ban the sale, manufacture or possession of any semiautomatic pistol with a “cruciform trigger bar,” which the bill’s backers say are particularly susceptible of being converted into machine guns with simple household tools.
Critics say the law is so broadly drawn that it would effectively ban an entire class of popular, safe handguns on the chance that they might be converted.
“What they’re punishing is the dealers and law-abiding Marylanders who purchase these extremely safe, reliable pistols because of actions of criminals, and that’s just wrong,” Pennak, an attorney and president of the gun rights group Maryland Shall Issue, said Tuesday.
Sen. Sara Love (D-Montgomery), the lead sponsor of the bill, said she is not worried about the challenges.
“I have confidence that the court will uphold the law,” Love said Tuesday. “We did a lot of research and review of Supreme Court precedence, and this bill falls squarely within them.”
Sen. Sara Love (D-Montgomery) testifies before Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee in February on Senate Bill 344. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
The latest challenge was filed Friday in U.S. District Court in Maryland by Glock, which pioneered the cruciform trigger more than 40 years ago, other gun manufacturers that use the design, a shooting sports foundation and a Waldorf gun shop.
The bill became law on Oct. 1, but the ban on sale and manufacture of guns with a cruciform trigger bar is not set to take effect until Jan. 1. It says a person or a retail business cannot “manufacture, sell, offer for sale, purchase, receive, or transfer a machine gun convertible pistol.”
The bill wouldn’t apply to current law enforcement officers or those who are retired, and those in the military. Also, current gun owners who own a Glock would be allowed to keep them.
That pistol converter is commonly known as a Glock switch, most often used on the popular Glock handguns. Glock is not targeted in the law, but is a lead plaintiff in the suit that claims the law violates the Second Amendment.
“That is because the Second Amendment protects the possession and use of weapons that are ‘in common use at the time,’ full stop,” according to the suit. “Efforts to ban an entire class of ‘arms’ that is overwhelmingly chosen by American society for [a] lawful purpose – such as cruciform-trigger handguns – thus fail constitutional muster under any standard.”
The suit also claims the law would hurt the state’s economy by banning a type of weapons that last year saw “tens of millions” of sales of cruiciform-trigger guns. One of the plaintiffs, Shadow Systems, couldn’t sell its pistols in California after July 1 due to the passage of Assembly Bill 1127, which, like Maryland’s law, prohibits the sale, transfer and delivery of a “semiautomatic machinegun-convertible pistol.”
The suit claims California has loss nearly $3.8 million of annual revenue, which represents 11% of Shadow System’s overall business.
The 35-page suit was filed against the Office of the Attorney General and Maryland State Police. Representatives from both agencies declined to comment via email Tuesday.
Supreme Court won’t take up Maryland gun rights case

Two separate lawsuits were filed in October challenging SB 334, but they were consolidated into one case in federal court naming the attorney general’s office, state police and Gov. Wes Moore (D) as defendants.
U.S. District Court Judge Richard D. Bennett last month declined to issue a preliminary injunction against the law in that case. His decision to let the law take effect was praised by Everytown for Gun Safety, which said in an Oct. 6 statement that convertors allow guns to shoot hundreds of rounds per minute.
“No matter how many reckless challenges the gun lobby launches in the hopes of selling more products, Everytown will always stand up for common-sense laws to keep Marylanders safe,” said John Feinblatt, president at Everytown for Gun Safety.
Pennak’s organization, Maryland Shall Issue, is one of the plaintiffs in the consolidated case. Pennak said Tuesday the case remains pending.
“We welcome their participation. I think it’s great that they’re there,” he said about the plaintiffs in Friday’s suit. “It may well be consolidated with other cases that are already brought and pending. So, we’ll see.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Gov. Jeff Landry goes quiet on LSU standoff with SEC
description: Gov. Jeff Landry remained uncharacteristically quiet Wednesday about the latest, and most dramatic, development in the intensifying standoff between LSU and the Southeastern Conference. The SEC has scheduled a Dec. 3 meeting of its 16 member schools to decide whether to expel LSU, one of its founding members. The conference says LSU violated eligibility rule[...]
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry took part in a Thanksgiving turkey giveaway Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026, at Nunez Community College in Chalmette. (Photo by Julie O'Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator)Gov. Jeff Landry remained uncharacteristically quiet Wednesday about the latest, and most dramatic, development in the intensifying standoff between LSU and the Southeastern Conference.
The SEC has scheduled a Dec. 3 meeting of its 16 member schools to decide whether to expel LSU, one of its founding members. The conference says LSU violated eligibility rules that prohibit athletes who have played professional sports when men’s basketball coach Will Wade played RJ Luis in a game last week against the University of Louisiana at Monroe. Luis was on the Boston Celtics’ roster during the 2025-26 preseason, totaling 8 minutes played over three games before he was waived.
The governor spent the day before Thanksgiving leading turkey giveaways in St. Bernard Parish and announcing a five-year waiver of tolls on the new Belle Chasse bridge. During those stops, he repeatedly declined to answer questions about the dispute between LSU and the Southeastern Conference and refused to say whether he agreed with Wade’s decision to play Luis.
“That’s a better question to ask the president of LSU and the lawyers,” Landry said. “Again, as we continue down this unfortunate path, we will unfortunately have to leave it in the hands of the lawyers.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
LSU System President Wade Rousse last week directed Wade not to play Luis again once the Southeastern Conference moved in federal court to exert its authority to expel the university from the league. Luis has since filed a lawsuit against the NCAA, the Southeastern Conference and its commissioner Greg Sankey.
The subdued tone from Landry is far more reserved than what he used in early September, when the conference first threatened to kick LSU out of the league over adding athletes to its football roster who had once been under professional contracts.
At the time, coach Lane Kiffin was considering suiting up the players for LSU’s season opener against Clemson, but Kiffin backed down following a contentious court hearing in Baton Rouge over whether the players were eligible.
Back then, Landry was defiant in his defense of LSU and Kiffin and clapped back at criticism online and in public appearances.
“Remember, LSU didn’t create the litigation in Louisiana. LSU didn’t create the litigation in Alabama. The SEC did,” Landry said during a Fox News appearance Sept. 10. “Our university has been stuck in the middle of this. Yet, the SEC tries to villainize LSU.”
Since taking office almost three years ago, the governor also hasn’t been shy about his general interest in LSU athletics.
A little over a year ago, he publicly blasted LSU’s then athletic director Scott Woodward at a news conference that went viral — the day before Woodward was forced out of his job.
Since that time, the LSU Board of Supervisors, whose members are appointed by the governor, has replaced the university’s athletic director, president, football coach and basketball coach with people who Landry has praised.
In April, Landry even hinted that he had a hand in LSU’s controversial decision to rehire Wade as the men’s basketball coach. LSU had fired Wade in 2022 when the NCAA charged him with recruiting violations.
When a columnist for The Times-Picayune asked Landry if he was involved in rehiring Wade, the governor responded, “I helped wherever I could.”
“Will and I are very close. I was sad that we didn’t pick him up last year (in 2025). It was something that irritated me. LSU missed an opportunity. It’s why there was a big change in leadership over there (in the athletic department),” he told the newspaper.
Yet on Wednesday, when Landry was asked if he agreed with the characterization that he is “intimately involved” with decisions about LSU athletics, the governor tried to change the subject.
“I’m intimately involved in getting the tolls off of the Belle Chasse bridge,” he responded, while leading a press conference in the Plaquemines Parish Government Center.
Venture Global, which operates massive liquified natural gas terminals in Plaquemines and Cameron parishes, has put up the $35 million needed to remove tolls on the bridge. An exact start date for the five-year waiver period wasn’t announced Wednesday.
