title: Developing: Army detonates degraded lead azide in Middletown
description: The U.S. Army intentionally detonated degraded, lead-based explosive Wednesday morning in southeast Iowa. The operation has drawn public criticism in Iowa, and across the country, due to concerns of the spread of lead, which is toxic, from the detonation. The Army decided to go ahead with the blast, after significantly increasing mitigation strategies and wo[...]
text:
A plume is visible from the detonation of nearly 5 tons of lead-based explosive material in Middletown, Iowa Nov. 25, 2026. (Screenshot via C-SPAN livestream)The U.S. Army intentionally detonated degraded, lead-based explosive Wednesday morning in southeast Iowa.
The operation has drawn public criticism in Iowa, and across the country, due to concerns of the spread of lead, which is toxic, from the detonation.
The Army decided to go ahead with the blast, after significantly increasing mitigation strategies and working to evacuate the area, because they determined intentional detonation was the best way to get rid of the material which was liable to detonate on its own.
The Army said it would update the public about the status of the operation by 11 a.m. at the latest.
The most recent maps from the U.S. Army showed lead particles released from the blast were likely to travel southwest of the site, as far as 100 miles over the next several hours. Dust with lead particles was expected to settle as far as 40 miles southwest of the blast site.
Folks in those areas have been advised to remain indoors, with windows and doors closed until the Army gives an all clear. Updates can be found online. The Army is also working with FEMA to distribute mobile notifications to people in the area.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Army have been in Middletown and surrounding communities taking samples and are slated to take samples following the detonation to determine how much lead was released by the blast.
EPA has published a dashboard with air sampling and monitoring.
This story will be updated as more information is released.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: ‘Wild West Mentality’: Kaʻū Unites Amid Insurance, FEMA Denials
description: Koali Street is emblematic of the southern portion of the Big Island, where survivors of Hurricane Lala struggle to cover the cost of recovery as they live in fear of another big storm.
text:
Three months after Hurricane Lala, the 100 or so residents of Pāhala’s Koali Street are exhausted. 
Their homes abut Pā’au’au Gulch and, on the night of the storm, water from several rivers flowed together, filling the gulch with fallen trees which in turn sent much of the water rushing straight to their homes. Many were trapped overnight, surrounded on all sides, watching floodwaters rise indoors and out. A man living at the top of the street had to break a window to escape.  
Once the water subsided on this southern outpost of the Big Island, the residents of Koali Street went to work. Like their neighbors all over Kaʻū, they have spent the last 102 days removing rubble, cleaning up and repairing their homes and yards, gradually replacing appliances and other important possessions that washed away in the pounding rain. And, for many, losing the fight against creeping black mold. 
Most had hurricane insurance, and yet they have been denied payment by companies that claim it was a flood that hit, not a hurricane. Then, last month, the Federal Emergency Management Agency rejected the state’s request to provide individual assistance for hurricane victims of either of this summer’s hurricanes. 
Some on Koali Street are waiting to see if the appeal the state filed two weeks ago will make a difference. Others are less optimistic; they see the FEMA denial as one more sign that Kaʻū — the largest, and one of the most rural districts in the state — is destined to be left behind. 
State and local lawmakers say they’re working to put plans in place to support the region, if not this time, then when the next big disaster hits. And Governor Josh Green has said the the state might be able to cover the costs.
The people who live on Koali Street are not waiting.
Falling Through the Cracks
This wasn’t the first flood to hit Koali Street, which at six blocks runs nearly the entire length of the plantation town, but it was the worst anyone could remember. 
Stephanie Correa, a third-generation Pāhala resident, said her father built a retaining wall around her family home years ago. It was damaged by the earthquake months before Hurricane Lala, which left visible cracks and cement bricks out of place. She received a quote for $85,000 to repair the wall, but it’s not the only cost she has to consider.
Stephanie Correa’s mother’s home on Koali Street borders the Pā’au’au Gulch, which became the source of flooding for surrounding residential areas when Hurricane Lala struck. (Ronit Fahl/Civil Beat/2026)
Mold on the walls and ceiling bloomed immediately after the home was partially flooded. Even after weeks of humidifiers and peroxide it’s still discolored. The home’s flooring has been warped in places and needs to be replaced, and the roof also needs repairs. 
“In this devastating time we’re trying to figure out how to rebuild, and then we have contractors who want to skin us alive. So that’s disheartening,” said Correa. She works  during the day and cares for her mother in the evenings. Now, at 56, she’s considering pulling money out of her retirement account to cover the repairs. 
Up the street a little ways, Delvin Navarro and his wife Shawnette had a rock retaining wall beside their one-story home to protect it from flooding, too, but Lala tore it apart as if it were made of Lego. They were quoted $55,000 to fix it. 
“Right off the bat when the insurance didn’t help anybody we kind of knew that the ball was in our court.”Delvin Navarro, whose rock retaining wall was torn apart by lala
Navarro, who farms coffee on a nearby plot of land and processes it entirely in his backyard, also lost a portion of his harvest. So in between long hours harvesting more coffee, he rebuilt the wall himself for $7,000 in materials.
Navarro saved the receipts, but he’s not expecting to be reimbursed. 
“Right off the bat when the insurance didn’t help anybody,” he said, “we kind of knew that the ball was in our court.”
He has heard that a number of the street’s residents are planning to relocate. But many don’t really feel they have that option. 
Take Graciano and Frando Libunao, two brothers in their 80s who live near the top of the street in a modest house elevated about 5 feet above the ground. Although they could stay with relatives if needed, they have no plan to move. 
On a recent Sunday, the Libunaos were sitting under a tarp in their carport. They said they had lost their brand new washer and dryer, most of their tools and nearly everything else they’d been storing in their yard — and they had given up hope of recovering any of it. 
Marcos Domingo, their neighbor in his 70s, offered a tour of his carport and shed, which had filled up with mud in the storm. Beside a shredded fence, his family was drying laundry and a pile of large burlap bags filled with dried coffee had turned black with mold. 
Down the street, Melani Manantan said her whole family is sleeping in their living room while her husband Carlo replaces most of the flooring and drywall in their home, between shifts at the Kaʻū hospital. He’s had some help from her dad, but it’s slow work. 
“It’s every day, one day at a time,” Manantan said. “It’s very tiring.” 
This culture of self-reliance has gotten many Kaʻū residents through rough times in the past, but it may also be part of why the district has received less support than it needs — especially now that the post-Lala influx of help has slowed to a trickle. 
Marcus Domingo’s carport and shed filled up with mud during Hurricane Lala. (Ronit Fahl/Civil Beat/2026)
“We largely avoided the number of casualties that we probably could have had if we didn’t have such a strong, tight-knit community that really activated and gave everything that they possibly could,” said Zed Aki, the newly elected County Council member for District 6, which includes Kaʻū and South Kona. “It’s this Wild West country mentality.” 
That cuts both ways, too, he added: Fewer fatalities also means the disaster will receive less lasting attention from communities outside Kaʻū. And because so many people sprang into action, and continue to make many of their own repairs, he worries that the damage may not have been documented in great enough detail to help the state justify the need for federal support. 
Latest From Civil Beat
State Rep. Jeanne Kapela, who represents a sizable district on the southern end of the Big Island, was on the ground in Kaʻū right after the storm, coordinating distribution of generators and other donated goods to residents right. Like others in positions of power and responsibility, Kapela has been looking back at what happened and how it might have contributed to the FEMA denial. 
Hundreds of Kaʻū residents showed up to support one another. It was chaotic, and effective at getting many people’s basic needs met, but there wasn’t always time for documentation, she observed.
“One of the biggest hubs was not taking any paperwork, so not one person that came in and out of that hub in the first two weeks filled out those Civil Defense report forms,” she said. “Those are the forms that we use to qualify for individual assistance.”
“You have these smaller communities that literally fall through the cracks. When you look at Kaʻū, the whole thing is a crack.”State Rep. Jeanne Kapela
As Kapela sees it, a big part of the problem stems from the absence of regional disaster plans in the county, which might have made for a smoother recovery process as well as more thorough documentation.  
“If FEMA requires that the closest agency acts first, which is technically the county, then it might be upon the state to come in and support the county in creating regional disaster plans,” she said.
Until that happens, she said, “You have these smaller communities that literally fall through the cracks. When you look at Kaʻū, the whole thing is a crack.”
Community members gather for a meeting in Pāhala in mid-November. Their homes were badly damaged when Hurricane Lala struck Pahala. (Ronit Fahl/Special to Civil Beat/2026)
The Community Meets To Talk Story 
On a recent afternoon, around 35 people gathered on an empty lot at the top of the street, near the edge of the gulch, to share their experiences of the prolonged recovery with Civil Beat, and to hear from one another. 
Correa had worked with Kerry Vekhov — a businessman based in Kailua-Kona who has volunteered his time and equipment in Kaʻū and interviewed dozens of residents about their recovery experiences for his social media account — to convene the gathering. Vekhov, who lent Koali Street residents his equipment to remove debris immediately after the storm, had no shortage of ideas to share about the collaboration needed to prevent an even larger disaster on the street. 
“We see that the county has done a lot of clearing of structures and roads, but at this point we see them slowing down,” Vekhov said. “If we don’t address the gulches, the issue can reoccur. It could be in two months, in six months, or two years, but now we have this time to assess, to look around, and to decide how we want to proceed. If the community is not involved and doesn’t step up together, I don’t believe much progress will happen on that front.”
Kerry Vekhov leads a meeting in Pāhala of community members whose homes were badly damaged when Hurricane Lala struck Pāhala. (Ronit Fahl/Special to Civil Beat/2026)
“Uncle” George Kailiawa, another coffee farmer from Wood Valley — the secluded farm community up the mountain from Pāhala — was there to share his concern about the downed trees. They became wedged under the bridge that connects Pāhala to the road to Wood Valley, in a part of the gulch owned by the Olson Trust and another private landowner, Robert Tom. 
“If that river plugs and the water decides to come down this road, it’ll kill everybody from the top of the street all the way down,” Kailiawa said.
That sentiment — and the fear it breeds — is just part of what it means to live on Koali Street now, or in other places downstream from the gulches in Waiʻōhinu and Nāʻālehu. 
“The Kona low storms started the work of widening the gulches, and then Lala finished it. Or let’s hope it finished it.” Stephanie Correa, whose mother’s home was damaged by lala
“All of Kaʻū has been redesigned,” Correa told Civil Beat before the gathering. “The gulches are tremendously huge, and Pāhala is pretty much surrounded by them now. The Kona low storms started the work of widening the gulches, and then Lala finished it. Or let’s hope it finished it.” 
Every time it rains, Correa added, she and her neighbors get nervous. She hasn’t unpacked her important papers and family photos since Lala because she doesn’t trust that she won’t need to pick up and run again soon. 
“They’re all still in containers, ready to go,” she said.   
Community member George Kailiawa and Councilman Zed Aki joined the meeting in Pāhala. (Ronit Fahl/Special to Civil Beat/2026)
As an incoming councilmember, Aki was also at the meeting to listen to Koali Street residents share their stories and concerns. When he takes office in a few weeks, he will be the chair of council’s public works and infrastructure committee. Protecting the street, and the broader region, would be a priority, he said, while acknowledging they have typically been deprioritized within the county. 
“We dodged a bullet,” Aki told the group. “We didn’t have any loss of lives here, but as storms continue, and maybe even worsen, we don’t ever want to see it get to that level again, right?” 
When C. Brewer and Sons, the sugar plantation in Pāhala, closed in the early 2000s, the dynamic in the town — and the conversation about whose responsibility it was to keep the town safe from flooding — shifted substantially.  
“The plantation used to do all of this,” resident Gwen Sorenson said at Sunday’s meeting. Now, she added, the county, the state and multiple landowners all play roles in maintaining different parts of the area. 
Olson Trust now owns the Kaʻū Coffee Company and about 10,000 acres in the district. The trust’s coffee and macadamia orchards weathered significant flooding and damage as did its gravity-fed water system, which originates high up on the slopes of Mauna Loa in the Kaʻū Forest Reserve. 
John Cross, Olson Trust’s land manager, told Civil Beat that it had contracted with a company called Forest Solutions recently to manage and remove trees along Pāʻauʻau Gulch and would advise the trustee on the challenges posed by the existing trees in the part of the gulch the trust owns. 
The cost of removing downed trees — especially large eucalyptus and ghostly ʻōhiʻa trees that had died before the storm due to rapid ʻōhiʻa death — requires significant investment, however — so it’s not always an easy call. Cross said a large tree can cost up to $20,000 to cut up and haul.  
Moving Forward Alone Or Together?
Even as many hurricane survivors have had to pick the pieces up on their own, some parts of the recovery process are still unfolding. 
Correa has worked with a caseworker from Vibrant Hawaiʻi who shares lists of resources, including grants and loans she can apply for to repair her home and information about what documentation is required to do so. It’s not help she takes for granted — and she doesn’t know anyone else on Koali Street who has a caseworker — but she said it would also be nice to have more personalized support with the application process.
The Domingo family lost bags of coffee to mold from Hurricane Lala. (Ronit Fahl/Special to Civil Beat/2026)
In addition to Vibrant Hawaiʻi, Kumukahi Health and Wellness has taken on dozens of Lala recovery cases this fall. But that organization is focused on supporting people who lost their homes and evacuated to hotels — some of whom are currently living in their cars, said Kumukahi Health and Wellness’ Chief Executive Officer Peter Tuiolosega Silva. 
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers also may play an important role in the recovery in Kaʻū, according to Darryl Oliveira, who recently completed his temporary role as the county’s Civil Defense director but plans to remain involved in the effort as a volunteer. 
Oliveira said the Army Corps will release a formal report on Hurricane Lala recovery within the next few weeks. He said he and Mayor Kimo Alameda hope the report clearly identifies the places where changes in the landscape after the storm may have put lives and critical infrastructure at heightened risk. They plan to host a community meeting on the findings. 
Now that Oliveira has stepped down, Public Works Deputy Director Neil Azevedo has begun his term as the acting Civil Defense administrator. The county has also hired Kanani Aton in a new role as its recovery officer — a role that will involve working with nonprofit partners such as United Way, Family Promise and Vibrant Hawaiʻi to support disaster survivors. 
A great deal hinges on FEMA individual assistance, which isn’t completely off the table yet. Oliveira said that Hawaiʻi County worked with the Hawaiʻi Emergency Management Agency to submit an appeal that looked at not just the cost of damages but also more qualitative justifications. 
“The Kaʻū district is one of the most impoverished districts in the state. The median household income, the number of residents using SNAP, the difficulties with employment because the storm impacted many of the agricultural and commercial businesses,” he said, are all important parts of the case the county has made.
Community members gathered to talk about damage, repairs and hopes for the future of Pāhala. (Ronit Fahl/Special to Civil Beat/2026)
If none of that moves the needle with the federal government, lawmakers including Kapela are looking toward the state’s green fee as a possible source of funding for disaster recovery. 
One third of the funds earned through the fees — a tax added on to stays in hotels, vacation rentals, and other short-term accommodations — is designed to go toward climate and hazard resilience, all efforts to harden infrastructure and protect people from future disasters. Kapela sees hurricane recovery as intrinsically related and she doesn’t think the green fee funding was well used in the last legislative cycle. 
“I want to make sure that this next year it’s used properly and for the people who need it,” she said. 
Kapela and Rep. Sue Lee Loy, who represents a district in Hilo, are also discussing introducing legislation to support disaster recovery, and they’re pushing House leadership to create a disaster preparedness and climate resilience committee.The governor’s recommended green fee budget includes close to $17 million in climate resilience funding, which on the surface seems tailored to support environmental restoration efforts in Kaʻū — including $10 million for community-based ahupuaʻa restoration, $2.6 million for statewide flood mitigation for vulnerable communities, $3 million for climate resilience crews and $1.25 million for environmental jobs and climate resiliency conservation corps. 
So far, none of it appears earmarked for individual disaster assistance. 
However, in an interview with Civil Beat earlier this month, Green said, “We still are waiting for individual assistance for Lala … but that’s such a small number compared to the larger, the over a billion dollars for Maui. 
“We’re talking about $14.4 million for the individual assistance for Big Island,” he said, “and I will simply include that in our state budget if necessary.” 
Kapela’s primary goal is making sure that everyone gets behind supporting the residents of Kaʻū, who, like those living on Koali Street, may be expecting very little from the government at this point. 
The hope, she said, is “that we can truly respond to a disaster while also working on preparedness for the next one.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: H-Power Operator’s National Track Record: Sued, Cited And Fired
description: Honolulu joins other jurisdictions around the country aiming to sever their relationships with Reworld. The company has long operated Honolulu’s H-Power plant but is now in hot water over a 400,000-gallon leak.
text:
The company at the center of the oil leak at Honolulu’s waste incineration facility has paid more than $3 million in penalties for environmental violations across the country, been the subject of a federal criminal investigation related to sketchy emissions data and faced several lawsuits, including by at least one state attorney general. 
Now they’re on track to lose their contract in Honolulu after a 400,000-gallon fuel leak that has alarmed the community and incensed the mayor.
Mayor Rick Blangiardi announced Tuesday afternoon that he plans to end the city’s decades-long relationship with the operator of its waste-to-energy incineration plant. Reworld, the plant’s operator, has been in charge of operations since the facility opened in 1990, but the spill — and the failure of company and government officials to immediately bring it to the mayor’s attention — caused Blangiardi to lose trust in them. 
“This is a failure in judgement and communication of the worst order,” Blangiardi said on Hawaiʻi News Now.
Honolulu’s move to back out of its longstanding relationship with Reworld follows a stream of lawsuits, violation notices and contract terminations across the country, as well as allegations that the company falsified records in at least three jurisdictions. 
The company signed a federal non-prosecution agreement and paid $200,000 to the state of Oklahoma to resolve record falsification allegations in 2018. And it’s now being sued in Pennsylvania by a former employee who alleges the company wrongfully fired him after he raised concerns it was misleading regulators to cover up pollution. 
Heavy equipment and trucks could be seen at the H-Power facility last Thursday. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
On Oʻahu, Reworld’s recordkeeping in Kapolei quickly became a point of local scrutiny, as the company was seemingly unaware it was losing 4,000 gallons of fuel per day for months. Records filed with the health department show discrepancies in the amount of fuel expected and the amount observed.  
It’s unclear whether or how the city can terminate the contract, which extends until 2032. The most recent contract extension was granted via a no-bid process for an unusually long term — 20 years — without city officials understanding what they were agreeing to, according to a decade-old city audit. 
Civil Beat requested a copy of the contract, but the city has not yet provided it. The city also has not outlined a plan for how H-Power would run if Reworld were to step aside. In another part of the country, a city is struggling to end its own contract with Reworld. 
“We recognize that terminating a contract of this magnitude is a complex process that will take time,” city Communications Director Scott Humber said in a written statement. “At the same time, we must ensure that H-POWER, a critical component of Oʻahu’s waste management system, continues to operate without interruption.”
On Tuesday, Blangiardi also strongly implied that Department of Environmental Services Director Roger Babcock may lose his job over the spill’s handling, though said he has not yet taken any official action on that front. 
Roger Babcock, fourth from right, listens to the mayor deliver a stern address to reporters regarding the fuel leak.  (Ben Angarone/Civil Beat/2026)
The cleanup could cost over $50 million and take over a decade, the mayor said. Reworld Vice President Michael Van Brunt said last week the company – not taxpayers – will cover the cost. 
Blangiardi said it’s too early to know whether any laws were broken, but that is a question his team is looking into. He also said the city is prepared to sue Reworld. 
Under its current contract, Blangiardi said, the city pays the company over $1 million a week. A private equity firm bought the company five years ago for a little over $5 billion, and a Singaporean sovereign wealth fund has since acquired a 25% stake.   
“They’re not a small company,” Blangiardi said. 
A History Of Environmental Violations 
In a written statement Tuesday afternoon, the regional chief operating officer at Reworld, Vincent Langone, said the company takes environmental compliance, workplace safety and operational responsibilities seriously. He did not respond directly to the mayor’s desire to end his company’s contract. 
“Regarding previous regulatory and operational issues, Reworld has consistently cooperated with the relevant regulatory agencies to address any concerns,” Langone said. “We are committed to operating our facilities safely, transparently, and in compliance with all applicable state and federal environmental regulations.”
Public records, however, paint a troubling picture. 
Reworld, which used to be called Covanta, has racked up more than $3.46 million in penalties stemming from at least 76 environmental and air pollution violations issued by state and federal environmental regulators over the last two decades, according to Violation Tracker, a database on corporate misconduct maintained by the nonprofit Corporate Research Project. 
Beyond H-Power, Reworld operates trash incineration plants around the country. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Those violations include illegal levels of highly toxic environmental pollutants known as dioxins and furans emitted from a Covanta facility in Connecticut in 2010 and more than twice the permitted level of nickel emissions at a Pennsylvania operation in 2006. Separately, Reworld was cited three times since 2019 with Clean Air Act violations at H-Power itself, ending in fines of $23,900.
In 2022, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency fined the company’s subsidiary Reworld Marine LLC more than $26,000 for a Clean Water Act violation: A facility in Texas that drains into the San Jacinto Bay didn’t have a plan to adequately prevent, mitigate and respond to oil spills.
The company has also faced dozens of lawsuits around the country involving allegations ranging from environmental problems to contract and employment issues. 
This September, Miami-Dade County sued Reworld seeking more than $750 million in damages related to a fire that burned for three weeks in 2023 at the company’s Doral, Florida facility. 
That county’s lawsuit accuses Reworld of failing to address fire safety issues despite years of warnings, including six fire code violations from local fire authorities. Miami-Dade ended their contract with the company in October after determining that it wasn’t financially feasible to rebuild the burned facility.
Several other jurisdictions have severed ties with Reworld for other reasons. Hennepin County, Minnesota and Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, both elected not to renew contracts with Covanta in recent years, citing increased costs. Financial considerations also ended the relationship between Covanta and Long Beach, California, after changes to state law removed waste diversion credits, the result of advocacy against trash incineration.
Following years of violations, hundreds of thousands of dollars in penalties and a $400,000 settlement with the Connecticut attorney general over illegal air emissions, the town of Wallingford stopped using Covanta’s facility as an incinerator around 2015. The operation transitioned to a transfer station before Covanta later sold it to another company. 
Taxpayers will not bear the cost of the cleanup, officials said. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Officials in Montgomery County, Maryland have found it difficult to separate from Reworld. The county has been trying to close a Reworld-operated facility for several years, as part of local zero-waste goals. Over the last year, the facility has repeatedly reported excess amounts of dioxins leaking from its boiler units. 
Finding an alternative proved difficult, and the date to shutter the facility kept getting pushed back. The original contract set to end in 2016 was extended three times, most recently until April 2031, to give the county time to explore alternatives. The county is currently planning to keep the facility open through the 2027 fiscal year, then transition to transferring waste out of the county. 
Claims Of Falsified Records  
Reworld has also been accused of deceiving regulators.
In 2016, one of the company’s subsidiaries, Covanta Tulsa Renewable Energy LLC, was the target of a criminal investigation by the EPA for “alleged improprieties in the recording and reporting of emissions data” at one of the waste combustion units at the facility in Tulsa, Oklahoma 
In a quarterly report filed with the federal government at the time, the company said its operations were in compliance with laws and regulations. Covanta Tulsa entered into an agreement with the U.S. Attorney’s Office in 2018 to stave off criminal charges if the company satisfied certain commitments for one year, including paying a $200,000 “community service” payment to the Oklahoma Department of Environmental Quality. 
In Philadelphia, former Reworld employee Eric Bazis, who had worked for 30 years as an operations supervisor at the facility in Chester, Pennsylvania – Reworld’s largest, he said – testified last week that the company had misled environmental regulators. 
“I was fired in July 2023 because I raised environmental and compliance concerns,” he said at a Philadelphia City Council committee hearing.
Reworld Vice President Michael Van Brunt showed reporters where the company has added monitoring wells to track the spilled diesel fuel. (Ben Angarone/Civil Beat/2026)
Bazis told Philadelphia council members that he believes trash incineration can be done safely if regulations are followed and equipment is kept up to date. But his facility didn’t live up to those standards, he said. 
“I remember opacity monitors and other measuring devices getting old and giving false measurements,” he said. “We were not told to replace them, just to make sure that they show the numbers that looked right.”
Bazis said Reworld misled regulators by operating differently during regulatory tests, including by mixing ash in an abnormal way during acidity testing and injecting more lime than usual into the system, which sticks to ultrafine particles and hides emissions. 
“Testing only works when it reflects how the facility is operated day to day,” he said. 
A court filing for wrongful termination shows that Reworld accused Bazis of making improper overtime hours submissions. 
In a statement given to WHYY, a Pennsylvia public radio station, Reworld spokesperson Jason Hahn said the company will defend itself against “meritless claims.”
“The claims do not accurately reflect our operations, values, or management approach,” he said. “The company looks forward to refuting these claims through the legal process.”
Bazis’ testimony came during a hearing about whether to remove Reworld from Philadelphia’s waste disposal contract. 
The City of Brotherly Love sends roughly a third of its waste to be incinerated in neighboring Chester, a small majority-Black town that environmental advocates say is unjustly saddled with poorer air quality from the fumes. 
Philadelphia City Council member Jamie Gauthier has been pushing to halt that practice. Last year, she introduced a bill to stop her city from contracting with companies that incinerate solid waste, though that fizzled, she said, as Reworld stepped up its lobbying efforts.
“That became too difficult to overcome,” Gauthier told Civil Beat.
A worker is seen at H-Power on the day the mayor’s office held a press conference to announce the massive fuel leak.  (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
She clinched a win last week, however, when the committee she chairs voted unanimously to cut Reworld from the city’s waste stream.
Bazis’ allegations echo those of another former employee who filed a whistleblower lawsuit in New York alleging that the company falsified test records to hide pollution by its facility in Nassau County, among other things.
A jury determined that the employee, Patrick Fahey, wasn’t fired in retaliation for whistleblowing. But an investigation by the state also determined that Fahey’s allegation was correct, that the company was out of compliance with state regulations to dispose of ash from its facility. Reworld admitted no wrongdoing but signed a settlement that required the company to pay $378,500 in penalties, as well as $500,000 to fund an environmental project.
What Are The Alternatives?
All the while, Oʻahu is grappling with a larger ʻōpala problem. The city’s only municipal landfill, in Nānākuli, is gradually running out of space and is projected to have capacity until late 2030, Babcock, the city director, said in a written statement. Blangiardi has pledged for years that he will site a new landfill, but so far no viable option has been found.
“We’re running out of room,” he said on Spotlight. 
H-Power is a key part of the city’s waste disposal strategy since it lessens the amount of trash that heads to the landfill. Blangiardi’s termination of the contract with Reworld would mean having to find a new operator – the first since the facility opened in 1990 – and, he acknowledged, will not be an easy task. 
As an interim solution, the city is once again looking into shipping trash off-island. The last time it was attempted, in 2010, the city’s plan to ship rubbish to Washington State failed because the planned destination was not fully approved.
A bulldozer smoothes ash from the H-Power incineration plant next to a pool of water at the Waimalao Gulch Sanitary Landfill, the island’s only municipal landfill. Roughly 80% of its intake is ash from H-Power. (Craig Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
Honolulu explored shipping trash again in late 2024 as the impending crisis inched closer  Blangiardi axed that plan after it became clear the cost would be too high. Now, the city is exploring it again.
The updated pricetag is scheduled to come in this January, Blangiardi said on Spotlight, but he’s already bracing for them to add to Honolulu’s untenably high cost of living. 
“I fear those numbers,” he said.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: When Disaster Strikes, Medicaid Work Rules Add Barriers for Potential Enrollees
description: New work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed last year, have put Medicaid enrollees living in disaster-struck counties at risk of losing health insurance.
text:
This story was reported by Ashley Mizuo
A month after Hurricane Lowell hit the island of Kauaʻi, downed trees, construction crews, and damaged homes dotted the neighborhoods. At the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort, where over 100 workers were laid off, heaps of sand blanketed the grounds, and the drained pool’s concrete deck crumbled into the beach, just steps away from the ocean.
On Kauaʻi, unemployment claims jumped from 69 before the September hurricane to about 1,800 nearly two weeks afterward, with widespread layoffs in the tourism industry amid a sharp decline in visitors. The number of Medicaid applications submitted by island residents jumped by about 50% in the following month, according to the Hawaiʻi Department of Human Services.
In times of emergencies, Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed last year, have put Medicaid enrollees living in disaster-struck counties at risk of losing health insurance. The law requires many nondisabled adults enrolled in Medicaid in 43 states and Washington, D.C., to work, volunteer, or attend school at least 80 hours a month, with eligibility checks starting in January.
In most states, residents impacted by a disaster can be granted a short-term exemption from Medicaid work requirements. Eligibility largely relies on a federal law that allows the president to issue a disaster or emergency declaration and authorizes federal assistance, but any declaration can take months or may not come at all.
Those who live in counties affected by natural disasters may not need to comply with the work rules — one of several carve-outs intended to provide limited, short-term exceptions. However, it’s unclear whether those who lost jobs after Hurricane Lowell would be eligible for that exemption so many months later. The Trump administration hasn’t offered clear guidance on how long a state can apply the natural disaster exemption to enrollees.
Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, and her boyfriend were laid off by Sheraton and are getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work. The union that represents the hotel’s hospitality workers secured them three months of health insurance. If Ganotisi isn’t hired back to her housekeeping job by then, she plans to apply for Medicaid, the federal-state program that provides health coverage to people with low incomes or disabilities.
Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, was laid off by the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort after it sustained significant damage from Hurricane Lowell. Her family is getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work.  (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News)
Hawaiʻi Gov. Josh Green, a Democrat and practicing physician, emphasized the importance of quickly issuing disaster declarations, especially as changes to Medicaid are set to take effect. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services allowed states to delay enforcing the work requirements until next July, but states are still expected to implement eligibility checks by Jan. 1.
“It would be devastating if suddenly 40,000 or 50,000 people didn’t have their Medicaid benefits,” he said. “It could affect our rural hospitals, our nurse practitioners, our doctors, so timeliness is key.”
Hawaiʻi officials said they will keep people who don’t meet the work requirements enrolled until July.
At least 34 states, plus Washington, D.C., plan to adopt the optional hardship exemptions to those work requirements. So far, four states — Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, and Ohio — do not plan to adopt the exemptions, according to KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. All four were issued disaster declarations for severe storms and flooding this summer.
CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster told KFF Health News in a statement that states can request a longer duration for a hardship exemption if they can prove that barriers to demonstrating work requirements persist in disaster areas.
Tom Cotter, CEO of Health Response Alliance, a nonprofit focused on improving healthcare access in disasters, said that when people lose coverage they end up using emergency rooms and charitable clinics, among the few places that will treat patients regardless of their ability to pay.
“All of these are really stretched thin during an emergency because their patient load goes way up,” he said. “That makes it even more expensive for the healthcare system that is being otherwise also burdened for the disaster.”
With additional work requirements, “it is going to slow the economic recovery of any particular community,” Cotter said. “It’s going to require people to be thinking about how they’re paying for healthcare when they have a lot of other things to worry about.”
Nebraska Work Requirements Begin
Once the president declares a disaster or emergency, the short-term hardship exception applies for the full month the disaster took place. Eligibility can apply retroactively after a disaster declaration, and enrollees can be reimbursed for expenses from previous months.
Nebraska implemented Medicaid work requirements early, in May, offering states a preview of how the hardship declaration might provide relief. For Nebraskans, that relief was delayed.
It took three months for Trump to declare a federal disaster for March and April wildfires. For severe storms, tornadoes, and flooding that occurred in May, he didn’t declare a federal disaster until August.
Six Nebraskans impacted by the disasters lost coverage because they did not comply with work requirements. In October, the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services reported it was reprocessing their eligibility now that they qualify for a hardship exemption.
Sarah Maresh, director of the Health Care Access program at the nonprofit advocacy group Nebraska Appleseed, said the early rollout of the Medicaid work requirements has been marred by uncertainty.
“This is part of the confusion that comes with the Medicaid work requirements, because it applies differently depending on your situation,” she said. “I think it’ll be very challenging for new applicants.”
Local economies and businesses can take years to recover after a natural disaster. About 90% of businesses fail within two years after being struck by disaster, according to the U.S. Small Business Administration. Housing shortages can hamper business recovery as employees repair their homes or are displaced to areas farther from work. Three years after the 2023 Maui wildfires that killed over 100 people, recovery is ongoing, with most storefronts still shuttered in what was once a bustling area.
After CMS published rules governing the exceptions to the work requirements, several Democratic states sued the agency. Their lawsuit cited the narrow time frame for securing natural disaster exceptions. The complaint argued that the lack of guidance burdens state Medicaid agencies determining eligibility.
In its response filing, CMS wrote that the restrictions ensure the exemption applies only when a disaster affects Medicaid enrollees’ ability to comply with work requirements.
Construction crews lined the roads on Kauaʻi a month after Hurricane Lowell, clearing debris and repairing damaged businesses, homes, and infrastructure.  (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News)
Disaster Delays, Denials
In Trump’s second term, he has denied nearly a quarter of disaster and emergency declaration requests as of mid-November, a denial rate higher than that of any other presidential administration in more than two decades, KFF Health News found. While decision wait times have increased across the country, they’re more acute in states with Democratic governors. Those states experienced both significantly higher denial rates and longer decision times than states with Republican governors, according to 2026 analyses from The Associated Press and Politico’s E&E News.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied any politicization in Trump’s decisions on disaster relief. She wrote that his response to requests from states ensures appropriate use of taxpayer money and that federal funds are used to “supplement — not substitute” states’ obligations to respond to disasters.
The presidential major disaster declaration for Kauaʻi was the state’s sixth disaster or emergency declaration this year. As of November, Hawaiʻi had received more disaster and emergency declarations than any other state in 2026. Trump’s disaster declaration for a 6.0-magnitude earthquake that damaged over 300 homes on Hawaiʻi Island took about three months.
A month after Hurricane Lowell in September 2026, sand still covered the grounds of the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort.  (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News)
Other states have waited longer for disaster declarations. New Mexico, where the Democratic Party controls the governor’s office and majorities in both legislative chambers, had one of the longest wait times for a decision — nine months for a presidential disaster declaration for severe storms and flooding in September 2025. Illinois, which also has a Democratic trifecta, waited over seven months and was denied. The state has yet to secure any major disaster declarations during Trump’s second term, despite several attempts.
Some who lost their jobs and don’t qualify for Medicaid have few resources to help them.
Oscar Cardova worked at The Terrace Hanalei, a restaurant on Kauaʻi’s North Shore that was significantly damaged in the hurricane. When the restaurant closed, he lost his employer-provided health insurance. Although he has a work permit visa from Peru, he was denied Medicaid because of his immigration status.
Cardova and his wife, Yesenia, live in their van. Yesenia has astigmatism and, without insurance, she will need to pay for glasses out-of-pocket, Cardova said. The cost is expected to be about $500.
The couple planned to work for two more years in the U.S. before returning to Peru. A month after the hurricane, they were still struggling to find work. In search of more job opportunities, they considered moving to Honolulu.
“Right now, we’re just surviving,” Cardova said. “We’re waiting to see what happens before making other decisions, because we can’t keep living like this.”
Have you tried to prove your eligibility for Medicaid under new rules that require people to show they are working, going to school, or participating in another qualifying activity? Click here to contact KFF Health News.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri proposal would establish statewide child safety standards
description: A Missouri child welfare task force has submitted draft legislation to Gov. Mike Kehoe that would define child safety in state law and require child welfare workers, judges and juvenile officers to follow a uniform process for identifying threats and determining when and how to intervene. Kehoe created the 18-member task force by executive order […]
text:
Members of a child welfare task force established by Gov. Mike Kehoe gather on Nov. 5 to discuss draft legislation that would require child welfare workers, juvenile officers, judges and service providers to use a consistent child safety framework (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).A Missouri child welfare task force has submitted draft legislation to Gov. Mike Kehoe that would define child safety in state law and require child welfare workers, judges and juvenile officers to follow a uniform process for identifying threats and determining when and how to intervene.
Kehoe created the 18-member task force by executive order in August, less than 24 hours before a bipartisan legislative committee held a hearing examining foster care deaths, child placements and turnover among frontline Children’s Division staff.
The proposed legislation describes the safety framework as a “sequential decision-making process” to identify safety threats, evaluate children’s vulnerabilities, assess a caregiver’s ability to protect a child and determine appropriate responses. Those could include community-based services, more structured intensive in-home services, temporary placements with relatives or longer-term removal from home. 
Missouri lawmakers press child welfare leaders on foster care deaths, staff turnover

It’s similar to the safety assessment already used by Children’s Division investigators, called Structured Decision Making. That safety assessment was developed by the division and the Office of State Courts Administrator based on a guide published by the American Bar Association.
In an email to The Independent, Baylee Watts, media director for the Department of Social Services, said that while SDM is already the basis of initial safety assessments, “the broader, ongoing goal is to embed the safety framework throughout all practice areas — including when a child is in alternative care.” 
The goal is to ensure that the reasons a child is considered unsafe — and what must change before that child can return home — are clearly described as the case moves through the child welfare system.
The legislation would require the division to establish the safety framework in state regulations and coordinate with the Office of State Courts Administrator to create standard forms for court reports and social service plans, as well as any other “uniform tools for the identification and evaluation of child safety.” The division would also develop training materials for juvenile and family courts, guardians ad litem, parents’ attorneys, law enforcement, medical professionals and child welfare agencies.
The legislation builds on efforts by division leadership to standardize child welfare practices statewide. Task force members said during the group’s Nov. 10 meeting that they plan to move forward with some changes, including developing standard forms, while lawmakers consider the legislation next year. Watts said the division also plans to begin promulgating rules needed to implement the proposed legislation.
Republican state Rep. Melissa Schmidt of Eldridge, who chairs the task force, has said throughout the group’s meetings that a shared framework and definitions will provide relief to overwhelmed division workers.
“I think we agree that what we’re currently doing isn’t working,” Schmidt said during the group’s Nov. 5 meeting. “And that’s why it’s not working — the inconsistency.”
Sara Smith, director of the Children’s Division, urged judges and juvenile officers to work with the division to standardize child welfare decisions, saying some judicial circuits have their own “blanket” policies.
“We have some courts that are saying there are no (parental) visits for three months, blanket, when a child comes into care,” Smith said. “There are circuits that are saying, if a parent tests positive for drugs, blanket, no visits until x, y and z, even if we can’t identify a safety threat.”
Smith told task force members that a shared understanding of safety is the “throughline throughout our agencies.”
“I’m trying to operate a statewide Children’s Division consistently for 46 judicial circuits,” Smith said. “…I think that’s what parents expect of Children’s Division — is that we know our policy and our practice and what our statutory authority is, and that we follow that no matter what circuit we are in.”
 Placement with parents

The legislation also narrows the circumstances under which judges can deny a child’s placement with a nonoffending parent — a parent not implicated in the alleged abuse or neglect — because of the parent’s history, if the placement would otherwise be in the best interest of the child.
Current law allows judges to reject a child’s placement with a parent with “a history of criminal behavior, drug or alcohol abuse, child abuse or child neglect, domestic violence or stalking within the past five years.”
Under the draft legislation, a judge could deny placement with a parent who, within the past five years, pleaded guilty to or was found guilty of a misdemeanor or felony involving drug use, domestic violence, child abuse or neglect or stalking — but not alcohol use. A judge could also count a preponderance of evidence finding of abuse or neglect or a full order of protection within the past five years against a parent.
Task force members debated whether to require the higher bar of a conviction for a child not to be placed with a nonoffending parent during a case of potential abuse or neglect.
Democratic state Rep. Ken Jamison of Gladstone, an attorney specializing in family law, initially called on the group to adopt the higher bar.
“From my experience and in other defense counsel’s experiences, it’s kind of trigger-happy to find any reason to not place with a parent who may have some sort of history,” Jamison said. 
Newton County Sheriff Matt Stewart opposed the requirement of a conviction, saying some domestic violence cases don’t result in convictions because the victim decides not to come forward.
An earlier draft would have spelled out in state law the division’s authority to create safety plans — agreements between caregivers and the division to prevent a child’s removal or work toward their return home. The division already uses 10-day safety plans authorized in department regulations. The task force removed the provision from its final draft after members disagreed about the potential burden on frontline division staff and how the plans should be monitored.
 Training and implementation

The task force plans to use its two remaining meetings in December to discuss recommendations for putting its proposed safety standards into practice.
The draft legislation would also establish a Joint Council for Child Safety to monitor the implementation of the safety framework and gather feedback from the public. The council would convene in April or May 2028 and include lawmakers, representatives of the Department of Social Services and Office of State Courts Administrator, juvenile officers, law enforcement, contracted child welfare providers, child welfare advocates, attorneys and judges.
Task force members emphasized the importance of training for division workers and the courts. They also acknowledged that it could be difficult to secure funding as Missouri faces a nearly $3 billion difference between departments’ initial spending requests and estimated tax revenue.
Smith said during the group’s Nov. 5 meeting that the division had talked with Casey Family Programs, a nonprofit foundation dedicated to reducing the need for foster care, about funding for initial multidisciplinary training. 
State Courts Administrator Kathy Lloyd said at the Nov. 8 meeting that the initial training could “get everybody at the table in one setting, by region,” bringing together division workers, judges, juvenile officers and law enforcement.
Training workers to put the new standards into practice, Schmidt said, is where the group’s work “either succeeds or fails.”
“We have to strike the training piece correctly without it being too cumbersome,” Schmidt said, “…because we can come up with the very best thing, but if folks don’t know how to implement it, we’re right back where we were.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC leaders plan to hike 100 miles to raise awareness of food insecurity
description: The hike will take place with nonprofit Hunters for the Hungry, which donates local venison to food pantries.
text:
A partnership between the state Department of Natural Resources and nonprofit Hunters for the Hungry is meant to raise awareness of a program to fight food insecurity with donated venison. (Photo courtesy of Liz Julian/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)State leaders will hike 100 miles over 10 days in an effort to raise awareness about food insecurity, according to the Department of Natural Resources.
The 100 Miles for the Hungry expedition will begin Jan. 8 and go through Orangeburg, Bamberg, Barnwell and Allendale counties, according to the agency.
The state agency is partnering with Hunters for the Hungry, a Spartanburg-based nonprofit that provides deer killed and donated by hunters to food banks, churches and other places where people might get free meals.
For 30 days, a nonprofit leads hikes and floats across SC. The goal is conservation.

The nonprofit pays the processing fees to turn the deer into venison before packaging and freezing it, executive director Rick Counts told the SC Daily Gazette.
Throughout the expedition, state leaders and members of Hunters for the Hungry will talk to local residents, businesses and churches about how to donate venison or volunteer to get food to people who might not have enough, Counts said.
The goal is to raise awareness of food insecurity, he said.
“This is a way to shine some light on the areas of the state that don’t get as much notoriety and press on what they need,” Counts said.
In 2023, roughly 14% of people in the state were food insecure, according to the most recent data from the Department of Public Health. Rural Allendale County has the highest rate of food insecurity, with more than 20% of residents lacking consistent access to healthy food, according to the agency.
The Department of Natural Resources often encourages hunters to donate extra deer to Hunters for the Hungry by dropping off carcasses at participating processing sites. The deer must have a state-issued tag to show they were legally hunted, according to the nonprofit.
Promotions from the agency have helped the nonprofit in the past, Counts said. When DNR shared a map of processors, a facility in Dillon County realized the area wasn’t covered and called Counts asking how to help sign up, he said.
Having as many processors involved across the state as possible is important because the nonprofit tries to keep donations local, so hunters can help their own communities, Counts said.
“We try to keep that deer meat in that county as much as possible,” he said.
This year, hunters received an extra tag for a doe when buying the regular deer tags in an effort to better balance the state’s population of deer. Most hunters don’t kill more than one doe each season, but having too many can disrupt local ecosystems, according to the agency.
If hunters already have as much venison as they plan to eat, state leaders encourage using as many of the tags as possible and donating the extra meat to Hunters for the Hungry.
“Most people, they’ve filled their freezers by now,” Counts said. “With our program, they can still go hunting and donate their does.”
The idea of hiking to raise awareness is similar to a program DNR runs with nonprofit South Carolina 7.
Every year, state officials, volunteers and members of the public walk, float and kayak more than 300 miles in an effort to get people outside and promote conservation.
