name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee lags by most measures in new federal foster care analysis
description: Tennessee lags behind a national benchmark to ensure there are enough foster homes for every child taken into state custody, according to a new federal scorecard system that tracks the effectiveness of child welfare systems in every state. As a result, a higher proportion of Tennessee kids in the custody of the Department of Children’s […]
text:
Department of Children's Services social workers attend child welfare presentation. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee lags behind a national benchmark to ensure there are enough foster homes for every child taken into state custody, according to a new federal scorecard system that tracks the effectiveness of child welfare systems in every state.
As a result, a higher proportion of Tennessee kids in the custody of the Department of Children’s Services are placed in institutional settings, contrary to federal directives to limit time in so-called congregate care settings. Tennessee also lags behind other states in prioritizing placing kids with relatives after they are taken from their parents as a result of suspected abuse or neglect, falling short of another goal set by the federal government. 
To promote transparency, the federal Administration for Children and Families released a  new state-by-state snapshots Monday showing how foster children are faring, a news release said. 
Blackburn taps child welfare advisory group to review Tennessee Department of Children’s Services

The scorecard system is also designed to “inspire some healthy competition” between states: states can earn between $1 million and $3 million from the federal government for maintaining or improving the availability of foster homes. 
The federal government has established a foster home-to-child ratio of at least 1 foster care space for every child. In Tennessee, where there are more than 7,500 children in state custody, the ratio stands at 1.7 foster kids for every home space, leaving many without places to go. More than 20% of Tennessee foster kids’ time is spent in institutional settings, versus a national average of 10%, according to the federal scorecard. And just 16% of foster children were placed with relatives or extended family, compared to a national average of 42%.
Tennessee, however, exceeded federal benchmarks in ensuring children were not repeat victims of child abuse or neglect: 1% of children in state custody were found to have been harmed again within six months. The national average is 4%.
The federal scorecard’s release coincides with incoming Gov. Marsha Blackburn’s decision to convene an advisory group to guide her on the future of the Department of Children’s Services, which has faced intense public scrutiny over reports of mistreatment of foster children in state custody, high caseloads and plans to build more residential care facilities.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Gov. Morrisey’s goal of bringing foster kids back to WV hits another roadblock
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey is intent on bringing foster children back home to West Virginia, but his key foster care reform focus faces yet another hurdle.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announces an update on his foster care reform initiatives Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025, at the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)Gov. Patrick Morrisey is intent on bringing foster children back home to West Virginia, but his key foster care reform focus faces yet another hurdle.
The Village of Barboursville says they’ll sue the state Department of Human Services to stop the Morrisey administration’s plan for a youth residential treatment facility in the heart of Barboursville Park. The facility, currently owned by the state, is expected to house up to 36 children in foster care next year.
Chris Tatum, mayor of Barboursville, is pictured on Tuesday, June 2, 2015. (Photo by Sholten Singer/The Herald-Dispatch)
“This is not an issue of whether people deserve treatment or not. This is about placement of said treatment in the middle of a park where there are thousands of kids and thousands of families,” Barboursville Mayor Chris Tatum said on Tuesday.
There are currently 519 children in foster care placed outside of West Virginia, and the majority of those children reside in residential facilities or psychiatric hospitals. These children are in facilities in Arkansas, California, Massachusetts, Texas, Washington and other states. 
West Virginia doesn’t have enough in-state facilities and homes for children in foster care, and the state has spent more than $62 million yearly for out-of-state care. 
West Virginia Department of Human Services Secretary Carl Ayers speaks before the Legislative Oversight Committee on Health & Human Resources Administration meeting in Charleston, West Virginia, on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“Bringing West Virginia children home has been one of Governor Morrisey’s top priorities since taking office, and that commitment hasn’t changed. These are our children, many of whom have been sent hundreds or even thousands of miles away from their families and communities. They deserve the opportunity to receive care closer to home,” DoHS Secretary Carl Ayers told West Virginia Watch.
“We’re moving forward with Barboursville, and we’re not going to allow reckless accusations or threats of litigation to derail our responsibility to these children. The facility served West Virginia children for nearly 40 years, and we’re committed to ensuring a safe, supportive environment for the children and the surrounding community.”
Earlier this year, the legislature declined to fund Morrisey’s $6 million “Bring Them Home” idea to move hundreds of foster children in state from out-of-state facilities. Some lawmakers cited a lack of details in the three-page proposal.
A fiscal note attached to the governor’s requested bill said the average yearly cost of one youth placed out of state is approximately $250,025 compared to the in-state cost of care, which is $120,333 per year.
Sen. Brian Helton, R-Fayette. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Two months ahead of the Legislative Session, Senate Health Chair Brian Helton said there is no specific plan to reconsider “Bring Them Home” legislation, but lawmakers will try again to tackle the issue of kids going out of state. 
“Per capita, we’re number one in the nation from kids being taken from the home, and it’s not even close. Until we figure out how to deal with that volume appropriately, we’re going to have challenges in West Virginia,” said Helton, R-Fayette.
There are 5,413 children in West Virginia’s foster care system.
“We don’t have the facilities. We don’t have the amount of psychologists, the amount of therapists, counselors to deal with this extreme volume, and we certainly don’t have enough foster families,” Helton said.
Examining Medicaid reimbursement rates, which help pay for foster children’s care, could be debated during the session as lawmakers try to increase the state’s capacity to care for children with complex needs. 
“You have to look at: do we actually have the bandwidth to do it? … You’re talking about potential lockdown situations, and how do you separate kids out appropriately by age group and by behaviors?” Helton said. 
Ayers said that the governor “will continue working with the Legislature to expand treatment options here in West Virginia.”
“Barboursville is intended to serve as a model for additional facilities, and we’re committed to bringing our children home,” he said.
The former Barboursville School is pictured on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, in Barboursville. (Photo by Ryan Fischer | The Herald-Dispatch)
Human Services secretary defends Barboursville decision  
The Cabell County site eyed by Morrisey for a new residential treatment facility previously housed foster children before closing last November.
The previous facility, operated by nearby River Park Hospital, served children in foster care with psychiatric disorders and in need of specialized, 24/7 care. The building is now vacant.
Tatum and some Barboursville residents are concerned because the new company taking over the site, Youth Health Associates, treats “higher-risk male youth, ages 12 to 18 years old, who engage in sexual misconduct with a broad range of sexual-offense behaviors and who are often sexually-preoccupied.” 
“In the middle of a park, 50 yards away from a splash park where young children play, is not the right spot for people with sexual misconduct in their past,” Tatum said.
“We’ve offered to purchase the property from the state so that they could do something, what I would consider state-of-the-art, with someone with a company from West Virginia who wants to serve these kids at a campus closer than Barboursville Park … They weren’t interested in those negotiations,” he added.
The state has entered a five-year lease with Youth Health Associates to operate the school. The facility plans to start accepting children in early 2027. 
Ayers said in a social media post that the new Barboursville School “will be a licensed psychiatric residential treatment facility, not a prison or detention center.”
“Every admission will be independently reviewed, and children will receive around-the-clock supervision from trained professionals under strict state licensing and safety requirements. Protecting these children and the surrounding community is a responsibility we take seriously,” he wrote on Friday.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: When getting by gets harder, healthcare shouldn’t be another worry
description: As West Virginia families prepare to gather around the Thanksgiving table, many will be doing what they have done all year: stretching every dollar, comparing prices at the grocery store, putting off purchases and hoping the next unexpected bill can wait.
text:
Thousands of West Virginians could lose their health coverage when Medicaid work requirements take effect next year. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)As West Virginia families prepare to gather around the Thanksgiving table, many will be doing what they have done all year: stretching every dollar, comparing prices at the grocery store, putting off purchases and hoping the next unexpected bill can wait. 
For some, even the holiday meal will require difficult choices. For others, the worry goes beyond what they can afford today. It is the electric bill coming due, the cost of keeping the heat on through winter or what might happen if a family member gets sick and needs care they cannot afford. 
These are not problems limited to one kind of household. Across West Virginia, working families, older residents living on fixed incomes and people doing everything they can to stay financially afloat are feeling the pressure of a higher cost of living. When household budgets are already stretched thin, healthcare can become one more expense people feel forced to sacrifice. 
And now, federal policy changes threaten to make that burden even heavier. 
Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, West Virginians covered by Medicaid who are subject to new federal work reporting requirements will face another hurdle to keeping their health coverage. Under H.R. 1, many adults ages 19 through 64 will have to document that they are working, volunteering, participating in qualifying activities or otherwise meeting applicable requirements, generally for at least 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. 
Supporters may call these requirements an incentive to work. But that framing overlooks a fundamental reality: many West Virginians who rely on Medicaid are already working. They are caring for children and aging parents, working hourly jobs with unpredictable schedules, managing health conditions or trying to hold onto employment in communities where opportunities can be limited. 
For these families, the problem is not necessarily a lack of willingness to work. It may be the difficulty of navigating another layer of paperwork, proving eligibility on time or understanding what information the state needs. People who qualify for coverage can still lose it if they cannot successfully navigate the reporting process. 
The consequences are serious. Losing Medicaid does not make a person’s need for medical care disappear. It can mean delaying a doctor’s appointment, skipping medication, putting off treatment or waiting until a health problem becomes an emergency. It can also leave families facing medical bills they have no realistic way to pay. 
In a state where healthcare access is already complicated by long distances, provider shortages and financial hardship, losing coverage can have consequences far beyond a single household. Hospitals and other providers depend on reimbursement to keep their doors open. Communities depend on those facilities for jobs, emergency services and essential care.
Medicaid is not a handout to people who have chosen not to contribute. It is a lifeline for children, people with disabilities, low-income workers, pregnant women and older West Virginians who need help paying for care. It also supports families who work hard but whose wages do not stretch far enough to cover the cost of living and health insurance. 
West Virginia has made meaningful progress in expanding health coverage over the past decade. Our state’s uninsured rate fell from approximately 18% before the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid expansion to about 5.9%. That progress helped more people see a doctor, manage chronic conditions and protect their families from the financial consequences of illness. We should be building on those gains, not putting them at risk. 
Thanksgiving is often a time to take stock of what matters most. For many families, that means having enough food, a warm home and the peace of mind that comes with knowing a loved one can get medical care when it is needed. Those are not extravagant expectations. They are basic ingredients of a secure and healthy life. 
But it is difficult to feel secure when the cost of everyday necessities keeps rising and access to healthcare becomes less certain. No family should have to choose between buying groceries and filling a prescription. No working person should lose health coverage because a complicated reporting process stands between them and the benefits for which they qualify. 
As the holiday season begins, policymakers should consider what these changes will mean in the real lives of West Virginians. States must make requirements as clear and accessible as possible, communicate directly with enrollees and help eligible people complete the necessary steps to maintain coverage. And all of us should pay attention to what happens when policies designed in Washington meet the realities of life in our communities. 
At West Virginians for Affordable Health Care, we believe that access to quality, affordable healthcare should not depend on how much money a person earns, where they live or how easily they can navigate government paperwork. 
This Thanksgiving, families across our state will do their best to make the holiday meaningful, even when money is tight. They deserve policies that make it easier to build a healthy, stable future, not policies that add another worry to an already full plate.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY counties face a fiscal ‘crisis’ to keep jails open. One solution has a big price tag.
description: Webster County Judge-Executive Steve Henry has been trying to find ways to invest in his Western Kentucky community, which he describes as a coal mining county without a coal mine. The last operational mine in the county closed in 2019.  But he said he’s limited in his county of 13,000 because of a growing fiscal […]
text:
Kentucky jails are facing a fiscal crisis. (Kenton County sheriff)Webster County Judge-Executive Steve Henry has been trying to find ways to invest in his Western Kentucky community, which he describes as a coal mining county without a coal mine. The last operational mine in the county closed in 2019. 
But he said he’s limited in his county of 13,000 because of a growing fiscal “crisis” at the local jail, something that’s “snowballed” over the past several years since the COVID-19 pandemic. 
If jail costs continue to increase, he foresees cuts across several county offices including the county sheriff, the local courthouse and more. 
“It is a crisis moment because we’re going to get to the point that these numbers have increased and continue to increase,” said Henry, the incoming president of the Kentucky Judge-Executives Association. “I truly feel that if nothing’s done in the next three to four years, Webster County will have to do a mass layoff.” 
Webster County isn’t alone in grappling with the costs of local jails. Kentucky’s 77 county jails have traditionally relied on money from housing state inmates in county jails, but that has declined.
Henry said the costs to house those inmates — food, medical costs and jail staffing — have only increased with inflation, and what the state provides in funding doesn’t come close to the actual costs. His county spent approximately $515,000 in fiscal year 2025 on local jail costs, about half of the approximately $1 million of the county’s annual property tax revenues that serve as the county’s primary revenue stream. 
A Kentucky Association of Counties analysis shows local jail costs have increased from $96.5 million in 2019 to $169.7 million in 2025, a 76% increase over that timespan. 
Different counties have sought different solutions. Some counties have merged their jail operations into a regional jail. Others have taken revenue from housing federal inmates and, controversially, also agreed to house Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees. 
One Republican state lawmaker, Rep. Michael Meredith, R-Oakland, has one potential solution: make the state government give enough funding to counties to cover the costs of housing state inmates. It’s got a big price tag, around $200 million each year, which is the main sticking point with getting his proposal passed into law. 
The proposal, filed as House Bill 557 in 2026, failed to get a hearing before the House Appropriations and Revenue Committee despite having 51 co-sponsors from both parties in the 100-member GOP-controlled House of Representatives.
Still, the proposal has the backing of the state associations for judge executives, county magistrates and county jailers, three groups that don’t always agree. 
“That is the biggest hurdle. It has always been the biggest hurdle,” Meredith told the Lantern about the bill’s price tag. “I think most people on their face think some of, or all of this, makes sense, and I think that’s why you’ve seen such a large number of co-sponsors.” 
Meredith plans to again file a version of HB 557 when state lawmakers meet in Frankfort in January, hoping the House budgetary committee can provide “guidance” on what can get passed. 
Seeking balance between the state and counties
HB 557 would have overhauled several aspects of how the state provides funding to county governments for housing incarcerated people in state custody. 
For example, under current law, the Kentucky Department of Corrections doesn’t have to pick up the tab for the costs of housing state inmates in county jails until after an incarcerated individual is sentenced. 
Henry, the Webster County judge-executive, said a man charged with murder sat in his local jail more than two years, with his county covering the costs of the man’s incarceration, until he was sentenced by the state for an amended charge of manslaughter. 
A statue of an underground miner honoring the region’s coal mining history stands in the center of Providence in Webster County. The former Dotiki coal miner who served as a model for the statue, Bobby Shoulders, died in October. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
HB 557 would require the state to enter into a contract with local jails that guaranteed reimbursement for state inmates. Currently, the state pays county jails $35.34 for each day a state inmate is held in a county jail. The Kentucky Association of Counties estimates that the actual per day costs are, on average, $63.44. 
In an emailed statement, Morgan Hall, a spokesperson for the Kentucky Department of Corrections, said the price tag of Meredith’s proposal can’t be implemented without a new appropriation. 
“The Department of Corrections works to carry out its mission under the current budget, even though it doesn’t control the number of inmates it must house nor the time in which they are in custody. Both are beginning to increase under recent legislation, which will increase normal recurring costs,” Hall said. 
Meredith’s bill would also provide new grants to encourage counties to create regional jails, something Meredith believes is another potential solution if the circumstances are right. There are only four regional jails operating in Eastern and Central Kentucky. 
Meredith said he understands “the pressure” that Republican budget leaders in the legislature, Sen. Chris McDaniel and Rep. Jason Petrie, have in trying to craft a balanced budget. 
In an October committee meeting, Petrie, the chair of the House Appropriations and Revenue Committee, told Meredith he believed the business model of county jails relying on state payments is “perverse and failed” but that he was cautious to allocate funding for a fix. 
“Are we rehabbing the model, or are we supporting the model?” Petrie said in October. “That’s going to be a continual conversation through today and on and on.” 
But Meredith doesn’t believe some county governments have much time to figure out growing jail costs on their own.
“I think as this has continued to develop and continue to be a bigger and bigger issue, I think that pressure is there for us to get something moving as quickly as possible,” Meredith said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: A Thanksgiving memory
description: This column was first published Nov. 27, 2024. Frankfort’s small army of state workers, fresh from four days off for Thanksgiving on Dec. 1, 1997, slipped from their cars in normal morning sun and almost as one looked to the sky with twisted, stricken faces. The Capitol Annex parking lot seemed misted with some indelible […]
text:
This is not the maintenance worker who responded to an unusual post-Thanksgiving emergency outside the Kentucky Capitol Annex. That incident went unphotographed, as far as we know, though not forgotten. (Getty Images)
This column was first published Nov. 27, 2024.
Frankfort’s small army of state workers, fresh from four days off for Thanksgiving on Dec. 1, 1997, slipped from their cars in normal morning sun and almost as one looked to the sky with twisted, stricken faces.
The Capitol Annex parking lot seemed misted with some indelible flesh-rot that despised humankind. It wasn’t just a smell but a Presence. It sucked life from you; your soul departed and you knew it would not return. Your eyes glazed toward opaque. You could not breathe but for shallow, burning gasps that presaged death rattle.
Of all possible causes, you wouldn’t at this moment imagine a turkey.
Yet. Over there, 30 feet yonder, a maintenance lad in a white haz-mat suit with a stout black bag and a muscular garbage picker crept toward a thing on the Annex lawn. It looked like a yellowed stew of plastic and flesh. It seemed to glow and quiver. Some brave parking-lot sufferer managed to croak out toward the creeping lad, “Dear God, son … What … Why?”
“Some a-hole threw a turkey on the lawn,” the lad said, in a voice that echoed death. It was a sentence as final and direct as, “They launched the nuclear missiles.”
When he’d kissed his wife goodbye that morning, the young man had no clue what this day would bring. He was about to be a hero. He retrieved the turkey. He lost his sense of smell. “Like starin’ at the Sun and goin’ blind,” he told the Workers Comp Board weeks later, I heard. It was a metaphor nailed down tight.
So this is a story I’ve been badgered to tell since then. It started when Rep. Jim Callahan of Southgate gave me a Thanksgiving turkey.
Jim was House Democratic Caucus chairman. In the happy event he liked you, you could have no finer friend in the stinging spin-drift of the Kentucky legislature. If he didn’t, he was one of the few people who could and would get you fired. A man to be trusted and feared. A perfect politician.
I had just lately and reluctantly been put in charge of the Legislative Research Commission’s Public Information Office, a communications shop whose future was in doubt because of some early Republican restiveness. They didn’t find the office deferential enough. It likely wasn’t.
I made it my strategic purpose in life to become indispensable to Jim, so he (and the House Dems, then lazy with a comfortable majority) would protect me against the new restive Republican hordes. I succeeded with Jim, the caucus obeyed his instructions re: me, and in late 1997 Jim started rewarding me for my many good works with appreciated tokens like holiday meats.
The day before this particular Thanksgiving — five days before the maintenance lad’s heroics — Jim’s lanky assistant presented me with my first turkey, laid the sweaty sucker on my desk, bagged in plastic, pristine, frozen and promptly forgotten.
Forgotten, that is to say, in my windowless, steam-heated office, 80 degrees at least, with four black holidays awaiting it and a billion turkey-flesh bacteria awakening to yawn, scratch themselves, and eat.
Flash forward: 9:27 p.m., Payton Residence, Louisville. Sat. Nov. 29.
Quick scene:
“Aw, MAN! NO!”
“What?”
“I forgot the damn TURKEY!”
“What turkey?”
“The one Jim C. gave me three days ago that’s sitting on my desk like a bomb about to explode, if it hasn’t already! I have to get it.’
(Indistinct squabbling).
Even quicker scene:
“You’re not driving a hundred miles round-trip to Frankfort in the dead of night to retrieve a turkey that’s wrapped in plastic and perfectly fine. No.”
Note to young husbands: There are many days coming in your marriage when you simply look at your wife’s slant eyes and surrender. I surrendered. Fifty miles east, the turkey-flesh bacteria ate and ate.
The rest of the weekend was like waiting for biopsy results. Monday morning I drove to work early, dreading what I’d find, hoping against hope the turkey hadn’t exploded but otherwise wanting to get things cleaned up and tended to as best I could before anyone else arrived. Pretty sure I was first in the parking lot slammed by the Presence, the living thing I’d birthed.
The Kentucky Capitol and Annex are in the author’s hometown of Frankfort along the Kentucky River. (University of Kentucky Libraries, Special Collections Research Center, Post Card Collection)
But hope withstood its first assault. As a Frankfort native, I was accustomed to its distilleries, specifically the smell of its distilleries burning mash. The signature smell of the Kentucky River valley. In many ways, Frankfort is a smell. It’s not necessarily a good smell; many find it rank. But all share in it. Every redneck boy, every doctor’s son, every lawyer’s daughter and governor’s privileged kid walks out on fall mornings into its egalitarian embrace. It is hillbilly Marxism: Share the stink.
So for no more than half a second I thought/hoped this stink might be mash. For the second half-second I thought, “Whew, did they throw some rotting sheep cadavers into the mash vats this morning?” Then of course I knew: Turkey. Hissing from my office. Into the Annex HVAC system. Leaking out the old building’s windows. Filling the river valley. Soon to make me the laughing stock of Frankfort. Republicans would say this proved my liberalism.
I try to be relatively accurate in memoirish accounts like this (facts are critically important until they interfere with a good laugh). So I’ll admit the next half hour is a blur that resists disinterment.
The grotesque bird was still on my desk, its plastic bag ripped open by the force of its eruption. I recall an echoey dripping sound onto the floor, a yellowish oozing slime, thick like molasses, that seemed alive itself (remember, it teemed with a billion chomping necrobiomes). It looked like some bad special-effects alien from the first season of Star Trek in 1966.
I cannot remember how I managed to scoop up the carcass itself, make some quick impossible decision about disposing of it, and rush it down the still-deserted Annex hall to the bronze entry doors, where I flung it mightily onto the front lawn and the Presence began spreading in earnest, as did its legend.
At some point the heroic haz-mat kid was called, he gave the remains their final scoop, yet the smell snaked through the Capitol campus (HVAC circulation and filters are eternal, and the river valley itself a thermal trap). Many workers went home for an extra day or two of Thanksgiving celebration. Every sentence at home began “You won’t believe…”
Me, I suffered the derision I deserved, and have at least once a year for 27 years been hectored into telling “Scott’s Turkey Story” to wildly laughing, knee-slapping audiences. I’ve hated it every time, knowing they’re not exactly laughing with me, and sworn for many years I’d “write it up” and just hand the sucker out at every such request.
So now I’ve done that. Here you are. Don’t ask again.
But.
Coda: There is more to the story, and it’s good, but it doesn’t belong to me. It belongs to a fellow Capitol staffer who worked a mysterious deskless job for people who seemed powerful. His name recalls that of a major world capital. He would “borrow” your desk without asking if he needed one. Jim Callahan gave him a turkey every year too.
This is a grand fellow, as all in politics must be, but a bit absent-minded, as most in politics are. To his credit though, and unlike me, he miraculously got his gifted bird to his car that afternoon. Threw it in the trunk. Promptly forgot it.
A week or so later, troubled by some mystery problem with the car — couldn’t quite put his finger on it, snap, snap! — he dropped it off at the repair shop.
From memory:
FRANKFORT STATE JOURNAL
Police Reports 12/8/97
Police responded at 8:19 a.m. to call from Willie and Joe’s Auto Service on East Main of a suspected dead body, decomposed in trunk of customer’s vehicle. Officers opened trunk, discovered turkey.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: In politics, men always get their flowers. Women, not so much.
description: This week, GOP Congressional Rep. James Comer announced his unsurprising bid to be Kentucky’s next governor. It was a curiously underwhelming announcement, with Comer standing alone before a banner emblazoned with his new campaign logo. No family by his side, no introduction by a prominent Republican, no applauding crowd, no slick video clip. Does Comer […]
text:
Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman speaks on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Austin Anthony / Kentucky Lantern) Flowers for Jamie

 This week, GOP Congressional Rep. James Comer announced his unsurprising bid to be Kentucky’s next governor. It was a curiously underwhelming announcement, with Comer standing alone before a banner emblazoned with his new campaign logo. No family by his side, no introduction by a prominent Republican, no applauding crowd, no slick video clip.
Does Comer have name recognition? Sure, if you consider how he smartly used his 2026 congressional campaign funds to spread his name statewide. That, plus he was a darling of rightwing media (Fox News, OANN, et al.) during the Biden administration when he served as Chairman of Oversight, investigating the all-encompassing bogeyman “Hunter Biden’s laptop” while ignoring the rampant corruption of President Trump, his family, and his administration.
While doing what, exactly, for Kentuckians?
And boy-howdy ain’t it curious that no one seems to want to run against Comer in a primary, even as GOP favorites like Secretary of State Michael Adams and Senate President Robert Stivers made early noises about running before slinking off stage like they’d been slapped. There is still time for a challenger, but it appears Comer has been handed his flowers while making minimal effort, and to a piteous puff of fanfare.
 Flowers for Rocky

 With the blue tsunami of the midterms behind us, I stopped by West Sixth in Lexington to not only hear Lt. Governor Jacqueline Coleman’s pitch as to why she’s the right choice in the Democratic primary, but to watch the crowd watching her.
 She is, in a word, electric.
On my way home I posted a photo on social media which I tagged #TeamJacqueline, and over the next couple of days got some interesting responses from the Rocky for Governor contingency. There appear to be two camps: (1) The “a woman can’t win” crowd, who have already forgotten how many next-generation candidates and Democratic women won seats in red states just two weeks ago, and (2) The “it’s Rocky’s time” crowd who believe Rocky has better name recognition across the state (does he?) and that it’s likely his last chance, at age 67, to get his flowers.
 I like Rocky. Who doesn’t. He’s a nice guy. I enjoy talking with him. I also recognize that we are in the midst of a political revolution, as clearly evidenced by both the Trump era and the 2026 midterms, and we ignore this era and the will of the voters — for new leadership, for new ideas, for diversity, for a new generation — at our peril.
At 44, Jacqueline Coleman is part of this new generation of leaders. She has served two terms as lieutenant governor alongside one of the most popular governors in the country. In 2018, well-before becoming Andy Beshear’s running mate, she stood with hundreds of citizens at the capitol and fought for teachers’ pensions. And when Covid-19 arrived in early 2020, Coleman was not only a brand new lieutenant governor, she was a brand new lieutenant governor with a newborn. And while running with Beshear the second time, in late 2023, she was quietly managing a breast cancer diagnosis.
 I don’t recall anyone handing Coleman anything in those days, including flowers. I just recall her doing what women do: her job.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Judge to decide Dec. 4 if Virginia’s reproductive rights constitutional amendment will stand
description: The fate of a legal challenge to Virginia’s voter-approved reproductive rights constitutional amendment will remain uncertain for a few more weeks, with a Tazewell judge planning to rule on Dec. 4.  Following a multi-hour hearing in the Southwest Virginia locality on Tuesday, parties will reconvene in a virtual meeting next month. On Dec. 7, the […]
text:
A lawsuit is seeking a preliminary injunction to block the certification of the reproductive rights amendment Virginians approved on Nov. 3, 2026 by alleging that the amendment's process was not properly filed and that its ballot language was misleading. (Photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)The fate of a legal challenge to Virginia’s voter-approved reproductive rights constitutional amendment will remain uncertain for a few more weeks, with a Tazewell judge planning to rule on Dec. 4. 
Following a multi-hour hearing in the Southwest Virginia locality on Tuesday, parties will reconvene in a virtual meeting next month. On Dec. 7, the state’s board of election is set to certify this year’s congressional election and three amendments voters advanced, including the one at the center of the lawsuit. 
About 62% of Virginia voters approved the reproductive rights amendment, which will enshrine access to abortion, contraception and fertility treatment in the state Constitution. 
The lawsuit is seeking a preliminary injunction to block the certification of the amendment by alleging that the amendment’s process was not properly filed and that its ballot language was misleading.
Founding Freedoms Law Center launched the lawsuit in April, but it has been stalled in court since June, after advocacy group Virginians For Reproductive Freedom successfully petitioned to join as a co-defendant.
Voter turnout for Virginia’s constitutional amendments transcended partisanship

Founding Freedoms is the political arm of the Family Foundation, a conservative advocacy organization that has opposed abortion access laws.
“It was supposed to be a three-hour hearing, and it ended up being closer to five,” Founding Freedoms lawyer Josh Hetzler said in an afternoon call following the hearing in Southwest Virginia. “That’s indicative, I think, of the volume and the complexity of the issues.” 
An argument of the case is whether Virginia’s retroactive repeal of old state code concerning constitutional amendment processes apply. 
A similar case brought forth by Liberty Counsel was dismissed over the summer in a different court, but the group is seeking an appeal. At the time of the dismissal, Senior Assistant Attorney General Erin McNeil emphasized that state lawmakers have authority to adjust the constitution and prescribe how they do it. 
“How can the General Assembly have this authority to prescribe a process but not have the authority to change that process?” McNeil said in court. 
The argument also surfaced as part of a successful effort to strike down a redistricting referendum voters had approved this past spring. Tazewell Judge Jack Hurley ruled on that case before it was heard by the state’s supreme court. He is the same judge who presided over the Family Foundation’s case. 
“Our position is that when you’re going to amend the state Constitution, there’s got to be strict compliance with the procedures,” Hetzler said. “We’ll see what the judge does.”
The ruling could also support or disprove Family Foundation’s assertion that the ballot language was misleading. 
The organization had four Virginians submit sworn declarations to the court that they felt confused by the language and would have voted differently if they’d better understood it, Hetzler said. 
Virginians for Reproductive Freedom, in a statement, accused the Family Foundation of bringing the “sham lawsuit against the amendment because they knew voters would protect reproductive freedom.” 
The group, a coalition of reproductive rights advocacy organizations, jointly added that the amendment passed with “62.87% of voters during a year of record midterm turnout. We are confident in our success.”

title: Dominion-NextEra merger hearings wrap up at the SCC, decision expected by Jan. 11
description: The evidentiary hearings for the unprecedented Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy proposal concluded Tuesday with a full day of testimony from supporters and opponents of the deal, leaving three commissioners to decide whether it will materialize in the state.  Over the last week, the two companies have faced questions from the over 30 intervening parties […[...]
text:
The State Corporation Commission building in downtown Richmond. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)The evidentiary hearings for the unprecedented Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy proposal concluded Tuesday with a full day of testimony from supporters and opponents of the deal, leaving three commissioners to decide whether it will materialize in the state. 
Over the last week, the two companies have faced questions from the over 30 intervening parties and have attempted to defend their proposal against arguments that it does not meet requirements of the Utility Transfers Act.
“Virginia has a big (energy) build need … to accommodate the generation that we see,” NextEra President and CEO John Ketchum testified. “We’ve got to have the right ecosystem and that ecosystem is enveloped in the commitments that we would be making.”
Heading into the case, the State Corporation Commission staff stated that as it was proposed, the merger should not be approved. Staff and Attorney General Jay Jones’ office presented the companies with a list of policy shifts and recommendations to put the deal in a better position. 
Dominion and NextEra accepted a majority of those recommendations, but rejected and altered some, mainly concerning financial “ring fencing” protections that would shield the state from fallout given credit shifts or bankruptcy.
The two companies were also pressured to provide calculations proving claims that combining the entities would enhance its ability to bulk-buy energy infrastructure and bring down costs to customers. 
But company witnesses said it would be difficult to calculate that metric and were not able to provide numbers. Some intervenors felt that without those calculations, the savings could not be guaranteed.
Dominion and NextEra emphasized that the deal also addresses short-term affordability, with a proposed four-year bill credit for residential customers. The original proposal was only for two years because large load customers, namely data centers, would also receive a credit. 
The companies offered to change it so that residential customers were chief beneficiaries, by rerouting the potential credits for large load customers back to the smaller rate classes. 
However, intervenors including Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration testified that those credits were not enough and did not guarantee that bills wouldn’t increase once the credits ran out.
The Florida-based company’s political past has been a defining feature of public discourse about the merger but on Tuesday was limited by commissioners.
NextEra recently paid a $150 million settlement over whether the company lied about its involvement in political interference schemes in Florida. Details of an internal investigation into the company leadership are contained in confidential evidence in the case called the “Robo Memo”. The commission ruled against an attempt to unseal it Nov. 24. 
NextEra Energy Resources, NextEra’s unregulated branch that produces energy infrastructure, has been noted as a more volatile business because it relies on the market price of power. 
Dominion’s Attorney Joseph Reid asked Michael Dunn, on behalf of the joint petitioners, whether the unregulated branch was an actual risk. Dunn said the extensive energy infrastructure business, which has major investments in renewable energy sources, have been a successful side of the NextEra entity.
“For NextEra Energy Resources, unregulated means long term, diverse, strong, stable cash flows,” Dunn testified Tuesday. “When I look at 49 states, you have 330 different projects, 400 different power purchase agreement offtakers.” 
At the heart of the three commissioners’ considerations is the Utility Transfers Act’s mandate, “that adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized” by combining the companies. 
They must make a decision by Jan. 11. The commission is expected to call post-hearing briefs from the intervening parties in December.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana’s quest for US Space Academy persists despite midterm setback
description: Louisiana is continuing its quest to become the home of the U.S. Space Force Academy despite the loss of key leadership positions in Congress that could have helped steer the project to New Orleans.
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry has proposed hosting the U.S. Space Academy on the campus of LSU New Orleans. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana is continuing its quest to become the home of the U.S. Space Force Academy despite the loss of key leadership positions in Congress that could have helped steer the project to New Orleans.
State leaders announced earlier this month have been working for much of this year on a proposal to host the new academy.
Gov. Jeff Landry, a Republican, proposed hosting the academy on the campus of LSU New Orleans, previously the University of New Orleans, which comes with considerable unused acreage and vacant office space.
The final decision on where to base the academy lies with President Donald Trump’s administration, but site selection is expected to involve political jockeying on Capitol Hill as the project would require significant federal spending.
Landry said he was confident in the state’s proposal when asked about whether the midterm election results, which will remove U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson and U.S. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise from leadership positions, would be a roadblock for the state,
“We are confident in the work we have done, the strong partnerships we have built and the compelling case Louisiana has made,” the governor said. “The Space Academy belongs to a state that builds rockets, supports our nation’s military and is now home to the world’s largest spaceport.”
During the space race of the 1960s, the NASA Michoud facility in eastern New Orleans built the first stages of Saturn rockets that sent Americans to the moon. The same location produced external fuel tanks for the space shuttles, and its most recent work has been on the core stages for the Artemis program that intends to take man back to the moon.
The LSU New Orleans campus, about 10 miles from the Michoud complex, is in the congressional district of U.S. Rep. Troy Carter, a Democrat who is in the running to be the next chairman of the Congressional Black Caucus. The powerful position could help turn the tides in Louisiana’s favor in the Democratic-controlled Congress that takes over Jan. 3.
“Count me as a champion of the state’s application to host USSA!,” Carter posted on social media. “Should the administration select LSU New Orleans as the next site of the U.S. Space Academy, it will have chosen the only university system in America that is a Land, Sea and Space Grant institution!”
LSU New Orleans will compete against proposals from at least two dozen other states, but officials hope the city and state offer some key advantages.
In addition to the city’s history with NASA, SpaceX has chosen to build a $100 billion launch facility in coastal Vermilion Parish. Dubbed Starbase Louisiana, its projects sending 30 rockets per day into space, according to the company.
“Louisiana is building one of the most consequential aerospace ecosystems in the country, and the U.S. Space Academy would give us the opportunity to build the talent pipeline alongside it,” Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois said.
In addition to a home on the LSU New Orleans campus, the state is offering assistance from the city of New Orleans, facilities at Southern University at New Orleans and Tulane University and a dedicated state fund to cover startup needs to lower the federal investment needed.
State Rep. Jack McFarland, R-Jonesboro, who leads the legislature’s budget committee, said he had not yet had discussions with the Landry administration about specific amounts of money the state would provide.

name: VTDigger
title: Appeals delay affordable housing for flood recovery in Montpelier
description:
The four single-family homes and 20 apartments are supported by federal flood recovery money, replacing homes that have been lost in recent years. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Appeals delay affordable housing for flood recovery in Montpelier.
text:
Construction is underway on four single-family homes on Heaton Street in Montpelier on Nov. 23. A nonprofit developer wants to renovate a former nurses’ dormitory next door into apartments, but a neighbor has appealed. David Littlefield / Vermont Public
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger.
An affordable housing developer has started construction on new homes on high ground in Vermont’s flood-prone capital city. But a series of appeals from neighbors is slowing its progress.
The nonprofit Downstreet Housing and Community Development is building the Montpelier project with over $6 million in federal flood recovery money, a funding source dedicated to helping replace homes the state lost to flooding in recent years. The location is high and dry – compared to where much of the city’s subsidized housing sits along its riverfront.
“It’s an affluent neighborhood out of the flood zone,” said Angie Harbin, Downstreet’s executive director. “It’s a perfect place for housing.” 
The site on Heaton Street was originally built as a nurses’ dormitory and most recently served as office space for Washington County Mental Health Services. Downstreet has begun construction on the first phase of the project: four new single-family homes next to the historic building. The homes will be sold as part of the nonprofit’s shared-equity program, ranging in price from $185,000 to $275,000 for qualified buyers. 
Next, the nonprofit plans to renovate the old dorms back into homes: It hopes to turn the underutilized office building into 20 permanently subsidized apartments.

Downstreet Housing and Community Development wants to convert an old nurses’ dormitory — pictured on Nov. 23 — into apartments. David Littlefield / Vermont Public

But those plans are currently on hold as the developer fights an appeal brought by neighbors. 
It’s the second challenge neighbors Lisa Mahoney and Peter Mancauskas have lodged against the project. The couple owns a property next door to the Downstreet development, according to city property records.
First, the couple appealed the Montpelier Development Review Board’s decision allowing Downstreet to subdivide the property in 2025. A judge ultimately affirmed the board’s decision and ruled in Downstreet’s favor, but the legal challenge delayed the project’s first phase by about a year, according to Harbin. The organization secured an additional $300,000 in flood recovery funding to cover the cost of resolving the appeal plus rising construction costs during the delay, she added.
The homeownership units were allowed to proceed in early 2026. But in September, Mahoney and Mancauskas appealed the DRB’s decision to approve Downstreet’s application to convert the former dormitory into apartments. 
At a June board hearing, Mahoney had expressed concerns about traffic impacts, pedestrian safety and noise from the new homes.
“It’s 20 units in a very quiet neighborhood. Nothing has been provided with respect to noise mitigation,” Mahoney said.
In their current appeal, Mahoney and Mancauskas asked state environmental court to weigh in on whether the Development Review Board appropriately considered issues like soil erosion, stormwater management, height bonuses for affordable housing projects and more when approving Downstreet’s application, according to court records. The case is ongoing.
Mahoney and the couple’s attorney did not respond to multiple requests for an interview. Mahoney owns a national environmental consultancy firm focused in part on helping clients navigate environmental regulation compliance, according to its website. 
For years, state lawmakers have debated how best to limit neighbors’ legal challenges to new housing in Vermont, but they’ve so far failed to agree on reforms.
Montpelier has taken steps to curtail some appeals on a local level. The capital had seen “a number of appeals of permits in the past in order to slow down and stop projects,” Montpelier planning director Mike Miller wrote in an email. “This created a reputation of Montpelier being a difficult place to build,” he said.
In 2025, the city raised the cost of appealing an administrative decision on a project to $1,600, better reflecting what it costs for staff to process appeals. The change is also intended to dissuade people from launching frivolous challenges, Miller said. (In cases where the appealing party wins, they get their money back.)
Yet that fee hike only applies to situations where someone appeals the city zoning administrator’s verdict to the Development Review Board. In circumstances like the Heaton Street project – where neighbors have appealed a DRB decision to court – the city fee does not apply.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Appeals delay affordable housing for flood recovery in Montpelier.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: This Thanksgiving, Imagine A Hawaiʻi Without Hunger
description: What if we all approached ending hunger the same way?
text:
As the season of gratitude arrives, we look forward to gathering with family and friends amid the aromas of spiced pumpkin pie and roasting turkey, yet across our islands, too many empty tables tell a different story.
On Hawaiʻi island, 43% of households experience food insecurity, and an estimated 62% of keiki live in households where children experience food insecurity. These are not distant statistics; they are our neighbors, our coworkers, and the next generation whose future we share.
A challenge of this scale can feel overwhelming, but Hawaiʻi has long understood that our strength lies in what we can do together.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

We see this in the Hilo lei, where strands of tī leaf are twisted together. A single strand is delicate, but joined with others, it becomes part of something stronger. This lei is also the centerpiece of The Food Basket’s strategic plan, and I confess I love a plan guided not by metrics but by a lei.
What if all of Hawaiʻi approached ending hunger the same way?
For generations, Hawaiʻi sustained thriving communities through agriculture, fishing, stewardship, and sharing. Fields of kalo and ʻuala, groves of ʻulu, and coastal fisheries nourished our islands through aloha ʻāina and reciprocity, because our kūpuna understood that abundance requires knowledge, cooperation, and shared responsibility. That history reminds us of what is possible.
Too many tables in Hawaii go empty too often. Pictured is a food bank in Kalihi. (David Croxford/Civil Beat/2025) David Croxford/Civil Beat/2025
We saw that spirit again this year. When the Kona Low storms, a magnitude 6.0 earthquake, and Hurricane Lala upended lives, neighbors checked on neighbors, volunteers mobilized, businesses stepped forward, and farmers shared their harvests despite losses of their own.
Yet these disasters also deepened hardship as power outages spoiled refrigerated food, missed workdays meant lost wages, and repairs stretched tight budgets further. For families already struggling, the burden grew heavier; others faced new worries about putting food on the table.
Hunger is a quieter disaster, one that arrives without storm warnings or headlines. It unfolds in kitchens where parents skip meals so their children can eat, and in working households where grocery money runs out before the month ends.
What if we brought the same urgency, generosity, and determination to ending hunger every day, not only in moments of crisis? The possibilities are already taking shape.
Farmers are growing healthy food for island families, while volunteers gather surplus produce from donor farms and backyard gardens and share it through food banks, pantries, and soup kitchens. Healthcare providers recognize nutritious food as essential to good health, and businesses are buying locally, strengthening the livelihoods of those who grow what we eat.
Teachers and cultural practitioners are reconnecting young people with the ʻāina, and neighbors continue to do what neighbors have always done: share what they have with aloha.
Acts Of Caring
At The Food Basket, Hawaiʻi island’s Food Bank, we are privileged to be part of these connections. More than half the food we distribute, is sourced on Hawaiʻi island, a commitment that nourishes families, supports farmers, ranchers, fishers, and local businesses, and builds a more resilient food system and a strong island economy.
Each act of caring is a strand, and each partnership strengthens the weave, but the lei is not yet complete. You do not need farmland, wealth, or specialized expertise to help end hunger, only the recognition that what you have to offer matters.
It might be ripe citrus from your backyard tree, a morning packing food boxes, choosing island-grown produce at the market, or a donation that helps a family through a difficult month. Perhaps it is sharing a meal with a kūpuna living alone, teaching a child to plant a seed, or inviting your workplace or school to join in.
We must also weave together larger changes: affordable housing, living wages, strong local agriculture, and public policies that help families thrive. This November, Oʻahu voters approved a Food Security Fund dedicating a portion of annual property tax revenues to improving access to locally produced food, an example Hawaiʻi’s other counties may wish to examine as they seek lasting food security.
Your voice matters, too, whether you contact an elected representative, testify at a hearing, or help shape local solutions. What transforms an island is not the scale of one gesture, but our willingness to braid our efforts into something larger than ourselves.
We must also weave together larger changes.
Imagine the strength of a lei woven with strands of nourishment, opportunity, and abundance encircling every keiki, kūpuna, and family with dignity. We know how to come together when disaster strikes, so let’s bring that determination to ensuring no one in Hawaiʻi goes hungry.
This season of gratitude, bring your strand and weave it with others, knowing that every contribution matters and every strand makes us stronger. Together, we can weave a Hawaiʻi where abundance is shared, aloha guides our actions, and no one goes hungry.

name: National
title: Ahead of Thanksgiving, more Americans struggle to put food on the table
description: KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards. As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and […]
text:
Andreas Leal and his wife peruse the shelves at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas. Food banks and pantries across the country are experiencing surging demand amid declining federal food assistance and higher grocery prices. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards.
As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and the hodgepodge of donated items on the toiletry shelves. A 75-year-old retiree, Leal said every bit helps when trying to keep up with rising prices.
“It’s very expensive,” he said. “Everything is expensive right now.”
Leal said his monthly Social Security benefit can’t keep up with rising costs. While the federal program boosted benefits by 2.8% this year, he said he just received notice that his residential property tax bill will jump 30%, costing him some $600. The increases require constant trade-offs. For example, to save on gas, the couple forgoes trips to visit their son who lives about 45 minutes away.
Leaders of Cross-Lines Community Outreach say such stories are more and more common. Its Community Market, a food pantry resembling a grocery store, serves about 1,900 families per month — a 35% increase over last year.  
“Daily, we have to turn people away,” said Executive Director Susila Jones. 
The market previously aimed to provide a couple pounds of frozen ground beef each month to every family. But those costs are now too high, pushing Cross-Lines to buy ground turkey or chicken — if prices are low enough.
People shop at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas.(Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
Cross-Lines serves people across Wyandotte County, one of the most populous counties in Kansas with a poverty rate that exceeds state and national averages. In recent years, the food pantry has become more lenient about its income requirements and welcomed people who seek aid from multiple organizations. 
“This is not what people want to do and so we really just let people come to us when they need to come to us,” she said. “Because we know even if you are working, if you’ve had steady income, just one paycheck can put you over the edge.”
Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance. At the same time, those charitable organizations are seeing a wave of Americans who have lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the nation’s largest food assistance program. 
About 5.5 million Americans have lost SNAP benefits since last July’s passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut taxes and federal safety net programs. The law changed SNAP eligibility rules, ended certain work requirement exemptions and shifted new costs to states that administer the federal program.
More people are expected to lose SNAP aid as the legislation is fully implemented in the coming years. And earlier this month, the Trump administration proposed enrollment rule changes that would cut eligibility for another 6.3 million people.
Without congressional action, few experts see much relief ahead, further stressing the nation’s patchwork of churches, food banks and nonprofits laboring to keep people fed.
“Unfortunately, it has become a big part of people’s lives because they keep cutting off SNAP benefits,” said Gina Plata-Nino, the SNAP director at the anti-hunger nonprofit Food Research and Action Center. “…And you have these volunteers at food banks trying to do their best, but they are suffering in terms of being able to keep up.”
‘A huge demand’
The line of cars waiting to pick up ingredients for a full Thanksgiving dinner stretched a mile long last week in Detroit’s East Side. 
The Capuchin Soup Kitchen had to close its line a few hours after opening when it became clear that the annual giveaway would quickly deplete its 500 turkey meal kits.
“If we had 750, we still would have to shut the line down,” said Brother Fred Cabras, director of social services at the nearly century-old Catholic nonprofit. “I imagine that whatever number we set, we will probably hit every time because there is a huge demand.”
Rising prices squeeze more Americans ahead of pivotal midterm elections

The organization serves about 1,000 hot meals each day across two locations and operates a food pantry for thousands of families. Food pantry visits have been surging in recent years. 
In 2022, the operation served about 15,000 families. Cabras expects that figure to reach 34,000 to 35,000 by the end of this year. 
“This is definitely worse than the pandemic,” he said. 
The surging demand — and food prices — mean the Capuchin Soup Kitchen spent about $20,000 more on the food it bought last month compared with September. But private donations have remained strong.
Cabras said the coronavirus pandemic and last year’s unprecedented disruption to SNAP benefits because of the federal government shutdown heightened the public’s awareness and compassion about growing hunger.
“People also realize it because they’re spending more money on groceries,” he said. “And they’re like, ‘Well if I have a decent job, and I’m struggling, I can’t even imagine for the folks who are not getting great wages how much they’re struggling.’”
Vegetables are available at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas.(Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
While people tend to donate more generously around the holiday season, high prices have also squeezed the budgets of many regular donors to charitable food groups.
“Everybody’s struggling. People who were not struggling a year ago are in a different space, just because of the rising costs,” said Courtney Goff, associate director of United Crescent Hill Ministries in Louisville, Kentucky.
The nonprofit, supported by local churches, businesses and individuals, serves about 50 people per day at its food pantry. That’s quadruple the amount of people it served last year, Goff said. 
With federal cuts to food pantry aid and rising prices for consumers, Goff said her organization is purchasing more food on its own and increasingly asking the community for cash and food donations.
Still, the food disappears nearly as quickly as it’s stocked because so many people are struggling to afford the basics. 
“You have people who maybe they make enough money to pay their rent, but rent is so high that that means they don’t have money for groceries or they don’t have money for gas,” she said. “And so they’re picking what is the most vital in that moment, and then trying to scramble together for the rest of it.”
Food banks increase spending 
St. Mary’s Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, which calls itself the World’s First Food Bank, has had to dip into its savings this year to meet rising diesel and fuel costs.
“We bought more food than we ever have before,” said Jerry Brown, director of public relations. “And just like everybody else who goes to the grocery store, that food is costing more.” 
The food bank serves hundreds of communities across Arizona, which has experienced the nation’s sharpest decline in SNAP benefits. Between July 2025 and July 2026, about 450,000 Arizonans lost SNAP benefits — a decrease of more than 50%. 
St. Mary’s has seen an influx from those who lost SNAP, Brown said. But it’s also experienced more visits from retirees who are unable to keep up with rising prices.
More Americans lose SNAP as Congress weighs food stamps’ future

“They thought they had enough money to retire on, and then the price of everything skyrocketed, while the amount of money that they receive remains the same,” he said. 
In Texas, some food banks have had to ration food in the face of overwhelming demand.
While individuals have lost SNAP benefits, food banks have grappled with separate cuts to federal food assistance. 
Last year, the Trump administration cut hundreds of millions in funding from a local food program for food banks and school meals. The U.S. Department of Agriculture also slashed $500 million that had already been allocated to food aid nationwide through The Emergency Food Assistance Program.
That’s pushed more food banks to purchase more of the food their communities need, said Celia Cole, CEO of Feeding Texas, a statewide network of 20 food banks.
“And that’s a real concern because it’s not really sustainable,” she said.
While she foresees no immediate relief from high food prices, Cole said politicians are increasingly recognizing the growing threat of hunger across the country. She’s hopeful that Congress will make changes to last year’s federal legislation cutting SNAP benefits.
“I think everyone recognizes the importance of having a well-nourished population and sees how these changes to SNAP are leading to people losing access to what’s really the backbone defense against hunger in our country,” she said. “So I see a light at the end of the tunnel there because I think there is a lot of bipartisan concern.”
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.
