title: McCollum to introduce bill requiring feds to share information with local law enforcement agencies
description: Democratic U.S. Rep. Betty McCollum will introduce a bill requiring federal agencies to cooperate with state investigators when federal agents are under investigation for violations of state law, the congresswoman announced Tuesday.  McCollum’s office said she plans to introduce the Federal Law Enforcement Information Sharing Act on Dec. 2, when members of C[...]
text:
Local police officers stand guard as Renee Good's car is towed away after ICE officers shot and killed a woman through her car window Wednesday, Jan. 7, 2026 near Portland Avenue and 34th Street. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Democratic U.S. Rep. Betty McCollum will introduce a bill requiring federal agencies to cooperate with state investigators when federal agents are under investigation for violations of state law, the congresswoman announced Tuesday. 
McCollum’s office said she plans to introduce the Federal Law Enforcement Information Sharing Act on Dec. 2, when members of Congress return to Washington after Thanksgiving. 
Minnesota law enforcement agencies are investigating a number of alleged crimes committed by immigration agents during the Trump administration’s crackdown earlier this year: The killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti; the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in north Minneapolis; the alleged kidnapping of U.S. citizen ChongLy “Scott” Thao; the brandishing of a gun at a driver on Highway 62; among others. 
In many of those cases, federal officials have blocked state and local investigators’ access to key pieces of evidence — including Renee Good’s car, and the identities of the masked agents who dragged Thao out of his home and into the snow wearing only a pair of shorts. In those cases, local prosecutors have sued for access to evidence. 
“Right now, the Department of Homeland Security and other federal law enforcement agencies — they’re impeding these investigations,” McCollum said, standing alongside Rep. Ilhan Omar, Ramsey County Attorney John Choi and incoming Hennepin County Attorney Cedrick Frazier. 
The bill would require federal agencies to allow state and local investigators to access crime scenes and run tests on evidence. (Federal agents blocked the state Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, which investigates law enforcement shootings, from accessing the scene of Pretti’s killing.)
The bill would also require federal agencies to share witness statements with their local counterparts and notify local authorities when they suspect an agent has violated state law. It contains exceptions for national security and privacy protections, according to a one-pager on the bill provided to the Reformer.
Information sharing between local and national law enforcement agencies has been standard practice for years, McCollum said — until Operation Metro Surge. 
“But now, because of the Trump administration’s unprecedented obstruction, this requirement — this courtesy, this working together — now has to be put into law,” McCollum said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska officials offer condolences after death of Bruce Fischer, senator’s husband
description: Bruce Fischer died “peacefully” while spending time outdoors on Sunday, Sen. Deb Fischer said in a statement. He is survived by the couple’s three children.
text:
U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb. June 6, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer’s husband, Bruce, died Sunday.
The senator said Bruce died “peacefully” while spending time outdoors. She didn’t provide additional details about his death. Bruce is survived by the couple’s three children.
“Our family is heartbroken by his passing, but we find comfort in the life we shared with him. I will cherish the decades we spent building a family in the Nebraska Sandhills. Above all, Bruce was a loving husband, a devoted father and grandfather, a man of faith and a rancher,” Fischer said in her statement Monday. 
Nebraska elected officials and others offered condolences. 
U.S. Rep. Mike Flood said Nebraska has “lost one of its very best.” 
“Bruce leaves behind a family that will forever be proud of the man he was. Mandi and I are heartbroken by his passing, and our hearts are with Deb, their boys, and the entire Fischer family.” Flood said in a statement. 
Gov. Jim Pillen said he and his wife, Suzanne, are keeping “Sen. Fischer and her family in our thoughts. We share our prayers as she deals with this great personal loss.” 
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts said, “Bruce left his mark on this world through his love for family, his faith and his ranch. Susanne and I send our deepest condolences to Deb, the entire Fischer family, and all their loved ones during this difficult time. The Fischer family is in our prayers.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: ‘We’re at a sensitive moment’: As legislative deadline nears, energy affordability negotiations enter scramble mode
description: As legislative leaders preemptively try to tamp down expectations for what Beacon Hill can finalize this session, top negotiators on the energy bill are warning that talks could fall apart, jeopardizing a deal.
text:
THE EXTRA TIME that lawmakers afforded themselves this year to put the finishing touches on legislation already approved by both legislative chambers hasn’t helped them manage to avoid a last-minute pile-up of 13 still-unfinished conference committee negotiations. 
The unfolding scramble is perhaps most fully crystallized on a high-stakes energy affordability bill. The two lead negotiators are starting to point fingers, and their views still appear to diverge ahead of a January 5, 2027, deadline to pass legislation this session. 
Hanging in the balance is the promise of savings for Massachusetts ratepayers, whose utility bills are among the highest in the nation and are contributing to a broader affordability crisis. Gov. Maura Healey filed her original energy bill 18 months ago, and with winter descending along with high heating costs this year, pressure is only mounting for elected officials to take concrete action as power demand rises and ambitious climate commitments look harder to meet.   
Yet as legislative leaders preemptively try to tamp down expectations for what Beacon Hill can finalize this session, top negotiators on the energy bill are warning that talks could fall apart, jeopardizing a deal. 
Sen. Michael Barrett, co-chair of the energy committee, said in an interview last week that there is a “50-50 chance” of getting a bill passed at all this session. 
“Things have not gone particularly well,” he said of the negotiations. “We could always turn this around, but the window is closing. We have not used our time well to date. We’re at a sensitive moment, and it could go either way.” 
Barrett is pinning some of the blame on a 20-page letter from Eversource, the largest utility in the state. Its top executives wrote in October that “neither of the bills pending before the Conference Committee will improve affordability” and that both would instead “set the stage for dramatic cost increases.”  
Eversource officials ticked through deep reservations about the price tag of energy efficiency, renewable energy, and electric vehicle programs funded through charges on utility bills and warned of the costs to customers of “compelling electrification through forced termination of natural gas service.” 
Barrett blasted the company’s comments as “reckless,” “careless,” and a “frontal attack on climate policy in Massachusetts as we know it” in a “carefully calibrated plan” to “torpedo” negotiations and “sink the bill.” 
But his counterpart, Rep. Mark Cusack of Braintree, said in an interview that it’s “standard operating procedure that stakeholders have a say and they weigh in.” 
“This freakout about a letter from a month ago is lost on me and is theatric,” Cusack said.  
William Hinkle, an Eversource spokesperson, said in a statement that “the surprised reaction by some legislators as to the scale and scope of charges” proves the company’s point that state energy policies “are not currently subject to public discourse, unbiased analysis or meaningful oversight” and that the letter is designed to show how much of a customer’s bill is not actually within the company’s control. 
Each version of the sweeping legislation filed by Healey and then approved by the House and Senate aims to save ratepayers around $10 billion over a decade by, among other provisions, expanding state procurement of energy resources and cracking down on competitive electric suppliers, third-party companies that sell power directly to customers, often at higher rates than utilities. 
But disagreement between the chambers on several big-ticket items quickly emerged last year. 
After a bid from Cusack to weaken the 2030 climate targets failed to advance last November, the House passed a bill that cut $1 billion from the current budget of Mass Save, the state’s energy efficiency program that collects a fee on customer utility bills to fund weatherization improvements and heat pump installations in homes and businesses. Environmental advocates called for Cusack to be removed from his perch as head of the House energy committee, and just last week some gathered to canvass in his home district. 
Environmental activists walk through the halls of the State House on February 26, 2026, criticizing a House energy bill that would cut $1 billion from Mass Save’s budget. (Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon)
The Senate’s version of the legislation didn’t include any cut to Mass Save but instead proposed to end by 2030 a gas pipeline replacement program that has seen its costs balloon in recent years. It also dropped a provision included in both Healey’s bill and the House version that would lift a moratorium on new nuclear power plants. 
Cusack said he is optimistic a deal can be struck and believes there is agreement on a host of provisions, ranging from interconnection reforms and third-party supply consumer protections to expansion of geothermal energy and ways to cost-effectively boost solar power.  
That means there’s at least a “base bill” that should be able to move forward featuring 60 to 70 percent alignment between all three versions of the bill — though there remains a “hashing out that needs to happen in the next six weeks if we’re going to actually save people money,” he added. 
“It takes two to tango, and that remains a question from across the hall,” Cusack said. 
 Barrett didn’t comment on the sticking points that remain in negotiations or what the two sides may have agreed on so far. 
Now, as the Eversource letter continues to reverberate, Barrett, Cusack, and other members of the negotiating team are sifting through incoming data and lobbying from entities pushing in the other direction.  
Top leaders at Acadia Center, a Boston-based environmental nonprofit, issued a rebuttal to what they called “selective and misleading arguments” by Eversource in a letter of their own to Barrett and Cusack last week. 
The group makes the case that infrastructure spending, ballooning gas system costs, and natural gas price jumps and volatility are to blame for high utility bills. Supply, transmission, and distribution costs account for more than 92 percent of overall bill increases for Eversource customers between 2018 and 2026, with only 8 percent due to clean energy, energy efficiency, and low-income assistance, according to Acadia Center. 
To Barrett, Democrats’ nationwide landslide in the midterm election has raised the bar here. 
“Expectations are high,” he said. “You’d hate to see Massachusetts fail to meet them. This is our own state-level test, and it’s unthinkable that we would fail it, but it could happen.” 
Lawmakers are hearing from others, too, about the importance of other pieces — including preserving Mass Save and finalizing a yearslong effort to crack down on third-party electric suppliers — in a potential legislative package. 
Boston officials have been making members of their delegation on Beacon Hill aware of new data showing the city is on track to meet significant energy efficiency targets — in large part thanks to Mass Save. 
The city, alongside utilities Eversource and National Grid, has installed more than 2,700 heat pumps and weatherized 5,000 homes over the last year through the Boston energy saver program, according to data shared with CommonWealth Beacon. That’s in line with Boston’s goals to install 5,000 heat pumps and complete 10,000 weatherizations by the end of 2027. 
The effort, launched last year, is designed to save residents money on their utility bills by insulating homes and shift them off of heating oil — which is 44 percent more expensive compared to last year — mostly through Mass Save funding. The program has also helped 500 Bostonians enroll in utility discounts, particularly important after Massachusetts implemented some of the most generous discounts in the country this month. 
Oliver Sellers-Garcia, Boston’s environment commissioner and Green New Deal director, said he’s been working “really closely” with the city’s representatives on Beacon Hill. It’s not lost on him that one of them, Rep. Aaron Michlewitz, the House budget chief and North End Democrat, is one of the most powerful lawmakers in the Legislature and is close with Mayor Michelle Wu. 
“When we talk with our legislators, we start with talking about the information about how well this program demonstrates the efficacy of Mass Save, and it often ends with, ‘Can we plan a community meeting together where we can do this immediately in my district?’” Sellers-Garcia said in an interview. “The numbers and the stories of people who use this program and save money are extremely compelling. This is definitely something that our representatives are well aware of.” 
And the Green Energy Consumers Alliance sent new data to the energy conference committee this week showing that the 25 percent of customers enrolled with third-party electric suppliers continue to pay more than those who get electricity through either their utility or municipal aggregation program. 
The data, compiled through filings at the Department of Public Utilities and the federal Energy Information Administration and shared with CommonWealth Beacon, show that residential bills from third-party suppliers rose by $112 million in Massachusetts in 2025 and cost households $183 more on average compared with the prior year. The state attorney general’s office has documented over a decade how these suppliers, which have been accused of deceptively targeting lower-income and non-English-speaking households, have cost customers $739 million more than they would have paid for basic service. 
Versions of the legislation already passed by the House and Senate both allow individual municipalities to ban these suppliers. Both also prohibit automatic renewals without customer consent and bar the suppliers from charging cancellation or early termination fees, with projected savings in the hundreds of millions of dollars. 
“If anyone’s thinking about why we should have no bill,” said Larry Chretien, head of the Green Energy Consumers Alliance, “this is just one huge example of why we still absolutely need action.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah dismisses criminal charges against Kalshi after the company blocks bets in the state
description: Utah’s Attorney General Office announced on Tuesday it moved to dismiss all 14 criminal charges against the prediction market platform Kalshi, a day after the company confirmed it had blocked its operations in Utah. The office last month filed 12 online gambling promotion felony charges, one count of pattern of unlawful activity, also a felony, […]
text:
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown speaks to reporters after a news conference announcing Utah's lawsuit against Kalshi at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Oct. 20, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Utah’s Attorney General Office announced on Tuesday it moved to dismiss all 14 criminal charges against the prediction market platform Kalshi, a day after the company confirmed it had blocked its operations in Utah.
The office last month filed 12 online gambling promotion felony charges, one count of pattern of unlawful activity, also a felony, and a misdemeanor charge for general gambling promotion against Kalshi and its founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara.
Before the dismissal, the charges followed a civil lawsuit the state filed against the platform, which is still pending in court.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The motion does not change the Office’s position: Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling,” the Attorney General’s Office said in a news release. “Utah’s Constitution bars any form of gambling, and state criminal law makes gambling a crime.”
With no legal wins so far, Kalshi blocks operations in Utah

The Attorney General’s Office filed to dismiss the case after Kalshi geofenced Utah. However, the office can still refile the charges if the company resumes operations in the state, the release says. 
“Utah does not allow gambling, and prediction markets are gambling,” Attorney General Derek Brown said in a statement. “Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges. Every company in this space should take note. If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable.”
Kalshi’s attorney Yaakov Roth said in a social media post company leaders were pleased with the move to dismiss criminal charges while proceeding with civil litigation.
“Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized,” Roth wrote. “We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets.”



Let us know what you think...


 


Utah has been fighting in court to enforce its anti-gambling policies since the state legislature passed a law in 2026 including proposition bets in the definition of the state’s constitutional gambling ban. 
That law has been the center of legal disputes, including one from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which argues that the federal government has the authority to regulate derivatives markets and has asked a court for a relief “holding that Utah gambling laws are preempted and unenforceable,” according to the complaint.
The list of legal challenges is still long as other states aim to regulate proposition betting within their boundaries. In Utah, a federal judge ruled in August the state may enforce its anti-gambling laws, even if they include bans of proposition betting. Kalshi unsuccessfully appealed that decision. But, criminal charges in other states, like Arizona, have also been blocked.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia immigrants file lawsuit challenging DHS re-detention policy
description: Two Georgia men are at the center of a lawsuit filed by the ACLU seeking to halt a new federal policy that allows immigrants who have previously been released by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to be re-detained for no clear reason. Under a decades-old policy, immigrants with pending immigration cases were generally not re-detained […]
text:
An ACLU lawsuit  challenges the Department of Homeland Security for re-detaining immigrants who are awaiting the outcome of their immigration cases. The case is being heard in Georgia where immigrants are held at the Stewart Detention Center, a facility run by the private prison company CoreCivic. (Photo by Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder)Two Georgia men are at the center of a lawsuit filed by the ACLU seeking to halt a new federal policy that allows immigrants who have previously been released by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to be re-detained for no clear reason.
Under a decades-old policy, immigrants with pending immigration cases were generally not re-detained by ICE as long as they were following all the conditions of their release, including appearing at court hearings and immigration check-in meetings. Officials would have to show that there had been a change in circumstances, such as a new criminal charge, before re-detaining someone, according to ACLU of Georgia staff attorney Raneem Ashrawi.
Democratic lawmakers call for closure of ICE detention center in southwest Georgia

But a lawsuit filed earlier this month in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia claims the Department of Homeland Security reversed course on that policy in May 2025. Under the new re-detention policy, officials can take immigrants into custody without assessing whether their circumstances had changed.
The lawsuit argues the re-detention policy violates the Fourth Amendment and leaves immigrants across Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina, where ICE’s Atlanta Field office has jurisdiction, vulnerable to being baselessly re-detained by immigration officials. The complaint also calls on the courts to block the policy, as a federal judge in California did last year.
The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment.
Two Georgia residents are among the four plaintiffs in the class action case. Two North Carolina residents are also plaintiffs. 
Alvaro Ibañez-Cardenas, a 35-year-old Venezuelan man who lives in Athens, was initially detained in 2022 upon arriving in the U.S. He was later released and was detained for a second time in September during a routine check-in at the Atlanta ICE field office, according to the lawsuit. Ibañez-Cardenas was transferred to Irwin County Detention Center before being released in October on a $20,000 bond. 
Three Georgia counties flagged by Trump administration for using non-English election materials

In a statement provided by the ACLU, Ibañez-Cardenas said he was greatly affected by the period of detention. He lost his job at a warehouse roughly three days after being detained, the lawsuit states. His pending asylum case, which was submitted in 2023, was also cancelled as a result of his re-detention.
“I feel very paranoid and worried all the time, but I have to keep going in order to make money to take care of my family,” he said in the statement. 
Ambrosio Trujillo Zavaleta, a 46-year-old from Mexico who lives in Savannah, was also detained by ICE in September along with his wife and adult son, according to the lawsuit. A plumber who has lived in the U.S. since 2004, he was arrested once in 2014 for driving without a license but was ultimately released, paid the fines associated with the charge and obtained his driver’s license. After his second arrest, he was sent to an ICE processing center in Folkston, which is located in South Georgia, where he was held for nearly a month before being released on a $20,000 bond.
Trujillo Zavaleta’s wife was also eventually released from detention, but their son is still in ICE custody. Their daughter, who is a U.S. citizen and a student at the University of Georgia, relies on him for financial support, the lawsuit said. 
Though he is now back at work, Trujillo Zavaleta said the detention has left a lasting impact on him and his family.
“My wife, who was also detained at the same time as me, now lives in constant fear of leaving the house,” Trujillo Zavaleta said in a statement provided by the ACLU. “I get very nervous going out in public or driving to work because I know ICE might choose to re-detain me at any time.”
Ashrawi, the ACLU of Georgia staff attorney, said the detentions have left both men and their families feeling unsettled.
“They relied on what they were told when they were released,” she said. “They followed the conditions of their release, and so to be abruptly snatched from their family and their community has shaken them.”

description: Powell’s work helping a client end a guardianship highlights the court’s role for Delaware families alongside its internationally known corporate work. The Delaware Court of Chancery has named attorney Jason C. Powell its 2026 Attorney Ad Litem Award for Service recipient, recognizing more than two decades of work on behalf of people with disabilities in gua[...]
text:
The Delaware Court of Chancery has named attorney Jason C. Powell its 2026 Attorney Ad Litem Award for Service: Image created with visual provided by the State of Delaware and formatted with AI on 11/24
Powell’s work helping a client end a guardianship highlights the court’s role for Delaware families alongside its internationally known corporate work.
The Delaware Court of Chancery has named attorney Jason C. Powell its 2026 Attorney Ad Litem Award for Service recipient, recognizing more than two decades of work on behalf of people with disabilities in guardianship cases.
Powell, of The Powell Firm, has served as an attorney ad litem in more than 60 Chancery cases since 2003, the court said. He has mentored new attorneys and helped resolve family disputes through mediation.
The case that prompted his nomination involved a client who had recovered from a disability. Powell took the case without pay and first asked the court to appoint a replacement guardian. He then worked with his client to end the guardianship, the court said.
“His thoughtful and respectful approach to his clients is immeasurable and genuinely appreciated,” Magistrate Jessie R. Benavides said in the court’s announcement.
Why the court matters
The Court of Chancery earned its international reputation by deciding disputes over how Delaware companies are run, including fights over mergers and the duties corporate directors owe shareholders. Judges who regularly hear those disputes decide them without juries. Their written opinions give companies and investors a record of how Delaware law applies when similar questions arise. That predictability matters well beyond the state. More than two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies call Delaware their legal home, according to the state Division of Corporations’ 2025 annual report.
That trust helps sustain Delaware’s corporate franchise, the business of serving as the legal home for companies. A court with experienced judges and a long record of written decisions gives businesses a reason to incorporate in Delaware and stay here. Delaware corporations pay an annual franchise tax even if they conduct no business in the state.
In the fiscal year that ended June 30, Delaware collected $1.33 billion in corporate franchise taxes before refunds. Together with taxes from limited liability companies and limited partnerships, the state collected $1.86 billion after refunds, about 27% of its net general fund revenue, according to the Delaware Economic and Financial Advisory Council. That revenue helps pay for state operations, including public education and public safety.
For Delaware families, the court can decide who has the authority to make medical or financial decisions for an adult who needs a guardian. The court can appoint an attorney ad litem to represent the person’s best interests. It can also end a guardianship when a person regains the ability to make those decisions. Powell’s case illustrates how that authority can help someone regain control over decisions that affect daily life.
The court established the annual award in 2022. At its most recent training for attorneys ad litem, Powell took part in a panel on working with clients sensitively, including across cultural differences.
To Go Box

What — The Delaware Court of Chancery’s 2026 Attorney Ad Litem Award for Service.
When — The court’s release was dated Nov. 24, 2026. It offers virtual certification training each fall and makes a recording available.
Where — Families can find forms and guidance on the Delaware Court of Chancery’s guardianship page.
Why — Court-appointed attorneys represent the best interests of people with disabilities in guardianship cases.
How to learn more — Delaware attorneys interested in certification can email Renee Kinsey at j.renee.kinsey@delaware.gov.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Canadian company exploring Chama Basin uranium expands claims, withdraws operations plan
description: A Canadian company that is seeking federal approval for uranium exploration in the Chama Basin last week announced it had expanded its claims in the area near Canjilon, as well as withdrawn a draft operations plan as it considers next steps.
text:
Gamma Resources, Ltd., a Canadian Company seeking to conduct uranium exploration in the Chama Basin, announced Nov. 19, 2026, that it had expanded its claims near Canjilon. (Photo of Canjilon Lake courtesy U.S. Forest Service)A Canadian company that is seeking federal approval for uranium exploration in the Chama Basin last week announced it had expanded its claims in the area near Canjilon, as well as withdrawn a draft operations plan as it considers next steps. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gamma Resources, Ltd., based in Vancouver, has prompted widespread opposition from northern New Mexico residents and elected officials over its Mesa Arc Project, which proposes to drill boreholes and conduct other exploration to confirm the existence of an estimated three million pounds of uranium across a four-mile stretch of land in the Carson National Forest. 
On Nov. 19, the company issued a news release announcing it had added 12 additional claims to its project area, bringing its footprint to 4,760 acres, as well as completed a study of detectable radon gas on the surface. Radon gas is produced during the radioactive decay of uranium. 
The claim expansion, according to the news release, is part of the company’s strategy of expanding its U.S. based uranium portfolio “at a time growing demand for domestic, responsibly sourced uranium supply.”
The same announcement also noted that the company in October had withdrawn its draft operations plan from the U.S. Forest Service’s consideration as it develops its “exploration targeting strategy.” The company’s initial operations plan sought federal approval to drill up to 12 boreholes up to 500 feet deep, as well as carve 800 feet of new roads and build temporary drill pads. 
In an email, Gamma Resources President Connor Messler told Source NM that the company is “still actively planning exploration programs” for the New Mexico project and will seek federal and state permits again when appropriate. 
“The timing of a new draft plan of operations being submitted is dependent on the review and interpretation of available data, and as such is currently unknown,” he said.
New Mexico US Rep. Leger Fernández’s bill would require mining companies to pay royalties

A spokesperson for the United States Forest Service confirmed to Source NM in an email Nov. 20 that the company had withdrawn its plan of operations, but the Forest Service is expecting a new plan by the end of the year. 
If the Forest Service deems the plan to be complete, officials would then evaluate how much surface disruption the company proposes and, as a result, the level of scrutiny the federal review will apply under the National Environmental Policy Act, according to the statement.
But U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), who has introduced legislation seeking to prohibit any uranium drilling in the Chama Basin, said in a statement to Source NM on Monday that he hopes the incoming Democratic majorities in the U.S. House and U.S. Senate will permanently project the Chama area from mineral development. 
“While Gamma is withdrawing its current proposal, its plans to pursue an expanded operation make clear that this fight is far from over,” Luján said. “I will not stand by while a foreign mining company threatens the land, water, and way of life of New Mexicans.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Collins agrees to pay $2,880 after ethics probe concludes his office improperly paid intern
description: Republican Congressman Mike Collins’ office broke House rules in paying more than $10,000 to an intern who was romantically involved with Collins’ then-chief of staff, according to a U.S. House Ethics Committee report. “The evidence in this matter demonstrates that Representative Collins was not sufficiently overseeing his Chief of Staff’s actions, both with[...]
text:
Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Collins speaks at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderRepublican Congressman Mike Collins’ office broke House rules in paying more than $10,000 to an intern who was romantically involved with Collins’ then-chief of staff, according to a U.S. House Ethics Committee report.
“The evidence in this matter demonstrates that Representative Collins was not sufficiently overseeing his Chief of Staff’s actions, both with respect to hiring, paying, and accepting volunteer services of the woman with whom he had a romantic relationship and his own travel expenses,” the report found.
Collins has agreed to return $2,880 to the U.S. Treasury based on the amount the committee estimated the woman was overpaid.
The ethics probe haunted Collins throughout his ill-fated campaign for the U.S. Senate, which he lost to Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff earlier this month.
Ossoff hounded Collins over the probe, but Collins dismissed it as partisan political theater.
“That ethics complaint is bogus,” Collins said during an October debate. “Anyone can file one. It is a nothingburger.”
The committee did not find evidence that Collins was directly involved in hiring the intern or using her services for official purposes, but it did find that he did not exercise sufficient oversight over his former chief of staff, Brandon Phillips.
The bipartisan panel said Phillips refused to cooperate with the investigation and evaded attempts by the U.S. Marshals Service to serve him with a subpoena. The committee recommended Phillips be held in contempt of Congress.
According to the report, Phillips helped arrange an internship for his then-girlfriend, despite her not submitting an application or being interviewed for the job.
The intern was paid under the House’s internship allowance for two short stints in 2023 and 2024, continuing to work full-time at Cox Communications throughout.
No other interns employed at that time in DC received comparable pay, and the committee heard testimony that most of the intern’s work was done remotely, which was against policy for interns. According to the report, multiple current and former members of Collins’ staff reported never seeing her in the office or copied on emails.
According to one interview in the report, a staffer recommended terminating her internship immediately, but Phillips said no and added “if anybody asks, I’ll apologize.”
The committee also investigated allegations that Collins’ office misused funds to pay for Phillips’ travel but did not find substantial evidence to back those claims.
Phillips was dismissed in May after making a social media post mocking an alleged victim of sexual assault.
A Collins spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment, and attempts to reach Phillips were not immediately successful.

text:
You can avoid the stress with these commonsense strategies with followed by a dose of patience. Follow these tips to help prevent holiday stress from ruining the most wonderful time of the year for you and your family.
Don’t let this holiday season be a time of stress and unhappiness for you. Here are six ways to embrace the positive aspects of the season!
by John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
NEWARK, Del. – The holiday season is here, and if you listen carefully, you’ll hear more than just the sounds of “Silent Night” playing in the background at your local mall. Those other sounds you hear are the cries of stressed-out shoppers, parents, salesclerks and children, who are overdosing on sweets and other holiday goodies.
But things don’t have to be that way in your house. You can nip the stress beast in the bud and prevent it from attacking you and your loved ones. It takes a little common sense followed by a large dose of patience. Follow these tips to help prevent holiday stress from ruining the most wonderful time of the year for you and your family:

The Right Attitude – Face it, with the wrong attitude, a trip to the mall or to cut down the Christmas tree can be disastrous. Everyone needs to have an attitude check at this time of the year, because with the right attitude, people are cooperative and respectful of each other. Parents should set a good example for their children by having the right attitude throughout the holiday season (and it wouldn’t hurt to continue that tradition throughout the rest of the year, either).
Be Flexible – The most common reason people become stressed around the holidays is because their expectations are not met. They thought the holiday meal with all the relatives wouldn’t end up with people arguing. Or they thought that their children would behave and stay happy while being dragged to marathon shopping trips to the malls and outlet stores. Flexibility is the key. When you are flexible, you realize that not everything will always turn out the way you hoped it would. When you are flexible, you realize that if things turn out differently, it’s not the end of the world. And when you are flexible, you don’t become stressed.
Eat Right – It’s not surprising that the average weight gain between Thanksgiving and New Year’s Day is 6 to 12 pounds. The holiday season is stressful enough without eating all the wrong foods. At this time of the year people tend to eat more because they are going out more. Try and limit the number of calories you consume at a party or holiday meal. Have plenty of lower-fat, lower calorie choices available such as raw vegetables and pretzels with fat-free yogurt-based dips or salsa-based dips. Offer fruit along with other desserts for a fat-free choice. Plan at least one healthy meal as a family every day. And when visiting the mall, don’t overdose on too many goodies.
Children and Routines – If you have small children in the family, you know how their routines will be disrupted over the holidays. The next time you are at the mall take a few moments and study the faces of the parents and their children. Chances are you won’t see too many “happy campers.” When a child’s routine is changed, for example, perhaps you’ve decided to do away with their afternoon nap and drag them to the mall to sit on Santa’s lap, stress can result. They may become cranky, uncooperative, and ruin the trip for everyone. Do your best to keep some sort of order and rituals for your children.
Get Physical – The best way to ward off a stress attack is by doing some type of physical exercise or activity. Turn off the television, stop playing video games and get up off the sofa. Find an activity that everyone in the family can enjoy together. Ice skating, walking or even putting in an exercise video and turning your living room into a fun-filled family exercise studio will help keep stress away.
Take Time to Laugh – Laughter is still the best medicine, and it is a very good way to beat holiday stress. Take time to read comics, watch a funny movie or video or even write your own jokes. Humor is contagious, too, and when people see you laughing you are doing your part to help beat their stress as well.

Don’t let this holiday season be a time of stress and unhappiness for you. Embrace the positive aspects of the season, keep the right attitude and always remember to put a smile on your face. When you do these things, your holidays will be merrier.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘Part of our DNA’: Book clubs promote community and Mississippi’s literary history
description: Aisha Carson reads during JXN Book Club's event at The Walk-In in downtown Jackson, Miss., on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.
text:
There’s an unexpected sound at The Walk-In, a downtown Jackson watering hole usually thrumming with first-date conversation and 2010s alternative music: The sound of pages turning.
Chris Kelly and Kimar Cain sit in a dimly lit, cobwebbed corner of the bar on a Sunday in mid-October, each engrossed in a book. The two founded JXN Book Club over the summer, hoping for good conversation and good reading. A few months later, the club has thousands of followers on Instagram. 
Christopher Kelly, left, and Kimar Cain chat about the book they and members of the book club they started are currently reading, Parable of the Sower by Octavia E. Butler at Lemuria Book Store, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
On this October afternoon, someone sits at every table in the bar with their nose buried in a book, a drink sweating nearby. 
Their book club is one of dozens around the city — spanning genre, race and age groups — and one of a handful that’s sprung up within recent years. 
Readers around Jackson say the surge of book clubs stems from a desire to connect and build community in our increasingly digital world. Other book club founders say they were inspired to dispel the myth that Southerners and Black people don’t read, and to create spaces that reflect the opposite. 
Ellen Rodgers Daniels, executive director of the Mississippi Book Festival, suspects the state’s strong literary tradition — represented by writers such as Eudora Welty, William Faulkner and Jesmyn Ward — also has something to do with it. 
Mississippians are storytellers by nature, she said.
“It’s part of our DNA,” Rodgers Daniels said. “Mississippians love their state, but they also have a super complicated relationship with it. A common way for people to reckon with that is to write — and to read.”
‘What Jackson could look like’
The story of JXN Book Club starts with Kelly going bald. 
Kelly lost his hair after moving to Jackson in 2021, and with it, the community of barbershops. 
“I didn’t have friends, I didn’t know anybody,” Kelly said. “For Black men, going to the barbershop is how you have that peer-to-peer talk. When I went bald, I wasn’t having that connection and didn’t talk to men my age anymore.”
An introvert, he forced himself out of his comfort zone and joined a group founded by Cain called Brother Helps Brother aimed toward fostering community between Black men. 
Shaun McDonough reads during JXN Book Club’s event at The Walk-In in downtown Jackson on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.  Credit: Devna Bose/Mississippi Today
The two hit it off. They discovered they shared an interest in reading and a desire to bring people together. The idea for JXN Book Club was born. 
Now, a few months later, Kelly marvels at the size of the crowd at their events and the crowd’s diversity. Cain said they intentionally opened the book club to everyone.
“There are a lot of niche book clubs around the city, but not one big general book club for everybody,” Kelly said. “This is something people wanted and needed … I really appreciate that it looks like what Jackson could look like.”
A similar desire prompted Nikita Nicholson and Shaketta Franklin to start their book club, Soulful Stacks JXN. 
Two years ago, the longtime friends were at Reading the Room, an event hosted by the Mississippi Humanities Council, when they looked around and noticed very few people who looked like them, two Black women. 
Soulful Stacks JXN bookclub members discussing their latest reads at Bonnie Sue’s Coffee Shop, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, in Pearl. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“We were an outlier in a lot of the spaces we were in,” Nicholson said. 
Nicholson and Franklin started Soulful Stacks JXN a few months later with people of color in mind, though everyone is welcome. Their monthly meetings at Bonnie Sue’s coffee shop in Pearl, Nicholson said, are a “whole vibe” — from the conversation, to the neosoul playing in the background and the laid back atmosphere.

Mississippi Humanities Council’s Community Reading Series
Welty at Home Virtual Book Club


Nicholson said it’s powerful for people to see a diverse group of Mississippians reading together. 
”It creates a counter narrative to things people assume what a reader looks like, what Mississippians in education and literacy look like,” she said.
Mississippi has drawn national attention for its fourth graders’ progress in reading over the past decade. 
Still, Franklin, a former teacher, said more work needs to be done to promote reading in Jackson among children and adults alike.
That’s why book clubs like Franklin’s and JXN Book Club matter, Kelly said. 
“Me and Kimar starting JXN Book Club is unconventional in itself,” he said. “You don’t see two Black men start book clubs. But representation always matters. I believe just us being there, people and kids seeing us do this, definitely matters.”
Finding community
Kenzie Ragland unintentionally created JXN Book Girlies when she moved to Mississippi from Nashville three years ago. Ragland was impatient to make friends, she said, so she created a Facebook group for women in the Jackson-metro area who liked to read. A few years later, the book club has about 150 members. 
JXN Book Girlies caters to everyone’s reading tastes — there are a number of subgroups for people who like to read a specific genre. For example, the romance group and fantasy group meet once a month.
JXN Book Girlies founder Kenzie Ragland, left, poses for a portrait with book club member Hannah Nugent at The Book Rack in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.  Credit: Devna Bose/Mississippi Today
Many of the women in the book club have grown so close that the group now hosts all sorts of events, no reading required. 
“Being actual friends has made it different,” Ragland said. “We go to Chili’s once a month. This past weekend, we went to Meridian for a retreat we called ‘Camp Bookish.’ We did tie-dye, crafts and karaoke.
“It’s become a community of its own.” 
Hannah Nugent, a therapist who joined the club last year, knows how important that sense of community can be. Many of her clients struggle with loneliness, she said. 
“I tell them to find some sort of club, find anything, just to go meet someone and make a new friend,” she said. 
A long and complicated literary history
Mississippians have long sought words to make sense of their home state and its complicated history, said John Spann, a historian who works for the Mississippi Humanities Council.

Those stories are the focus of the council’s Community Reading Series group, which discusses a book, usually nonfiction, during weekly meetings over the course of a month. So far, they’ve read “The Barn” by Wright Thompson, “When It’s Darkness on the Delta” by W. Ralph Eubanks and “I Don’t Like the Blues” by B. Brian Foster. 
The conversations have been difficult but rewarding, Spann said. 
“Even though sometimes truth is hard to digest, the Mississippi writer has a way of portraying hard truth to Mississippians in a way that is digestible,” he said.
Soulful Stacks JXN bookclub co-founders Shaketta Franklin, left, and Nikita Nicholson during a club meeting held at Bonnie Sue’s Coffee Shop, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, in Pearl. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Anna Traylor believes Eudora Welty, one of the state’s most well-known authors, was particularly skilled at writing about the difficult truths about Mississippi. Traylor works at the Eudora Welty House and manages the organization’s book club.
A few locals started meeting in 2013 to read Welty’s books and novels by authors she inspired. But in 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the gatherings moved online, which allowed people outside of Jackson to join. That’s when the group became the Welty at Home Virtual Book Club and started drawing members from all over the country.
People find value in reading stories about Mississippi because our state’s struggles are universal, Traylor said. 
Mississippians know about their state’s rich book culture, Rodgers Daniels said, but it often comes as a surprise to people outside of the state. Watching them discover authors from Mississippi gives her a deep satisfaction, she said. 
JXN Book Club co-founder Kimar Cain reads as daughter Kimari Cain watches videos during the organization’s event at The Walk-In in downtown Jackson, Miss., on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.  Credit: Devna Bose/Mississippi Today
“It’s like a state secret or something, but of course, anybody who’s ever thought about literature in this country knows about William Faulkner and Eudora Welty and Richard Wright and Jesmyn Ward and Kiese Laymon,” she said. “What do you think made those people?”
Cain knows, because the same state that made them authors made him a reader. In October, when he looked around the bar full of Jacksonians thumbing through books, Cain saw the best of his home state. 
“The things on these pages bring so many people together,” he said.

title: 19 Nebraska lawmakers join call for special session to address Medicaid cuts coming Jan. 1
description: LINCOLN — A letter signed by 19 state senators was submitted to the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office Tuesday calling for a special legislative session intending to address pending cuts to Medicaid set to take effect Jan. 1. State Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha announced the effort at a press conference in the Capitol rotunda, […]
text:
State Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha announces she and 18 other senators have signed onto a letter asking for a special session to address pending Medicaid cuts at a press conference Nov. 24, 2026. (Erin Bamer/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A letter signed by 19 state senators was submitted to the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office Tuesday calling for a special legislative session intending to address pending cuts to Medicaid set to take effect Jan. 1.
State Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha announced the effort at a press conference in the Capitol rotunda, saying she pulled the letter together within roughly 24 hours with the help of Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln. She said all 15 Democratic senators have signed on, along with nonpartisan Sen. Megan Hunt of Omaha, and Republican Sens. Tom Brandt, Myron Dorn and Merv Riepe.
“If your senator is not on here, it’s not because they didn’t want to be on here,” Cavanaugh said to the roughly 100 attendees Tuesday. “It’s just this happened very quickly.”
The backlash is in response to an announcement late Friday from Gov. Jim Pillen’s administration, proposing a 3% reimbursement rate cut to physicians, dentists and other providers who accept Medicaid starting Jan. 1. Another 3% cut is to follow the next fiscal year.
In addition to the 3% cut in provider reimbursement rates, concerns include:

New copay requirements for people receiving certain Medicaid services
Cuts to mental health and substance use treatment reimbursement, and changes to certain behavioral health services
Changes to inpatient and outpatient hospital reimbursement
Changes to specialty drug reimbursement
New limits on adult dental coverage, capping Medicaid benefits at $2,000 annually
A 4% cut in in provider rates in 2027 and again in 2028 for those who receive services through the Developmental Disabilities Waiver

SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
According to the letter, the purpose of the special session would be “to adopt or enact statutory modifications, including temporary suspensions, relating to purported changes in the Medicaid and related healthcare programs.”
Now that the letter has been submitted, supporters of the effort have 10 days to gather 14 more senators to join the call for a special session. If they get 33 senators on board, the letter would then be sent to Pillen, who would have five days to call the special session, Cavanaugh said.
The earliest the special session would begin is Dec. 10, and any special session must last a minimum of three days. Cavanaugh said the intention is to have a proposal ready to introduce on day one.
Pillen’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Scott Colom’s ‘pick another protein’ ad poses dilemma for people supporting animal rights, professor writes
description: A mother and calf
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.

In February, a TV interviewer asked Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith what Republicans were doing about the price of beef. “You know,” she replied, “you have so many proteins to choose from.”
Scott Colom’s campaign turned that line into a viral ad urging Mississippians to “pick another senator.” Colom is now senator-elect and will become the state’s first popularly elected Black U.S. senator in January when he is sworn in to replace Hyde-Smith.
Beef was everywhere this election. In addition to wrong-footing Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, it helped elect a Methodist minister in Kansas and supplied the right’s favorite insult in Texas
 For those of us who care about human rights and about the lives and safety of animals, the results are worth celebrating, but they also pose a dilemma. The new Democratic majority was built partly on the anger of cattle country and on high meat prices. What policy changes does that majority owe, and to whom?
Consider Texas, where James Talarico spent the campaign fending off smears that he was vegan and gay. In truth, he is neither, but what if he were?
On election night he celebrated at Whataburger with Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, whose historic election as the state’s first Latina governor repudiated years of xenophobic policy. The burger stop was good politics. It was also a reminder that, in 2026, eating plants still works as an accusation.
In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist minister, will become the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 1932, despite wave after wave of attacks on his faith. He won because he was an outstanding candidate, and because the Trump Administration’s tariffs and its war of choice in Iran sent diesel and fertilizer prices soaring across the Farm Belt.
Then the administration waived tariffs on imported beef in an attempt to bring grocery prices down. This economically quixotic move did almost nothing for shoppers, while ranchers watched their cattle sell for less at auction. Iowa, where Democrats flipped both a Senate seat and the governorship, tells a similar story.
Here is the problem. Industrial agriculture’s institutionalized brutalization of animals, its massive pollution and its carbon footprint are well documented. This is an industry desperately in need of rigorous regulation and oversight. Yet the last thing Democrats want is to alienate a voting bloc that has perhaps finally recognized that the Republican Party does not truly represent its interests.
Meanwhile, millions of vegans voted Democratic even as their dietary choices became an epithet and a punchline. Veganism became something from which candidates fled, and the political discourse treated opposition to animal cruelty as a character flaw. For the plant-based community (ironically, not unlike the ranchers), political allegiance seems fraught.
The way through starts with noticing that ranchers and animal advocates share an adversary. Four meatpacking companies, JBS, Cargill, Tyson and National Beef, control roughly 85% of the U.S. beef industry. That concentration squeezes ranchers on the price of their cattle, squeezes families at the meat counter, and leaves the treatment of animals and the pollution of the industry’s largest operations in the hands of a few firms that answer to almost no one. Even President Trump has called for an investigation of the packers.
A Democratic majority could start there: vigorous antitrust enforcement against the packers, real enforcement of environmental law against the largest feeding operations and serious public investment to help ranchers who want to diversify or transition out of cattle. All of that moves us toward a food system that treats farmers, animals and the land as more than inputs, and away from the slow-motion catastrophe brought on by our national agriculture and energy policies.
Regardless of political affiliation, the vast majority of Americans want their leaders to refrain from self-dealing and crony capitalism, end wars of choice and leave their children a world with clean water, clean air and a climate that does not present an existential threat. They also want animals not to be brutalized and slaughtered as if nonhuman lives had no meaning other than as a protein source for humans.
There’s clearly common ground here. The trick is to focus on it. Democrats must realize that political strength lies in listening, not pandering, and in treating voters with respect, even when that means embracing positions that feel uncomfortable. In short, the party must become one of principle rather than politics.
Barack Obama famously quipped at the 2006 Gridiron Club dinner that “People say that Democrats don’t stand for anything. That’s not true; we stand for anything.” It was funny because it was true. This election gives Democrats a chance to prove otherwise. They have so many proteins to choose from, but they should pick a principle.

David Cassuto is a professor of Law at Pace University’s Elisabeth Haub School of Law, where he is a member of the Global Center for Environmental Legal Studies. His work focuses on the intersection of animal and environmental law. He is also the class of 1962 distinguished visiting professor of environmental studies at Williams College.  He lives in the foothills of the Berkshire Mountains in upstate New York, where his neighbors include bears, turkeys, coyotes and porcupines.

name: VTDigger
title: Balint introduces bill on data privacy protections, tech guidelines for schools
description:
“Companies have to be held accountable when they fail to protect students’ information,” Vermont’s congresswoman Becca Balint said in an interview.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Balint introduces bill on data privacy protections, tech guidelines for schools.
text:
U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vermont, speaks during a press conference at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Tuesday, January 27, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt, introduced a bill Tuesday designed to ensure big tech companies protect personal student data. 
The bill would require tech companies that provide services to schools and other educational institutions to keep identifiable student information private. The bill also gives the government explicit permission to bring civil lawsuits against tech companies who violate those data privacy protections. 
“Companies have to be held accountable when they fail to protect students’ information. And the social media companies have been operating in a big wild west from their inception,” Balint said in an interview with VTDigger Tuesday. 
The bill would allow the government to sue technology companies that violate the privacy protections for up to $5,000 in damages for each student whose personal information is compromised. 
In recent years, a number of popular technology platforms used by schools have seen major data breaches, compromising the private information of millions of students and teachers. 
A 2024 data breach of Powerschool, an online attendance and grading platform, is alleged in lawsuits from school districts to have leaked the data of 50 million students and teachers, according to Bloomberg Law. That breach likely included students in Vermont. Another online education platform, Canvas, suffered a major data breach this spring that left its 30 million users across North America without access to class materials and assignments, according to NPR. 
“The massive Canvas data breach was, I think, a wake-up call,” Balint said. 
Only 40 calendar days remain in the current Congress and bills that do not pass will die this session. Catherine White, a spokesperson for Balint’s office, said the congresswoman plans to reintroduce the bill in the new Congress, which is set to begin Jan. 3. 
Along with data protections, the bill also seeks to provide schools and education agencies with better national guidance on best practices for using technology in education. 
Students need to be protected from technology that’s designed to be addictive, Balint said. But teachers and districts are already overburdened, so the responsibility of auditing and vetting products shouldn’t fall on them, she said. 
“Teachers are being asked to assess these products that they don’t have enough hours in the day or enough expertise to be able to make these determinations. They need support,” she said. 
The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology, along with the national Department of Education, to research guidelines and create model contracts for education agencies to use when contracting with technology companies. 
The bill would also set aside $3 million in grant funds for experts and academic researchers to evaluate tech products that are being used in schools.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Comptroller-elect Bailey names transition team ahead of taking office Jan. 1
description: Democratic state Comptroller-elect Jessica Bailey has picked one of her campaign advisers as her office chief of staff and named a bipartisan group of transition advisers.
text:
Jessica Bailey, right, speaks alongside Coumba Kebe after winning the Democratic nomination for Indiana comptroller in June. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Democratic state Comptroller-elect Jessica Bailey has picked one of her campaign advisers as her office chief of staff and named a bipartisan group of transition advisers.
Bailey, who is currently the Porter County clerk, takes office Jan. 1 after defeating Republican Comptroller Elise Nieshalla in this fall’s election.
Bailey announced Tuesday that her transition team will be led by Kaleb Hagen, who was senior adviser and consultant for Bailey’s campaign and will join the comptroller’s office as chief of staff. Hagen is the founder of Valparaiso-based TBH Strategies, a consulting firm for political, business and nonprofit clients.
The comptroller, formerly known as the state auditor, is responsible for accounting, disbursing and reporting how Indiana spends its $26 billion in annual state general fund revenues.
Bailey said in a statement that Nieshalla and her staff had “been very helpful in making sure services for Hoosiers and office operations continue without disruption.” 
“I have never seen this office as partisan — all Hoosiers deserve to know their tax dollars are being watched closely and spent wisely,” Bailey said.
Bailey released a list of 14 transition advisers who she said would assist in organizing priorities, planning policy initiatives and reviewing current office operations. 
Among those advisers are three Democratic legislators — Reps. Cherrish Pryor and Greg Porter of Indianapolis and Sen. Rodney Pol of Chesterton — and former Republican Sen. Greg Walker of Columbus.
The advisory team also includes Sarah Riordan, a former Indianapolis city controller under Democratic Mayor Joe Hogsett; Republican Huntington County Clerk Shelley Septer; and Brian Tabor, a former president of the Indiana Hospital Association.
Bailey will join Secretary of State-elect Beau Bayh as the first Democrats to hold any Statehouse executive branch office since the end of 2016.

Carleigh Beriont, who serves on the Hampton Select Board and ran unsuccessfully for Congress this year, is one of three Democrats vying to be New Hampshire's next secretary of state. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Carleigh Beriont is the Democrats’ unofficial pick to be New Hampshire’s next secretary of state.
Beriont, who serves on the Hampton Select Board and ran unsuccessfully for Congress this year, is one of three Democrats publicly vying for the position. She won a nonbinding straw poll of Democratic state lawmakers, according to an email sent by the party to all members-elect. Beriont has been pitching herself to lawmakers as a candidate who will promote voter registration among the youngest voters, modernize election technology, and push for nonpartisan redistricting committees and campaign finance reform (though the latter would require the Legislature to act).
New Hampshire elects its secretary of state by a vote of the state Legislature, as opposed to a direct election by citizens, as in many states. On Dec. 2, both the House and Senate will meet for an official vote on the matter as part of Organization Day. The straw poll was nonbinding, but the goal is for Democrats, who control both chambers of the Legislature by wide margins after November’s election, to coalesce around one candidate to avoid splitting their votes. State law requires the vote be made “without regard to the party affiliation of the candidate.”
In the email, which was shared with the Bulletin, Democratic Party Chairman Ray Buckley wrote that the party will not be releasing individual vote counts “per our agreement with all the candidates.” However, Beriont was “the clear winner,” though both her opponents Patrick Long and James Butler “had strong showings.”
Announcing the Winner of the NHDP Secretary of State Straw Poll
 
Butler told the Bulletin after the announcement he is dropping out of the race. He wrote in an email to lawmakers: “Carleigh has my full support, and I encourage everyone who voted for me to support Carleigh for Secretary of State.” Long did not immediately respond to the Bulletin’s phone call or text messages.
Republican David Scanlan, who has served as secretary of state since 2022, is again running for reelection. Before becoming secretary of state, he was deputy secretary for 20 years under his predecessor, Bill Gardner. Scanlan has tried to pitch himself as a nonpartisan actor with the most experience who can ensure continuity in the office. He points to Gardner, a Democrat who served for almost 50 years, being reelected by several Republican majorities.
Scanlan is likely to secure most if not all of the Republican votes, but he’ll need Democratic votes to survive. He said he knows he has at least some support in the caucus. The question is whether it will be enough to overcome the new Democratic supermajority. If the Democrats unite behind Beriont, he’ll lose the seat.
“What the results clearly showed,” Buckley wrote in his email, “was that if those that voted for James and Patrick in the straw poll unite behind Carleigh on Organization Day, there is no doubt that there will be a new Secretary of State.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: DHS contract for downtown Hartford parking under review
description: The Capital Region Development Authority is reviewing a Hartford parking lease signed by the Department of Homeland Security.
text:
The Capital Region Development Authority is reviewing a parking lease signed by the Department of Homeland Security with the company that operates CRDA-owned parking garages in Hartford after concerns were raised by local residents and officials.
ProPark Mobility has operated the CRDA’s garages since 2021, including managing “long-term space leasing.” The company, which does not have to get CRDA staff or board approval to enter lease agreements, signed a contract with DHS effective Oct. 1, according to CRDA spokesperson Terryl Smith.
The lease is for space in Bushnell South garage at 120 Capitol Ave. The facility is near the Hartford Immigration Court located at 450 Main St.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have become a regular presence in the city, particularly near the courthouse, since President Donald Trump ramped up efforts in his second term to detain and deport more people.
News of the contract has drawn concerns from Hartford officials, with Mayor Arunan Arulampalam, who is on the CRDA board of directors, advocating for the agency to end the contract when he was “made aware” of the lease.
“Mayor Arulampalam was recently made aware of this contract as a CRDA board member. He immediately requested the agency take the necessary steps to end the contract, and will continue to push for that resolution,” the mayor’s office wrote in a statement to The Connecticut Mirror. “The City of Hartford has and will always be a welcoming place for all of our residents, regardless of their immigration status.”
In February, Arulampalam asked the Hartford Parking Authority to terminate a contract with ICE for use of a city-owned parking lot at 141 Sheldon St.
The 5-year lease with ProPark for the Bushnell South garage has annual payments of $122,168, but “the lessee may terminate the agreement at any time after the third year,” Smith said.
CRDA’s executive director, David Steuber, found out about the lease “just over a week ago in response to an outside inquiry,” Smith told the CT Mirror in an email. 
“In recognition that arrangements involving federal immigration enforcement agencies are a sensitive matter for many members of our community, CRDA is actively reviewing the circumstances surrounding the agreement, including its terms and the options available to us. We take these matters seriously and will proceed accordingly,” Steuber wrote in a statement.
ProPark Mobility did not respond to a request for comment.
Former Hartford mayor and current U.S. Representative-elect Luke Bronin, in a statement, urged the CDRA to distance itself from DHS’s immigration enforcement activity. 
“Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security’s immigration enforcement is lawless, dangerous, and out of control, and in light of that, every public entity in Connecticut, including CRDA, should do everything possible to separate themselves from anything associated with it,” he said.
The CRDA aims to stimulate economic development and growth in the city of Hartford and surrounding area. The agency is partly funded by public dollars. In recent years, CRDA received $25 million annually in state bond authorizations.

Killed in the crash on Dec. 22, 2023 was Adrian Tucker, 34, an advanced manufacturing technologist […]
text:
Nancy Tucker has spent the past three years trying to get the truth of what happened in her son's death. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Jamie Lucke)The Kentucky Parole Board on Tuesday rejected early release for a driver who sped through a Hopkinsville industrial park at 90 mph, crossed the center line and slammed into a vehicle that had just left a factory parking lot.
Killed in the crash on Dec. 22, 2023 was Adrian Tucker, 34, an advanced manufacturing technologist at an auto plant.  
His mother, Nancy Tucker, waged a years-long battle to uncover the facts surrounding the fatal crash, as the Lantern reported last month. Nancy Tucker used the Kentucky Open Records Act and a state Supreme Court ruling in a different case to finally obtain investigators’ files from the Hopkinsville Police Department. The state legislature in 2025 quickly undid the Supreme Court ruling for other Kentuckians by allowing police to reject records requests without a detailed explanation of why.
Adrian Tucker was an advanced manufacturing technician working at an auto plant in Hopkinsville. (Photo courtesy Nancy Tucker)
The driver, Jaden Johnson, 21, pleaded guilty to second degree manslaughter and agreed to serve 85% of a five-year sentence. The judge stipulated in writing that Johnson was to serve 85% of the sentence. His term began Oct. 24, 2025, according to state records.
Nancy Tucker and other family members and friends submitted written statements opposing Johnson’s release and also appeared before the parole board Monday.
Nancy Tucker said she was told during the Monday hearing that because of credits Johnson will become eligible for mandatory supervised release as early as April, which she said felt like a “slap in the face.”
Police found a liquor bottle and evidence of marijuana use in Johnson’s car but he was never tested for drugs or alcohol after being airlifted to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. 
Johnson told the parole board Tuesday that he had suffered a dislocated hip in the crash.
