name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi lawmakers: Redistricting maps nearly done, special session up to Reeves
description: A crowd of residents attended a legislative redistricting public hearing in Tupelo on Aug. 18, 2026.
text:
The two lawmakers leading Mississippi’s redistricting efforts say they are prepared to convene for a special session whenever Gov. Tate Reeves calls one.
Republican Rep. Noah Sanford of Collins and Republican Sen. Dean Kirby of Pearl told Mississippi Today that they are close to finishing redrawing the state’s legislative districts and have been meeting with some lawmakers individually to show them the districts.
“We’re actually on hold waiting for the governor to call a special session,” Kirby said. “We don’t know anything, or even whether he’s going to call one or what he’s going to call it on.” 
Reeves’ office did not respond to a request for comment, but he recently told WLBT that he still has “every intention of there being a special session for redistricting.” 
FAQ: Mississippi redistricting. Why does it matter? What’s being considered?
The governor could call a special session to redraw state legislative, congressional and-or state Supreme Court districts. 
But the two legislative leaders said they don’t believe there’s an urgent need for the governor to call a special session for congressional redistricting because lawmakers can tackle that issue during the regular session, which begins on Jan. 5. 
Lawmakers want to tackle legislative redistricting in a special session because the timeline for candidates to file their paperwork to run for a legislative seat begins on Jan. 4, one day before lawmakers convene for the regular session. 
If lawmakers wait until the regular session to redraw legislative districts, it could lead to confusion with candidates filing paperwork to run in districts even as the Legislature changes them. 
A federal three-judge panel in 2024 ordered the Legislature to redraw its legislative districts. Lawmakers complied with that order in 2025, but the U.S. Supreme Court later overturned the three-judge panel’s order. 
After the U.S. Supreme Court’s order, lawmakers formed a joint redistricting committee that conducted a series of public hearings across the state in the summer and fall to gather input. 
A redistricting push in Mississippi and elsewhere was set in motion by the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais decision, which removed protection for majority-minority districts and cleared the way for state legislatures to redraw political lines for partisan advantage. Republican leaders believe the court’s decision ended the practice of allowing race to be considered when drawing political maps.   
Some Mississippians told the committee they wanted the Legislature to redraw districts that were “race neutral,” but most people who spoke at the hearings told lawmakers they did not want legislators to redraw the districts. 
Some Democratic politicians have speculated that these hearings caused a surge in Black voter turnout in the recent U.S. Senate election where Democrat Scott Colom ousted Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Sanford said the redrawn House map he’s proposing won’t look radically different from the current map. His priorities in redrawing the districts are putting small counties back together and reducing the number of split voting precincts. 
Kirby said his priorities for the Senate map are making sure districts are compact and roughly equal in population, and that the committee is looking at how districts have voted in the last three statewide general elections rather than race.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Retiring Kansas water engineer anticipates more legal conflict as resource scarcity grows
description: Retirement of Kansas' chief water engineer arrives as the state enters what may be a more contentious era as private and public interests collide on water policy.
text:
Earl Lewis, chief engineer of the Division of Water Resources at the Kansas Department of Agriculture, enters retirement as the state's challenges with water supply and consumption escalate. In this Nov. 16, 2026, image, Lewis stands outside the Kansas Capitol. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Newly retired Kansas Department of Agriculture chief engineer Earl Lewis expects escalating demand for water to trigger more legal disputes as aquifer depletion, reservoir siltation and climate change compromise the supply.
Lewis, chief engineer for the past six years in the department’s Division of Water Resources, has been responsible for enforcement of water management and conservation laws, regulations and policies. He administered 30,000 water rights, monitored four interstate compacts and had oversight of thousands of dams. His career in state government covered nearly 35 years.
Lewis said water was a resource often taken for granted as long as drinking water emerged from the kitchen faucet, farmers had plenty to nourish crops or livestock, and economic development recruiters could offer prospective businesses a stable supply. He said threats to water resources, including climate-influenced drought, topsoil runoff into reservoirs and aggressive pumping of the Ogallala Aquifer, created tension between holders of senior and junior water rights. Those individual interests were likely to clash more frequently with public interests in the future, he said.
“We’re gonna have more legal disputes about water rights. Water scarcity is going to get to be a bigger and bigger issue over time,” Lewis said.
Lewis, who grew up on a farm in Osage County, said there had been reluctance, primarily for political reasons, to exercise sweeping state authority to impose remedies designed to preserve water resources.
“I think we’re reaching a critical mass where it’s like, ‘OK, we’ve got to do something. We’ve got to take action,’ ” he said.
Lewis said reliance on statutory authority to invoke the public’s interest in water conservation could trigger lawsuits “sooner rather than later.”
“We think there’s a part of the law that says: ‘Yes, in the public interest, we can create an overall system that says. No, you’ve got to use less than what your water right says.’ At some point here … we’ll do that and there will be a legal challenge by all the folks that don’t want to change,” Lewis said.
 
Aquifer contraction
Lewis said decades of research led to greater general public awareness about implications of pumping too much groundwater to irrigate crops in western Kansas. Irrigation accounts for 85% of the state’s water consumption, but as much as 95% in western counties in Kansas. Farmers in western parts of the state need to look no further than their own wells to see the perils of overconsumption, he said.
The growth of dairies and feedlots in western Kansas could be viewed positively in terms of business development, he said, but those projects were heavy water consumers and prompted crop production shifts by farmers keen to provide corn or hay to those confined feeding operations.
He said the potential of state-mandated crackdowns on water use prompted some farmers to intensify pumping of well water to maximize short-term profit. Farmers anxious about potential of restrictions in the future kept their baseline water consumption high so calculations of a cap wouldn’t be as detrimental to their bottom line, he said.
“There’s probably people in southwest Kansas pumping today on corn stalks,” Lewis said. “There’s nothing there other than they’ve got some water left under their water right. They’re going to keep their water use up.”
He said unwarranted irrigation of fields was shortsighted because the practice diminished the overall water supply, which was the fuel source of the region’s economic engine.
“It’s kind of this belief that the water right is more important than the water,” Lewis said. “What does western Kansas look like without water, without irrigation? You go down to New Mexico, parts of eastern Colorado, where you just drive for miles and miles and never see, you know, a house or anything. There’s nothing magical about those places versus Garden City or Liberal or Hugoton other than there was water in Kansas and not those other places.”
 
Reservoir reserves
Large reservoirs dotting eastern portions of Kansas, including Milford, Tuttle Creek and Perry, didn’t justify complacency, Lewis said. With population growth comes economic development and a greater concentration of consumers or businesses depending on surface water supply from lakes, rivers or streams, he said.
“In eastern Kansas, you really don’t have a huge savings account like you do with the Ogallala Aquifer. It’s all stream flows and very little groundwater. When you get into a drought, the stream flow goes away,” Lewis said.
He said the reservoirs, built to deter flooding, offer recreational opportunities and boost water reserves, were magnets for topsoil pushed off fields during heavy rains. He said $20 million invested in removing sedimentation in John Redmond Reservoir southeast of Emporia extended the life of the reservoir a mere three to five years.
“The fact is our climate is changing,” Lewis said. “All of our understanding of how much water we’re going to have, how long those reservoirs would give us … how does that play out in a different climate setting?”
Lewis said the state’s chief engineer was responsible for monitoring water compacts with Nebraska, Colorado and Oklahoma. There was no pending litigation with those states about equitable distribution, he said, but that could change because some states were “very creative” when documenting usage.
It was incumbent on downstream states to prove how another state was not abiding by deals, he said.
“That’s always the question. Are they in compliance with the compact?” Lewis said. “That’s a very complex system. A lot of times it’s really difficult to determine we’re getting the water that we’re entitled to.”
The state’s chief engineer held responsibility for 2,600 dams dotting the Kansas map. Perhaps one-fourth could threaten a home or significant road if there was a failure, he said.
The state for about 30 years invested $15 million to $20 million annually in water infrastructure projects, but the Legislature and Gov. Laura Kelly added $35 million in 2023.
“Spread it over 105 counties and 3 million people. Twenty bucks per person in the state is basically what we’re spending on water in Kansas, at least at the state level. Is that an adequate investment?”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT sues HUD over rule stripping aid from mixed-status immigrant families
description: CT, other states are suing to block a federal rule change that would strip housing assistance from 'mixed-status' families.
text:
A coalition of 22 states is suing to block a federal rule change that would strip housing assistance from “mixed-status” families — those including U.S. citizens and people without legal immigration status.
Under the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule, any household that includes one member without lawful  status would be cut off from housing assistance. Currently, subsidies are pro-rated to include only eligible recipients, a provision enacted by Congress. The rule, if unblocked, goes into effect Dec. 14.
The states argue that HUD’s new rule violates federal law. “HUD lacks authority to rewrite federal law to exclude families this Administration disfavors from federal affordable housing programs,” the lawsuit says. 
HUD argues the rule would allow the department to redistribute tenant subsidies from mixed-status families to what the new rules classifies as eligible households. Secretary Scott Turner said the rule “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”
“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing,” Turner said in a statement to Stateline. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”
California accounts for the largest share of affected families, followed by Texas and New York. In these states, thousands of households that currently receive prorated rental assistance could lose eligibility entirely if the rule is finalized, rental housing advocates warn. 
Nationwide, nearly 20,000 mixed-status families would be affected by the rule. Most would leave assisted housing voluntarily while nearly 1,000 households would require formal eviction, HUD estimated.
Advocates and plaintiffs in the suit say of the total 78,000 people affected by the new rule, 55,000 are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, a population that skews toward the youngest of renters. 
HUD figures listed in the complaint say that 65% of eligible people in mixed-status households are children and that mixed-status families are a small share of households that receive federal housing assistance, less than 1%.
The states also argue that the rule will shift costs of housing the displaced people onto state and local governments and make it harder for eligible people to keep their housing by requiring them to prove their legal status. 
Plaintiffs in the 22-state lawsuit include the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, as well as the governor of Pennsylvania. It was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts.
“For decades Congress has recognized the importance of keeping families together even if not every member of a family qualifies for assistance,” Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes, a Democrat, said in a statement. “The Trump administration does not get to unilaterally change those protections.” 
Tenant and immigrant rights groups, as well as a coalition of cities from across the country, also have sued over the HUD rule.
This story was first published Nov. 23, 2026 by Stateline.

name: National
title: Golden Girls bills could bring together older and younger roommates
description: Twenty-five-year-old Californian Regnar Madarang wants to own his own home someday. But the Bay Area’s rent of $2,000 and up for a single room wouldn’t allow him to save up for a downpayment, he said.  Three months ago, Madarang learned from a friend about the California-based homesharing platform JoeyCo, which connects homeowners with students and […]
text:
Twenty-five-year-old Regnar Madarang rents and lives with Eileen and Gary Ruppel, who are in their 70s, in Palo Alto, California, through a homesharing agreement. Some states are passing laws to allow more unrelated people to share a home. (Photo courtesy of Regnar Madarang)Twenty-five-year-old Californian Regnar Madarang wants to own his own home someday. But the Bay Area’s rent of $2,000 and up for a single room wouldn’t allow him to save up for a downpayment, he said. 
Three months ago, Madarang learned from a friend about the California-based homesharing platform JoeyCo, which connects homeowners with students and young people who rent a room and do spare work around the house. He now lives with Eileen and Gary Ruppel, who are in their 70s, in Palo Alto. He particularly likes visiting local museums with the couple and says they have allowed him to find community. 
“I’ve learned so much from them and it’s a living situation where I get to help around the house and build community with people who know so much about the neighborhood … and it doesn’t hurt the budget,” Madarang said. “Homesharing is a give and take. They opened their home to me so I also want to add whatever I can to their life.”
Beyond private apps, some cities, including San Francisco, Boston and New York City, have homesharing programs that promote intergenerational living. So do some states such as Pennsylvania and Vermont. But many other areas have laws limiting the number of non-related people who can live in a home.
To address that barrier, lawmakers in several states have introduced or enacted so-called Golden Girls legislation, named after the hit TV show about four older women who share a home. The measures create a statewide standard that allows unrelated individuals to live in the same home. Local jurisdictions still could set occupancy limits based on health and safety standards.
Supporters say these bills can boost the housing supply and open up a living arrangement that can help tackle the high cost of housing and combat senior loneliness. But opponents say that statewide mandates override local authority on housing and zoning issues and could allow single-family housing to be turned into crowded boarding homes. 
Several groups are advocating for similar versions of Golden Girls model legislation they want states to pass, including the American Legislative Exchange Council or ALEC, the Metropolitan Abundance Project and the Pacific Legal Foundation. 
In Pennsylvania, a Golden Girls bill sponsored by Democratic Rep. Tarik Khan passed the House 123–78 in June, but stalled in the state Senate. Some fellow Democrats voted against it, saying they wanted to protect local zoning authority.  
Khan said his first post-college home was a two-bedroom apartment that he shared with three other guys and cost them $2,000 in monthly rent while he worked retail jobs. Khan believes uncapping the amount of unrelated people who can live with each other is one of the ways to lower the cost of housing without additional funding or construction.
“We could increase the availability of housing by doing this,” he said to Stateline. “We can lower the cost of housing without breaking the bank.”
Older adults want to ‘age in place,’ but their options are limited in most states

Pennsylvania Republican state Rep. Jeremy Shaffer had concerns about a Golden Girls bill overriding local authority and undercutting occupancy limits intended to enforce health and safety standards.

“Basically, this bill would allow any single-family home to essentially become a de facto small apartment building,” said Shaffer, as reported by the Pennsylvania Capital-Star.
A report by the conservative Pacific Legal Foundation found that nine of the 10 largest Pennsylvania cities limited the amount of unrelated roommates to three or four people. Thirty-two states have enacted no laws protecting unrelated roommate living arrangements, and municipalities in all those states have restricted how many unrelated people can share a home, according to a July 2026 analysis by the foundation, which advocates removing those limits.
“Most states are silent on this topic,” said Kyle Sweetland, a research manager for property rights at the foundation, which takes cases on limited government, property rights and individual rights. 
Since 2017, Colorado, Iowa, New Hampshire, Oregon, Texas and Washington have passed laws prohibiting some local governments from limiting the amount of non-related residents that can occupy a single home. 
In Connecticut, a Golden Girls measure that would have required towns to allow homeowners to rent rooms to long-term tenants passed the state Senate with bipartisan support this year. But Democratic House Speaker Matt Ritter declined to bring it up for a vote in the House, according to the CT Mirror.
Ritter worried about how a provision requiring homes to be owner-occupied would be enforced and feared people would buy housing as rental property and lower homeownership rates in cities like Hartford, the outlet reported.
JoeyCo’s founder Alison Donnally believes homesharing is an underutilized housing option that could help bridge generational lines among younger and older adults affected by a multifaceted housing crisis. 
“You walk the dog, you pick up the groceries, you act as a good roommate, basically, you get paid to be a good roommate, right?” said Donnally. “You’re not just sort of drifting and floating in this housing market and you’re able to connect and put down roots in a way that is hard to find in other housing options that are available right now.” 
City limits 
In Maryland, Annapolis Alderman Brooks Schandelmeier, a Democrat, said the city’s newly-passed ordinance “Bedrooms for People Act” allows homeowners to rent spare bedrooms without risking $1,000-a-day fines. Schandelmeier once rented a bedroom in a home to afford to live in the city, and said his legislation was inspired by an older constituent of his who needed income by renting a room in her home. 
“This is already happening throughout the city but it was just happening off the books,” he told Stateline. “People may ask, ‘Who would want to live with strangers?’ but I was once that person and it suited my life at the time. Others should also have a chance option if they want it.”
He recalled a former councilmember boasting that previous enforcement of the law prompted the removal of five people from a home when a neighbor complained.
“I’m hearing this story here and all I’m thinking about is that five people were thrown out onto the street and she’s bragging about it,” he said. “I don’t think the city should be interested in enforcing an outdated law that removes people from a shelter that was offered to them.”
PadSplit, which says it’s the largest co-living room rental platform, is in favor of Golden Girls measures and any policy that lifts roommate or home sharing caps. 
Corporate investment in residential housing may be another hurdle for first-time buyers

Its founder Atticus LeBlanc thinks Golden Girls legislation is good low-hanging fruit for housing policy on the state level and should be a bipartisan solution for accommodating changing housing habits and affordability. 
“Pretty much everybody should be able to support that one,” LeBlanc said about Golden Girls legislation. “That’s a series of actions on the state level where it shouldn’t matter where you fall on the political spectrum.”
LeBlanc told Stateline that he recently emailed the Arlington City Council in Texas about neighbors’ opposition to more than four unrelated people sharing a house. 
“I think there’s a misconception that it’s this sociability piece driving this housing behavior when it’s almost entirely financial,” LeBlanc said. “Your housing option shouldn’t be restricted based on how many relatives you have.” 
Arlington City Council held sessions this year during which some city officials said they are leery of these types of housing options. Arlington’s definition of family is a single housekeeping unit with “no more than four individuals unrelated to the head of household by blood, marriage or adoption.”
In August, the city’s Code Compliance Services Director Alex Busken said investors and companies were purchasing single-family homes and renting them to multiple tenants, sometimes with more than five occupants. Some owners had obtained permits to add bedrooms. 
Housing pressures across generations
According to the Urban Institute, the share of young adults ages 25 to 34 who are homeowners fell from 40% in 2005 to 29% in 2024.
Jung Hyun Choi, a principal research associate in the Housing Finance Policy Center at the Urban Institute, said higher borrowing costs and lower savings have reversed some of the progress young adults made toward independent living and homeownership between 2019 and 2022. One part of that equation is the relationship between home prices and interest rates. 
“So we’re in this market where it’s like both are very, very high, so it’s very challenging for younger adults to find a home that they can purchase,” she told Stateline.
Older adults face their own headwinds in today’s housing market. In 2023, more than a third of households led by someone 65 or older spent over 30% of their income on housing. About half of these households, or 6.7 million, spent over 50%, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies.
The US needs homes. But first, it needs the workers to build them.

The center’s 2026 State of the Nation’s Housing report found that households headed by someone 65+ are now dissolving at a rate of 1.4 million per year due to deaths, move-ins with family or entry into care facilities. Those households also have the highest housing cost-burden rate of any age group. 
Younger adults are trying to afford their first homes, while older adults face rising costs that threaten their ability to remain in familiar homes and communities, said Jenn Jones, vice president for financial security and livable communities in AARP’s office of government affairs.
“Who knew that sort of housing affordability would be bringing generations together, right?” she said. 
Madison Daniels, a senior external relations adviser for AARP, told Stateline the organization advocates for laws that support home sharing, which can generate supplemental income for older homeowners and be more affordable than living alone. 
Back in Palo Alto, Madrang has three months left until his contract with the Ruppels is up. Both sides seem keen to re-up.  Homeownership is still in the sights for Madarang but for now, he’s found a home and a family that is worth delaying that milestone for.
“I dream of one day owning property and not having to rent anymore. But the reality is that it might not be possible at this moment,” Madarang said. “For where I am now, homesharing works for me. It’s home.” 
Stateline reporter Robbie Sequeira can be reached at rsequeira@stateline.org.

name: California
title: What the blue wave could mean for California’s economy
description: A Democrat-controlled Congress could change Trump administration policies that affect the state’s agriculture, wine, tech and other industries.
text:
In summary
A Democrat-controlled Congress could change Trump administration policies that affect the state’s agriculture, wine, tech and other industries.


From agriculture to small businesses to the technology industry, the blue wave could have a significant impact on California’s economy. 
That is, if a Democrat-controlled Congress and President Donald Trump can compromise on the different factors that have driven up prices and affected business and the labor force in a variety of industries. 
Leaders and business owners around the state agree that the results of the midterm elections could bring about changes as the president loses the Republican-majority Congress that gave him outsized power — but not all the possible changes would be welcome to them.
Here’s a look at the potential effects on four key sectors of California’s economy. 
Agriculture and the wine industry
The state’s agricultural and wine industries are hurting from inflation brought about by tariffs and the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, and are hoping for some relief. 
“Tariffs have had a tremendous impact on agriculture, depending on what people are growing and selling,” said Shannon Douglass, president of the California Farm Bureau. “We need consistency in our trade relations. We want more markets and more ability to sell our products.” 
Take the U.S-Canada trade war: The state’s vegetable and melon exports to that country dropped about 27% in 2025 from the previous year, falling from $1.14 billion to $837 million, according to data from the International Trade Administration. 
Likewise, California winemakers have lost overseas business. 
“The American brand was so damaged by tariffs and the toxic politics of the day,” said Matt Licklider, owner of LIOCO in Healdsburg, a winemaker that gets its grapes from small vineyards around the state. “We have done almost no export business since Trump took office (the second time).”
Licklider said not all of his fears about what tariffs would mean materialized. He did not have to reduce staff. Despite losing most of his ability to export, which he said made up about 10% of his business, he was able to adjust by focusing his efforts on the domestic market. 
Matt Licklider, owner of LIOCO Wines, at the winery’s tasting room in Healdsburg on Nov. 21, 2026. Photo by Chad Surmick for CalMatters
But tariffs — some of which were struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court — combined with the Iran War led to higher costs for just about everything, such as transportation and supplies. And the next “tariff shock” could come after the holidays, after the suspension of a U.S.-China trade truce expires, according to a new study by the Port of Long Beach and an institute at University of Southern California. 
All of it has cut into LIOCO’s bottom line.
“As good of a year as we had from a revenue standpoint, from a profit standpoint, the champagne is not on ice,” Licklider said. “It’s pretty heartbreaking after having worked so hard all year.”
Licklider also worries about the long-term effects on global trade. 
“I think the rest of the world is watching what happens in the next election, and wondering ‘can they trust America’?” he said.
AI and Silicon Valley
There’s a big question mark around the tech industry and whether the artificial intelligence boom is about to burst, which would among other things affect the state’s budget. 
Wall Street has had a mixed reaction about what the changes in Congress mean for Silicon Valley. Even before Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang’s resignation (and reinstatement) threatened the nexus of the boom — think of the chip company as the sun around which all other AI companies revolve — the stock markets saw big declines over fears Democrats would enact tougher AI regulations. Opposition to data centers that power the AI boom influenced voters around the country during the midterm elections, contributing to the blue wave. 
Considering California laws tend to become models for the rest of the country, the tech industry is doing its best to advocate for itself in its home state.
“There’s confusion (around data centers), and we’ve been part of legislative efforts where there has been misinformation that we believe has not provided community members with an accurate picture of what responsible development looks like,” said Ahmad Thomas, CEO of Silicon Valley Leadership Group. The group’s members include the world’s biggest tech companies. 
Thomas said data centers in San Jose show how such development can feature renewable energy and recycled water, and include community incentives and utility-cost goals. Yet the city decided last week to pause data center development. 
On Democrats being more keen to pass laws reining in AI, including those related to how it affects and sometimes eliminates jobs, Thomas said it’s important to invest in training today’s workers for jobs with the new tech reality in mind.

Almost immediately after the election, Trump said of the new Democratic majority: “Maybe we can work something out.” He also acknowledged that his approach to immigration, which has included sweeping raids and deaths of detainees and others, may have been “too tough.”
Then he appointed Stephen Miller, widely known to be behind his administration’s hardline immigration policies, to be his new chief of staff.
“Trump has responded to these midterms in some schizophrenic and kind of incoherent ways,” said Giovanni Peri, a professor of international economics at UC Davis.

name: California
title: Does Gavin Newsom have any regrets? He’s not saying as he looks to 2028
description: Gavin Newsom is winding down his time as California governor and preparing to run for president in 2028. He defended his record at the Sacramento Press Club.
text:
In summary
Gavin Newsom is winding down his time as California governor and preparing to run for president in 2028. He defended his record at the Sacramento Press Club.


Gov. Gavin Newsom’s unofficial campaign pitch for president boils down two main themes — California is amazing, and President Donald Trump is dangerous.
In an exit interview Monday night with the Sacramento Press Club, attendees got a glimpse into how a potential candidate Newsom would field questions on his California record 
The soon-to-be ex-governor took every opportunity to tout his administration’s ambitious policy agenda. He praised California as a national leader on the development of artificial intelligence — and its regulation — as well as renewable energy and housing policy. 
And he pivoted any thorny questions into attacks on Trump. 
When asked for his response to the news that tech giant Nvidia just reappointed its scandal-ridden founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, Newsom called Huang an “extraordinary talent” whose company’s success has boosted state revenue. He denounced Trump for reportedly pressuring the Nvidia board to rehire Huang, ostensibly to keep a wayward stock market from tanking further following Huang’s acknowledgement of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
“This is more about Trump, in many ways, than even Jensen himself,” Newsom said. “I’m concerned about selling our national security for a quick buck.”
Newsom raised his national profile significantly when he and his team embraced the Trumpian strategy of trolling critics online, a move that disgusted some followers and thrilled others. He signaled that his total embrace of “new media” — podcasts, social media videos, direct-to-camera appeals — wasn’t going anywhere.
“A lot of you wrote that this was unbecoming of a governor. That I should wash my mouth out with soap. And you were partially right, fair point,” Newsom said. “Direct to camera, social media, using those portals become the only mechanism to which we can actually tell the story about our state.”
Careful to not appear too eager to move on from his day job before Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra takes office, Newsom refused to close the door on a long shot special session to address two of his chosen issues — wildfire liability and AI regulation. Newsom has never had the coziest relationship with state lawmakers and has oftentimes tried to squeeze big policy proposals through at the last minute. 
But if legislative leaders showed signs of being open to a special session, he said he’s “ready to move at a moment’s notice” and has drafted proposals. 
“I would love to do it. But I need to have partners,” Newsom said, seemingly pointing to the two legislative leaders, Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Senate Pro Tem Monique Limón. “You know their attitudes at this point.”
He was reluctant to name any regrets from his eight years in office. Yes, even if he had a redo, he would 100% still have Charlie Kirk and Stephen Bannon on his podcast. 
The closest he came was how the state handled education during the COVID-19 pandemic, when California kept schools closed longer than some other states. 
“I want that five months back,” Newsom said, speaking of the period when schools were shuttered and students fell behind on learning. 
Newsom since his first run for governor embraced headline-grabbing goals, such as building 3.5 million homes, reducing homelessness and bringing thousands of people with severe mental illnesses into treatment. He also changed California’s criminal justice system by moving to commute death sentences and closing prisons. Some of those policies and promises could be fodder for his opponents in a national presidential campaign.
Quoting the Italian artist Michelangelo, Newsom said he and his team strived to aim high and make partial progress rather than set the goal at an attainable level. 
“We want to take big swings, and the vast majority of the time we actually connect.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts can close the racial homeownership gap
description: We are calling on corporate leaders, financial institutions, and elected officials to dream bigger with us—and with the thousands of first-generation homebuyers who are ready to become homeowners.
text:
OVER 10 YEARS ago, a landmark study on the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston and research partners was released and we missed the moment. Badly. 
An updated Federal Reserve Bank of Boston report released in August found a still-staggering racial wealth divide in Massachusetts: median net wealth of just $7,800 for Black households and $1,200 for Hispanic households, compared with $550,000 for white households.  
Homeownership is not the only factor driving that disparity, but the enormous racial homeownership gap is a major contributor. Massachusetts has long had one of the largest gaps between the percentage of white households owning a home (70 percent) compared to Black (37 percent) and Hispanic (32 percent) households. 
What is different now? We already have a program showing us the way forward. 
In the last six years, Saving Toward Affordable Sustainable Homeownership (STASH) has helped 469 first-generation, all below-median-income Massachusetts homebuyers purchase homes. It’s a matched-savings program that is simple, direct, and packs a powerful punch. First-generation buyers save and learn about homeownership from peers who have been there. We match those savings and those potential homebuyers get a fairer shot at buying a home. 
Nearly half of STASH buyers are Black and another third are Hispanic. These are precisely the households that have historically been left out of homeownership—and, as a result, left out of one of the most powerful engines of wealth creation in America. 
That matters enormously in Massachusetts. And STASH is closing that gap. 
The program began in 2019 with support from Boston Children’s Hospital followed by the City of Boston, and expanded by ARPA state funding and, most recently, with the support of The Boston Foundation Racial Wealth Gap Partnership and banks like M&T and Wells Fargo. The program has grown further with commitments from banks, individual donors, and municipalities. But it remains nowhere near the scale needed to reach the thousands of first-generation buyers still sitting on the sidelines. 
That is the opportunity before us. 
Massachusetts is a state that knows how to innovate. We are home to the country’s first public school, the first university, the first public park, and the first public beach. We invented basketball. 
And Massachusetts has a proud history of leading on housing. In the 1980s, Gov. Michael Dukakis and state leaders stepped forward when the federal government dramatically cut housing programs. The Commonwealth chose to act when Washington walked away. Our organization helped to pass the first state-level Community Reinvestment Act for independent mortgage companies. And in 2019, we launched STASH, the nation’s first homeownership program aimed at first-generation homebuyers.  
We look forward to building on that legacy of leadership together. 
The STASH program, operated by the Massachusetts Affordable Housing Alliance, works. Combined with the ONE Mortgage Program administered by the state Massachusetts Housing Partnership, which our organization worked with lenders, the city of Boston, and the state to create in 1990, STASH is the most powerful tool we have to close the racial homeownership gap. 
The combination of low interest rates and other affordability features in ONE Mortgage means increased buying power, and STASH enables people to get to the closing table with the cash they need. Add in the state’s Commonwealth Builder Program, administered by MassHousing, which produces affordable homes, and you have a trio of programs that can be difference makers.  
Now we need to take it to scale. 
We are calling on corporate leaders, financial institutions, and elected officials to dream bigger with us—and with the thousands of first-generation homebuyers who are ready to become homeowners but cannot overcome the upfront costs of buying a home in one of the nation’s most expensive housing markets. 
Massachusetts has an $8 billion rainy-day fund. It has been raining hard for first-time and first-generation homebuyers. 
Let’s invest $100 million in state dollars in STASH to help 2,000 first-generation homebuyers become homeowners—and, at the same time, build a sustainable funding model that makes serving 2,000 families a year an enduring commitment of the Commonwealth. 
And let’s open our biggest affordable housing construction programs to communities that want more homeownership opportunities.   
With leaders like Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Ayanna Pressley poised to assume key leadership roles in Congress, it is time to revisit the $10 billion First Generation Down Payment Fund first introduced in Congress in 2021. 
That is not a handout. It is an investment in families, neighborhoods and the future of Massachusetts. 
Imagine what happens if we do this year after year. Two thousand families become homeowners. Then another 2,000. And another. 
Children grow up in homes their parents own. Families begin building equity. Neighborhoods gain stability. More Black and Hispanic families have an opportunity to pass wealth to the next generation. And, finally, the numbers begin moving in the right direction. 
We missed the moment once. We cannot miss it again. Massachusetts has the programs. We have the partners. We need the resources and the commitment to scale what works. 
Symone Crawford is executive director the Massachusetts Affordable Housing Alliance. Cathy Mercado is executive director of the Merrimack Valley Housing Partnership.

name: California
title: CalPERS is changing the rules for retirees with part-time jobs. Here’s why
description: California limits how much retirees can work while receiving a pension, but people — and employers — often make mistakes. CalPERS is trying to clarify the rules with two new policies.
text:
In summary
California limits how much retirees can work while receiving a pension, but people — and employers — often make mistakes. CalPERS is trying to clarify the rules with two new policies.


Working part-time after retirement can backfire for former California government employees who are collecting pensions. 
They — and their employers — must adhere to California pension law or risk costly penalties that can derail their plans. 
Take, for instance, Sacramento, which laid off 41 reserve police officers last year after an audit by the California Public Employees’ Retirement System. 
Or, government workers who received letters from their retirement fund demanding that they repay hundreds of thousands of dollars in pension income because they ran afoul of those rules. 
CalPERS is trying to make the rules a little easier to understand with a pair of new policies clarifying who can work while receiving a pension and for how long. Its board approved the proposals last week, but they are not final and are subject to a public comment period.

The first lays out a clear timeline for how long a government agency can hire what CalPERS calls a retired annuitant, meaning someone who works while receiving a pension. Previously, retired part-timers could work for a “limited duration.” If CalPERS formally adopts the new policy, agencies could hire a retired annuitant for two years and then apply up to three one-year extensions.
The second change would help retired police and firefighters move into part-time positions by clarifying their retirement age. It eliminates a conflict with federal tax law and designates an employee’s retirement age as the one set by the place where they spent the majority of their careers.

“These proposed regulations would give employers and retirees a more consistent framework to follow and help prevent avoidable violations,” CalPERS President Theresa Taylor said in a written statement after the board advanced the two policies. “Just as important, they would make the approval and reporting process more transparent and accountable.”
Government employers, however, have reservations. 
Cory Sazillo, the legislative director for the California State Sheriffs’ Association, called into last week’s board meeting to stress that law enforcement agencies sometimes turn to retired officers for hard-to-fill positions. He urged the board to leave flexibility for public safety. 
“County sheriff offices utilize annuitants in many ways, in cold cases, specialty units and court services,” he said.
The Sacramento reserve officers who lost their part-time jobs last year were a good example. The city was not able to rehire any of them after the audit, a spokesperson said.
Organizations representing cities, counties and special districts wrote to the CalPERS board asking for modifications, including a hardship extension for positions that cannot be filled after recruitment for a full-time employee. 
But the agencies also commended CalPERS for trying to clarify the rules.
“We do not oppose a defined limit on post-retirement service. A clear standard serves employers and retirees better than ambiguity, and it serves the system’s interest in preventing abuse,” the agencies wrote.
Disputes over how CalPERS polices work-after-retirement rules have been building up for several years. Gov. Gavin Newsom in August signed a law backed by one of the state’s largest public employee unions, the California School Employees Association, that will require CalPERS to give better notice when it audits an agency.
And, several CalPERS retirees are suing the pension fund over notices they received when it determined they violated working-after-retirement rules. One of them received a letter demanding she repay $1 million in pension income she received while working part-time. The lawsuit is underway in San Francisco Superior Court.

name: Nevada Current
title: Kalshi partnership costs problem gambling council another member
description: Nevada’s chronically underfunded problem gambling efforts could get a boost from casino industry giants such as MGM Resorts International and Aristocrat Gaming pulling their membership from the National Council on Problem Gambling over the organization’s partnership with Kalshi. MGM informed the National Council last week that it’s not renewing its membershi[...]
text:
Kalshi photo illustration, Tuesday, April 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Nevada’s chronically underfunded problem gambling efforts could get a boost from casino industry giants such as MGM Resorts International and Aristocrat Gaming pulling their membership from the National Council on Problem Gambling over the organization’s partnership with Kalshi.
MGM informed the National Council last week that it’s not renewing its membership because of the organization’s embrace of Kalshi, a prediction market that is fighting efforts by Nevada and other states to require it to comply with gambling regulations.
Aristocrat Gaming announced in September that it had “shifted its support from the National Council to local organizations that provide direct prevention, education, and treatment services within their communities.” Aristocrat cited “differing views on prediction market policy” as the reason.
Aristocrat increased its contribution to the Nevada Council on Problem Gambling by 50%, says the council’s executive director Trey Delap. 
In May, the Nevada Current reported that the National Council formed the Financial Services and Trading subcategory with Kalshi, its first member, funding a $2 million, two-year investment to “support a strategic initiative focused on trader health and safety.”  
That contribution from Kalshi, a company valued at $40 billion, amounts to about half of what Nevada allocates to problem gambling each year. 
MGM’s departure from the organization comes months after the Nevada Council on Problem Gambling cut ties with the national organization because of its partnership with Kalshi. 
“MGM’S decision reinforces concerns we raised months ago about credibility and consumer protection,” says Delap. “Casino operators look their customers in the face every day, and when someone calls a helpline, they need real help from people in their own community. Consumer protection is a responsibility, not a PR exercise.” 
The National Council did not respond to a request for comment. 
The need for a national organization that supports local work remains, says Delap. “Research, advocacy, and coordination all matter. But problem gambling affects people where they live, and that’s the front line for prevention, treatment, and support. The bigger question now isn’t who stays or goes. It’s what we do next.”
In its letter to the National Council, MGM wrote that “by welcoming Kalshi, NCPG actively confers legitimacy on its business model and leaves the public with the mistaken impression that prediction markets adhere to the same consumer protections, licensing requirements, responsible marketing standards, and regulatory oversight as legitimate sports betting operators.”
Nevada is one of more than a dozen states that maintain Kalshi is subject to state gaming regulations and prohibitions. 
A panel of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in Nevada’s favor in August, finding that sports bets accepted by the platform are likely not swaps, as defined by federal law. This month, the Court denied Kalshi’s request for a rehearing, setting up a likely appeal by the platform to the U.S. Supreme Court. 
“Legal operators obtain state gaming licenses and adhere to strict regulatory guidelines that help protect consumers and game integrity,” MGM wrote. “Kalshi openly flouts these regulatory safeguards and brags about offering sports trading ‘in all 50 states’ – whether states allow them or not.”
Kalshi’s marketing, the letter says, undermines a key tenet of responsible gambling advocates  — “the foundational principle that gambling is entertainment, not an investment or a path to meeting financial obligations.”
A Kalshi ad in which a player boasts he was unable to pay his rent but won enough on Kalshi to pay for two years “blurs this line,” MGM wrote. “Suggesting that sports betting on Kalshi is an easy ticket to financial success is an open invitation to every form of problem gambling that NCPG and responsible gaming programs are supposed to confront, not legitimize.”
Kalshi accepts wagers from bettors as young as 18, the letter notes, and refers in TikTok ads to bets as a “money hack” or “side hustle.”
Young people between 18 and 24 are the source of about half of the callers to the U.S. National Gambling Helpline, says Delap of the Nevada Council. 
The Nevada Council has long endured inadequate funding. The problem has been exacerbated by the proliferation of alternative forms of gambling. 
Funds for problem gambling awareness and treatment are predominantly paid for by licensed casinos and from gaming taxes, MGM wrote, adding that Kalshi and other prediction markets, by ignoring state regulations, “pay only a pittance in taxes compared to legal gaming companies, which ultimately reduces funding for problem gambling initiatives.”
The proliferation of gambling outside the lines drawn by state regulators is exponential, as is the Pandora’s Box-like potential for harm, say experts. 
Standard options for gambling – legal casinos, legal apps, and illegal websites or bookies – have been upended in recent years by gambling-adjacent activities such as stock daytrades, crypto and meme coin trading, and the ubiquitous prediction markets.
“The state-regulated gambling industry — both online and land-based — is now competing, to varying extents, with all of these things,” prediction market expert and journalist Dustin Gouker wrote earlier this month.“And the idea that you are going to be able to stop, slow or regulate all of these verticals feels out of reach.”

title: $61M paid out for insurance claims after historic WA flooding
description: Insurers paid over $61 million to cover Washington homes damaged in record-setting flooding late last year, state Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer announced this week.  Across Washington last December, 33 rivers reached flood stage, and three broke records, though not to the catastrophic level some feared. The record-breaking flooding forced evacuation o[...]
text:
Debris floats down the Nooksack River in Ferndale, in the flooded area around Hovander Homestead Park. (Photo by Eli Voorhies for Washington State Standard)Insurers paid over $61 million to cover Washington homes damaged in record-setting flooding late last year, state Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer announced this week. 
Across Washington last December, 33 rivers reached flood stage, and three broke records, though not to the catastrophic level some feared.
The record-breaking flooding forced evacuation orders for over 100,000 Washingtonians and damaged nearly 4,000 homes, according to the state. Of those, 1,056 homeowners filed approved insurance claims totaling more than $61.3 million.
Many Washingtonians don’t have flood insurance. Fewer than 45,000 homes are covered, despite many more facing a risk of flooding. Nearly 40% of residents live in a 100-year floodplain, meaning areas with a 1% chance of flooding in any given year, according to an Urban Institute analysis. Homeowners’ insurance typically doesn’t cover flooding.
About two-thirds of those covered have policies through the National Flood Insurance Program, managed by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. It provides coverage with limits of $250,000 for building damage and $100,000 for personal property damage, and has a 30-day waiting period before taking effect.
Starting last month, FEMA began allowing homeowners to buy a National Flood Insurance Program policy online. 
These insurees accounted for nearly $41 million of the losses linked to the 2025 flooding: about two-thirds. 
The remaining $20.5 million came from residents with flood policies through private insurance companies. 
Whatcom County accounted for the most claims: 353, totaling $24.5 million in paid losses. Of those, 258 were filed through the federal insurance program. 
King, Skagit and Snohomish counties also had over 100 claims reported. A few counties, including Cowlitz, Yakima, Grays Harbor and Thurston saw fewer than 10 claims that were paid out. 
The insurance company data doesn’t include damage to commercial properties, including those owned by a business and rented out. Its release by Kuderer’s office comes as flood season begins, and on the heels of one of the state’s worst wildfire years. 
“Climate change is pushing floodwaters into areas that may not have a history of flooding,” Kuderer said in a statement. “Even if your home has never flooded before, it’s important to prepare for the possibility that your home could be damaged in a flood — and that your flood risk could change after a wildfire.”
The geographical distribution of federal flood insurance is unclear, but the state collects data on those with private coverage. As of last December, King County had over 2,800 private flood insurance policies, followed by Skagit County with 2,035, Grays Harbor County with 1,588, Snohomish County with 1,150 and Pierce with 1,109, according to the insurance commissioner’s office.
Insurance hasn’t been the only recovery tool for residents. State and federal aid has also been available.

Of $2.5 million in cash assistance from the state, less than half was given out as of this week, due to tight restrictions on who can access it. Another pot with $1 million from the state was quickly doled out to over 2,600 households. 
On the federal side, as of June, the deadline to apply, FEMA distributed $11 million to more than 1,200 households, after President Donald Trump approved a request from Gov. Bob Ferguson for the federal help. That sum has likely increased, as more applications were processed. 
Trump didn’t OK all of Ferguson’s asks, however. The Trump administration denied Washington’s request for federal funding to prepare for future floods. The state appealed the rejection, but hasn’t heard back, said Karina Shagren, spokesperson for the Washington Military Department.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s new interim education commissioner sparks debate over political influence
description: Missouri’s 1945 constitution put the selection of the state’s education commissioner in the hands of an appointed board, a change intended to insulate education leadership from partisan politics. The State Board of Education’s decision last week to name Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin as interim commissioner has renewed questions about whether thos[...]
text:
Missouri Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O'Laughlin — pictured during the inauguration of Gov. Mike Kehoe Jan. 13, 2025 — will step into a new role as interim commissioner of education Dec. 1 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri’s 1945 constitution put the selection of the state’s education commissioner in the hands of an appointed board, a change intended to insulate education leadership from partisan politics.
The State Board of Education’s decision last week to name Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin as interim commissioner has renewed questions about whether those safeguards are working as intended.
O’Laughlin, a Shelbina Republican, breaks from a tradition of career educators leading the department. Critics worry her appointment could bring partisan politics into an agency designed to operate independently.
“The Missouri Constitution includes an independent State Board of Education to keep politics out of the commissioner hiring process,” the Missouri State Teachers Association wrote in a statement Friday. “Today’s decision puts it right back in.”
The association’s advocacy extends back to the 1940s, when Missouri held a constitutional convention that, among other things, reshaped how the state’s education department is governed.
The group endorsed a new constitution, approved by voters in 1945, which created an eight-person State Board of Education and the education commissioner position. Previously, the department’s chief was an elected superintendent of schools chosen on a partisan ballot.
A pamphlet circulated to voters at the time advertised that the constitution “takes the State Department of Education out of politics.” 
“Education is so important that we don’t want it handled in a partisan fashion,” Duane Martin, an attorney whose law firm EdCounsel represents public school districts, told The Independent. “We want education policy for this state to be above partisan politics, and that insulation has been removed.”
State Board of Education President Brooks Miller has defended O’Laughlin’s appointment, pointing to her experience on a local school board, as a business owner and as a legislative leader. He said those skills will benefit the department and Missouri students.
 Constitutional convention

Concerns about political influence were central to the debate over Missouri’s education system more than eight decades ago.
“One of the fundamental principles in our system of government is to remove as far as possible, educational matters from partisan consideration,” William L. Bradshaw, a teacher from Columbia, said as delegates in the constitutional convention debated the education framework May 1, 1944.
That day, delegates debated whether the state should continue to have an elected superintendent of schools or create a state board that would appoint a commissioner of education. Ultimately, they chose the latter, but not before considerable debate over the best way to insulate the position from political interference.
George W. Kirk, a lawyer from Sikeston, advocated for an appointed commissioner, saying the best candidate is likely someone who would not want to campaign or be at the mercy of election cycles.
To him, the commissioner would be “a man high in education circles, a man who has no political aspirations, a man in all probability who would never present his name to the voters of the state but a man qualified for the high office.”
 


O’Laughlin is not the first politician to become commissioner. In 2024, state Sen. Karla Eslinger took the role after a long career in education.
Eslinger had worked as a teacher, principal, superintendent and education policy advisor prior to joining the legislature.
According to her Senate biography, O’Laughlin has worked “as a school bus driver, an administrator at a local Christian school and as a member of her local school board.”
Many delegates in 1944 argued that the commissioner should have extensive experience in education, and that an appointed position would allow the state to search more broadly for qualified candidates.
But some worried that a board appointed by the governor would feel pressure to carry out the governor’s agenda. Supporters of the proposal argued that staggered terms and political balance would limit any one governor’s influence.
“It seems to me that it definitely takes (the position) out of politics,” Kirk said. “We have a bi-partisan board. That bi-partisan board is given… an eight year term, a staggered term, the purpose of it being so that no governor of this state could appoint more than four members of the board.”
At the time, a governor could not be elected to two consecutive terms — a restriction voters eliminated through a constitutional amendment in 1965.
Gov. Mike Kehoe has appointed members to seven of the eight State Board of Education positions. When he took office last year, multiple board members were serving on expired terms, and he was able to select four new members right away.
A similar situation occurred in 2017 when former Gov. Eric Greitens appointed board members who voted to oust then-Commissioner Margie Vandeven. When Greitens was forced from office in 2018, the board rehired Vandeven.
The Missouri Constitution bars the board from having more than four members of the same political party. In 1944, delegates spoke about the board as having “four Republicans” and “four Democrats.”
But the constitution does not require an equal number of Republicans and Democrats. The department currently lists three Republicans, two Democrats and two independents on the board, with one voting seat vacant.
The state’s first two education commissioners and two original State Board of Education members shared their opinions in a 1973 research report that the political balance of the board is an “essential requirement.”
“In their opinion, education is not a partisan issue; hence, a politically balanced board ensures that all viewpoints are considered,” wrote the report’s author Dewey Wahl, who worked for Purdue University and the Indiana State Department of Public Instruction.
 Political independence

Missouri’s first commissioner of education, Hubert Wheeler, who participated in the report, was particularly sensitive to political pressures. 
Everett Keith, who was one of the first members of the State Board of Education in 1946, said Wheeler was “sensitive that the department be kept out of politics” in a 1996 interview as part of an oral history project by the University of Missouri and the State Historical Society of Missouri.
“He was an ethical guy, all the way,” he said. “He did not dabble one bit in politics.”
Some worry O’Laughlin will see her role as interim commissioner as an extension of her political career.
As a state lawmaker, she has advocated for policies that use public funds for private schools and sought stricter consequences for schools whose students score poorly on standardized tests.
“Her appointment raises questions about how (the department) will balance these policies with its responsibility to support traditional public schools and the nearly 900,000 Missouri children they serve,” the Missouri Retired Teachers Association wrote in a call to action.
But for some, O’Laughlin’s break from the norm is welcomed.
Tony Leutkemeyer, a Republican from Parkville who served as Senate Majority Leader during O’Laughlin’s time as president pro tem, lauded her work in the legislature “to expand school choice, improve student literacy and increase teacher pay.”
“Cindy has the experience, vision and leadership to take (the department) in a bold new direction focused on parents, students and academic achievement,” he wrote on X.
Tom Estes, chief of staff to Republican state Sen. Rick Brattin, celebrated her appointment.
“The house is about to get cleaned,” he wrote.
O’Laughlin will begin work as interim commissioner Dec. 1. The board is continuing its search for someone to fill the role permanently.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: ‘Mr. Johnson’ is off to Washington. His students helped him get there.
description: A few years ago, when Jake Johnson noticed that the Mayo High School girls tennis team regularly made the state tournament but drew less fanfare than sports like football, he decided to do something about it. He organized a bus to take students to cheer on the team.  That year, a bus packed with eager […]
text:
Jake Johnson and Nik Marda play chess in New Ulm during a break in the day in June 2025. (Courtesy photo)A few years ago, when Jake Johnson noticed that the Mayo High School girls tennis team regularly made the state tournament but drew less fanfare than sports like football, he decided to do something about it. He organized a bus to take students to cheer on the team. 
That year, a bus packed with eager students made its way to the state tournament. Last year, the school sent two.  
It was the kind of thing he was known for, alongside his challenging math classes and the string of student clubs he advised. So when Johnson’s campaign manager, Nik Marda, realized that Johnson’s underdog race against U.S. Rep. Brad Finstad might come down to a few Rochester precincts where Johnson’s former students and their families lived, he felt a surge of confidence.
Sure enough, the precincts pushed Johnson ahead by 324 votes, flipping a district that President Donald Trump won in 2024 by nearly 12 percentage points.
Marda called the congressman-elect, who had returned home for the night to be with his wife and four sons. 
“Jake, we’re up by over 300 votes,” Marda told him. “You’ve won.”
The win, certified on Nov. 19, was a culmination of a campaign built, in large part, around a network Johnson had developed long before entering politics: his former students. 
For them, congressional candidate Jake Johnson was not so different from “Mr. Johnson,” the math teacher who made a notoriously difficult math class feel manageable — even fun, for some — and who never shied away from a good challenge. 
Now that he’s met the challenge of riding the blue wave to Washington, Johnson’s already got another undertaking on his hands: re-election. Voters in the 1st District, which spans southern Minnesota from South Dakota to Wisconsin, will want swift action on affordability, even though Johnson won’t have much influence at the Capitol and few immediate tools to bring down prices. He’ll also have to navigate the district’s conservative leanings: The district’s base may look askance at a Democrat too close to party leadership, even though he’ll need to cozy up to leadership to get anything done for its interests. In other words, he’ll need to be a quick study.
‘Mr. Johnson’
When Marda arrived at John Marshall High School in 2013, he heard about the tough but fair math teacher Mr. Johnson. He had also heard about what a grind AP Calculus BC could be. 
“You sort of go through the ringer in a class like that,” Marda said. 
Marda took the class his sophomore year and was  drawn to Johnson, whose classroom Marda would visit even after he was no longer his student. 
Jake Johnson’s old classroom at Mayo. (Photo by Maya Betti/Minnesota Reformer)
At the time, Marda was also part of John Marshall’s flailing math league team, which had dwindled to just four members and was being coached by a non-math teacher. 
“It wasn’t an endeavor that was designed to be successful,” Marda said. 
Marda thought Johnson could help. He asked him to take over as coach, and the two set about rebuilding the team. By Marda’s junior year, it had grown from four members to 40 and had become the fourth-best team in the state.
High expectations then followed Johnson to Mayo High School, where he began teaching in 2022. 
Jack McCauley, who graduated in 2024, remembers what Johnson said on his first day of class. 
“He was very upfront in that it was going to be a difficult class, and we would learn to struggle, but we would all kind of come out better for it,” he said. “To be honest, it’s still to this day, the hardest class I’ve ever taken.”
Johnson, for his part, made sure students had what they needed. He (in)famously held 5:30 a.m. study sessions for extra help. McCauley attended about a third of them, often arriving to find Johnson already there, prepared to teach.
“It was an experience,” McCauley said. “I was like, “Oh, he’s actually here at 5:30.’”
Johnson’s commitment wasn’t just reserved for his math classes. During the school’s annual Give One For All fundraiser, he won the inaugural “Professor Mayo” competition, an elimination-style bracket in which teachers competed to raise money for local charities, including the Rochester Women’s Shelter and the Dorothy Day Hospitality House.
In a prelude to his congressional run, Johnson did a Tom Sawyer trick and raised $15,284 — more than any other teacher — by enlisting students to sell donated treats and drinks. 
“It was kind of a really militant operation,” said Rocco Ruggeri, who was student body president at the time and creator of the “Professor Mayo” tagline. “He was like a very disciplined leader. And everyone wanted to do it because he was so inspiring.” 
Students gravitated toward  him, said Travis Krahn, a math teacher and former colleague. 
“He’s got that personality that kids gravitate towards, and they want to do work for him,” Krahn said. “It starts with building a relationship with the kids, and that’s what he does very well. He picks up on what they enjoy.” 
Throughout his time at Mayo, Johnson hosted a walking club; a “Supercell Club for students who played mobile games such as Clash Royale and Clash of Clans; and a “Chips and Politics Club,”  where students discussed current events over chips. And of course the buses to back the girls’ tennis team. 
Congressional candidate Jake Johnson
After graduating from John Marshall High School, Marda went on to Stanford University before beginning a career in Washington, D.C. He and Johnson stayed in touch, usually catching up over brunch at Denny’s when Marda returned to Rochester for holidays.
For years, it was a once-a-year tradition. 
That changed the day after the 2024 presidential election.
Marda gave Johnson a call. 
“I just sort of had this ninth sense that like I should call Jake,” Marda said.
The two spoke for about an hour, lamenting what the next few years entailed. Marda remembered something Johnson used to tell his students: Think about how they could use their skills to make the world better. 
“I remember telling Jake, like, ‘Hey, I think you should think about what you can do at this moment, too,’” Marda recalled.
At the time, Johnson had already gotten a small taste of politics. He helped organize support for a 2024 Rochester Public Schools levy referendum, which passed and provided more than $19 million annually for the district over the next decade. 
But running for Congress was a different ballgame. Johnson would be challenging Republican Finstad in a district he had won reelection in 2024 by 17 percentage points. 
Johnson sat down with his wife and sons and gave each of them the opportunity to veto the idea. If any one of them objected, Johnson would not run. They agreed. 
Then, Johnson called Marda. 
“I think I said something to the extent of, like, ‘I have a job now. Do you want me to write a check and make a contribution?’” Marda said. “Jake said something like, ‘No, I want you to move back home and run this campaign.’”
Nik Marda gets Jake Johnson set up for a video interview. (Courtesy photo)
Marda quit his job, moved back to Rochester and got to work. He wasn’t the only one. 
Ruggeri took time away from his junior year at the University of Minnesota to join the campaign, followed by McCauley, who took a leave of absence from his junior year at the University of Southern California to help.
By the end of the campaign, over 50 former students were involved in some way. They helped with social media, knocked on doors, raised money and joined Johnson at town halls across southern Minnesota.
Ruggeri was skeptical of Johnson’s chances. As a political science student, he understood the district’s Republican lean. 
“This might be a good try, Mr. Johnson, but, you know, we’ll see what happens,” Ruggeri recalled thinking when he first heard the announcement. 
But as he spent more time with Johnson on the campaign trail — often riding with Johnson in his dinged-up minivan from one county to the next — his feelings changed.  
“Once I started working on the campaign and I started spending more time with him. I’m like, ‘This guy’s got it.’” 
For Marda, the students and Johnson’s network are a part of the reason why he won. 
“So many people who had known Jake at some point in his life all came through for him at the end of this campaign,” Marda said. 
Johnson needed to do well in Rochester and Stewartville — where Johnson was born and raised — and he blew through his goals in both. 
Members of Jake Johnson’s campaign, many of them his former students, wait for results from the final precinct on election night. (Courtesy photo)
US Rep.-elect Jake Johnson
After a celebratory breakfast at Denny’s and some sleep, Marda introduced his former teacher to a crowded room full of supporters at the campaign’s victory party. 
“This thing that started out is such a sort of long-shot aspiration that became real, and to have the people in the room that made it possible,” Marda said. “It was just truly one of the most inspiring and fulfilling moments of my entire life.”
Although Finstad has requested a recount following the Nov. 19 certification of election results, the 324-vote margin separating the candidates makes a reversal unlikely, and Johnson has begun preparing to take office. In mid-November, he attended a 10-day orientation for incoming members of Congress in Washington, D.C., and signed a letter urging party leadership to adopt a day-one ban on members of Congress owning or trading stocks.
McCauley, who hopes to join Johnson on Capitol Hill next semester, said he expects that his former teacher will continue to set high expectations for himself and for those around him. 
“He was right there with us at 5:30 a.m., and I really feel like he’s willing to do the same work, really roll up the sleeves to get stuff done in D.C.,” McCauley said.

title: Commentary: This Thanksgiving is a time to remember, rejoice and get ready
description: Thanksgiving has always been a special holiday, but this year, our national landscape is clouded by virulent partisan politics, economic challenges and growing uncertainty about what America stands for. The results of the midterm election, while encouraging, do not guarantee that our country will move closer to what we aspire for it to be. Some […]
text:
(alexkich/iStock Images)Thanksgiving has always been a special holiday, but this year, our national landscape is clouded by virulent partisan politics, economic challenges and growing uncertainty about what America stands for.
The results of the midterm election, while encouraging, do not guarantee that our country will move closer to what we aspire for it to be.
Some leaders appear determined to double down on divisive politics rather than work in a spirit of cooperation and goodwill to improve life for the people they serve.
On the national level, the Trump administration is making it clear it has no intention of changing the way it operates despite the outcomes of the midterm election.
In Missouri, some Republicans are already considering new efforts to restrict abortion and revisit congressional redistricting and changes to the initiative petition process where voters have made their position clearly known.
The steady diet of vitriol, accusations and divisiveness is taking a toll on our collective spirit.
Beginning with Thanksgiving and throughout the holiday season, let us take time to get our minds and spirits in a state of readiness to fight to promote and protect our well-being as citizens, and for the America that we love.
At a time when we need leaders on both sides of the political spectrum who will help us bridge our differences and find a path forward, many are perpetuating the discord.
It is little wonder the public is exhausted and wondering when it will end.
What are the odds of us seeing meaningful change when the state legislature and Congress reconvene in January? Those odds do not seem great.
At least, not without our collective resolve to get ready and commit to intervene and insist on the changes we desire.
More and more, the public is finding it difficult to determine what to believe, how to sort facts and truths from the lies, distortions, misinformation and disinformation that seem to rule the day.
Many of us are feeling drained, overwhelmed, discouraged, and exhausted by it all.
We cannot afford to become overwhelmed by the never-ending negative dialogue, actions and other forces that seem to dominate the political, economic, and social environment.
Rest assured lawmakers are already drafting bills and legislation to hit the ground running in January. Lawmakers in Missouri can begin prefiling bills on December 1. The incoming Congress has also choreographed what their agenda will be.
In addition to following lawmakers activities in Missouri and Washington, how do we personally become battle ready to take on those elected officials who persist in doing their will and not that of the people?
Many of us go through extraordinary measures to avoid any discussion about politics during Thanksgiving and holiday festivities.
Our discussions need not become uncomfortable, difficult, discordant or disruptive.
First, we need to pause, think about and discuss with family and friends how we can remain hopeful about the future of our country and the quality of our lives as we navigate the current storms.
We can take time to recall and remember better, more hopeful times.
We can revisit our favorite family games and memories, or our favorite books, readings, music, television programming, to remind us of those things that are important to our mental, emotional and physical well-being.
More importantly, we can recognize and be reminded of how we cannot take them for granted.
We can find comfort in knowing that we have overcome many challenges, politically, professionally and personally in the past. We can find strength and resolve in knowing that we will get through these challenging times, too.
Thanksgiving is just the beginning of our most treasured holiday season, culminating with the celebration of a new year.
With the new year, a new state legislature and new congress will be sworn in, taking oaths to make life better for the constituents they represent in our state and nation as a whole.
Let us take this holiday season, amid the festivities, to get ready to discharge our patriotic duties as we prepare to work with our state legislators and members of Congress..
There is no better time to get in our best state of readiness than beginning with Thanksgiving, remembering why and how we are able to celebrate, and continuing that mindset throughout the holiday season.
Rest assured, elected officials are using this holiday season, amid the festivities, to gear up for the policy and legislative initiatives they want to advance in the year ahead.
So should we.

title: ‘Invaluable’ crisis intervention services reduce burdens on Oklahoma first responders
description: Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide and mental health crises.
