text:
COPES case manager Andrea Potter, left, and crisis therapist Anthea Miller visit a client, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide and mental health crises. If you or someone you know needs help, call or text 988, the U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline, or access online chat at 988lifeline.org.  
TULSA, Okla. — Living in a cluttered Tulsa hotel room, an Oklahoma woman struggling with feelings of hopelessness called an emergency health crisis line seeking help. 
The woman, who mental health professionals knew had a history of suicide attempts, substance use and hallucinations, had lost access to her healthcare provider and needed help being reconnected to her doctor and support system. 
But rather than sending a police officer, social worker and crisis therapist Anthea Miller and her colleague, case manager Andrea Potter, were dispatched to her hotel room. 
The two Community Outreach Psychiatric Emergency Services employees spent an hour assessing the woman’s mental health while listening to her speak at length about past traumas, health- and career-related issues, a pervasive feeling of hopelessness and an unwillingness to live. 

This is the third of a three-part series on Oklahoma’s certified community behavioral health clinics.

At the end of the visit, Miller told the woman that someone with her team would return to check on her. 
Being present is huge in a crisis and can put someone at ease, even in moments of trauma, she said. 
“We try to keep things conversational,” Miller said. “She was willing to work on a safety plan but if the intent to harm herself was there, we would have worked on an inpatient assessment.” 
Community Outreach Psychiatric Emergency Services, better known as COPES, serves the Tulsa area and is one in a statewide network of mental health crisis mobile response units operated by Oklahoma’s certified community behavioral health clinics.
COPES case manager Andrea Potter drives to visit a client, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
The crisis units, which respond for free, are designed to allow trained professionals to tackle mental health needs. This frees up law enforcement to focus on their communities’ more pressing public safety needs, allows others with more specialized mental health training to respond and alleviates strains on emergency rooms, hospitals and jails. 
Last year, employees of these mobile crisis units operated by certified community behavioral health centerswere also dispatched to the vast majority of the tens of thousands of calls made to Oklahoma’s 988 mental health crisis helpline, including in rural areas of the state.
‘Invaluable’
Tulsa Police Capt. Malcolm Williams, who oversees the department’s mental health unit, said he can’t imagine what his job would look like without the “invaluable” COPES partnership.
COPES clinicians help people connect to services and make follow-up appointments, freeing up officers from responding to noncriminal calls, Williams said. 
The program also keeps more people out of the criminal justice system and results in fewer unnecessary hospital visits, he said. 
“The big thing for us is that it has allowed officers to get back in service quicker, which means that we’re not tying up resources on a call for maybe an hour or two,” he said.
Emily Farmer speaks about the COPES program at Family & Children’s Services, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
Between October 2025 and the end of September 2026, COPES’ partnership with 911 diverted more than 5,100 mental health-related calls away from first responders, saving Tulsa-area emergency personnel over 10,100 hours during that year, according to a report from the Tulsa Police Department. 
Emily Farmer, senior program director for COPES, said she’s been with the program since 2017 when she started out helping with calls focused on children. 
COPES, which has a team of about 80 employees that specifically serve the Tulsa area, is also a field response team for the 988 suicide and crisis hotline and works with local first responders such as the Tulsa Police and Fire departments to embed clinicians to handle some mental health-related 911 calls. It also operates its own direct hotline for Tulsa-area calls. 
On average, COPES alone receives about 7,000 calls a month on its direct hotline. Employees make about 3,000 follow-up phone calls a month, Farmer said. During the last budget year, COPES worked 17,500 cases with adults and 2,700 with children. 
Crisis calls do not always mean someone is actively suicidal. 
“I could answer the phone, and it could be someone who’s saying, ‘Everything’s fine, I just need to know how to get connected with mental health help.’ Or ‘I’m not suicidal, but I really am struggling, so can you just talk to me for a moment?’ All the way up to someone on the phone who’s imminently suicidal,” Farmer said.
Tulsa and the surrounding communities are safer because of the crisis intervention program and its partnerships with first responders, Farmer said. 
“We’re able to make sure that the right person is there to provide the right response at the right time, that our law enforcement resources aren’t tied up dealing with mental health,” she said. “And that also means that our community is safer because the experts are dealing with mental health crises.”
‘Somebody stepped in and helped’: Advocates press to keep Oklahoma’s mental healthcare ‘safety net’

A federal model 
For nearly a decade, the programs operated by certified community behavioral health clinics have served as a lifeline for hundreds of thousands of Oklahomans who need access to mental health or substance use treatment. 
The federally designed model, which among other things requires community behavioral health providers to offer 24-hour crisis intervention services, now plays an integral role in addressing Oklahoma’s mental health crisis. The state has some of the nation’s highest rates of mental illness, substance misuse and suicide. 
From Oklahoma’s selection for the pilot program in 2017 through most of 2025, the federal government paid for around 90% of the operating costs to help get the healthcare model off the ground. But when the pilot period ended, states saw that reimbursement rate shrink to 67%, leaving providers and local and state officials with an increased bill to the tune of tens of millions of dollars. 
Certified community behavioral health clinics must provide care regardless of an individual’s ability to pay, and until about a year ago, the state helped cover the cost of some uncompensated care. That support abruptly dried up, creating uncertainty about the long-term viability of these statewide services. 
COPES crisis therapist Anthea Miller speaks to a client at Family & Children’s Services, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)COPES case manager Andrea Potter drives to visit a client, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)COPES case manager Andrea Potter, left, and crisis therapist Anthea Miller visit a client, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)COPES case manager Andrea Potter talks to a client during a field visit, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)COPES crisis therapist Anthea Miller listens to a client during a field visit, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)COPES magnets on a filing cabinet at Family & Children’s Services, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)A view of COPES at Family & Children’s Services, Wednesday, June 10, 2026, in Tulsa. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
Crisis intervention
Across the state, each certified community behavioral health clinics’ mobile response team partners with the state’s 988 crisis help line, said Maria Chaverri, a spokesperson with the Mental Health Department.
During the 2026 budget year, there were 50,755 calls to 988 in Oklahoma, she said. Oklahoma’s 988 line launched in July 2022. 
More than 80% of the 4,800 calls requiring a mobile response are answered by the teams associated with Oklahoma’s certified community behavioral health clinics. 
Oklahoma City Police Lt. Tim Land leads his department’s crisis intervention team, which he said has been around since the early 2000s. 
Before the certified community behavioral health clinics, the Oklahoma City police were the ones responding to mental health calls, he said. 
“It’s night and day, almost, from when I started to what we have now with all the resources and all the people that can come out and help,” Land said. “I think that helps keep people from being involved in the justice system.”
He said the partnerships with local certified community behavioral health clinics make the process more “seamless” and help people get services much faster. 
“Now we’re just a resource and now we are assisting the (clinics),” Land said. “And the people that are going out are mainly for public safety, and sometimes if it’s an involuntary treatment-type thing, we may need to be used to intervene in that.” 
Oklahoma Voice is part of the Mental Health Parity Collaborative, a group of newsrooms that are covering stories on mental health care access and inequities in the U.S. The partners on this project include The Carter Center and newsrooms in select states across the country.

title: Commentary: Want Oklahoma kids to read better? Give their teachers a trained coach.
description: At a literacy training in Oklahoma City this summer, I realized that for the last 10 years I’d been teaching a key reading skill the wrong way.  Our curriculum called for 15 minutes a day of phonological awareness drills, where kids practice breaking words into their component sounds. But our instructor said the exercise should […]
text:
An elementary school teacher shows cards she uses to teach reading comprehension in Tulsa on April 9, 2024. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)At a literacy training in Oklahoma City this summer, I realized that for the last 10 years I’d been teaching a key reading skill the wrong way. 
Our curriculum called for 15 minutes a day of phonological awareness drills, where kids practice breaking words into their component sounds. But our instructor said the exercise should take only three to five minutes.
It was a revelation because I’d been stretching this out for 15 minutes, and my students had been looking at me like I was crazy. It was one of many light-bulb moments where a familiar practice suddenly clicked and made more sense.
This year, my school, the Academy of Okmulgee, is one of 10 in the state participating in the Oklahoma Literacy Initiative, a pilot run by the Oklahoma State Chamber Research Foundation that trains and supports reading coaches who work in their own schools. 
The stakes are high. Just 23% of our state’s fourth graders read proficiently, according to the latest National Assessment of Educational Progress. And starting next school year, third graders who score below basic on the state reading test and fail a second screening will be held back unless they fall under a narrow set of good-cause exemptions. 
I’ve always been passionate about helping kids become strong readers. I once set up my 3-month-old daughter in a pack and play next to me in the school gym so I could attend a science of reading workshop. 
So, last year, when my school’s leaders asked me to become a literacy coach, I jumped at the chance. Our trainers were passionate literacy experts who showed us how each idea connects to how students learn to read. This wasn’t a check-the-box training where you take a quiz and get your certificate in the mail. This was valuable work that felt urgent. 
What has happened since the training is just as important. 
Back at my school, I’m bringing new strategies and a sense of urgency into my real-time coaching with teachers. 
Last week, I sat in on a lesson where a teacher showed students how to form a lowercase f, but not quite the right way. 
“Do you think we should start at the top and go around and down?” I asked. 
She agreed, and we corrected it on the spot. I told her I’d made the same mistake early in my career, but I didn’t have a coach to show me the right way. 
What could have been a tense moment wasn’t because I’ve taught alongside these teachers for years. They know I’m not there to judge. I’m there to help them figure out what to try next. And if I don’t have the answer, I have a coach, too: a literacy expert who visits our school twice a month to help me solve problems and give extra support to teachers who need it. 
The Oklahoma Literacy Initiative approach works because it skips the shame.
I never say, “You’ve been doing it wrong this whole time.” Instead, I say, “I see the work you’re putting in, but we can do better.” 
That kind of grace matters because it’s hard for teachers to admit what we don’t know. Many of us went through college and certification programs and still felt unprepared for the challenges we faced in the classroom. Only one of my professors talked about phonics and the science behind it.
Now teachers stop me in the hallway with questions so often that I carry a notebook with me to keep track. 
My colleagues feel comfortable asking for help. To me, that’s a huge victory. And we get to figure it out together. 
This fall, when the test results came back, I helped teachers pinpoint which phonics skills students were struggling with so they could target interventions during small-group time. 
Our students are already feeling the difference. Recently, a second grader who lacked confidence in reading sounded out a word on his own after three days of practice. He looked so proud that I still get chills. 
That’s the kind of progress I want to build on. We would never teach a lesson once and assume our students had mastered it. Teachers deserve the same patience and sustained support. Great training is a start, but what changes instruction is having a well-trained coach in the building every day who knows the teachers and knows the kids. 
Right now, 10 Oklahoma schools have this resource. 
Every school should.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Nearly 5K helped by state-funded legal aid program for immigrants, NJ says
description: New Jersey says nearly 5K people received aid from a state-funded legal aid program for immigrants in the last fiscal year.
text:
Elizabeth Detention Center as seen in on July 2, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Nearly 5,000 New Jerseyans got free legal help, guidance navigating deportation hearings, or other assistance from the state’s Office of New Americans in the last fiscal year, according to a state report released Monday.
Some 2,400 low-income residents benefitted from a detention and deportation defense program, which handled roughly 1,500 legal matters on their behalf, while another 2,400 young people got help from a program for unaccompanied minors, which submitted more than 200 state court petitions to enable abused or abandoned kids to remain here legally, the report says.
The aid included securing release for some immigrants from the state’s two detention facilities in Newark and Elizabeth, the state says.
The findings come less than two weeks after Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, announced the allocation of more than $20 million in state funding for pro-bono legal services for immigrants facing deportation or detention, more than double the amount New Jersey committed to this work between July 2025 and June 2026, the fiscal year covered by the report.
NJ distributes $20M for legal aid for immigrants facing deportation, detention

Sherrill said the additional investment was needed, given the Trump administration’s deportation effort.
“Given the gravity of the situation, no detained member of our state should be left to fight removal without a lawyer by their side,” Lori Nessel, a Seton Hall University law professor and director of its immigrant rights clinic, said in a statement from the Sherrill administration.
Seton Hall received grants to expand its existing work with the Office of New Americans. Funding for a similar law clinic at Rutgers University nearly doubled, officials said, and other groups, like the New Jersey Office of the Public Defender and Catholic Charities in Newark, got money for the first time. In all, ten organizations got state support.
Alexandra Gonçalves Peña, legal director for the American Friends Service Committee, an immigrant advocacy group that has long done this work, also welcomed the increased investment.
“Bringing more partners into this vital statewide effort builds on that strong foundation. It means more attorneys to increase access to justice, fewer families who must face the threat of deportation alone, and a stronger, collaborative statewide network of defense,” Gonçalves Peña said in the statement.

name: WyoFile
title: Nonpartisan government jobs should be open to anyone, despite what the Freedom Caucus says
description:
Republican hardliners the state’s hiring policies should only reward "real" Republicans, columnist Kerry Drake writes.
The post Nonpartisan government jobs should be open to anyone, despite what the Freedom Caucus says appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

In the runup to November’s election, Wyoming’s far right did everything it could to discredit Eric Barlow and Robert Short, two candidates who don’t conform to the rigid ideology that GOP hardliners demand. Voters didn’t care, electing both men by huge margins.
Now many politicians who opposed the campaigns of Gov.-elect Barlow and Secretary of State-elect Short are up in arms because they had the temerity to appoint key members of their offices who have [insert gasp here] made donations to Democrats.
This has exposed a fundamental flaw in the extremist Freedom Caucus’ view of how state government’s nonpartisan positions work, as well as a major reason why voters soundly rejected their leadership only two years after giving them control of the House.
I gave the caucus too much credit for understanding why most of its members were given the boot in August, only because it seemed so obvious. If a small faction of a political party rabidly believes only people who hold their same beliefs are fit to govern — and everyone else is unworthy of performing public service jobs — why would any electorate keep them in power?
It’s an arrogant view that defines the petty partisan politics preached by the caucus members and aptly demonstrates why it should be dismissed as sour grapes, not legitimate grievances that merit attention.
Why is the Freedom Caucus arguing that there’s something wrong with the concept of elected leaders selecting the person they believe is best qualified to do a job, regardless of political ideology? Or that whose political campaign someone contributes to should even be a factor when assessing their qualifications?
Voters rejected most House Freedom Caucus members’ reelection bids, nixed their attempts to move to the Senate and rebuffed their efforts to gain statewide office. They loudly said no to the idea that the party has a right to impose litmus tests on candidates and, if they fail, ridicule them as “RINOs,” or Republicans in name only. Barlow and Short each earned a whopping 68% of the vote in November, a clear sign that voters weren’t as obsessed with ideological purity.
In expressing his outrage that Barlow picked a lifelong Democrat as the state’s attorney general, former House Speaker Chip Neiman, R-Hulett, a Freedom Caucus leader who lost his Senate bid in the August GOP primary, penned a guest column for the Open Range Record calling for the Wyoming Senate to reject the nomination of Walter Eggers. 
It’s a treatise on a theme Neiman and like-minded Republicans unsuccessfully trotted out for over a year: Barlow supposedly isn’t conservative enough to be Wyoming’s governor.
But they couldn’t defeat him. Their only means to attack him now is to try to keep Barlow from appointing people he believes are critical to the success of his administration.
I agree with only one thing Neiman wrote: People should pay close attention to state senators’ confirmation votes on Eggers. Don’t allow these proceedings to degenerate into partisan attacks on the integrity and character of the governor and his nominee.
Eggers has represented oil, gas, coal and trona industries in Wyoming for nearly a quarter-century. For Neiman to dismiss his solid record as “generic experience in energy law” is an insult that should not be allowed to stand. It is beyond pathetic.
There’s a good reason why the Legislature has repeatedly rejected bills — including ones sponsored by Neiman — to make the attorney general an elected official.
In the Cornell Law Review, attorney Marissa A. Smith articulated it well: “While this partisanship may garner national attention and party approval for state attorneys general, it comes at the expense of their states and constituents, particularly those constituents that fall outside their voter block.”
Both Republican and Democratic governors have appointed AGs from outside their own parties in Wyoming. Democratic Gov. Mike Sullivan chose the GOP’s Joseph Meyer, who served for both of his terms. Republican Gov. Matt Mead appointed former Democratic legislator Greg Phillips, who is now a judge in the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals.
Both men served Wyoming honorably, and are prime examples of why Neiman’s preemptive criticism of Eggers is merely partisan posturing by a man totally out of touch with his former constituents. 
And it’s important to remember that lawyers are ethically bound to represent the interests of their client — the state of Wyoming, in this case — and not their own. Attorneys often advocate for positions they might personally disagree with, but that’s the point. Their job is to make the case for their client, not on behalf of their own political beliefs.
The attacks on Short’s appointment of a registered Republican, Cara Boyle Chambers, to serve as deputy secretary of state appear to be based solely on donations the attorney made to Democratic candidates. Her critics completely ignore her record of accomplishments since she graduated from the University of Wyoming Law School in 2005.
Chambers has served as director of the Wyoming Attorney General’s Division of Victim Services, and chair of Gov. Mark Gordon’s Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons Task Force. She’s also worked on task forces dedicated to combatting human trafficking and reviewing maternal mortality factors.
Wyoming will benefit from her leadership and diverse experience.
The Freedom Caucus seriously wants Wyomingites to believe Chambers isn’t qualified to serve in Short’s office based on her donations to former President Joe Biden, former Maine U.S. Senate candidate Graham Platner and Britney Tennant of Cheyenne.
Criticism of that last contribution is particularly telling and indicative of just how low some Republicans will go to track members’ alleged disloyalty to claim she doesn’t deserve the job. Tennant, who won the House District 11 seat, is one of only seven Democrats in the 62-member House.
Are they so threatened by the idea that state government might include people with political beliefs that aren’t their own? Do they really believe that Democrats can’t hold nonpartisan positions in state government? 
There’s an inherent threat to all members of the Wyoming GOP in these mind games. What better way is there to discourage donations to any candidate should they be judged for some unforeseen reason? 
What’s next on their agenda: tracking what books someone checks out of the public library to root out alleged communists applying for nonpartisan jobs? U.S. Sen. Joe McCarthy died years ago, folks, but his disgusting tactics are still practiced.
During his campaign for secretary of state, Short made it clear after he won the GOP primary that he plans to serve the public, not engage in partisan attacks.
“I think that Republican voters are tired of vitriol and just talking points,” he told the Torrington Telegram. “They want people who are willing to do the work to get results that matter to the people of Wyoming.”
Short also explained that he will demonstrate his loyalty to Wyoming residents rather than a particular political narrative.
Short’s appointment of Chambers to serve as his deputy speaks volumes about his commitment to do exactly what he promised. 
Barlow’s nomination of Eggers also dramatically shows that he’s not beholden to any party leaders who want to enact a spoils system or limit his ability to make the appointments he believes will benefit the state of Wyoming.
We can’t reward ideologues who want to punish anyone with beliefs outside their own. We just jettisoned some of the worst examples of this type of politician. They will use any means they can to drag us down that path again. It would be pure folly to give them that opportunity.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Federal official highlights Idaho’s success in increasing foster home-to-child ratio
description: Idaho’s former state health director, now a federal official in the Trump administration, is highlighting Idaho’s success in increasing the ratio of foster families to foster children to kindle “healthy competition” among state child welfare programs.  Federal Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex Adams traveled to Boise on Monday[...]
text:
Assistant Secretary at the Administration for Children and Families Alex Adams speaks to a group of state, local and nonprofit officials about Idaho's success in improving the ratio of foster children to foster families on Nov. 23, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido / Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s former state health director, now a federal official in the Trump administration, is highlighting Idaho’s success in increasing the ratio of foster families to foster children to kindle “healthy competition” among state child welfare programs. 
Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Alex Adams joins state officials and business leaders to announce the Idaho State Park Foster Family Passport at Lucky Peak State Park, in this file photo. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
Federal Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex Adams traveled to Boise on Monday to meet with state, local and nonprofit officials to discuss the Gem State’s changes to the foster care system and announce a federal competition among the states. 
“We put out the first incarnation of the scorecard showing each state’s performance on those measures, and perhaps not surprisingly, Idaho is currently in the pole position,” Adams said Monday.
The federal administration’s recently launched child welfare “scorecard” shows certain metrics: foster-home-to-foster-children ratios, family placement (known as kin placement, in which the foster child is placed with a relative) rates, use of congregate care facilities, recent maltreatment case percentages, and disrupted home placement rates. 
As of Monday, Idaho ranked first in its ratio of foster homes per foster child, at 116 homes for every 100 foster children in the system. Data for 27 states was available Monday, and all 50 states would be added by the end of December, Adams said. 
From Oct. 1, 2027, to Sept. 30, 2027, the Administration for Children and Families will host a challenge for state child welfare systems, in which the state with the highest foster-home-to-foster-child ratio will win $3 million from the federal agency, followed by $2 million for the second-highest, and $1 million each for the two states with the most improved ratios.
“When we announced this competition, it was really that we wanted healthy competition across state lines for the betterment of child welfare outcomes,” Adams said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho’s foster ratio increased substantially statewide. Some regions still lack enough foster homes. 

Before Adams was tapped for his federal post within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, he served as director of Idaho’s state Department of Health and Welfare for just over a year. 
At the time, he highlighted a major focus on ensuring that there was at least one foster home available for every foster child entering the system. The Legislature in 2025 approved an additional $23 million to the state agency for child welfare changes, including an increased focus on prevention and recruitment and retention of foster parents. 
The state has improved its ratio statewide, but in some regions more than others. In Boise County, the ratio is more than seven homes available for every one foster child, according to the federal scorecard. Latah County has about three homes available for every foster child. In several other counties, there are fewer homes available than there are foster children. 
Nez Perce County has an estimated ratio of about .71 homes-to-children, or 71 homes for every 100 foster children. Bonneville County’s ratio is around .88. Several rural Idaho counties had lower ratios. 
 Adams: Foster scorecard metrics meant to show a ‘balance’ 

Idaho health officials have sought to improve Idaho’s ratio by tackling both sides of the equation — increasing the number of foster families who get licensed and stay, as well as decreasing the number of children who enter the system. 
Adams said that the required reporting of recent maltreatment cases is meant to show that states aren’t improving one metric at the cost of child safety. 
“We picked these five measures as a delicate balance to demonstrate whether or not states are doing it the right way,” Adams said in an interview. 
Jean Fisher, administrator of Youth Safety & Permanency at the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (Courtesy of Right on Crime)
On Monday, officials highlighted that 25% of children who are referred to the department are served through prevention case plans. These cases may involve providing the family with services to keep the child safely in their home to prevent removal. 
Jean Fisher, administrator for the Division of Youth Safety and Permanency, said the agency has tried to promote prevention services when possible, including working with schools to learn when services may be more appropriate than a call to Child Protective Services. 
“Not everything is abuse and neglect,” Fisher said in an interview. “… it could be mental illness. We’ve got a family struggling for food. We’ve got families trying to find shelter. That doesn’t mean that they don’t love and support their children. They need support in a different way, and they don’t belong in the system.” 
Idaho foster child advocates concerned abuse is worsening amid policy and law changes 

Advocates for children in the Idaho foster care system have previously raised alarms that some prevention policies may be leaving some children in more dangerous situations for longer, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
Volunteers called court-appointed special advocates, or CASAs, who advocate for children in the welfare system said that abuse rates weren’t increasing, but the severity of that abuse seemed to be. The advocates named a number of potential factors contributing to this, including an increased focus on prevention as well as a court decision that limited Idaho law enforcement’s role in removing children without a warrant. 
The agency – which cannot remove children or make final placement decisions but makes recommendations to the courts – has implemented a new system to try and reach a resolution on cases quicker. 
Fisher said the agency has worked with courts to share case information to show if a family shows “poor performance” indicators for being successfully reunified, or “early reunification” indicators, to help determine an outcome more quickly. 
“The courts make those decisions,” Fisher said. “And so what I think really is helpful, especially with this new tool, is that it’s giving the court the information. It’s giving us the information, and we do our job by giving it to them and then letting them decide what to do.”

title: Alabama lawmakers plan bills regulating license plate readers in coming session
description: State lawmakers plan to file legislation addressing privacy concerns over license plate readers in the coming legislative session. Both Rep. Ron Bolton, R-Northport, and Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, said their bills will place time limits on data collected by plate readers; require audits of the database that tracks vehicle information and establish penalties[...]
text:
Flock Safety license plate readers are typically mounted on tall poles, with a camera and solar panel on top. Alabama lawmakers plan to file bills in the coming session to address privacy concerns over the cameras while allowing law enforcement to use the technology in an appropriate manner. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)State lawmakers plan to file legislation addressing privacy concerns over license plate readers in the coming legislative session.
Both Rep. Ron Bolton, R-Northport, and Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, said their bills will place time limits on data collected by plate readers; require audits of the database that tracks vehicle information and establish penalties for officers who abuse their authority when they obtain information.
“We have got to protect people’s rights, but also we are using the tools that are available for law enforcement to solve crimes,” Bolton said in an interview Wednesday. “I have got an ever-increasing list of things that have been solved, very important things.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Flock, an Atlanta-based company that manufactures license plate readers, said in a statement Wednesday that the technology provides an important tool to address public safety and signaled it would support regulations.
“We support thoughtful legislation and strong privacy, transparency, and accountability guardrails that ensure technology is used responsibly while preserving law enforcement’s ability to use effective tools to keep people safe,” the company said.
License plate readers capture an image of a vehicle’s license plate, then convert it to text. The system can then record the plate number of the vehicle as well as the date and location.
Privacy advocates have become increasingly concerned as the technology’s capabilities expand to allow it to retain vehicles’ location histories. That information can then be used to trace where people have been.
Several law enforcement officers have been charged with using data obtained by license plate readers to surveil current and former romantic partners. The system has also misidentified people. In Wisconsin, a person was pulled over at gunpoint after the camera flagged the vehicle in a homicide case. Milwaukee police said the incident was caused by an employee who failed to remove an alert on the vehicle and was not because of the system.
Bolton and Orr said they proposed the legislation to address some of the concerns.
“It really allows law enforcement to use the technology in a very narrow manner, and it doesn’t inhibit them from doing their job,” Orr said in an interview Wednesday.
The bills are still being finalized, but both legislators said the bills would include sanctions for law enforcement officers who abuse the system.
“There are going to be levels of criminal offenses depending on the severity of the violation,” Bolton said.
Both bills will also require audits of the system periodically, but neither Bolton nor Orr outlined who would perform the audits or the process. Orr said law enforcement officials would need authorization from a court before using the system, unless the situation is urgent.
“You would have to have a judicial warrant,” Orr said. “If you are coming from out of state, let’s say Mississippi, and you want to access our cameras in Alabama, you would need a warrant, domesticated by an Alabama judge.”
Both bills also limit the time the system retains license plate data before automatically deleting it. Bolton said he is still speaking with people to determine the appropriate timeframe. Orr said his bill allows the data to be retained between one to three months.
For their part, law enforcement said they are willing to accept regulations imposed by lawmakers.
“We have no issues with regulation, creating better regulation, creating more rules, or even holding the data,” said Michael Moore, president of the Alabama Association of Chiefs of Police and chief of the Enterprise Police Department, in an interview Wednesday. “We completely understand that. There has got to be a legitimate length that assists us on both sides.”
Moore said he believes that having access to the data for 90 days would be reasonable. The data could then be retained for two years but would require a court order or warrant to be able to access the information.
Many of the elements proposed by Bolton and Orr are part of the recommendations from the Institute for Justice, a nonpartisan, libertarian-leaning public interest law firm. The firm is representing residents in two federal lawsuits who are challenging the use of license plate readers.
The organization advocates time limits for keeping the data, requiring police to obtain a warrant or receive permission from the court for access, and ensure a record is created each time a person reviews information.
“At the end of the day, the Fourth Amendment is the balance,” said Robert Frommer, senior attorney for the Institute for Justice, in an interview Tuesday. “The idea is that we do not want officers in the field to have this roving power. And we want to maintain a degree of privacy and security that people had at the time of the founding.”

title: Tennessee House Republicans stick with top leaders
description: The Tennessee House Republican Caucus is maintaining the status quo, selecting the current speaker and GOP leader to continue heading up the state House in 2027.  The 69-member caucus, which holds a supermajority in the House despite six losses to Democrats in the November election, unanimously nominated House Speaker Cameron Sexton of Crossville to continue[...]
text:
Republican Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton, left, and Republican House Majority Leader William Lambert, right, during the 2026 legislative session. (Photo: John Partipilo/ Tennessee Lookout)The Tennessee House Republican Caucus is maintaining the status quo, selecting the current speaker and GOP leader to continue heading up the state House in 2027. 
The 69-member caucus, which holds a supermajority in the House despite six losses to Democrats in the November election, unanimously nominated House Speaker Cameron Sexton of Crossville to continue as the chamber’s leader in the next two-year session, according to a caucus release. The entire 99-member House will vote on his nomination when the legislature convenes Jan. 12.
Entering a fourth two-year term as speaker, Sexton said the state has made “great progress” in several areas, though he didn’t specify those in a caucus press release.
Under Sexton’s leadership, the state created a new private-school voucher program and expanded it this year after he initially opposed a limited voucher plan for low-income children in Memphis and Nashville. The two programs cost about $310 million. 
The legislature also passed a “truth-in-sentencing” law at Sexton’s direction that requires people convicted of certain crimes to serve 85-100% of their terms. In addition, Sexton supported a constitutional amendment giving judges discretion to decline bail for people charged with felonies for which they would have to serve at least 85% of the sentence. The measure passed by a 67-33% margin in the early November election. Previously, judges could refuse to set bail only for capital offenses of first-degree murder and child rape.
Republicans also voted unanimously for Rep. William Lamberth of Portland to continue serving as House majority leader in the coming session. 
With the retirement of Rep. Jeremy Faison, the caucus chose Rep. Tim Hicks of Gray as caucus chairman, putting him in charge of Republican campaigns in the state’s 99 districts.
The caucus chose Rep. Clark Boyd of Lebanon as majority whip, a post that ensures members vote in line with the caucus, and Rep. Pat Marsh of Shelbyville as speaker pro tempore.
Rep. Mark Cochran of Englewood was selected to a third term as assistant majority leader; Rep. Paul Sherrell of Sparta as floor leader; Rep. Kip Capley of Summertown as caucus vice chair; Rep. Fred Atchley of Sevierville as secretary; Rep. Rebecca Alexander of Jonesborough as treasurer and Rep. Noah Smith of Jacksboro as assistant floor leader.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Commentary: A lawsuit led to Meta’s child safety standards. YouTube, TikTok and Snapchat should match them.
description: As parents, we do everything we can to protect our children. We teach them right from wrong, warn them about dangers and prepare them for a world that isn’t always safe. But raising children in today’s digital world presents challenges previous generations never faced. Technology offers extraordinary opportunities to learn, communicate and connect. Unfortuna[...]
text:
The parent company of Instagram and Facebook agreed to settle a nationwide lawsuit by paying up to $17.1 billion and implementing safety features on its platforms to protect children. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)As parents, we do everything we can to protect our children.
We teach them right from wrong, warn them about dangers and prepare them for a world that isn’t always safe.
But raising children in today’s digital world presents challenges previous generations never faced.
Technology offers extraordinary opportunities to learn, communicate and connect.
Unfortunately, it also exposes children to harmful content, online predators, cyberbullying and potentially addictive algorithms, often with little warning.
For years, parents have demanded stronger safeguards, greater transparency and meaningful tools to protect their children.
Now, we’re beginning to see what accountability can look like.
This summer, South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson helped secure a historic multi-state settlement with Meta alongside a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general, valued at up to $17.1 billion.
SC to receive upwards of $247M in Meta settlement over child safety on social media

South Carolina alone is expected to receive nearly $247 million.
Wilson deserves thanks for his work alongside attorneys general across the country to hold powerful technology companies accountable.
Their collective effort demonstrates what can happen when state leaders prioritize children’s online safety.
But the agreement’s significance extends beyond its financial terms.
Meta must implement daily screen-time limits, mandatory breaks from endless scrolling, overnight access restrictions, stronger age verification and expanded parental controls.
Additional safeguards address bullying, sextortion, eating disorder content and material promoting suicide or self-harm. Notifications will also be restricted during school hours.
Most importantly, these are enforceable requirements, not voluntary promises.
But protecting children on two platforms does not solve an industry-wide problem.
According to Pew Research Center survey in 2024, 90% of American teenagers used YouTube, 63% used TikTok and 55% used Snapchat.
Roughly one in six reports using YouTube or TikTok almost constantly.
Our children move between platforms throughout the day, often encountering similar content, engagement-driven algorithms and risks. What good does limiting harmful exposure on one platform accomplish if a child can simply move to another with fewer safeguards?
The Meta settlement must be a starting point, not the finish line.
If these safeguards are necessary to protect children using Instagram and Facebook, then children using YouTube, TikTok and Snapchat deserve comparable protections.
A coalition of more than 90 child-safety advocates has called on these companies to adopt similar measures.
Their message is simple: protecting young users should not depend on which company runs the platform.
Where voluntary safeguards fall short, state attorneys general should continue examining whether enforcement action is necessary.
But meaningful reform cannot stop at individual platforms.
We must also address how children gain access to applications.
The proposed federal App Store Accountability Act would require app stores to verify users’ age categories and obtain parental consent before minors download applications.
Why the App Store Accountability Act is a child safety imperative

The bill advanced through the House Energy and Commerce Committee in March but has not yet received a vote on the House floor.
The legislation extends beyond social media to gaming services such as Roblox, artificial intelligence applications and other digital products children may access.
These risks are not confined to social media feeds. They exist in private messaging, gaming communities, AI interactions and applications parents may not even realize their children are using.
The App Store Accountability Act and Meta settlement address two distinct concerns: parental involvement before an app is downloaded and safeguards once children begin using it.
Together, they could establish a more comprehensive framework for online child safety.
Parental responsibility and corporate accountability are not competing ideas. They must work together.
As a mother, I firmly believe parents have both the right and responsibility to guide their children’s digital lives through conversations, boundaries and education.
But in an ever-changing digital world, it is nearly impossible for parents to understand every platform, monitor every interaction or anticipate every risk.
We need meaningful tools, accurate information and safeguards that support our ability to protect our children while respecting privacy and parental authority.
No legislation or corporate policy can replace parental involvement.
But parental involvement should not excuse technology companies from accountability. We should not have to choose between allowing our children to benefit from technology and protecting them from preventable harm.
The goal is not to eliminate technology from their lives, but to create an environment where they can learn, communicate and explore more safely.
Attorney General Wilson and his fellow attorneys general have taken an important step toward that goal.
Now the responsibility extends to the rest of the technology industry and Congress.
YouTube, TikTok and Snapchat should adopt comparable protections, and Congress should seriously consider the App Store Accountability Act as part of a broader approach to parental oversight.
As a mother and co-founder of S.C. Family First, I believe protecting the next generation requires more than promises.
It requires education, parental involvement, responsible legislation, corporate accountability and governing with our next generation in mind.
South Carolina has demonstrated what is possible when protecting children becomes a priority.
Now we must build on that progress.
Our children’s safety should not depend on which app they open, which company owns it or whether their parents can keep up with the latest technology.
The standard has been established. It’s time for the rest of Big Tech to follow.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: What’s the price of the government? Nobody really knows, analysis shows
description: According to the state constitution, the only law they must pass is the budget. And a lot of the laws, whether it be improving the public school formula or cutting taxes again, can cost money.
text:
The West Virginia state Capitol in fall 2021. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)In January, the West Virginia Legislature will convene for 60 days to pass laws. 
According to the state constitution, the only law they must pass is the budget. And a lot of the laws, whether it be improving the public school formula or cutting taxes again, can cost money. 
The West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy has found the system for assigning a price tag to those laws is deficient, resulting in legislators approving measures without really knowing the true costs of them. 
It all comes down to the “fiscal note” — which can be requested for any piece of legislation that spends money. Sean O’Leary, a policy analyst for the center, said while other states have an independent office that handles it, West Virginia is one of just a few where the agency that would implement law formulates the price tag. 
“So when you have an agency that’s responsible for the new program to also estimate its fiscal impact, it creates an opportunity for bias,” O’Leary said. “Not saying that they’re all biased, but it creates an opportunity for that, they can include subjective information in the fiscal note instead of just the objective costs.” 
Del. John Williams, D-Monongalia, served eight years on the House Finance Committee. He said he’s seen agencies tip the scales on fiscal notes first hand. 
“I’ve seen a lot of oversells on implementation, but also undersells too,” he said. “I mean, you don’t know how these conversations come about if they’re told to slant it one way or another to help kill it or help get it through, and that’s the problem,” he said.  
O’Leary’s analysis noted that the Legislature has an office for independently formulating fiscal notes, but they haven’t done so in the last two legislative sessions. 
Bills, as they go through the legislative process, also change. O’Leary said they generally don’t revise the fiscal note as lawmakers add and subtract from legislation. 
“Bills can change dramatically, and the price tag can change dramatically, but the fiscal note is what the fiscal note says, and that’s all the way back to the beginning of the bill process,” O’Leary said. 
The legislative session will begin Jan. 13, 2027.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Kids Count survey shows education levels rising in West Virginia
description: Reading and math skills appear to be rising, according to the latest West Virginia Kids Count Survey.  The annual survey measures the wellbeing of children across the Mountain State, looking at poverty, education and health. As a part of a national survey by the Annie E Casey Foundation, the state survey is performed by the […]
text:
Inside a Kanawha County elementary classroom in West Virginia. (Photo by Lexi Browning/West Virginia Watch)Reading and math skills appear to be rising, according to the latest West Virginia Kids Count Survey. 
The annual survey measures the wellbeing of children across the Mountain State, looking at poverty, education and health. As a part of a national survey by the Annie E Casey Foundation, the state survey is performed by the West Virginia Center on Budget & Policy. 
Sean O’Leary, a policy analyst for the center, said anyone concerned about the welfare of children or the future of the state should take a spin through the report. 
“It’s a reflection of how we’re doing as a state as a whole, and it predicts how we’re going to do in the future,” O’Leary said. “Those who are struggling with poverty, struggling with education, struggling with their parents having difficulty working, having difficulty finding childcare, that all follows them throughout their lives, and we know that.” 
He said big takeaways he saw this year is the dip in educational attainment during the COVID-19 pandemic appears to be rebounding.
“It sort of shows that the dip we saw during COVID was temporary, and we’ve seen the numbers come back up to where they were before COVID,” O’Leary said. “Now they’re still not great, but we’re showing progress, which is good.” 
He also noted that less than 3% of children are without health insurance. But nearly half the children that do have health insurance are on Medicaid, he said.
“Any threat to Medicaid, like these work requirements that are starting Jan. 1 can threaten that number because we know when parents lose health insurance their children usually also lose health insurance even if they’re not the target of the policy,” O’Leary said. 
O’Leary said lawmakers heading into session in January should take a look at the report.
“We ought to take a look at programs, at policies that really improve the lives and outcomes of children and we can use these indicators to determine what those policies might be and how well we’re implementing them,” he said. 
A follow-up report on what it would cost to implement programs that could improve the lives of West Virginia children is forthcoming, O’Leary said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Elissa Slotkin understands the Democratic mandate. Does the rest of her party?
description: U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin gets it. Slotkin appears to understand that the “blue tsunami” that swept through the country on Nov. 3 is, in many ways, like an actual tsunami. Its initial force can be devastating, but eventually, the water recedes. What remains is what those who rode the wave to power intend to do […]
text:
WASHINGTON, DC - DECEMBER 11: Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) walks into the Senate Chamber on December 11, 2025 in Washington, DC. Two opposing health care bills intended to avert rising health care premiums have failed. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin gets it.
Slotkin appears to understand that the “blue tsunami” that swept through the country on Nov. 3 is, in many ways, like an actual tsunami. Its initial force can be devastating, but eventually, the water recedes. What remains is what those who rode the wave to power intend to do with the opportunities it has created.
Having built her political reputation by eking out victories in a politically competitive mid-Michigan congressional district, Slotkin was not necessarily someone many observers expected to emerge as a leading voice for systemic change in the hidebound U.S. Senate. She has often been characterized as a centrist whose political instincts were shaped by the need to win over voters who don’t necessarily even identify as Democrats.
Yet she has increasingly been out front in demonstrating that pragmatism does not have to mean endless rounds of trying to build a consensus with those who view compromise as a dirty word.
Facing new DOJ threats, Slotkin uses anniversary of illegal orders video to decry intimidation 

When Slotkin announced last week that she would support Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s challenge to longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader, she did more than just add her name to a growing call for a new generation of party leadership. She took the extra step of challenging Democratic leaders to explain what they intend to accomplish during the first 100 days of the new Congress. 
As she put it, voters aren’t looking for “small nibbling at the edges.” They want bold policies that put more money in people’s pockets, and they want it fast.
That is a significant and long overdue departure from the political playbook Democrats have followed for much of the past three decades.
For too long, the Democratic Party has occupied a carefully calibrated political center, making incremental changes designed not to inspire those who voted them in, but instead to avoid scaring away voters who might otherwise lean Republican. This so-called Third Way politics popularized during Bill Clinton’s presidency got its name by Democrats triangulating against their political opponents but also what were viewed as the extreme members of their own party. 
But the wave that swept Democrats into power didn’t just wreak havoc on the Republican Party and the MAGA movement. It also swept away, whether its leaders care to admit it or not, the assumption that Democrats must continue to be guided by a political framework developed in the 1990s, before most of the 18 to 29-year-olds that powered the blue tsunami were even born.
The threat matrix facing Democrats now isn’t that they will overreach by pursuing an ambitious legislative agenda. It is that they will fail to respond to the clear mandate for change that voters gave them.
And this is where Slotkin’s background in the intelligence field is particularly useful.
Intelligence analysis is, at its core, about assessing threats and recognizing patterns. By anticipating what comes next and distinguishing between the immediate crisis and the larger strategic picture, that analysis, if used properly, can be used as a map of where the pitfalls are and how to most effectively achieve the objective.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And the objective for Democrats must be to demonstrate that democratic government can actually deliver meaningful improvements in people’s lives.
So instead of looking back 30 years for inspiration, the party might best look back nearly a century to the first 100 days of Franklin D. Roosevelt’s presidency in 1933.
FDR inherited a country in the depths of the Great Depression, with failing financial institutions and mass unemployment. But more importantly, the country had serious doubts about the future of democratic self-government. Whether we want to admit it or not, that is largely where we find ourselves today. But faced with that doubt, FDR didn’t cautiously advance modest reforms, but instead moved with unprecedented urgency, pushing through a series of sweeping legislative and executive actions that fundamentally reshaped the federal government’s relationship to its citizens.
What we know now as The New Deal was not a single legislative achievement, nor was it perfectly executed. Many of its programs were challenged and later had to be revised or even curtailed. But the lesson of those first 100 days was that Roosevelt wasn’t interested in preserving the political status quo. He understood that the mandate from voters was to change it.
Slotkin ‘seriously’ considering presidential bid, says decision could come soon

That is the kind of ambition Democrats should be discussing now, not modest adjustments designed primarily to avoid offending the opposition. And while President Trump will hold the veto pen, making it unlikely much legislation will actually become law, Democrats need to make him use it. 
Ending the undeclared war with Iran, rolling back the incomprehensibly stupid tariff regime, raising the federal minimum wage and unwinding the termination of ACA tax credits should only be the beginning. Making a concrete case for Medicare for All and putting it to a vote has to be a priority. If the votes aren’t there to pass it, then let its opponents, including Sen. Slotkin, be on the record and explain why. But in each of these cases, the excuse that Trump will just veto it can’t be a reason not to try. 
Slotkin’s support for Van Hollen is significant not because the Senate leadership contest will determine the future of the Democratic Party, but because it reflects a larger debate about what the party intends to do with its newfound political power. Her insistence that prospective leaders present a concrete plan for their first 100 days is exactly the kind of demand for accountability that Democrats should be championing.
The political waters will eventually recede. The question is whether Democrats will have built something durable on the ground they gained, or whether they will simply watch the tide go out and wonder where their opportunity went.
Slotkin seems to understand the difference. The rest of her party would be wise to catch up.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas Explained: What to know about the Dec. 1 runoff election
description: Election season in Arkansas is not over just yet. Runoff elections are set for Dec. 1 to determine the winners of dozens of mayoral and city council races in more than 30 counties.  Although Johnson County doesn’t have any runoff elections scheduled, there will be a special election on Dec. 1 for Clarksville voters to […]
text:
Vote here signs along with campaign signs adorn the grounds outside of the Dunbar Recreation Center in Little Rock, Arkansas on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Election season in Arkansas is not over just yet.
Runoff elections are set for Dec. 1 to determine the winners of dozens of mayoral and city council races in more than 30 counties. 
Although Johnson County doesn’t have any runoff elections scheduled, there will be a special election on Dec. 1 for Clarksville voters to consider two ordinances that would authorize a combined $55 billion in bonds for a data center project. 
Early voting begins Tuesday and continues until Nov. 30. The runoff is Dec. 1.
Here’s what you need to know about voting in next month’s runoff elections:
 
Why does Arkansas have runoff elections?
County and municipal races result in a runoff whenever there are more than two candidates and no candidate receives a majority of the votes cast, according to state law. 
The two candidates with the highest number of votes compete in a runoff. If the two candidates tie in a runoff, the county board will determine the winner by lot at a public meeting. “By lot” means a random procedure to break a tie, such as drawing numbers out of a bowl, which is how election officials broke a tie for the Elm Springs mayoral race runoff in November. 
A 2025 law repealed a provision that allowed county and municipal candidates who received 40% of the vote to avoid a runoff if they obtained at least 20% more than the second-place candidate. 
There are no runoff elections for state or federal offices in Arkansas. 
 
Which counties will have runoff elections?
According the secretary of state’s office, 32 counties will hold runoff elections on Dec. 1:  
Arkansas, Ashley, Baxter, Benton, Chicot, Craighead, Crittenden, Cross, Faulkner, Franklin, Hot Spring, Howard, Jackson, Lincoln, Lonoke, Mississippi, Monroe, Ouachita, Phillips, Poinsett, Pope, Pulaski, Randolph, Saline, Scott, Sebastian, St. Francis, Union, Van Buren, Washington, White and Woodruff.
Johnson County’s special election regarding two bond issues for a Clarksville data center project will coincide with the Dec. 1 runoffs. 
 
Can I vote in the runoff if I didn’t vote in the general election?
Yes.
Registered voters are not required to have participated in November’s election to be eligible to vote in the December runoff.
 
When is early voting?
Early voting begins Tuesday and will be available Wednesday, Friday and Monday, Nov. 30. 
According to state law, early voting occurs during the county clerk’s regular office hours. You can contact your local county clerk for details here. 
 
When is the runoff election?
The runoff is Dec. 1 and polls will be open from 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.
You can check your voter registration, view sample ballots and locate polling sites at www.voterview.ar-nova.org.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Commentary: Lung cancer screening deserves attention for asbestos-exposed veterans in Idaho
description: Without a doubt, the strength of the nation’s security is significantly rooted in the courage of citizens who endured the rigors of war zones and the vastness of the sea while fulfilling their commitment to fighting for liberty. In that spirit, the Navy’s birthday offers Idaho and the rest of the country a fitting opportunity […]
text:
Naval Facilities Engineering Command Southwest public works employees inspect containment on a 2013 asbestos abatement project at Naval Base Coronado in California. (Photo by Mario T. Icari/U.S. Navy)Without a doubt, the strength of the nation’s security is significantly rooted in the courage of citizens who endured the rigors of war zones and the vastness of the sea while fulfilling their commitment to fighting for liberty. 
In that spirit, the Navy’s birthday offers Idaho and the rest of the country a fitting opportunity to honor those who answered the call to serve. Yet beyond tribute, this occasion is also an opportunity to remember that some of the profession’s consequences can last long after their retirement, especially for those previously stationed aboard older ships built with asbestos. 
Valued for its heat and corrosion resistance, asbestos became widely used in military applications. It is now known to be a lung cancer risk decades after exposure, raising questions about whether they have adequate access to screening and information about their options.
 Idaho’s asbestos past reaches into military service

Idaho’s connection to military service is embodied in its roughly 121,300 veterans representing generations of Americans whose careers brought them into a range of branches, assignments and workplaces. For many of these retirees, however, their dedication may have also placed them in environments that heavily depended on asbestos. 
Valued for its insulating and fireproofing properties, this natural mineral was extensively incorporated into countless structures and products the Navy relied on, especially in building ships prior to 1983, as well as in shipyards operating from the 1930s to the 1990s. 
With this, it is not surprising that facilities such as the Naval Surface Warfare Center Detachment in Bayview contained asbestos materials. This pervasive presence has cost many lives before science revealed the toxicity of asbestos. Those exposed have become susceptible to lung cancer and other debilitating diseases even decades later. 
Consistent with this, an interactive map indicates that just between 1999 and 2017, nearly 1,500 Idahoans have already succumbed to asbestos-associated illnesses, with 1,068 residents impacted by lung cancer and 267 and 161 more individuals lost to mesothelioma and asbestosis, respectively. 
The reality is stark. The toll of this crisis is profound, and lung cancer accounts for the largest share of the deaths — surpassing both mesothelioma and asbestosis. 
 Veterans’ lung cancer screening must consider more than smoking history

In practice, smoking has long been recognized as the leading cause of lung cancer — making this history a critical part of determining who may benefit from routine tests. 
Yet it is not the only established root of the disease, as asbestos is also a notorious carcinogen that can increase malignancy risk. And that distinction is particularly relevant for veterans whose military service typically involved exposure to such a harmful mineral. 
Even so, the current screening framework continues to place its emphasis on tobacco use, with the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force only recommending annual low-dose CT screening for adults ages 50 to 80. The guidelines also underscored that patients must have accumulated 20 pack-years of smoking and still smoke or have quit within the past 15 years to receive an A or B grade — categories that may facilitate preventive measures without compelling out-of-pocket payments. 
By these same criteria, a veteran with prolonged asbestos contact but no qualifying smoking record may not be eligible for the screening despite the fact of asbestos toxicity. 
Acknowledging this doesn’t mean that smoking should be disregarded, but it changes perspective about how a veteran’s complete service and health history is understood when lung cancer risk is assessed. 
Simply put, a sailor who spent years around asbestos, for example, may carry an alarming occupational exposure even without ever having smoked. 
Conversely, those who both smoked and encountered asbestos may face an even greater combined risk — bringing both narratives together as part of a broader conversation about veterans’ health and well-being.
That said, as we honor the men and women who devoted part of their lives to safeguarding the country, it is also an appropriate moment to remember the environments where they have lived and worked for an extended period. 
For Idaho veterans who may have endured serious contamination, that history should not disappear simply because this happened decades ago.
 Honoring their sacrifices must also mean keeping sight of the health risks that their service may have carried — and ensuring that significant asbestos exposure remains part of the conversation when considering who may benefit from earlier lung cancer screening.

title: New cypress trees grow in Kerr County, bringing hope and healing after floods
description: After deadly floods devastated Kerr County, Texans are replanting native trees along the Guadalupe River to restore its ecosystem and help communities recover.
text: Bald cypress trees in fall color line the North Fork of the Guadalupe River at Camp Stewart for Boys in Hunt on Nov. 12, 2026. Seeds collected at the camp were grown into saplings at the San Antonio Botanical Garden for replanting.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV House Dems ask Morrisey to take advantage of Medicaid work requirements grace period
description: Democrats in the West Virginia House of Delegates have called on the governor to take advantage of an optional 6-month grace period for new Medicaid work requirements that go into effect next year.
text:
The West Virginia Department of Human Services' website, wvmedicaidhelp.org, explains the changes coming to the program in January on Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)Democrats in the West Virginia House of Delegates have called on the governor to take advantage of an optional 6-month grace period for new Medicaid work requirements that go into effect next year.
House Democrats asked Morrisey to help “prevent thousands of West Virginians from losing their health insurance” in a news release Monday afternoon. 
Del. Hollis Lewis, D-Kanawha, told West Virginia Watch Monday that it’s important that the state’s systems — including its online Medicaid management system PATH and the state’s volunteer network — have time to prepare for the changes.
“The system itself needs time to get caught up,” Lewis said.
Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, with some exceptions, low-income people aged 19 to 64 who are part of the expanded Medicaid program will have to work, volunteer or train for at least 80 hours per month in order to keep their health care. The new requirements are set to begin Jan. 1. 
The federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid announced on Nov. 13 an optional “hold harmless” period through June 2027, during which states will assess whether individuals meet the work requirement, but not deny applications or disenroll people who are otherwise eligible for the program based on the work requirements. 
The grace period will give states time to “improve and refine their systems,” and give them the “opportunity to learn from the early months of implementation to identify and address workforce training needs and improve the beneficiary experience,” CMS said in a news release. 
The state Department of Human Services told West Virginia Watch last week it was still evaluating whether to take advantage of the grace period. 
Lewis said he’s concerned that people who are subject to the new requirements aren’t aware they’re happening, and some people are trying to figure out how to meet the requirements. 
The state has said an estimated 40,000 people are not currently meeting the work requirements and are not exempt from them. 
“This affects 40,000 West Virginians specifically …but also even those who have the exemption, those individuals still have to show proof and have to do things within the system to prove that they are exempt,” he said. “So even if you’re not susceptible to these changes, you still could be impacted.”
Lewis said the state has made strides treating substance use disorder and preventing drug overdoses, but that work could be affected by the changes to Medicaid. People in drug treatment for less than five years are exempt from the work requirements, but Lewis noted they’d still have to prove that.
“My fear is that we don’t want to create a situation in which you have those individuals who are dead focused on their recovery and sobriety and different things of that nature be undercut from programs simply due to clerical and paperwork barriers,” Lewis said. 
States are required to tell the federal government by Dec. 11 if they plan to use the hold harmless period. 
In an email to West Virginia Watch, Lars Dalseide, a spokesman for Morrisey, said “We will continue to evaluate all options to ensure the best interests of taxpayers and Medicaid beneficiaries are protected.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: New Huntsville-area Democratic Senator plans to use public service background in first term
description: Jared Sluss worked on affordable housing projects in the public and private sectors before deciding to run for office.  “I am new to politics, but I am not new to serving people,” Sluss, a new Democratic state senator from Huntsville, said in a recent interview. “All politics is an extension of service. That I’m very […]
text:
The Alabama Senate chamber in the Alabama Statehouse as seen on April 8, 2026. Voters in Senate District 7 chose Jared Sluss, D-Huntsville, over incumbent Sen. Sam Givhan, R-Huntsville, in the general election. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector) 
 New members
This is part of an ongoing series profiling the Alabama Legislature’s freshman lawmakers.


Jared Sluss worked on affordable housing projects in the public and private sectors before deciding to run for office. 
“I am new to politics, but I am not new to serving people,” Sluss, a new Democratic state senator from Huntsville, said in a recent interview. “All politics is an extension of service. That I’m very used to doing, and there’s a lot of overlap. You’re forming relationships, you’re solving problems. That, I’m very much not new to. I’m excited to use some of that skill set to get some good things done.”
Voters in Senate District 7 chose Sluss over incumbent Sen. Sam Givhan, R-Huntsville, in the general election. Sluss got about 30,200 votes (50.5%), and Givhan got about 29,700 votes (49.5%), according to unofficial returns. 
Sluss is one of six new senators joining the 35-member body. Republicans maintain a supermajority with 24 members and a conservative independent, and Democrats will have 10 members with two gains on Nov. 3.
At 29, Sluss will be the youngest member of the upper chamber. 
Sen. Jared Sluss, D-Huntsville, is the newly-elected senator for Senate District 7. (courtesy of Sluss)
New members are thinking of committees they hope to serve on for the next four years. Sluss said he wants to make the”biggest impact possible,” but also recognizes his limits as a Democrat and a first-term lawmaker. Knowing that, he said he’d like to serve on the Senate Healthcare and budget committees. 
Sluss’ campaign focused on the rising costs of healthcare and focusing on funding public education. He said he would support any effort to expand Medicaid. 
“There’s things like expanding Medicaid that I’ve talked about several times on the campaign trail that would lower healthcare costs, increase healthcare access, and help keep our rural hospitals open,” he said. “Then it’s just a matter of determining what’s feasible given the current state of things.”
Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville, a Republican, has said that he will not support that effort. One thing Tuberville and Sluss agree on is a state lottery, though the uses for the revenue may differ. In 2024, the vote for a lottery failed by one vote.
Tuberville last week said he is considering calling a special session of the Legislature to pass a gambling package, though he did not say when.
Sluss said that he would like a lottery to specifically fund healthcare, education or another initiative, not a “slush fund.” If he had his pick, it would fund the state’s First Class Pre-K program. 
“The fact that we have a system of have- and have-nots because it’s not fully funded, I think, is a really grave injustice,” he said. “That’s something the lottery could fully fund.”
Alabama is the last state east of the Mississippi to not have a lottery. According to a 2021 projection from the Legislative Fiscal Office, a lottery in Alabama would generate $272 million to $358 million. 
Although Sluss does not have any specific ideas for legislation, he said anything would have to be bipartisan and promised to work with the Madison County delegation – which has two Democrats and three Republicans – for any local bills. 
“It’s important to approach all the other senators and House reps with just a lot of humility and recognizing that I’m a quick learner, but that ultimately, I still have to grow into this and make sure I can deliver,” he said. “When it comes to this area, I really think it’s a lot less partisan than people think, and it’s just working to deliver good things.”
The Legislature will convene for the 2027 Regular Session on Feb. 2.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: After shedding jobs for almost a year, Tennessee sees an uptick
description: Tennessee’s economy added nearly 20,000 new jobs over the past three months, reversing a nearly year-long trend of job losses.  From December 2025 to July, Tennessee’s unemployment rate remained low at 3.5-3.6%, which is below the national average. The number of people employed fell by nearly 55,000 over that period.  Starting in August, the state’s […]
text:
Tennessee’s economy added nearly 20,000 new jobs over the past three months, reversing a nearly year-long trend of job losses.  (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s economy added nearly 20,000 new jobs over the past three months, reversing a nearly year-long trend of job losses. 
From December 2025 to July, Tennessee’s unemployment rate remained low at 3.5-3.6%, which is below the national average. The number of people employed fell by nearly 55,000 over that period. 
Starting in August, the state’s economy added jobs, a trend that has continued through October, according to data released Friday by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, or BLS.
Don Bruce, a professor with the University of Tennessee’s Boyd Center for Business and Economic Research, told the Tennessee State Funding Board that Tennessee’s job market spent nearly a year “bumping along,” and is now showing signs of “positive growth.”
“The economy in Tennessee got out of the gate post-COVID on fire,” said Bruce. “When things started to slow down, we slowed a little bit more quickly, and that started with the labor market.”


State job gains over the past few months were driven mainly by construction and government jobs. Leisure and hospitality jobs declined slightly over the past few months, while the other sectors tracked by the BLS held steady. 
The BLS also released its monthly inflation data, showing that across the southern United States, inflation came in at 3.4% for the 12-month period including October, which is slightly below the national average of 3.6%.
