name: Maine Morning Star
title: Grassroots groups that fueled Democratic wins call on King to rescind support for Schumer
description: Grassroots groups and progressive organizers are calling on U.S. Sen. Angus King to retract his support for Chuck Schumer as majority leader, arguing that Mainers made clear earlier this month that they were voting for change. Ahead of the Dec. 1 closed door leadership vote, dozens of Mainers rallied outside King’s Portland office on Monday, […]
text:
Crystale Lapham of People Powered Maine addresses the crowd outside Sen. Angus King's Portland office on Nov. 23, 2026. The rally-goers, holding Indivisible and “People Over Party” signs, are calling on the independent to retract his support for Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. (Photo by Jenna Valente for People Powered Maine)Grassroots groups and progressive organizers are calling on U.S. Sen. Angus King to retract his support for Chuck Schumer as majority leader, arguing that Mainers made clear earlier this month that they were voting for change.
Ahead of the Dec. 1 closed door leadership vote, dozens of Mainers rallied outside King’s Portland office on Monday, encouraging the independent to instead back Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer for the role. That followed another demonstration last week outside his Augusta office as part of a nationwide day of action against Schumer.
King has been forthright in his support of Schumer, arguing in a statement earlier this month that much of Democrats’ success in the midterm elections should be credited to the New York senator. 
“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” King asked. 
But that statement “did not sit well with the volunteer organizers and the organizers around the state who worked extremely hard,” said Crystale Lapham, founding member of People Powered Maine, an independent group established by former volunteers of Graham Platner’s campaign, which led a statewide, volunteer-run field organization to turn out voters this cycle.
Former Platner volunteers turn grassroots energy into independent organizing machine

Lapham told Maine Morning Star that the experience of volunteer organizers in Maine “has very much been that Chuck Schumer is not the reason why we were able to retire Susan Collins.” If it were up to Schumer, she said, “we would have had Janet Mills on the ballot.” 
The outgoing governor was backed by Schumer for the U.S. Senate race but suspended her campaign ahead of the June primary, citing a lack of funds though she had been trailing in the polls. After winning the primary, Platner stepped down following accusations of sexual assault, which he denies, and was replaced by Troy Jackson on the Democratic ticket in July. 
After a flurry of 11th-hour organizing by Jackson’s campaign, as well as independent groups including labor unions and People Powered Maine, the former logger and state Senate president ousted five-term incumbent Republican Susan Collins.
Lapham and Lakes Region Indivisible Founder Amy Strum met with King’s staff to deliver a petition signed by more than 1,900 people. An accompanying open letter noted that the groups’ volunteers talked to voters, including independents, in all 16 counties who said they want universal healthcare, an end to forever wars, and an economy that works for regular people, not billionaires, among other issues.
“Delivering on these issues will take a unified, forward-looking majority, willing to take on entrenched interests in both parties,” it reads. “Chuck Schumer has not proven himself to be that leader, and Mainers have no reason to expect a different result from the same leadership.”
During the meeting, Lapham said they could hear the roughly 50 rallygoers gathered four stories below chanting that Schumer has to go. Kelli Brennen, co-president of the Maine State Nurses Association, Maine Rep. Rafael Macias (D-Topsham) and author Neal Gabler also spoke during the event.
King’s office did not respond to a request for comment on the petition.
Lapham said that despite King’s stated support for Schumer, they still believe it’s worth the effort. 
“We believe it is our job to use our collective voices and to communicate where the people of Maine are at, and it’s up to him if he chooses to listen, or not listen, or change his mind,” she said. “But at least he knows where his constituents stand.” 
Jackson has repeatedly said he does not support Schumer, but has so far withheld committing to Van Hollen. 
The senator-elect told Maine Morning Star last week that he had a “good conversation” with the Maryland senator but that he wants “to make damn sure that my vote counts.”
Local activists with the national organization Showing up for Racial Justice held a rally outside Sen. Angus King’s Augusta office on Nov. 20 as part of a nationwide day of action against Chuck Schumer. (Photo courtesy of Elle Gates)

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Once seen as long shots, these Democrats in historically red districts helped turn Georgia blue
description: One grassroots political action committee played an outsized role in establishing a Democratic majority in the Georgia House of Representatives for the first time in more than 20 years. The Fighting Fifty – named after the 50 state House districts Republicans had previously run in uncontested – recruited and trained five of the 10 Democratic […]
text:
Fifty Fighting-backed candidates are shown here clockwise starting top left: David Dillie, Elisa Lassiter, Chris Luchey, Mishael White, Cynthia Starke-Jones and Scott Soracco. Luchey's race had not been officially called as of Monday. Photos were provided by the candidatesOne grassroots political action committee played an outsized role in establishing a Democratic majority in the Georgia House of Representatives for the first time in more than 20 years.
The Fighting Fifty – named after the 50 state House districts Republicans had previously run in uncontested – recruited and trained five of the 10 Democratic candidates who flipped historically Republican districts, with a sixth race yet to be called and an additional 11 candidates that came within three percentage points of victory. But a previous success story, state Rep. Eric Gisler of Watkinsville, also lost his reelection bid. 
Watkinsville Democratic Rep. Eric Gisler speaks during the 2026 legislative session. Gisler won a special election in 2025 in an upset but lost his reelection bid this year. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
House Democrats currently have a slim one-seat majority, with three races still not officially resolved. 
“We feel like it was the perfect storm. You know when the blue wave came we feel like we already had these fabulous candidates in place,” said Pam Woodley, co-founder of the Fighting Fifty. “The House would not have flipped without our candidates.” 
Woodley, with co-executive director Bob Herndon, formed the Fighting Fifty ahead of the 2024 presidential election. The group contacts local Democratic parties to recruit candidates in heavily Republican districts that traditionally see uncontested Republican candidates cruise to the state Legislature. The organization provides a support network and holds informational sessions on campaigning, handling donations and fundraising efforts. 
The idea is to energize lonely Democrats living in these districts through a local candidate at the bottom of the ticket, Woodley said. In turn, statewide races benefit from the increased turnout. 
In 2024, the damage from state Democrats ceding rural counties to Republicans became obvious, making the group’s mission more important, Woodley said. 
“When Kamala lost and just didn’t get enough votes, we realized we can no longer rely on urban voters,” Woodley said. “We’ve got to do something about our brand in these rural areas because voters tend to love Democrats’ policies if they don’t have the word Democrat attached to them.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This time around, Fighting Fifty represented candidates Cynthia Starke Jones in Dallas, Elisa Lassiter southwest of Atlanta, Mishael White southeast of Atlanta, David Dillie near Savannah and Scott Soracco in Hall County, all flipped state House seats. Another candidate, Chris Luchey, is narrowly leading in a metro Atlanta race that still had not been called as of Monday.  
Where other Democratic political action committees focus on flippable districts, the Fighting Fifty aims its efforts at districts that have backed Republicans with as much as 80% of the vote, said political director for the Democratic state House caucus, Andrew Heaton.
“There are limited resources that we have and limited staff to be able to put into a certain number of races that we think are our best path and best chances to get the majority,” Heaton said about how the Fighting Fifty has the time and funds dedicated to go beyond that.
The volunteer-led group used their shoestring budget – $294,000 this election – to get candidates in the unlikeliest of places off the ground.
“It’s important to have Democrats locally on the ballot to help energize local Democrats in areas where they might not have a reason to come out,” Heaton said.
Doubling down on these turnout efforts will be especially necessary to defend the statewide positions Democrats gained in a midterm election with record-breaking turnout, Heaton said. 
Running in ‘Trump Country’
In northwest Georgia, counties overwhelmingly voted for President Donald Trump just two years ago. It’s considered such friendly turf for Trump that he visited Dalton last month to urge his supporters to “pretend” he was on the ballot in an effort to boost GOP turnout. Northwest Georgia Congressman Clay Fuller called the region “Trump country.” 
And this year, some Republican incumbents here faced Democratic challengers for the first time in nearly a decade.  
In one of the most conservative areas in the country, one legislative race was so close that the Republican incumbent congratulated his Democratic opponent on winning, believing he had lost before the last votes were tallied and the roles reversed.
Dalton’s Quentin Postell, a Fighting Fifty recruit who separated from the group before the primary, came within 500 votes of beating incumbent state Rep. Kasey Carpenter in the Whitfield County-based House district. 
Postell held the lead for the better part of election night, and thinking he had won, Postell said he called Carpenter asking to meet in the week following the election, which Carpenter declined before congratulating Postell on his supposed victory. Shortly after the call, Carpenter closed the gap and officially won the race after trailing all night.
It was the first time a Democrat ran against Carpenter since he was elected in a special election in 2017. 
“There is just so much pressure coming out of Washington that the moderates just left and went to the other side,” Carpenter said. “They were hitting the blue button because they had enough.”
After losing, Postell said he plans to run again and is grateful the Fighting Fifty pushed him to run for the state House. Most Fighting Fifty recruits, who are running for office in the nooks and crannies of Georgia, know they don’t stand a chance, but it doesn’t stop them from trying. 
Rasmus Jensen heeded that call, losing the state House District 5 race in Gordon County by almost 50 percentage points but improving on the last Democrat’s performance in 2018 by eight percentage points. It’s a small gain, but one Jensen said he is proud of. 
Rasmus Jensen. Photo courtesy of the candidate
“You have to be willing to run and lose, and come back, run again, lose by less, and do that however many times it takes until you start winning. It doesn’t just have to be one candidate,” Jensen said.
A little more than a quarter of the funds Jensen raised came from the Fighting Fifty. That $6,000 in seed capital helped build necessary campaign infrastructure, he said. 
“They did an awful lot with a little. It was probably one of the best investments in Democratic politics in recent Georgia history,” Jensen said about the impact the money had. “It’s worth a lot more than throwing millions and millions and millions at TV ads.”
Fighting Fifty introduced him and the other candidates to the mechanics of state politics but granted them the freedom to run their own campaign how they saw fit for their district. Northwest Georgia’s voters have very different concerns from their counterparts in South Georgia, Jensen said.
Through campaigning, Jensen said he found a community of like-minded voters – people who are politically active and outspoken. The number of active Democrats is small, but they found camaraderie, Jensen said. 
“We all of the sudden made it okay to be a Democrat here,” Jensen said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Food insecurity could increase in Ohio under proposed rule on SNAP eligibility
description: Those who are trying to help Ohioans who struggle to afford food during the holidays and year round are bracing for more struggles amid the impact of food assistance cuts in federal budget legislation and a proposed change to the biggest federal assistance program. Cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), also known as […]
text:
Photo by Steph Quinn/States Newsroom.Those who are trying to help Ohioans who struggle to afford food during the holidays and year round are bracing for more struggles amid the impact of food assistance cuts in federal budget legislation and a proposed change to the biggest federal assistance program.
Cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), also known as food stamps, have been top of mind for anti-hunger advocates since the federal spending legislation called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act was championed and signed by President Donald Trump in 2025.
The bill included the biggest cuts to the program in its history, and experts estimated millions would be left without food assistance because of the changes, including hundreds of thousands of Ohioans.
Already, more than 1 million children in the U.S. have lost access to SNAP, and the cuts were projected to spill over into the free breakfasts and lunches children have access to during the school year.
 

If you or someone you know is in need of food assistance, visit the Ohio Association of Foodbanks’ website for more information, and to search for your county’s food bank location. 

Currently for most Ohioans, to be eligible for SNAP one must have a household monthly income at or below 130% of the federal poverty level. Families with elderly or disabled members, or with other eligibility factors are able to receive assistance up to 200% of the federal poverty level, according to the state.
For a family of four at 200% of the federal poverty level, their household income would be $5,500 per month.
A 2026 study released by the Ohio Association of Foodbanks found that more than half of Ohio households surveyed said they were forced to choose between paying for medicine or food, and 6 in 10 had to make the choice between buying food or utilities while also dealing with health problems and other financial struggles.
“Ohio families are visiting food pantries as they work hard to keep up with rising food costs, inflation, and other external pressures,” association executive director Joree Novotny said when the survey was released.
According to Feeding America, more than 1.8 million Ohioans experienced food insecurity in 2024, the most recent data released. That amounts to 15.3% of Ohioans, with an estimated 60% of those living above the poverty level threshold to qualify for SNAP.
In a report released in July, Feeding America found that the national average cost for a meal was $3.70 in 2024, but the national food budget shortfall was more than $33 billion that year.
In Ohio, the average meal was slightly less than the average, at $3.53. The annual food budget shortfall in the state was $1.22 billion in 2024.
“Food insecurity is often linked to one or multiple factors, creating a cycle that can be hard to break,” the report stated. “These factors may include limited income or income instability as well as the high cost of food and other essentials like housing, healthcare, utilities, and child and dependent care.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Other barriers to food security can include health emergencies, limited access to community resources, and “historical and ongoing discrimination,” according to Feeding America researchers.
The data cited in the report came from the USDA’s Current Population Survey Food Security Supplement, an annual survey the agency has now cancelled, meaning data about the status of food insecurity on a national level may not be as readily available in the coming years.
“Given the broader social and economic impact of food insecurity, it is vital that local governments, public health agencies, school districts, and workplaces understand the level and distribution of food insecurity in their communities,” Feeding America’s report stated.
The SNAP cuts from the federal spending bill come alongside Medicaid cuts and new work requirements that will also cause some to be ineligible for help, and now a proposed rule change to restrict the ways in which which low-income families can receive help.
The new proposed rule released by the USDA would “impose significant benefits cliff penalties on working families with low income, and eliminate states’ ability to align income and asset limits that match local economic conditions,” according to the Ohio Workforce Coalition.
Families and individuals who are eligible for SNAP can also be eligible for programs under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program, another federal assistance entity.
Under the proposed rule, “broad-based categorical eligibility” would be eliminated, taking away a policy that the the national Food Research & Action Center said “streamlines the administration of (SNAP).”
“(Broad-based categorical eligibility) lets SNAP align eligibility thresholds for income and assets with TANF’s eligibility thresholds,” the center’s Gina Plata-Nino and Dory Thrasher wrote in a statement.
Eliminating the eligibility would increase administrative costs and processing delays, shift bigger cost burdens to the states, intensify food insecurity, and undermine work incentives, Plata-Nino and Thrasher said.
According to Keith Barnes of the Beyond the Cliff Coalition, a national anti-poverty group of which the Ohio Workforce Coalition is also a member, the proposed rule would reduce the amount of SNAP benefits being distributed by about $14 billion in the first full year.
That boils down to a loss of about $340 per month on average for impacted households, Barnes said, citing the USDA’s own estimates.
The proposal would mean 3.7 million more households who are currently receiving SNAP would no longer be eligible, with a “disproportionate impact on working families,” according to Barnes.
For households with children, nearly 18% of those currently on SNAP wouldn’t be eligible.
An analysis of the rule by the Children’s Defense Fund found that the proposal “would risk the food security of more than six million children in America.”
The rule would be inserted into an already confusing bundle of public assistance rules and regulations, a benefits system that Barnes said is “not particularly cohesive or sometimes even coherent for families navigating it.”
“Instead, it’s a patchwork of programs, and families with low incomes are left to piece together multiple programs often administered by different agencies with different access points and applications to make ends meet,” Barnes said.
Along with keeping households from having the monetary assistance, individuals who are no longer eligible for assistance could also find themselves barred from using programs like employment and job training provided through SNAP under the new rules.
“So individuals who lose SNAP eligibility could find themselves, you know, potentially midstream in a program that’s designed to help them get ahead suddenly having to disenroll from that program,” Barnes said.
If the rule is approved, the coalition projects Ohio would lose 10% to 15% of its SNAP caseload, but the caseload decline could be even larger than that, according to the coalition.
“To be fully transparent, this is a cost of living problem that impacts every state and community in the nation,” Barnes said.
The proposal was released for public comment on Nov. 10, with a deadline for public comments set for Dec. 10, and an expected implementation date of Oct. 1, 2027, if the rule is approved.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Commentary: This was a healthcare election — and the polling proves it
description: Healthcare was on the ballot in this year’s midterms elections. And voters in every region of the country delivered their verdict on this issue in historic fashion — powering historic wins for Democrats in Wisconsin and beyond. The reasons behind such an overwhelming “wave” election like this one are not all that complicated. Rising healthcare […]
text:
Protesters in Wisconsin used a decommissioned ambulance to display their message opposing healthcare cuts. Voters in the 2026 midterms said healthcare was a top issue. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Healthcare was on the ballot in this year’s midterms elections. And voters in every region of the country delivered their verdict on this issue in historic fashion — powering historic wins for Democrats in Wisconsin and beyond. The reasons behind such an overwhelming “wave” election like this one are not all that complicated.
Rising healthcare costs were among the foremost drivers of families’ struggles to afford daily life and Donald Trump and the Republican Congress took full ownership of the issue with the largest cuts to healthcare in American history. 
Americans aren’t stupid. They see a Republican administration start a dumb war in Iran with no pushback from Republicans and they’re going to blame higher fuel prices on the party in charge. It’s the same with healthcare. Except that it’s perhaps even more insulting to voters’ intelligence than the misguided Iran war. Because the rationale for the healthcare cuts was yet another massive handout via the tax code to billionaires and mega corporations. The only way to even pretend those giveaways were ‘paid for’ was to slash $1 trillion dollars from Medicaid and end the working and middle-class healthcare tax credits that were ensuring access to health insurance was affordable.
On Election Day, the bill came due for the fallout from Trump’s centerpiece OBBB legislation: 8 million people have lost the insurance coverage they relied on and over 1,250 hospitals, clinics, and essential service providers nationwide have cut services, closed their doors, or are at risk of doing so. 
Here in Wisconsin, nearly 70,000 people have already lost their Medicaid, CHIP, or Affordable Care Act (ACA) coverage — just shy of 24,000 lost Medicaid and CHIP and more than 45,500 dropped ACA coverage. 
Voters didn’t just notice. They felt it and they made healthcare a deciding issue in this election.
New polling: this was a healthcare election 
Exit polling conducted by Protect Our Care and SEIU across nearly 60 battleground congressional districts found that healthcare was a major priority in the midterm elections, with more than 7 in 10 voters identifying it as a top issue, second only to the overall cost of living and ahead of issues like the war in Iran or tariffs. Nearly half (45%) of voters reported affordable healthcare as one of their top three voting issues, including 51% of moderates, 45% of independents and 48% of late deciders.
Republicans’ healthcare agenda proved to be deeply unpopular. The exit polling found that among 10 Republican policy positions, including the war in Iran, tariffs and funding for ICE, voters expressed the strongest opposition to Republicans’ healthcare agenda. In fact, 66% of voters were against cutting funding for local hospitals, 62% opposed ACA premium increases, and 61% opposed slashing funds for Medicaid. 
In contrast, healthcare was Democrats’ greatest advantage, tipping the scales in the country’s most competitive battlegrounds and delivering historic flips in states that were long considered Republican strongholds, including in both the 1st and 3rd Congressional Districts in Wisconsin. 
According to the poll, voters overwhelmingly trusted Democrats over Republicans to fight for affordable healthcare, with 60% of voters trusting Democrats to take the right approach compared to just 26% of voters who trusted Republicans. 
What’s next? 
Crashing ashore everywhere from Ohio to Texas and Mississippi to South Carolina, this blue wave is more than a historic defeat for Republicans and MAGA-ism — it is an opportunity for a genuine turning point for American healthcare.
The American people are demanding change — 83% of voters say they want the new Congress to take decisive action to lower healthcare costs, including 80% of voters who support capping insulin at $35 and two-thirds of voters who support reversing Medicaid cuts and restoring the ACA subsidies.
Democrats at the state and national level must hit the ground running, turning their campaign promises into a decisive agenda focused on lowering costs, protecting hospitals, and moving our country closer to universal, affordable healthcare coverage.
